Andre Pedroso Kowacs and Marielle Aparecida Silva develop new math tools in a paper published on arXiv in 2025. They study functions that are almost periodic, repeating after a shift combined with a twist, a pattern described by two parameters. Fourier analysis, which breaks signals into pure waves, is well understood for plain periodic functions but not for this broader class.

The authors build that Fourier theory and prove key properties, including a Poincare-type inequality. They then apply it to differential operators, which are rules that act on functions using their derivatives. They show an operator on these twisted periodic functions is globally well-behaved exactly when the matching operator on ordinary periodic functions is. They also settle the question completely for a class of first-order operators.
arxiv-2512-16174:
Kaito Kobayashi proves theorems about random networks in a 2025 mathematics paper posted to arXiv. Bond percolation flips a coin for each edge of a grid: open edges link sites into clusters. Away from the critical probability, clusters stay finite, and Kobayashi studies the largest cluster diameter inside a growing box.

He proves the maximum diameter grows like a constant times the logarithm of the box size, with the constant set by how fast connection chances decay with distance. He also proves a large deviation principle, which prices the odds of clusters much wider than typical. Finally, he counts how many vertices sit in clusters with large diameters. The results sharpen the mathematical picture of percolation off criticality, a regime used to model spread through random media.
arxiv-2512-16474:
Thijs Beurskens and three co-authors improve a shape comparison method in a paper that appeared on arXiv in 2025. Sequences of terrains over time, from shifting landscapes to growing data, need compact summaries and fair comparisons. Merge trees summarize a terrain's hills and valleys as a branching structure, and the interleaving distance measures how far apart two such trees are.

An optimal interleaving gives one global shift number, but its matching can ignore local similarities between the trees. The authors define locally correct interleavings, which let the shift vary across the trees to reflect local likeness. A generalized residual interleaving distance, allowing extra constraints on the matching maps, makes the definition work. They prove constructively that a locally correct interleaving always exists. Better matchings mean terrain evolution can be tracked feature by feature, not just scored.
arxiv-2512-16674:
Saverio Monaco and coauthors use Pauli propagation to pre-train quantum circuits on classical computers. Quantum machine learning often needs costly training on quantum chips, and gradients are hard to get. Pauli propagation instead writes what a circuit measures as a formula in its settings.

That formula grows fast with depth, but smart circuit shapes and cuts on term size keep it usable. The team shows the method can reach system sizes past classical state simulation, letting gradient training run before any quantum run. On the variational eigensolver for the ANNNI spin model with 32 qubits, the pre-trained circuits found ground state energies with strong accuracy at low cost.
arxiv-2512-16874:
Tomáš Souček and a Meta team present Pixel Seal, a state-of-the-art system for invisible image and video watermarking, used to trace where digital content came from. Training such models is hard because proxy losses for invisibility fail to match human sight.

Pixel Seal trains with adversarial loss alone, dropping pixel-wise losses that leave visible marks. A three-stage schedule splits robustness and invisibility work to steady training. For high resolution, a just-noticeable-difference scaling and training-time simulation remove upscaling artifacts. Across image types and edits, it beat prior tools on both robustness and invisibility, and a time pooling step extends it to video with ease.
arxiv-2512-16974:
Ailsa Robertson and coauthors map the shift to quantum-safe cryptography as a social and governance problem, not just a technical one. Quantum computers could open data harvested today, so banks, hospitals, and states must migrate, yet no single actor owns the job.

Drawing on an expert workshop in Amsterdam, the team charts twelve actor groups in the Dutch case. Regulators hold the strongest direct sway, while standards bodies matter most through indirect paths. Several duties have no clear owner, the missing sticks of the title, and rewards are weak, the irrelevant carrots. The map is offered as a guide for other countries facing the same tangled move.
arxiv-2512-17074:
Tao Ji and a large team measure the mass of clumps in accretion bursts onto TW Hya, a nearby young star watched for decades. Single-filter surveys see the flicker but cannot turn brightness into accretion rate without help.

By calibrating TESS and ASAS-SN g-band light curves against same-time spectroscopy, they convert flicker to flow. High-cadence TESS data show clump masses from about 10 to the minus 13 solar masses up to 3 times 10 to the minus 11. Bursts last 1.8 days on average, longer than a plain thermal guess, so flicker tracks live accretion. Eight years of near-daily data show seasonal swings at about half the short-term scatter.
arxiv-2512-17374:
Fatima-Zahrae Akhyar and three co-authors build generative models that respect a chosen summary measure of a complex system. Scientists often boil a molecule down to a few collective variables, such as a distance or an angle. The question is what full arrangements remain likely once that summary is pinned to one value, a slice called a level-set.

Their method learns the slice models for many pinned values at the same time, rather than one costly run per value. Rare slices, where data runs thin, get a boost from enhanced sampling data borrowed from physics simulations. Worked examples show the models stay accurate across slices. The approach suits molecular systems in biophysics, where rare shapes often carry the real interest.
arxiv-2512-17674: Dietmar Ferger studies the peak of a classic statistical curve: the standardized uniform empirical process, which compares observed data against a uniform law. He proves the height of the peak and the spot where it occurs settle into a joint limit law as samples grow. The two parts turn out independent. The peak position lands at either end with equal chance, while the peak height follows a Gumbel distribution, the law of extremes.
arxiv-2512-17774:
Saikat Roy and six co-authors argue that in medical image AI, the network's bones matter as much as the size of its training feast. Labs now pretrain segmentation models on huge scan archives, yet few checked whether their favorite backbone actually learns well at that scale. The team benchmarked backbones first, then scaled the winner.

Their model, MedNeXt-v2, grows a 3D ConvNeXt in depth, width, and context together, with a normalization module tuned for volumes. Pretrained on 18,000 CT scans, it then topped six hard CT and MR benchmarks covering 144 body structures, beating seven public pretrained rivals. Backbone strength before pretraining predicted strength after it. The models ship inside the popular nnUNet toolkit, ready for hospitals and researchers.
arxiv-2512-17874:
Mohamed Belfkir studies events where two Higgs bosons appear at once at the Large Hadron Collider, then decay into bottom quarks and photons. Events of this kind are rare, and they carry clues about how the Higgs field behaves. His paper is the first focused study of the fast moving, or boosted, form of this event type.

Belfkir tests two ways new physics could show up: a shifted strength in the link between Higgs and gauge bosons, and a heavy new particle that decays into the Higgs pair. The boosted view sharpens the search in the high mass range. It tightens limits on the shifted link and extends the reach for heavy new particles.
arxiv-2512-18474:
Dmytro Kuzmenko and Nadiya Shvai ask when a robot should refuse a human's request. Blind obedience can cause harm, but refusing too often erodes trust. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and accepted at the HRI 2026 conference, introduces the Empathic Ethical Disobedience Gym, a testbed that scores both refusal safety and social acceptability.

Inside the Gym, agents weigh risk, feelings, and trust, then choose to comply, refuse with or without an explanation, ask for clarification, or offer a safer option. Tests show that action masking removes unsafe compliance, while refusals that explain themselves keep trust intact. Constructive styles earn the most trust, and safe reinforcement learning improves robustness but makes agents overly cautious. The team releases code and preset scenarios so others can repeat the tests.
arxiv-2512-18874:
Dirk Erhard, Tertuliano Franco, and Wanessa Muricy complete a classification Feller began in the 1950s: what is the most general Brownian motion? Away from zero it must wander like ordinary Brownian motion, but at zero it may reflect, stick, skew, or be killed. Feller settled the half-line case, a mixture of those behaviors. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, settles the full line and two half-lines joined at zero.

On the whole line, the answer is the skew sticky Brownian motion killed at zero, a process already in the literature. On two closed half-lines, they identify a new process they call skew sticky killed snapping out Brownian motion, extending Lejay's 2016 snapping out construction. Knowing the full menu of possible motions matters wherever diffusion meets an interface, from physics to finance.
arxiv-2512-18974:
M. Prado, A. Manjavacas, F. A. Pinheiro, and W. J. M. Kort-Kamp show that disorder, arranged just so, beats order at moving heat with light. At the nanoscale, nearby hot objects exchange energy through near-field radiation, and the pattern of particles shapes that exchange. Their structures are Vogel spirals, aperiodic arrangements where one parameter dials the spatial correlation. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, tracks how correlation strength reshapes the modes and the transient dynamics of the coupling.

Aperiodic configurations outperform both random scatterings and neat periodic arrays at controlling radiative heat transfer. Deliberate aperiodic order, the result suggests, is a design tool in its own right: neither crystal nor chaos, but a tunable middle. Chip coolers, thermal switches, and energy harvesters all live or die by nanoscale heat flow, making this a platform worth watching.
arxiv-2512-19074:
Joanne Hughes and co-authors hunt for stars torn from the globular cluster NGC 6569, deep in the Milky Way's bulge. They took spectra of just over three hundred stars around the cluster with the Anglo-Australian Telescope. Targets were picked from survey photometry and Gaia positions and motions.

Forty stars match the cluster in motion and chemistry, marking them as likely debris. The seven best cases share the cluster's iron and alpha-element pattern. Read as freshly stripped stars, they imply the cluster loses roughly one to one and a half solar masses per million years. Orbit models explain why stars just outside the edge can already be unbound.
arxiv-2512-19274:
A. Cimarelli, N. Marras, B. Niceno, and Y. Tessier propose one frame for judging turbulence models of every kind. Coarse-grained flow equations always need a closure, a rule for the stresses the grid cannot see. Statistical and scale-resolving models have grown apart, with no shared yardstick.

The exact formalism of time-filtered Navier-Stokes equations supplies that yardstick. In their reading, turbulent stress acts like a time filter on the solution, an operator that slides smoothly between the two camps. From it they derive a dynamic closure that serves both. Tests capture tricky physics better, including transition to turbulence and how free-stream turbulence moves separation points.
arxiv-2512-19874:
Stefan Kluth, Wolfgang Ochs, and Redamy Perez-Ramos hunt for a subtle QCD signature inside top-quark jets. Heavy quarks radiate fewer gluons straight ahead, a dead cone whose angle shrinks with the quark's energy, and the effect is established for charm and bottom jets. The top quark's far greater mass opens a new kinematic regime, but its fleeting lifetime complicates everything, since it decays before hadronizing.

In the decay to a bottom quark, lepton, and neutrino, the bottom quark radiates too and partly veils the top's dead cone. Guided by the leading-order decay amplitude, the authors separate radiation from the two dipoles involved and extrapolate momentum distributions to zero decay angle, where decay radiation should vanish. Tested with the Pythia generator, the method reproduced the expected relation at parton level and matched at hadron level within roughly fifteen percent.
arxiv-2512-19974:
Borui Du, Kawon Han, and Christos Masouros defend a sensing system from its own signal. New networks merge sensing and communication in one waveform. That opens a privacy hole. A spy can run her own passive sensing on the signal and track targets. Sensing security, apart from message secrecy, is little studied so far.

The team models three parties. They are the base station, the user, and the sensing spy. They then build a detection metric from Kullback-Leibler divergence. It weighs mainlobe, sidelobe, and noise parts of both sides' ambiguity functions. A tuned matrix then shifts amplitude and phase over time and frequency. Simulated annealing does the tuning. The spy's detection odds fall by over half. The cost to the true sensor stays small, and trade-offs with data service stay tunable.
arxiv-2512-20074:
Quamran Hasan leads a five-author team building clinical AI that must explain itself as it decides. Support systems need sharp predictions. They also need reasons that match those predictions. Self-rationalizing models drift into reasons that do not fit their own outputs. That flaw is called exposure bias. Reason2Decide is a two-stage training frame built against it. It also fights the habit of keeping prediction and explanation apart.

Stage one trains rationale writing. Stage two trains prediction and rationale work jointly. A sampling schedule eases the shift from gold labels to the model's own calls. On three medical data sets, one a private triage set, the method beat fine-tuned rivals. It also beat some zero-shot giants on prediction and on rationale quality. It did so with models forty times smaller than today's foundation models.
arxiv-2512-20174:
Hao Guo and six colleagues give document search a natural-language front door. Finding a document image in a gallery has traditionally meant querying with another image and settling for coarse category matches, newspapers versus receipts. Real users describe what they want in words, often with fine-grained detail. The team introduces the NL-DIR benchmark to close that gap, with matching evaluation metrics.

Its dataset holds forty-one thousand authentic document images, each paired with five high-quality, fine-grained text queries drafted by large language models and checked by humans. Zero-shot and fine-tuned evaluations cover mainstream contrastive vision-language models and optical-character-recognition-free document understanding models, and a two-stage retrieval method is explored for better performance at reasonable time and space cost. The benchmark, presented at CVPR 2025, targets the visual document understanding community.
arxiv-2512-20374:
Yujia Fu and co-authors automate a scoring job that colonoscopy doctors currently do by eye. The Boston Bowel Preparation Scale rates bowel cleanliness, but manual scoring is subjective and varies between observers. The team assembled a dataset of over two thousand colonoscopy images from several hundred patients, each labelled with expert-agreed scores.

Their approach adapts the CLIP vision-language model with lightweight adapters and adds a branch dedicated to stool-related features. Global image features are fused with textual priors about fecal appearance, so the model scores cleanliness without needing pixel-level segmentation. Tests on their dataset and the public NERTHU dataset beat existing benchmarks. The authors position the system as a step toward dependable computer-aided colonoscopy assessment.
arxiv-2512-20874:
Meysam Ghanbari and six co-authors survey a shared weakness of the narrow beams that future networks will depend on. Free-space optical, millimeter-wave, and terahertz links all aim energy in tight directions, and all lose reliability when transmitter and receiver drift out of alignment. Each field has studied these pointing errors with its own definitions and models, which blocks comparison across fields.

The survey unifies the topic with consistent terms and a cross-technology taxonomy, reviews misalignment models and their effect on performance, and lists fixes with a focus on optical systems. Dedicated sections cover orbital angular momentum links and quantum optical links, where the impairments take mode-dependent and measurement-bound forms. Open challenges close the agenda for designers of next-generation directional systems.
arxiv-2512-20974:
Jingyang You and Hanna Kurniawati remove the approximation error from a popular way of teaching agents to adapt. Meta-reinforcement learning infers a hidden model of each new task, but most deep Bayesian approaches lean on variational posteriors, whose looseness distorts the task representation. Their framework, GLiBRL, instead models tasks with generalized linear models over learnable nonlinear basis functions, a pairing chosen so the Bayesian updates stay exact.

Posterior updates arrive in closed form, sequentially, and identically regardless of the order experiences arrive in, and the method plugs into both off-policy and on-policy algorithms. A learned task representation obeys an exact kernel identity linking distances between tasks to kernel discrepancies. Against eight rival methods, GLiBRL posts the best aggregate zero-shot scores on the MuJoCo locomotion and MetaWorld manipulation benchmarks.
arxiv-2512-21474:
Shota Ono looks for hidden two-dimensional materials inside compounds that seem to have no layered structure. Carbon motivates the search: graphite is layered and peels into nanosheets, while diamond is non-layered and forms under high pressure. Ono revisits metal dichalcogenides known for a non-layered, pyrite-type structure, asking whether a layered form might secretly be more stable.

Working with zinc diselenide, he finds that ultrathin films of the pyrite-type material spontaneously transform into a layered phase. That phase is the true ground state. A single layer stretches unevenly by direction and has a semiconducting band gap about twice the pyrite value. The energy landscape along a distortion path has two valleys, which hid the layered state. Many other two-dimensional materials may likewise be concealed inside non-layered compounds.
arxiv-2512-21574:
Ammar El Falou examines the security of sixth-generation mobile networks whose base stations fly on drones. Unmanned aerial vehicles launch quickly to restore coverage in underserved or disaster-hit regions, making them part of non-terrestrial networks. Moving the base station off its fixed, wired tower changes the threat picture.

A flying base station runs on limited energy and computing power, which leaves it more exposed to denial-of-service attacks. Its dependence on wireless backhaul links and satellite navigation opens the door to jamming, interception, and spoofing. Because it is central to emergency communications, it is an attractive target for spoofed emergency alerts. Its mobility enables attacks, such as manipulating the handover of users between cells. El Falou maps these attack surfaces in detail. He then outlines principles for mitigating each threat, aiming to guide the design of UAV-based 6G systems before they are deployed.
arxiv-2512-21674:
Tsubasa Kondo, Hidehiro Kaneda, and their co-authors survey hydrocarbon dust in nearby galaxies using near-infrared spectra from the AKARI satellite. Dust rich in aromatic and aliphatic hydrocarbons glows at fixed wavelengths, and the balance between the two kinds records how strongly radiation and shocks have processed the dust.

The team fitted spectra from hundreds of star-forming systems across three brightness classes, plus hydrogen-rich regions in our own galaxy as a reference. The ratio of aliphatic to aromatic emission varies far more among systems than in the reference regions. The ratio falls as total infrared brightness and hydrogen glow rise. Galaxies with bluer colors near four micrometers show higher ratios, suggesting dust shielded from harsh ultraviolet light. Some merging, very luminous systems show very low ratios, which the authors attribute to blended emission and absorption around a hidden nucleus. The survey maps dust chemistry against setting.
arxiv-2512-21874:
Michael J. Cervia, Henry Lamm, and their co-authors improve the codes used for magic state distillation, an overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computing. Distillation purifies noisy resource states using quantum error-correcting codes with transversal gates. Qudits, quantum units with more than two levels, promise lower overhead, but earlier codes demanded dimensions above one hundred, far beyond current experiments.

Using a lifting procedure, the authors construct the first family of good triorthogonal codes on a finite-field alphabet that beats a classical coding bound, the Tsfasman-Vladut-Zink bound. The codes support transversal CCZ gates, enabling magic state distillation with constant space overhead at qudit dimension sixty-four. They single out one concrete code with forty-two qudits encoding fourteen logical ones at distance six. They show a distilled state can be converted to a smaller alphabet with a shallow Clifford circuit using few gates and measurements.
arxiv-2512-22374:
Xin Yu and eight co-authors introduce Self-E, a text-to-image model that grades its own homework while it learns. Flow and diffusion models learn only from local signals and so need many steps at generation time, while distilled fast models require a pretrained teacher. Self-E instead evaluates its own generated samples using its current score estimates, acting as a dynamic self-teacher alongside usual flow matching training.

Trained from scratch with no teacher, the model produces strong images at very low step counts yet also matches leading flow matching systems at fifty steps. Quality improves always as more steps are allowed, so one model covers both ultra-fast drafts and careful long runs. The authors describe Self-E as the first from-scratch, any-step text-to-image model.
arxiv-2512-22574:
M. Looshorn and a thirteen-author team measure what happens when one photon knocks many electrons out of a lanthanum ion. At a synchrotron light source, they merged photon and ion beams. They recorded cross sections for double through tenfold ionization of singly charged lanthanum. The energy range ran from 820 to 1400 electronvolts, where inner M-shell excitation or removal drives resonances and thresholds.

Such readings benchmark the atomic theory needed to model exotic plasmas like kilonovae, where calculations must supply most data. The team upgraded the Jena Atomic Calculator and ran large-scale computations of photoabsorption and of the de-excitation cascades following an inner-shell hole. Theory largely matched the experiment, though calculated charge-state distributions came out somewhat narrower than the measured ones, likely from necessary simplifications.
arxiv-2512-23174:
Peter Koroteev, Myungbo Shim, and Rahul Singh open a geometric study of the Bethe ansatz for spin chains with open ends. In the geometric q-Langlands picture, spaces of q-opers, special connections on the projective line, correspond to solutions of Bethe ansatz equations for closed spin chains with twisted periodic boundary conditions. Open chains, whose ends reflect instead of wrapping around, had no such geometric treatment.

The authors define a space of q-opers whose defining sections stay invariant under reflection through the unit circle, in a chosen gauge, mirroring the chain's open boundary. Under nondegeneracy conditions, that space of reflection-invariant opers is described exactly by the corresponding Bethe ansatz problem. The construction is carried out for type A, with the general case promised in a sequel. Comparisons with known results in integrable systems and representation theory are included, situating the objects inside the duality landscape.
arxiv-2512-23474:
Junyu Chen, Pratik Nag, Huixia Judy-Wang, and Ying Sun want better maps of the air quality index, the combined measure of several pollutants used in regulation. Monitoring stations are sparse, and the index does not follow the neat bell-curve statistics that classic mapping methods assume. Their goal is a full predictive distribution at every location, not just a single best guess.

They propose deep classifier kriging, a deep learning method that estimates distribution functions for spatial data without assuming a shape for them. A data fusion mechanism merges accurate station readings with continuous but biased model output, and handles pollutants measured at different places. In simulations the method beat conventional approaches, and applied to air quality data it supports estimates of extreme-event risk for policy decisions.
arxiv-2512-23574:
Melvyn Nathanson poses a question in additive number theory about infinite intersections of sumsets. Take a set inside an additive structure and form its h-fold sumset, all sums of h of its elements. Now take a strictly decreasing chain of sets, one inside the next, and intersect them all to get a limiting set.

The question is when forming sumsets commutes with that intersection: for which h, if any, does the sumset of the limiting set equal the intersection of the sumsets of the whole chain? Equality can fail in principle, because an element might be representable at every finite stage using elements that drift away and never land in the limit. Nathanson's paper, corrected and expanded in this version, investigates exactly when the interchange is justified.
arxiv-2512-23774:
Vinoth Punniyamoorthy and seven co-authors design an architecture for running API gateways consistently across many cloud clusters. Gateways are where security rules, governance policies, and traffic limits get enforced. In multi-cluster and hybrid deployments those settings drift apart, policies propagate slowly, and behavior turns unstable under changing load.

Their design starts from intent: administrators declare security, governance, and performance objectives in high-level form, and the system translates them into enforceable gateway configurations for each cluster. Policy verification and telemetry feedback continuously check that reality matches intent, while bounded, policy-compliant adaptation handles variation. In a prototype spanning several Kubernetes clusters, policy drift fell by up to about forty percent, configuration changes propagated about a third faster, and latency overhead stayed low under variable workloads.
arxiv-2512-23874:
Şenol Tarhan and Gabriel Goetten de Lima redesign a component of the machines that make Bose-Einstein condensates, clouds of atoms cooled until they act as a single quantum object. Production starts in a magneto-optical trap, where anti-Helmholtz coils supply the trapping magnetic field. With the traditional single pair of coils, the field's peaks fall outside the region experimenters can actually reach, wasting the geometry.

A double-pair configuration instead shapes a clean field potential centered exactly at the accessible midpoint. The authors follow the full cooling chain, Doppler cooling, trapping, and evaporative cooling to sub-microkelvin temperatures. Through theory and simulation they optimize coil geometry plus operating parameters such as laser detuning and saturation intensity for rubidium-87. Their design reaches final temperatures near sixty nanokelvin with about a hundred thousand condensed atoms, giving builders systematic guidance.
arxiv-2512-24274:
Souvik Chatterjee, Prasenjit Deb, Chandan Datta, and Pankaj Agrawal distribute special entangled states across quantum networks. Multipartite entanglement powers many quantum information tasks. The three-qubit W state is famously robust to losing one qubit. It resists deterministic distribution, though. That blocks deterministic communication protocols.

The authors turn to a non-symmetric cousin, the W-mod state. It carries one ebit across a chosen split. Deterministic teleportation and superdense coding become possible. Several distribution protocols are described. A central node prepares the state locally first. Individual qubits then travel to the end nodes. Fidelity measures performance under every kind of noise. The protocols are also compared against distribution with no central node. The work guides how W-class resources should be spread through a network.
arxiv-2512-24374:
William Eckner and six colleagues assemble a many-body quantum state atom by atom. Quantum simulation needs low-entropy systems that classical computers cannot mimic. The team starts with a cooled array of single strontium atoms. Optical tweezers hold and rearrange up to fifty of them. The array then connects smoothly to a two-dimensional optical lattice.

The connection is adiabatic, so order survives the transfer. The result is an itinerant Bose-Hubbard superfluid. Quantum Monte Carlo calculations at finite temperature provide the comparison. The estimated entropy per particle is low, near two Boltzmann units. Temperatures match a significant superfluid fraction. The authors stress the novelty. Itinerant many-body systems had never been prepared from rearranged single atoms before. Bottom-up assembly of neutral-atom and molecular systems now looks feasible.
arxiv-2512-24574:
Zhenyu Zhang and five colleagues steer the thinking of reasoning language models. Long chains of thought solve hard tasks but waste tokens. Trajectories wobble between underthinking and overthinking. Shallow, inconsistent steps alternate with repetitive, verbose loops. The authors study the structure of these trajectories. Specialized attention heads correlate with distinct cognitive behaviors.

Verification and backtracking each have their heads. Light intervention on those heads steers the model at inference time. Their method, CREST, needs no training. An offline step identifies the cognitive heads and builds steering vectors. At inference, hidden states are rotated to suppress the bad components. Reasoning behaviors adapt as a result. Across benchmarks and models, accuracy rose while token use fell sharply. Faster, more reliable reasoning is the payoff.
arxiv-2601-00374:
Samuel W S Johnson, Ruth E Baker, and Philip K Maini model how a group of embryo cells, called cranial neural crest cells, moves as a collective. Many models split the cells in advance into leaders at the front and followers behind. Their 2026 paper questions that fixed split, since real cells seem able to change roles, yet leader-like cells do persist in living tissue.

Their model gives every cell the same rules. Each cell carries a polarity vector that changes with its average exposure, over time, to a chemical signal. In simulations, a leader-follower split appears on its own, with no built-in difference between cells. The behavior also matches what is seen in chick embryos, giving a grounded account of the pattern.
arxiv-2601-00574:
Junlan Shi, Li Chen, Jiani Zhang, and Botao Fu predict an unusual partnership of properties in bilayer indium selenide, a two-layer semiconductor. Materials that are both ferroelectric, holding a switchable electric polarization, and ferromagnetic, holding magnetism, are rare and prized for new devices. Using first-principles calculations, the authors study the favored stacking of the two layers.

That stacking spontaneously breaks mirror symmetry, producing a switchable polarization with a low switching barrier. Surprisingly, light electrostatic doping strengthens rather than weakens the polarization, against the usual screening expectation, because of how electrons occupy the layers. Doping also switches on traveling-electron ferromagnetism, helped by the band's Mexican-hat shape. The findings suggest one material could host both orders, tunable by charge.
arxiv-2601-00674:
Kei Yuen Chan continues a series on the representation theory of general linear groups over a non-Archimedean local field, the setting behind much of modern number theory. For an irreducible smooth representation, a construction called a Bernstein-Zelevinsky derivative produces simpler representations, and certain multisegments label simple quotients of those derivatives.

A preceding article showed the set of multisegments giving the same quotient has a unique smallest element under the Zelevinsky ordering. Chan's main result here concerns commutativity properties of the corresponding minimal sequence, and further properties that follow from it. The article ends by conjecturing a module structure that minimality seems to force, offering a target for later work in this classification program.
arxiv-2601-01074:
R. J. G. Elbertse and four co-authors join two tools that rarely meet. Scanning tunneling microscopy reads surfaces atom by atom through a sharp tip. MEMS devices are tiny machines whose parts move at much larger scales. The team uses the microscope tip both to excite and to sense the motion of millimeter-wide membranes with very sharp resonances.

Working at very low temperatures, they read the sound modes of these membranes with precision down to trillionths of a meter, with no lasers and no electric coupling. The tip barely disturbs the motion and adds almost no heat, so the team sees the natural behavior of oscillators that weigh mere millionths of a gram. They show three ways to measure, each with its own strengths. The method could serve many delicate mechanical and quantum devices that need a gentle readout.
arxiv-2601-01274:
Haque and 4 co-authors design a smarter bus system aimed at cities where riders get few live updates. Buses that stop at random places add danger and block roads, and blind spots near large vehicles raise crash risk. Their plan links the bus, its stops, and a central server.

A camera-based warning system spots objects in blind spots, and the bus can tell when it reaches a real stop. Solar-powered stops show how many riders wait, while cards record where each rider gets on and off. Tests reported near-perfect blind spot warnings and energy savings at the stop, pointing to safer daily travel.
arxiv-2601-01374:
Lizhe Wan and Jiaqi Yang study the Muskat problem, which models one fluid pushing another through a porous medium. Their twist: the interface between the fluids is elastic and resists bending like a membrane. They treat both a one-phase version and a two-phase version, in two dimensions, following a framework set up in earlier work by Nguyen.

Locally in time, they prove the problem is well-posed for any starting shape of a stated smoothness: a solution exists, is unique, and depends sensibly on the data. Globally, for small starting shapes, the one-phase case and the stable two-phase case, where the upper fluid is no denser than the lower, also admit solutions for all time. Well-posedness results are the license other researchers need before trusting simulations of such flows, which model oil recovery, groundwater, and elastic membranes in fluids.
arxiv-2601-01574:
Ahmadi-Azar, Atazadeh, and Eghbali solve the equations for a flat, expanding universe model that includes the cosmological constant. The model, named by its four founders' initials, tracks how the universe's scale changes over time. Rather than attack the equations head-on, the team uses invariants drawn from the Hamilton-Jacobi method, a classic tool from mechanics.

Those invariants act like conserved quantities for a single particle moving in a simplified space. Finding them gives the full solution, plus the model's action and energy functions. The authors also solve a reverse problem about when such an action exists, without the usual extra conditions. A symmetry view gives the same result, uniting both routes.
arxiv-2601-01674:
A future Muon Collider running at ten trillion electron volts could measure the Higgs boson with unusual precision, including how often it decays into two tau leptons. Kevin Dewyspelaere, Giacomo Da Molin, Giovanni Battista Marozzo, and Michele Gallinaro estimate how well that decay's rate could be measured, using a dedicated tau-finding algorithm.

The study reconstructs taus that decay into hadrons, finding identification efficiency above eighty percent for one-prong decays and about half for three-prong decays. Comparing the signal with background processes and fitting the reconstructed mass gives a projected uncertainty of about one point three percent on the rate, stated as a relative error near one percent. Comparisons with other planned colliders round out the case.
arxiv-2601-01774:
Engineering runs on equations that no formula solves directly, from pipe friction to orbital position, and practitioners increasingly ask language models to just give the number. Sai Varun Kodathala and Rakesh Vunnam test six leading models on one hundred such problems. The problems span seven engineering domains. Two approaches compete. One asks for direct prediction. The other is a hybrid: the model sets up the equation, and a classical solver iterates.

Direct answers were far off, with mean relative errors around or above one in the worst cases. Letting a Newton-Raphson solver do the arithmetic cut errors by roughly two thirds to four fifths, with the biggest gain in electronics and the smallest in fluid mechanics. The lesson: today's models excel at symbolic setup and recalled knowledge but should hand precision arithmetic to real solvers.
arxiv-2601-02174:
Ergodic theorems say time averages settle down. Rate-giving versions say how fast. The noncommutative versions replace functions with operators. Guixiang Hong and three co-authors develop a framework here. It covers mean ergodic theorems with rates. The setting is actions of amenable groups and semigroups on noncommutative Lp spaces.

The engine is a set of square function inequalities for ergodic averages. The groups have polynomial volume growth. Proofs run through endpoint estimates and semi-commutative harmonic analysis on non-doubling spaces. Calderón-Zygmund arguments and a transfer method for group actions appear. As applications, averages from Lamperti forms get explicit rates. The authors also extend a dilation theorem of Fackler and Glück. It grows from single operators to commuting families. Ergodic theorems for large classes of operator semigroups unlock.
arxiv-2601-02274:
Sébastien Campagne studies the Schrödinger equation in its semi classical limit on closed curved surfaces known as Riemann surfaces. The question is where solutions concentrate, described through the resolvent, a tool that links the equation to its spectrum. Most earlier work assumed the potential, the landscape term in the equation, was smooth.

Campagne allows a potential that is only bounded, with no smoothness at all. He smooths the potential in a controlled way and proves a local to global estimate. In plain terms, the estimate measures how roughness of the potential in a small patch affects concentration of the solution over the whole surface. That bridges results proved for smooth settings and the rougher cases found in practice.
arxiv-2601-02374:
Melissa Tessa and six co authors build a food recommendation system whose suggestions come with explanations a non expert can follow. A recommender may rank meals well yet leave users unsure why an item was chosen, which weakens trust. Their process works after the recommendation is made, turning the reasons behind it into clear language.

They combine a large language model with a hybrid method for finding which input features mattered most, using SHAP values that assign credit to each feature. The language model then writes a fuller, more convincing explanation from those key variables than earlier systems produced. The authors argue that clearer explanations raise transparency and trust for lay users of food recommendation tools.
arxiv-2601-02574:
Haoran Wang and four co authors improve fact checking for large language models, whose fluent answers still contain invented facts. Existing checkers fetch outside proof for each claim, and miss what the model already knows well and sometimes adding irrelevant noise. The authors argue, by analogy with human checking, that a model should first judge its own confidence in a claim and only search when that confidence is low.

Their framework, probabilistic certainty and consistency, estimates confidence from two signals, how probable the model's answer is under its own distribution and how consistent its reasoning stays. Confident claims are answered directly, while uncertain or inconsistent ones trigger targeted retrieval aimed at the specific gap. That adaptive strategy focuses effort where errors are likely, instead of checking all claims the same way.
arxiv-2601-03174:
Debraj Dutta and Urna Basu show that a spread in self-propulsion strength can reorganize a crowd of active particles into ordered patterns. They study a binary mixture of active Brownian particles with two different propulsion strengths, attracting each other over short range. Depending on the interaction range, the two strengths, and the mix ratio, the system settles into one of three phases.

One phase is disordered. In a second, the slower particles assemble into a ring while the faster ones diffuse randomly around them. In the third, two concentric rings form, one of faster and one of slower particles, giving complete spatial and orientational order. Using a truncated harmonic potential as an example, the authors map the phase boundaries analytically and identify the order parameters behind each transition.
arxiv-2601-03374:
Tieguang Zi, Mostafizur Rahman, and Shailesh Kumar examine extreme mass-ratio inspirals as probes of physics beyond vacuum general relativity. In such a system, a small object slowly spirals into a massive black hole. Two kinds of deviation are considered together. One is an astrophysical environment, such as cold dark matter around the system, which adds drag and changes the gravitational wave flux. The other is modified gravity, in scalar Gauss-Bonnet theory, where the inspiraling object carries a scalar charge and radiates it away.

Using a two-timescale analysis, the authors compute leading-order corrections to the energy fluxes. They work with circular equatorial orbits, and build the corresponding waveforms. They then measure how much the signal drifts out of phase with the vacuum prediction, and how large the waveform mismatch grows. Such dephasing is what space-based detectors would use to spot environmental or modified-gravity effects.
arxiv-2601-03474:
José Isidro and six co-authors revive an old training task, next sentence prediction, to split long texts into topical sections. Splitting text well helps summarization, search, and question answering, but topic boundaries are fuzzy and writing styles vary. Next sentence prediction was dropped from modern pretraining, yet it directly models whether one sentence follows another, which is exactly what boundary detection needs.

Their system, SegNSP, predicts whether the next sentence stays on topic without needing topic labels. A segmentation-aware loss and harder negative examples sharpen its sense of discourse flow. The design avoids extra task-specific supervision that other recent methods require. Clean segmentation is quiet infrastructure: many language tools work better once long documents are cut into coherent parts.
arxiv-2601-03574:
Mamdouh Alenezi, writing alone, presents a framework for making DevOps automation auditable, so teams can defend why each automation was built. Automation speeds software delivery, yet firms often struggle to justify projects in terms of waste cut, predictable delivery, teamwork, and customer quality. The framework joins three established tools into one traceable chain.

Value Stream Mapping charts the whole delivery flow and measures delays, rework, and handoffs. The Goal-Question-Metric approach then turns stakeholder aims into a small set of useful measures, including DORA delivery metrics. Finally, automation targets the bottlenecks the data actually shows, in small reversible steps. Priorities are ranked by expected impact, confidence, and cost, which gives managers a defensible record instead of gut-feel choices.
arxiv-2601-03674:
Yuanying Chen and three co-authors study regression where both the inputs and the outcome are whole distributions, not single numbers. Several distributional predictors may drive one response distribution, as when income patterns in different regions shape an overall outcome spread. Such problems are hard because the space of distributions has curved shape, described by the Wasserstein distance.

Their built-in method combines each predictor's moved distribution through a weighted mean defined inside that curved space. The weights are clear, showing each source's share, and the model does not depend on free construction choices like a reference distribution. The authors prove the regression map can be pinned down and give guarantees for estimating it, using a predictive measure tied directly to forecast accuracy.
arxiv-2601-03774:
Chu Wang and six co-authors show that machine learning force fields, which simulate molecules at near quantum accuracy, stumble on very large molecules because they only look within a fixed distance cutoff. Long-range forces dominate in macromolecular systems, and the authors demonstrate that force errors grow steadily with system size under that locality constraint, exposing an architectural bottleneck.

They built the MolLR25 benchmark from high-fidelity quantum calculations, covering molecules up to twelve hundred atoms, and designed E2Former-LSR, an equivariant transformer with explicit long-range attention blocks. It kept error scaling stable, captured non-covalent decay well, and stayed precise on complex protein shapes. Its efficient design also brings speed gains noted in the work. Reliable force fields for proteins open faster drug and materials simulation.
arxiv-2601-03874:
Anthony Lamelas, working alone, tests whether small decoder-only language models can handle grammar correction and text simplification well enough to replace far larger models. Big models are costly to run, hard to deploy, and awkward to secure, so a capable small model would be valuable in schools, offices, and on private devices. The experiments try the small models as shipped, after fine-tuning, and in sequential pipelines.

Testing used the JFLEG set for grammar and the ASSET set for simplification, scored with established metrics. The small models learned some behaviors well but stayed below strong baselines and current large models overall. They also struggled to preserve meaning and sometimes hallucinated content. Lamelas concludes that, despite their efficiency, today's small models are not yet competitive for rewriting tasks, and further advances are needed.
arxiv-2601-03974:
Anubha Goel, working with Amita Sharma and Juho Kanniainen, tests whether portfolios built from shape-based methods beat standard choices. Their approach uses persistence landscapes, which summarise how the shape of return data changes over time. From that summary they define a new measure called topological risk.

The team builds a portfolio that lowers this new risk and tests it on nearly ten years of S and P 500 data. Their portfolios earn higher extra return and better financial ratios than seven popular models and two simple benchmarks. The gain holds across different holding sizes and time spans. Readers get a clear case that shape can add information beyond usual statistics.
arxiv-2601-04074:
Hanna Bartel, Martin Burger, and Marie-Therese Wolfram model how opinions form when people hold views on many topics at once. Each person carries both opinions and importance weights that say how much each topic matters to them. Opinions shift through pairwise encounters between individuals.

The novelty is the coupling: change on one topic depends on weighted likeness across the whole opinion vector, not just that topic. The three authors write the kinetic equation for the process and derive a mean-field partial differential equation for the crowd as a whole. Analysis and simulations show several distinct steady end states. Which end state appears is set largely by the importance weights people carry, a point with clear lessons for polarisation studies.
arxiv-2601-04274:
Alina Vozna, Andrea Monaldini, Stefania Costantini, Valentina Pitoni, and Dawid Pado schedule medical appointments with Answer Set Programming, a logic method that finds assignments meeting all stated rules. Clinics need scheduling that is efficient, light on office work, and centred on patients. Vulnerable patients need extra personal care in how slots are offered.

Their framework weaves Blueprint Personas, profiles that capture such personal needs, into the scheduling model. Planning sits inside one ASP model, which keeps availability current in real time and guarantees conflict-free assignments. The design also aims at smooth connection with existing health platforms, since planning operations are centralised in the logic model. The five authors present the system as a route to fairer, calmer booking for patients who need the most support.
arxiv-2601-04474:
Bill Marino and Nicholas D. Lane argue that obeying AI regulation will become a computing problem, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Rules for artificial intelligence are arriving, but checking and steering real systems by hand, with lawyers and paperwork, cannot keep pace with systems that update constantly and operate at machine speed. Compliance, they claim, will have to be done by algorithms running across an AI system's whole life cycle.

The paper is a blueprint for that research field, which they call computational compliance for AI regulation. It specifies design goals for the algorithms that would steer systems toward compliance as conditions change, and a benchmark dataset for measuring quantitatively whether a given algorithm meets those goals. The authors offer both to crystallize a domain they consider inevitable, and to provoke the investment it will need.
arxiv-2601-04774:
How fast the universe expands is still disputed, and one new route combines two very different kinds of evidence. Felipe Andrade-Oliveira and 3 co-authors report a 2026 measurement of the Hubble constant, the number that sets that expansion rate. They join gravitational-wave standard sirens, whose signals give distances, with weak lensing and galaxy clustering data.

For the lensing part they use the Dark Energy Survey Year 3 release, and for the waves the fourth Gravitational-Wave Transient Catalog. One famous event, GW170817, also brings host-galaxy information. Joining the probes in a single analysis gives a first combined value and a check on single-method results.
arxiv-2601-05174:
Yiji Zhao and 7 co-authors present FaST, a forecasting framework for huge spatial-temporal graphs, in a 2026 paper. These graphs model networks such as traffic sensors or power grids evolving over time. Existing models mostly predict short horizons, and scaling them to long horizons over large graphs brings notorious computational and memory costs that block practical use.

FaST uses a heterogeneity-aware mixture-of-experts design, routing different parts of the problem to specialised sub-models. The authors report it unlocks week-ahead prediction at fine time granularity across thousands of nodes. Long-horizon forecasts on large networks support planning in transport and energy systems, where operators need next week's picture, not only the next hour's, to schedule resources.
arxiv-2601-05874:
Santosh Srinath K and 4 co-authors address in 2026 a practical obstacle in building small language models for low-resource languages from large ones: catastrophic forgetting, where new training erases older abilities. Their setting adapts large models into small multilingual models, and the forgetting problem is the central challenge they target.

Their continual learning strategy combines parts-of-speech-based code-switching with a replay adapter. Code-switching mixes languages within text, while replay revisits earlier material during training to protect it. Experiments covered vision-language tasks such as visual question answering alongside language modeling. The authors report that the proposed architecture mitigated the forgetting gap successfully in those tests, offering a route to capable small models for languages with limited data.
arxiv-2601-05974:
Goran Muric and Steven Minton present in 2026 a real-world approach for deciding which classification cases a machine should settle alone and which need a human reviewer. Automated systems increasingly keep human oversight for uncertain cases, but review is expensive. A single confidence cutoff wastes that resource on cases that are nearly certain either way.

Their double-threshold policy auto-accepts cases above an upper threshold, auto-rejects below a lower one, and routes only the ambiguous middle to humans. Formulated as an optimization balancing accuracy against review cost, the approach is analyzed mathematically and through Monte Carlo simulations. Different confidence distributions create regions of diminishing returns where extra review adds little. Applications range from fraud detection to medical triage and content moderation.
arxiv-2601-06374:
Nikolai Parvatov studies how many edges a hypergraph can have while avoiding short cycles in a 2026 combinatorics paper. A hypergraph generalizes a graph: its edges can join any number of vertices, here a fixed number r of at least three. Girth is the length of the shortest cycle, and the question asks for the maximum edge count at a given girth.

Parvatov focuses on girth at least six and at least eight, with the number of vertices growing large. Constructions come from generalized polygons, highly symmetric geometric structures. The results give lower bounds on the maximum edge count as explicit powers of the vertex count, with small correction terms that shrink as the count grows. These bounds advance knowledge of the asymptotic behavior of the extremal function.
arxiv-2601-06574:
A pic tool that must please four judges at once will slight some of them. Dongliang Chen and 10 co-authors name the two faults that cause the slight in a 2026 paper. Their field is text-to-image tools taught to prize more than one trait: crisp text in the pic, true looks, and charm.

Fault one: a prize with wild swings grabs more than its share of the teach signal. The rest starve. Fault two: the aims pull in clashing ways, so the tool seesaws and none of them gains ground. Their tool, APEX, calms each prize in two steps, then ranks the aims on the fly. Rank rests on room to learn, a clash toll, and need. On a top pic tool, the four aims rose in a fair spread. Text stayed sharp while looks and charm gained.
arxiv-2601-06674:
C. Gallesco and two co-authors sort chains of states for data in fixed classes in 2026. Such data, like words or gene codes, change step by step in time. Most models for them are chains whose next step rests on the past few steps.

Work in the past dwelt most on chains with just one step of past. Yet the traits of longer chains can be read through the short ones. One maps a long chain to a short one on a blown-up set of states. The paper works out that map and sorts the chains by what they share. This tells those who model such data which chains act the same at heart. The scope runs from gene codes to speech and far past both. A clear sort saves time when a new chain must be picked.
arxiv-2601-06874:
Changli Wu and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with MVGGT. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Most existing 3D referring expression segmentation methods rely on dense, high-quality point clouds. While real-world agents such as robots and mobile phones operate with only a few sparse RGB views and strict latency constraints.

The authors introduce Multi-view 3D Referring Expression Segmentation. Where the model must recover scene structure and segment the referred object directly from sparse multi-view images. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-06974: Research by Quoc-An Nguyen and co-authors was posted on arXiv in 2026. It deals with UETQuintet at BioCreative IX - MedHopQA. The preprint joined the arXiv PAPERS collection in 2026. Biomedical Question Answering systems play a critical role in processing complex medical queries. Yet they often struggle with the intricate nature of medical data and the demand for multi-hop reasoning. The authors propose a model designed to effectively address both direct and sequential questions. For specialists, the preprint offers a compact account of the problem and the authors' approach.
arxiv-2601-07074:
Pedro Abdalla and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers robust mean estimation under quantization. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. The authors consider the problem of mean estimation under quantization and adversarial corruption. The authors construct multivariate robust estimators that are optimal up to logarithmic factors in two different settings.

The first is a one-bit setting, where each bit depends only on a single sample, and the second is a partial quantization setting. In which the estimator may use a small fraction of unquantized data. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07374:
Andrea Ferrara and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers possible evidence for a pair-instability supernova nature of ultra-early JWST sources. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Recent JWST observations have revealed a population of unexpectedly bright sources at ultra-high redshift , challenging current models of early galaxy formation. One extreme example is Capotauro.

An F356W-dropout identified in the CEERS survey and initially interpreted as a luminous galaxy at z 30 z 30. But subsequently found to be variable over an 800 800 day baseline. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-07674:
Xingran Chen and colleagues defend decentralized learning against a playful-sounding but serious attack. Random walk algorithms are popular in distributed systems for their low overhead and scalability. They now support decentralized learning, where data stays on local devices. Their weakness is reliance on local interactions, which malicious nodes can abuse. The team's 2026 preprint names the threat the Pac-Man attack.

In this attack, a malicious node probabilistically swallows any random walk that visits it. The proposed defense uses self-creating random walks, which can replace the ones destroyed. The contest between attack and defense is studied directly. Such work matters as learning moves onto untrusted networks of devices. The paper speaks to distributed systems and security scholars.
arxiv-2601-07974:
Yuxi Xia, Kinga Stańczak, and Benjamin Roth explain why detectors of AI-written text fail on new material. Such detectors score highly on familiar benchmarks. They often struggle with unseen prompts, model families, or domains. Prior work reported these generalization gaps but offered few explanations. Their 2026 preprint presents a systematic study using linguistic analysis. The goal is to explain the behavior, not just measure it.

Detectors lean on linguistic cues that may be artifacts of one generator or genre. When conditions change, those cues vanish or mislead. Knowing which cues carry the signal helps build detectors that travel better. It also warns against trusting detector verdicts in schools and courts. The paper serves NLP scholars and anyone who deploys AI text detection. It shifts the question from accuracy to mechanism.
arxiv-2601-08074: Xavier Hernandez proposes a new way to tune twelve musical tones in his 2026 arXiv paper. Standard equal temperament cannot give exact perfect fifths in every key. The math is stark: twice two to the seven-twelfths power does not equal three. So the second harmonic of a fifth can never match the third harmonic of the root note. Hernandez uses elastic overtones to build a twelve-tone system that keeps fifths exact. The paper speaks to readers in music theory, acoustics, and tuning design.
arxiv-2601-08474: Marcelo Coniglio, Francesc Esteva, Joan Gispert, and Lluis Godo wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on fuzzy logics built by Godel. Godel fuzzy logic grades truth on a scale. The team studies the degree-preserving companion of that logic, in a form with an involution, a flip that twice applied gives back the start. They sort the logics that sit between that companion and classical propositional logic, and do the same for their finite-valued forms. The study covers paraconsistency, where a clash need not cause collapse.
arxiv-2601-08774:
Christian Bernert and three co-authors count whole number points on a rough shape from algebra. The shape is a quartic del Pezzo surface, a surface set by a fourth degree rule. They count points whose height stays below a set cap. The count must work over any number field, not just the plain whole numbers.

They prove a growth rule for that count. The proof is hard in a plain way. The shape that guides the count breaks into a huge set of small blocks. Like a jigsaw, those blocks fit back into one large block. A reader in number work gets both the rule and a new view of why the blocks must fit.
arxiv-2601-09174:
Kaue Cardoso studies a graph built from a hypergraph, where each link can join more than two points. Take each such wide link as a point in a new graph. Join two new points by as many lines as the wide links share in points. The new graph is called a line multigraph. It codes how wide links cross and share.

He proves traits of these graphs, both in shape and in their spectra. Spectra here are sets of counts that code how a graph waves and links. Such graphs can model group ties, where one tie binds a whole team. A reader in graph work gets a new class with firm first laws to build on.
arxiv-2601-09974:
Seoyeon Kim and Jaehyung Kim study how a language model can track a user over time. Most tailoring tools rest on fixed user facts. They fetch past text or tune the model once. But what a user likes can drift week to week.

A model that fails to drift with the user grows stale. A model that retunes too much can lose old likes. The pair give a plan that does both jobs in parts. It picks which weights to tune for new likes. It also blends in fetched past text at reply time. The aim is tailoring that moves with the user and keeps the past.
arxiv-2601-10374:
Tuomas Lappi, Risto Paatelainen, and Mikko Seppälä work out a two loop split rule for quarks and gluons. As a fast grain hits a proton, its parts share its push. Split rules say how that share shifts with scale. They are core to collider math.

The team use light cone methods, a frame where one push part is plus at all times. That trait makes some poles easy to tame. A plain cut off does the job, and it drops out of the end math. They get the next to lead split rule. The work shows the frame can bear two loop tasks.
arxiv-2601-10474:
Optimal error bounds are proved for a Galerkin method on curved edges with straight meshes. The method splits a field into parts on each cell. It is named discontinuous Galerkin. It is strong for laws with sharp fronts. But a curved edge cut by straight cells can lose grade.

The loss comes from the gap twixt the true edge and the mesh. Past runs oft drop one full grade from that gap. The paper gives best bounds for that case. It shows when the full grade can be kept. The work guides mesh picks for rigs with curved walls.
arxiv-2601-10674:
Lorenzo Ricci and Raman Sundrum use energy correlators to probe strongly coupled field theories. A correlator tracks how energy flows out in set patterns after a clash. For theories that are nearly conformal, direct math is hard. Holography offers a dual picture in terms of curved spacetime, where the math can be done.

The authors study warped geometries, spaces that bend away from pure anti-de Sitter form. They also study cut-off versions that mirror a mass gap in four dimensions. These features match what realistic theories beyond the standard model would need. The results show what energy flow can reveal about hidden strong dynamics.
arxiv-2601-10774:
Mathis Gerdes and Miranda C. N. Cheng design building blocks for normalizing flows. Flows turn simple random noise into rich data by a chain of smooth, invertible maps. Each scalar map in the chain must be expressive, smooth, and easy to invert with a known Jacobian. Existing choices force trade-offs among those needs.

Affine maps are smooth and easy to invert but weak. Splines give local control yet are only piecewise smooth and work on bounded ranges. Residual flows are smooth but need slow numeric inversion. The authors seek analytic bijections that keep all the good traits at once. Better blocks mean flows that train faster and sample more faithfully.
arxiv-2601-11274:
Sylvia Novo, Rafael Obaya, and Ana Sanz revisit families of rough ODEs. Their 2026 preprint deals with Caratheodory differential equations. Such equations allow rough, jumpy terms on the right side. Precompact families of them are the focus of the study.

The team builds a space of parametric b-measures for the work. Fit topologies on that space set the stage. From it they define a new class of generalized ODEs. The class is given by those parametric b-measures. Nonautonomous dynamical systems tools then do the heavy lifting. That route gives a fresh way to handle the families. The work sits in the core theory of differential equations.
arxiv-2601-11374:
Furkan Sahinuc, Subhabrata Dutta, and Iryna Gurevych grade scientific writing by machine. Their 2026 preprint builds reward models for that task. Scientific writing is expert work with strict demands. It needs deep domain knowledge and sharp reasoning at once.

Making scientific text by machine has been widely studied. Grading such text is still an open, hard problem. A reward model scores drafts so systems can learn from scores. Scores must track task specs, not just fluent style. The team tackles what a good reward for science prose is. Sound grading could lift AI help for authors and reviewers. It could also flag weak claims dressed in fine words.
arxiv-2601-11474:
Olivier Benoist proves a negativity claim about resultant divisors in this work. His 2026 preprint sits in birational geometry, a pure math field. Fix two degrees d and e, with d the smaller one. The space in play parametrizes pairs of polynomials.

Each pair holds homogeneous polynomials in two variables. One has degree d and the other has degree e. The higher one is set only up to a multiple of the lower. That gauge freedom shapes the parameter space's geometry. Resultants test when the pair shares a common root. The divisor they form is shown to be negative here. Negativity results guide how such spaces can be mapped and split.
arxiv-2601-11774:
Haoyu Xie, Jichao Fan, Zarif Ahmad Razin Bhuiyan, and their co-authors report a new kind of sensor for handed forms of molecules. Many drugs and scents come in left and right hand forms. Light based tests for which form is present are weak, and past boosts add hard steps.

Their sensor joins two effects in one stack built at wafer scale. One part uses twisted carbon tubes, and one part can change phase. Taking in molecules shifts the light read-out. The team frame this as a new route to sense work that is fine, large in scale, and open to control.
arxiv-2601-11874:
Suchana Datta, Dwaipayan Roy, Derek Greene, and their co-authors link search science with cultural analytics for fair access to old texts. They use the British Library BL19 set, with more than 35,000 works from 1700 to 1899. The set holds both fiction and non-fiction from the 19th century.

They build a test bed for shifts in words, terms, and search over that span. Old terms can hide works from modern search terms. The test bed can show where search fails past users. It aims to open old culture to all readers on fair terms.
arxiv-2601-11974:
Xinmeng Hou, Peiliang Gong, Bohao Qu, and their co-authors give language model agents a way to improve with less waste. Agents today rest on fixed prompts made by humans. That caps how well they can adapt to new tasks.

Past self-improve tools use loops that run many turns and cost much compute. The team take a cue from human meta-cognition, our skill at thinking about our own thought. Their method uses brief self-review to guide change. A leaner loop could make agents adapt at lower cost.  Brief self checks keep the cost of each task in bounds.
arxiv-2601-12174:
Haiman Guo, Cheng-Yi Li, Yuli Wang, and a large clinical team build a multitask agent to read right upper quadrant ultrasound. Ultrasound is a key tool in emergency and liver-bile care. Yet its reads rest much on the operator and are time pressed.

Their vision-language agent helps across the full read workflow. It does many linked tasks in one system, not just one label call. A broad aide could cut missed signs and speed reports. The work tests it on multi-frame scans from real care.  The agent is built for multi frame scans, not still shots.
arxiv-2601-12274:
Mahdi Eslamimehr joins concolic testing with large language models to guide path search in big programs. Concolic testing runs code with both real and symbolic inputs. It is strong, but path counts explode and constraint solving is costly.

His frame uses a language model to pick which paths to try and to ease solving. That pairing aims to make the method work on large, real software. Better test coverage finds flaws before release. The work sets out the algorithm and its claims.  LLM guides may cut the cost of search by a lot.
arxiv-2601-12374:
Akram Elbouanani, Aboubacar Tuo, and Adrian Popescu take on the task of bias checks in large language models. Past checks face a hard trade off. Fake prompts give tight control but do not match real use. Real tasks match real use but lack scale and rigor. The field needs a way to get both at once.

The team builds a framework that uses named entities as probes. Names of people, places, and groups can be swapped in a planned way. That swap lets them test how model behavior shifts across groups. The design aims to be large in scale and firm in method. It seeks gaps in how a model treats distinct sets of entities.
arxiv-2601-13074:
Shi-Cong Mo, Hongyi Yu, and Wei Wu study a rare route to superconductivity in flat layered matter. The route is the Kohn-Luttinger path, where pairs form from pure push away forces. In the plain form, pairs carry high spin like waves and form only at very low heat levels.

The team finds a new case in a stacked model of flat electron sheets. Such stacks stand in for layered van der Waals matter, sheets held by weak forces. In their model, pairs form in a plain s wave form with no spin like twist. The heat level for the change is also much higher than in the plain case. The result hints that layered matter may host this rare pairing at more apt heat levels.
arxiv-2601-13274:
Akinlade Akintunde and Stewart A. Mallory trace self spread in active matter back to hits between bits. Active matter is made of bits that move on their own, like cells or bots. Much is known about how crowds of them act as a whole. Far less is known about why one bit spreads as it does.

The pair build a frame that ties self spread to hit forces. They also track how those forces link over time, their memory. Both the plan of hits and their memory shape the spread. The frame gives a micro cause for a bulk trait. For staff who design smart stuff or study cell crowds, that cause is a design knob.
arxiv-2601-13374:
Bao-An Li reads the trace anomaly of dense matter from two harsh realms. The score is set by the gap of one third less the ratio of pressure to energy density. It marks how far dense stuff strays from a scale free form. That stray steers both fluid reply and star hold.

Li draws on two data pools. One is bulk flow in heavy ion crashes in the lab. The next is bulk traits of neutron stars, such as mass and size. By join of the two pools, he pins the score across a wide density span. Few scores can be tied from both a lab crash and a dead star at once.
arxiv-2601-13774:
Yan-Cheng Wang, Zheng Yan, and Xue-Feng Zhang probe a candidate quantum phase change point in 2026. Their setting is an extended hard-core Bose-Hubbard model on a kagome lattice. A kagome lattice has a woven pattern of triangles and hexagons. The point in question is a deconfined quantum critical point, or DQCP.

They use quantum Monte Carlo simulations to study the point. Two probes guide the work: entanglement entropy and the U(1) disorder operator. Both can reveal hidden order at a phase change. Firm proof at this point would test bold ideas in quantum matter theory.
arxiv-2601-13874:
Shijie Zhong, Yikun Yang, Da Gong, and Jiangfeng Fu refine a key statistic for two-sample testing in 2026. Maximum mean discrepancy, or MMD, compares two samples via kernels. Its inferential accuracy hinges on how well its variance is known. Past estimators differ under null and alternative hypotheses, and for balanced or imbalanced data.

The team gives a unified unbiased variance estimation for MMD. They target robust finite-sample performance with imbalanced data. They also give exact acceleration under both hypotheses. A single sound estimator could make two-sample tests simpler and more trusted.
arxiv-2601-13974:
Shih-Yao Lin builds a new way to judge which video frames a system picks in 2026. Frame sampling is a core step in video understanding and video-language pipelines. Judging the quality of sampled frames remains challenging. Old metrics focus on perceptual quality or reconstruction fidelity of single frames.

They do not test if a frame set captures informative, representative content. Lin's STEC is a reference-free spatio-temporal entropy coverage metric. It needs no ground-truth frame set to score a sample. Better frame picks could make video models faster and more accurate at once.
arxiv-2601-14174:
Myung-Sin Song and James Tian attach a notion of content to wavelet packet trees in 2026. Wavelet packets split a signal into a tree of finer frequency bands. The team gives a simple way to attach content to the tree's nodes, given a positive operator. At a fixed packet depth, packet projections split the operator.

The split yields positive pieces of the original operator. This decomposition induces a boundary measure on the packet path space. Vector-dependent densities show how energy distributes across the tree. Such maps help analysts see where an operator's strength concentrates.
arxiv-2601-14274:
Anh-Tuan Mai, Cam-Van Thi Nguyen, and Duc-Trong Le work on emotion reading in this 2026 paper. Their task is multimodal emotion recognition in conversation. A system must judge feelings from speech, text, and face cues at once. Each cue type can add its own facts.

Some facts are unique to one cue type. Some are shared across types. Some appear only when types are combined. The authors use those three kinds, named unique, redundant, and synergistic. A good system should use all three in balance, but that balance is hard to reach. Their divide-and-refine method aims to improve both the mix and how well the system can explain its calls.
arxiv-2601-14374:
Daniella van der Boom and Doron Kushnir revisit a key distance in this 2026 paper. The galaxy NGC 4258 holds a water maser system, gas clouds that beam microwaves. Tracking it gives a geometric distance to the galaxy. That distance is commonly reported as about 7.6 megaparsecs, with percent-level accuracy.

The value anchors the extragalactic distance ladder. It also feeds recent measures of the Hubble constant, the rate at which the universe expands. The authors reanalyze the maser system by tracking individual maser components. Their aim is a fresh check on a number that much of cosmology leans on.
arxiv-2601-15074:
Srinath Srinivasan, Tim Menzies, and Marcelo d'Amorim build a smarter judge for fuzz testing. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with differential fuzzers. These tools run the same input through rival versions of one spec, such as JavaScript interpreters, and flag where outputs differ.

Someone must decide which output is right. That judge, the oracle, is built by hand for JavaScript tests. Hand work is slow, costly, and prone to false alarms, and it must be redone when the spec changes. Their SmartOracle uses an agentic approach to cut that noise down.
arxiv-2601-15374:
Shravya Shenoy, Daniel J. B. Smith, and co-authors ask what sets the radio brightness of a star-forming galaxy. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with the radio continuum to star formation rate relation. Radio light offers a view of star birth that dust cannot hide.

New evidence hints that stellar mass bends that relation. The authors ask which other galaxy properties shape it too. They build a new calibration from the LoTSS-DR2 survey data. A cleaner relation means radio surveys can read star formation rates with far more trust than ever before.
arxiv-2601-15474:
Md Nabi Newaz Khan, Abdullah Arafat Miah, and Yu Bi study attacks on graph neural networks in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such networks do well on hard tasks in many fields. Yet they can be fooled by backdoor attacks. In these attacks, a hidden trigger is planted in the model. The model then acts as the attacker wants when the trigger appears.

Past work on graph classification mostly covers single-target attacks. There, one trigger is implanted by swapping in a subgraph. The title signals the step this paper takes. It moves to multi-targeted attacks, with more than one target in play. For defenders, that shift matters. A guard built for one trigger may miss a broader attack.
arxiv-2601-15774:
Mathew Duong and four co-authors build a yardstick for firmware fuzzers in a 2026 arXiv paper. Monolithic firmware runs countless devices. Fuzz testing it is an active research field. New methods claim gains in this hard domain. Checking those claims is messy, though. Metrics like code coverage and unique crashes are unreliable guides. Two fuzzers can post similar coverage while finding very different bugs.

Their answer is FirmReBugger, a benchmark framework. It is bug-based rather than coverage-based. A benchmark keyed to real bugs measures what users care about: found flaws. Fair comparison speeds progress across the field. Firmware flaws are security risks in routers, cameras, and industrial gear. Better fuzzers, honestly ranked, mean safer devices.
arxiv-2601-16074:
Annemarie Jutte and Uraz Odyurt ask how to trust machine learning in plant systems. Their 2026 preprint deals with plants and grids that join code and real gear.
