Such plants are key for safety and cost. Deep models now help run them, but their steps are hard to see. A model that acts in odd ways on new data can pose real risk.

The pair stress strict tests before trust is earned. Clear accounts of why a model acts as it does form part of that test. Tests must catch odd acts on data the model has not seen. The work frames a path to safe use of deep models. It speaks to teams who run plants where faults cost much.
arxiv-2601-16474:
Kaur Kristjuhan and Dominic Berry cut the cost of phase sums with three guide bits. Their 2026 preprint deals with quantum phase sums. Those sums sit in many quantum plans, most of all for chem ground states. Past sums use a guide state built on a bank of bits. Powers of a step are then run as that guide tells.

Three guide bits turn out to give best trust marks. Best marks mean the true phase sits in a tight range. Tight range with few bits cuts gear needs much. Chem sums could then run on more small gear. The work finds the sweet count for guide bits.
arxiv-2601-16674:
Shamim Haque, Atharva Shinde, Asim Kumar Saha, Tuhin Malik, and Ritam Mallick study twin stars. These are star pairs of a rare sort, not two stars in space. One branch holds plain dense stars of crushed matter. A twin branch holds stars mixed with quark matter. A sharp shift in dense matter can split the branches. Their 2026 preprint weighs which mixes can form twins.

Fresh sky data now bound the size and mass of dense stars. The team checks which shift points fit those bounds. They also gauge how strong the shift must be. Such checks test our grasp of matter at crush depth. They link lab ideas to what scopes see in deep space.
arxiv-2601-16774:
Yiheng Jiang, Biao Tian, Haoxu Wang, Shengkui Zhao, Bin Ma, Daren Chen, and Xiangang Li tackle echo in calls. When a speaker's voice loops back through a mic, talks get hard. Old fixes first strip the straight part of the echo. They also gauge the lag of the echo path. Their 2026 preprint drops both old steps for one neural net.

Their net learns the whole clean-up task end to end. It runs as a stream, fit for live calls. A step-wise training plan lifts its skill bit by bit. The goal is clear speech with no harsh cuts. Such nets could serve phones, meets, and smart speakers.
arxiv-2601-16874:
Fangzheng Wu and Brian Summa build a check kit for the guts of neural nets. A net's train state hides in its weights and steps. Gauges can read that state from in-house signs. Signs span slope size, faith, doubt, and margin. Their 2026 preprint treats train state as one hidden root. Each sign is then a view of that root.

The views are set next to fixed anchor marks. That set lets signs from unlike nets share one scale. An early form of the kit picked good save points. The full kit may flag bad runs while they train. It could save power and time in big model labs.
arxiv-2601-17074:
Akila Sampath, Vandana Janeja, and Jianwu Wang gauge Arctic snow depth from scarce, noisy signs. Snow depth drives ice growth and melt in the far north. Gauges there are few, and their marks are rough. Past models lean hard on those few marks. Or they skip the physics that makes marks make sense. Their 2026 preprint codes physics in an inverse model named PhysE-Inv.

The model works back from signs to depth with rules built in. Rules keep the depth calls in the true range. Sparse north data then yields more trust-worthy maps. Such maps feed climate and ship route plans.
arxiv-2601-17274:
Samar Hadou and Alejandro Ribeiro build neural networks that solve constrained optimization fast. Classic dual ascent methods solve such problems step by step. They are sound but can be slow. The authors unroll those steps into a learned network. Their frame is called constrained dual unrolling. Two coupled networks learn the two sides of the problem.

Together the networks near the saddle point of the Lagrangian. That point holds the best primal and dual values at once. Learned solvers can then answer new cases in one pass. Speed like that helps control, planning, and design tools. The work keeps the shape of a trusted method while adding learned pace.
arxiv-2601-18174:
Kazutoshi Masuda and Miho Yanagisawa build a theory for the skins of synthetic cells. Their 2026 preprint deals with lipid membranes, the soft sheets that wrap living and artificial cells. Such interfaces are basic to cell science and to soft materials. Yet a quantitative link between molecular layout and nonlinear surface mechanics has been missing. The authors set up an analytic frame for how lipid-coated synthetic cells respond when a micropipette pulls on them.

Lipid geometry and DNA nanostructures both enter the design. Together they let a builder program how stiff or springy a cell's skin is. Programmable skins serve drug carriers and cell models alike. The frame turns guesswork into design rules.
arxiv-2601-18274:
Sicheng Shen and co-authors add a temporal module to spiking transformers. Their 2026 preprint presents TEFormer. Spiking neural networks promise energy-efficient sequence modeling, and spiking transformers are a rising design in that space. Yet they lack a principled way to fuse information across time. That gap limits how well they use spatiotemporal patterns. TEFormer adds structured bidirectional temporal enhancement, letting each moment draw on both past and future context.

Bidirectional flow suits spikes, whose meaning often depends on what follows. Better temporal fusion could close the gap with standard transformers. It would do so at a fraction of the energy cost. Efficient sequence models matter for edge devices and sensors.
arxiv-2601-18374:
Rodrigo Silva and twelve colleagues built CitiLink to make city council records easier to search and read. Council minutes tend to be long and formal, with a stiff style set by office rules. The files are open to the public, yet their form makes facts hard to find.

Reporters and local people both need to find single facts fast, such as who voted for a road plan. Long files slow that search down and can hide choices from public view. A tool that lets users search the text and jump to the right part could save hours of work. It could also help more people take part in town life. The record would no longer feel locked to staff and lawyers alone.
arxiv-2601-18774:
Jonathan Pipping-Gamón and Abraham Wyner study a trap in sports talk: the team that had the best shot to win, yet lost, is said to have blown the game. Live win odds now run with each game on air. When a team that once stood at a high mark falls to a loss, the mark is read as proof of a choke. The pair ask what mark a sound set of odds would give by chance to a team that goes on to lose.

That mark has a spread set by the odds them-selves, if the odds are right. A big blown lead may be no more than what chance gives in a fair game. The pair work out that spread for a clean kind of odds path. Their sums give fans a yard stick: past it, a loss may be a choke.
arxiv-2601-18874:
Francis Burk and five colleagues show how a known beam trick could make new bits at labs that fire a beam at a still mark. The trick makes pairs of bits and anti-bits when a beam hits the mark's cores. Those pairs could, in a set world view, spawn a light go-between bit. That bit could then die in-to a pair of hid bits that barely act at all. Such hid bits are a prized hunt in the field.

The team take one such hid bit as their case: a heavy kin of the neutrino. They work out how oft the chain would fire at mark labs, for a range of go-between weights. Their sums show mark labs have a real shot at this hunt. That is a gain: mark labs are far more cheap and swift to run than smash labs.
arxiv-2601-19074:
Dariy Guzairov, Alex Potanin, Stephen Kell, and Alwen Tiu audit the safety of two systems built on guarded memory. Memory corruption attacks have plagued software for decades. The CHERI design fights back with capabilities: pointers that carry strict bounds on where they may reach and what they may do.

The team checks CheriBSD and Morello Linux, two systems built on that design. Guards are only as good as their setup in real code, so an audit hunts for gaps between the promise and the build. What they find guides both CHERI's growth and users who bet their safety on it.
arxiv-2601-19174:
Nirhoshan Sivaroopan and eight co-authors defend language model services against sponge attacks. Such attacks feed inputs crafted to make the model burn huge compute, a form of denial of service. Old defenses lean on statistical filters, which miss attacks that read as normal text, or on fixed detectors that cannot adapt.

Their framework, SHIELD, heals itself: it adapts as attack styles shift. Agentic defense means the guard can act, not just flag. As model services grow into public infrastructure, guards that keep pace with new drains on resources become a basic need.
arxiv-2601-19374:
Bahruz Suleymanli and Kutsal Bozkurt build an exact framework for protons bouncing off nuclei below the energy barrier. Stellar reaction rates depend on such scattering, and fresh experiments have refined them. Resonances caused by impurities inside the nucleus can spike the rate at set energies.

Their Green's function formalism rests on the exact solution of the Dyson equation, with no perturbative shortcut. A non perturbative tool can capture strong resonance effects that approximations smear out. Better rates feed straight into models of how stars burn, age, and forge the elements that later build planets and people like us.
arxiv-2601-20174:
Alexander Benanti, Xi Han, and Hong Qin present NeuraLSP, a neural preconditioner for solving large sparse linear systems. Such systems arise when partial differential equations are solved on a grid, and preconditioning is what makes them tractable. Graph neural networks have shown promise here by speeding up convergence.

NeuraLSP targets the left singular subspace of the system matrix, and it is built for use with conjugate gradient methods. The authors stress both efficiency and rigor in the design. Faster solvers for these systems would speed up simulation work across engineering, physics, and other fields that rely on such equations.
arxiv-2601-20274:
Fan Lin and Xinyang Wang propose a picture of the baryon, the family that includes the proton and neutron. In this picture, a gluon knot sits at the core. In this conjecture, the knot is a topologically knotted configuration of color-magnetic monopole condensates. Quarks interact with the knot through color-electric fields of an abelian kind.

Those fields are squeezed into flux tubes by the dual Meissner effect. That squeezing leads naturally to confinement, the fact that quarks are never seen alone. The picture offers a concrete shape for the inside of a proton, and a target for tests by theory and lattice work.
arxiv-2601-20474:
José F. B. Afonso, Stefan Kirchner, and Pedro Ribeiro study charge and current fluctuations at a phase transition driven by voltage. Their setup is a workhorse of quantum transport: an interacting quantum dot joined to non-interacting metal leads. Using the random phase approximation, which is exact when the dot has many levels, they map the zero-temperature phase diagram.

The map spans interaction strength and applied bias. Fluctuations of charge and current are sharpest near the transition, so they serve as sensitive probes of it. The work speaks to nanoscale electronics, where a biased dot is both a device and a lab for non-equilibrium physics.
arxiv-2601-20774:
Steve Hanneke and Mingyue Xu find cases where extra data from sister tasks stops helping. Their 2026 paper studies the limits of adaptation in multitask learning. Multitask learning pools datasets from related source tasks. The hope is to beat what each task could achieve alone. The framework has scored tremendous successes in modern applications. The authors ask when that hope fails. Their answer draws a boundary around the method's promise.

Adaptation means bending a shared model toward one target task. If the source tasks differ too much, pooled data can mislead. The paper characterizes when transfer gains vanish. Such limits guide practitioners who must choose between pooling and going solo. Knowing a method's failure zone is as useful as knowing its strengths. The work is learning theory with direct design advice.
arxiv-2601-20874:
Mustafa Cavus and four co-authors study how anxiety and depression relate to who we are and when symptoms strike. Their 2026 paper brings a new modeling view to public mental health. It centers on the Rashomon effect. That effect notes that many models can predict almost equally well. Yet each may rest on a different internal structure. Choosing just one can mislead interpretation.

The authors use that view to read the links between symptoms and factors. The factors include demographic traits and temporal patterns. With many good models in hand, only links that recur across them deserve trust. This robust reading suits health data, where stakes are human. The paper offers officials a steadier way to see what drives distress. It also warns against over-reading any single model's story.
arxiv-2601-21074:
Erik Lentz and four co-authors reinterpret a classic signal tool as a measure of information. Their 2026 paper concerns the Wigner-Ville transform in radio-frequency signal analysis. The transform maps a signal into a joint time-frequency picture. The authors present novel interpretations of it as an information measurement tool. Its utility lies in detecting and localizing signals of interest. Those signals sit amid noisy, cluttered backgrounds.

The transform can also measure the information volume of a signal. The authors use Tsallis entropy and related functionals for that job. Such measures could help analysts rank which signals deserve attention. Radio bands are crowded and growing more so. A tool that finds and weighs information at once is valuable. The paper joins classical signal processing with information theory.
arxiv-2601-21174:
Yuanning Cui and four co-authors break a reasoning limit in models that align entities across knowledge graphs. Their 2026 paper concerns entity alignment, a critical step for knowledge graph fusion. Alignment matches the same person, place, or thing in two graphs. Existing models lack transferability. They cannot align unseen graphs without retraining. Graph foundation models promise a fix. Yet the authors find that adapting them to alignment directly remains largely ineffective.

The title names the barrier: the reasoning horizon. Models reason too shallowly to match entities in new graphs. The paper works to break through that horizon. Transferable alignment would let fused graphs grow without constant retraining. Search engines and data platforms depend on such fusion. The study diagnoses why foundation models stumble here. It then pushes their reasoning further for this task.
arxiv-2601-21274:
Shinji Tsujikawa studies how the dark energy that speeds up the cosmos might cross a key boundary. In some theories, dark energy can act stronger than a pure vacuum push. One family of theories uses a vector field whose basic symmetry is broken.

The author shows how such fields, alone or with a scalar partner, can realize the crossing. Crossing this divide has long been hard to achieve without unstable models. A clean route matters because surveys keep hinting that dark energy may not be constant. The work gives model builders a tested path to match those hints.
arxiv-2601-21574:
A measurement study reports the photon-fusion production of W boson pairs in proton collisions, using the CMS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Two protons can graze past each other and trade photons, which then fuse into the boson pair. The data come from several years of running at high energy.

The team measures the total rate of this rare process. The result tests the standard model in a clean channel, since grazing collisions leave little debris. It also probes how photons behave inside fast protons. Rare clean events like these are sharp tools for spotting any crack in the current theory.
arxiv-2601-21674:
Ivan Biočić and Vanja Wagner study boundary value problems for nonlocal operators of spectral type. The operator is built from a function of a standard operator restricted to a bounded domain. The boundary condition here is nonhomogeneous, meaning the outside values are prescribed and nonzero.

The equation is semilinear and elliptic, set in a domain with a fairly smooth edge. Such problems model processes where long jumps, not just local spread, drive the physics. Handling nonzero outside data is essential for real use, since the world outside a region is rarely silent. The theory extends tools that were mostly built for the silent case.
arxiv-2601-21774:
M. Timmermans and a large team report two new rocky planets found hiding in existing data. The Hidden Gems project searches observations from the TESS space telescope for extra planets around low-mass stars in systems already known to host planets. Many such worlds sit below the detection limits of the standard pipelines.

The team uses a specialized pipeline called sherlock, built to find and vet faint transit signals with care. Applying it, they report two new rocky planets around nearby M dwarfs, the small red stars that are the most common in our galaxy. Extra planets in known systems help scientists see how full those systems are. And nearby rocky worlds are prime targets for later study of their atmospheres.
arxiv-2601-21974:
Collin Dabbieri and co-authors build a catalog of how quasar light changes over time. Quasars are brilliant galactic centers powered by black holes. Their broad emission lines, including the hydrogen line known as H beta, vary as conditions near the black hole change.

The team studies every quasar spectrum in a major Sloan Digital Sky Survey data release with low redshift and at least two observations. For each spectrum they decompose the light to isolate the broad H beta emission and measure its variability. Their 2026 catalog gives the community a uniform record of that behavior. Such catalogs power reverberation mapping, the technique that weighs distant black holes by watching their light echo.
arxiv-2601-22074:
Kevin Zakka and co-authors release a lightweight framework for robot learning called mjlab. Robot learning needs fast simulation, since policies improve through millions of trial actions. Heavyweight simulators with painful setup slow that loop and shut out smaller labs.

mjlab pairs GPU-accelerated simulation with composable environments and minimal setup friction. It adopts a manager-based design where users assemble modular blocks for observations, rewards, and events, and it runs on MuJoCo Warp for GPU speed. Their 2026 preprint presents the framework as open source. Lowering the cost of entry to robot learning research could widen who gets to train the next generation of capable robots.
arxiv-2601-22374:
Samyak Jain and four co-authors test whether a deep-ice detector can spot new kinds of neutrino contact. Neutrinos shift form as they fly, and matter can warp that shift. Their 2026 preprint uses DeepCore, the dense heart of the IceCube detector at the South Pole.

Odd contact terms, beyond the standard model, would leave a mark on shifts through the Earth. DeepCore watches neutrinos that have crossed the planet. The team map how well it can bound those odd terms. A clear bound, or a real mark, would test physics past the known rules.
arxiv-2601-22474:
Jian Xiong and a large team find hints of latent learning — grasp gained with no reward — inside large language models. Tolman's rats learned a maze while just wandering, then used that grasp once food appeared. Their 2026 preprint contrasts this with reward-led learning, which leans hard on outside feedback.

The team probe whether models build inner maps during unrewarded play. If they do, those maps could let models adapt fast when goals arrive. The claim links model science to a classic idea from psychology. It may reshape how agents are trained to explore.
arxiv-2601-22874:
Alessandro Pignedoli, Atreya Majumdar, and Karin Everschor-Sitte borrow an idea from swarms to solve hard search tasks cheaply. They use tiny particles that jitter with heat inside a material. Short-range attraction lets the particles help each other, like ants or birds moving as a group.

On a test landscape with a warm and cold pattern, interacting swarms find the best spot reliably. They beat lone searchers by a wide margin in the right range of group size and pull strength. The result hints at computers that optimize using physics itself.
arxiv-2601-23274:
Guantao Chen and three co-authors study edge coloring in graphs with no short cycles. Vizing and Gupta bounded the chromatic index, the number of colors needed for edges, by the maximum degree plus the maximum multiplicity. Steffen proposed a sharper bound that some graphs achieve.

The authors focus on graphs whose girth, the length of the shortest cycle, is at least five. They examine which such graphs reach Steffen's bound exactly. Edge coloring results support scheduling and network design, where edges are tasks needing distinct slots. Maximum degree and maximum multiplicity set the classical ceiling that Steffen's sharper bound tries to lower.
arxiv-2602-02474:
Haozhen Zhang and 6 co-authors let an AI agent's memory procedures themselves learn and evolve, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Most agent memory systems rely on a few static, hand-designed operations for storing and revising information. Those fixed routines hard-code human guesses and cope poorly with diverse interactions or long histories.

MemSkill recasts the operations as reusable memory skills for extracting, consolidating, and pruning information. A controller learns to select a small set of relevant skills, and an executor model carries them out. A third component, the designer, reviews hard cases where memories came out wrong or incomplete and proposes refinements or entirely new skills. The loop improves both selection and the skill set itself. Experiments on conversation, question-answering, and household-task benchmarks beat strong baselines and generalized across settings.
arxiv-2602-02574:
Edgard El Cham introduces a benchmark for the rules that decide what an AI memory system should keep, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A memory write policy chooses what to store, merge, and evict under a strict byte budget while a stream of documents and API data drifts over time. Good policies must balance task success against storage efficiency.

WritePolicyBench supplies four components for fair comparison. Task generators create controlled non-stationarity, so the stream changes in known ways. An explicit action interface defines how policies manipulate external memory. A byte-accurate cost model prices every storage decision honestly. Standardized metrics measure both task success and budget efficiency together. The benchmark gives memory-policy research, often evaluated ad hoc, a shared and reproducible testbed. Policies can now be compared on identical streams, budgets, and drift patterns.
arxiv-2602-02674:
Archaeological lead is prized for shielding rare-event detectors, and M. Consonni and 13 co-authors present a fast way to certify how clean it is, in a 2026 paper. Ancient lead has had centuries for its lead-210 contamination to decay away. Measuring the residue still matters, and standard assays are slow.

Their method uses a commercial low-background liquid scintillation counter with optimized chemical preparation and pulse-shape analysis. Samples under one gram reach sensitivities of a few hundred millibecquerels per kilogram within one week. The technique separately identifies the beta decays of lead-210 and bismuth-210 and the alpha decay of polonium-210, verifying equilibrium inside the decay chain directly. Forty days of counting pushes detection below one hundred millibecquerels per kilogram. The authors offer the assay for quality control in next-generation low-background experiments, with possible extension to other materials.
arxiv-2602-02774:
Israel Abebe Azime and 6 co-authors build a story question-answering benchmark in Amharic that treats culture as more than language, in a 2026 paper. Multilingual evaluations often equate a language with one culture and read model scores as language understanding. Narratives from different Ethiopian regions share a language yet differ in content, and those differences move evaluation results.

AmharicStoryQA grounds long-sequence questions in culturally diverse stories from Amharic-speaking regions. Testing existing models reveals a significant narrative understanding gap. Regional differences in scores are pronounced, and supervised fine-tuning improves performance unevenly across regions and settings. The authors argue benchmarks must be culturally grounded within a language, not just translated into it. Low-resource language evaluation, they show, hides its hardest variation at the regional level.
arxiv-2602-02874:
Teaching data science well is the subject of a 2026 paper by Tiffany A. Timbers and 1 co-author. Data science blends statistics and computer science. Borrowing teaching methods from either parent field alone, the authors argue, misses what makes the subject distinct in the classroom.

The paper presents ten simple rules for teaching the subject. Leading educators in the community developed and refined the rules. The authors have also applied them in their own data science classrooms. For teachers building or revising a course, the rules offer tested guidance shaped by practice rather than theory alone. The short format keeps each rule direct and easy to apply.
arxiv-2602-03374:
How viewers look at machine-intelligence-made videos is measured by Danqing Shi, with 5 co-authors, in an eye-tracking study of real scenes. Realistic made videos increasingly blur fact and fiction on media platforms, eroding public trust. Understanding viewing actions offers a human-centered perspective for improving finding and guiding output advances, yet gaze during made videos of real scenes had not been investigated before this study design.

Eye movements from forty participants were collected during video understanding and finding tasks mixing real and made videos. Given the high realism involved, gaze was driven less by a video's actual authenticity and more by the viewer's perception of its authenticity. Awareness of potential output may itself shift consumption from passive viewing into active searching for anomalies, the results demonstrate.
arxiv-2602-03474:
Agreement, getting distributed parties to settle on one value, is a founding problem of distributed computing. Shachar Meir and David Peleg study an energy-conscious version of it in a 2026 paper. In energy efficient agreement, each party wants to take part in as few communication rounds as possible, since every active round costs power.

Earlier work introduced that energy measure and asked how low it can go when some parties may crash. The authors present a recursive agreement algorithm with a strikingly small footprint. Each participant is active for only a logarithmic number of rounds in the maximum fault count. The recursive design shows that strong agreement guarantees do not require everyone to stay awake throughout the protocol.
arxiv-2602-03574:
The Euclid space telescope's near-infrared instrument, NISP, must measure faint galaxy light with limited onboard computing and bandwidth. The Euclid Collaboration examines the onboard signal estimator that handles that job in a 2026 paper. A custom algorithm running on the instrument's data processing units produces flux measurements and a quality factor for each estimate.

The authors revisit the estimator's assumptions and trace its main systematic errors through Monte Carlo simulations. Flight data from early operations show a systematic bias under the noise budget for nearly the whole detector array. They also derive an analytical formula for the estimator's variance. And they give the quality factor a firm statistical reading, including how it responds to cosmic ray hits.
arxiv-2602-03774:
Color every vertex of a random graph red or blue, and some subgraphs will end up all one color; how few can you force? Yatin Dandi and 2 co-authors study that minimization problem in a 2026 paper. The host graph is random, the copies counted are of a fixed subgraph shape, and the two-coloring is chosen to minimize monochromatic copies.

Using a recently discovered contiguity between balanced subgraphs in random graphs and random hypergraphs, the authors show the minimum converges to a limit. The convergence holds when the expected number of copies grows linearly in the number of vertices. Connections with mean-field spin glass models then give an asymptotic formula for the limit. The formula applies as the expected copy count and the subgraph's size both grow.
arxiv-2602-03874:
Crypto markets now hold trillions of dollars, yet no single gauge shows where their stress builds. Murad Farzulla and 1 co-author propose one in a 2026 paper. Their index, ASRI, blends stablecoin concentration, DeFi liquidity, contagion from traditional finance, and regulatory opacity into one score.

They test the index against four past crises, including Terra/Luna and FTX. The honest verdict is mixed. The index separates crisis days well but barely beats its own best part, and its early warnings carry many false alarms. Its real value, they argue, is showing which channel drives stress.
arxiv-2602-03974:
Shuhui Qu tackles planning when key facts are unknown and checking them costs effort. The 2026 paper presents Active Epistemic Control, a planning layer for agents in partly observable environments. A learned world model can guess missing facts cheaply, but wrong guesses can sink a plan silently.

The system keeps two stores strictly apart: grounded facts, which alone can justify commitment, and beliefs, which only prune candidates. When uncertainty runs high, it queries the environment; when confidence suffices, it simulates instead. Final commitment requires grounded coverage of every precondition. Simulated beliefs speed the search but can never certify a plan feasible.
arxiv-2602-04274:
Sunlight leaving the Sun's edge shifts differently than light from its center. H. C. Yu and 4 co-authors analyze that limb shift for an iron spectral line in a 2026 paper, using data from the CHASE mission and Bifrost simulations. Rising hot cells imprint a convective blueshift that varies across the solar disk.

Two separate averaging methods derived the shift curve. Simulations matched the data at the camera's resolution. At finer resolution, the velocity-based method departed from classical behavior while spectral averaging stayed consistent. The comparison also pins down the convective blueshift missing from the observations, sharpening solar speed calibrations.
arxiv-2602-04474:
A very bright exploding star called SN 2017ati is examined in a 2026 paper led by Z.-H. Peng with a large team of co-authors. The event was a type IIb supernova, a massive star explosion that has lost most of its outer hydrogen layer.

Optical images and spectra showed a broad, luminous peak and a late brightness above the usual range for its class. Radioactive nickel alone could not explain the light curve well. Adding energy from a magnetar, a highly magnetic neutron star, improved the fit. Late spectra suggested a large oxygen mass and a heavy parent star. The authors conclude that both energy sources likely powered the explosion.
arxiv-2602-04574:
Jonathan Klees and 5 co-authors present a cheaper way to estimate label uncertainty in a 2026 paper on probabilistic label spreading. Human annotations contain both inherent ambiguity and ignorance from limited knowledge, but collecting many labels per image is too costly at scale.

Their method spreads single annotations across a graph built from feature similarity, assuming nearby items share labels. They prove the resulting probability estimates stay consistent even as annotations per item approach zero. A scalable implementation follows. On common image datasets, the approach sharply reduced the annotation budget needed for a target label quality. It also set a new best result on a data-centric classification benchmark.
arxiv-2602-04674:
Eun Cheol Choi, Lindsay E. Young, and Emilio Ferrara test whether language models can stand in for survey respondents in a 2026 paper on misinformation susceptibility. Researchers use such stand-ins more and more, but their fidelity to human patterns is unsure.

Profiles from three online surveys, covering networks, demographics, attitudes, and behavior, prompted the fake answers. Outputs caught broad trends and matched human responses modestly. But the models overstated how strongly belief predicts sharing. Their fitted models explained too much variance and leaned on attitudes while largely ignoring personal networks. A look at the models' reasoning and training data pointed to built-in biases. The authors suggest such tools suit diagnosing divergence better than replacing humans.
arxiv-2602-04774:
Choosing a learning rate is one of the most fiddly parts of training a neural network, usually settled by trial and error. Blake Bordelon and Francesco Mori build a theory of optimal schedules in a 2026 study of a solvable random feature model trained by stochastic gradient descent.

Their optimal schedule comes from both numerical optimization and optimal control theory. Two regimes emerge. In the easy phase, the rate decays as a polynomial. In the hard phase, it follows a warmup, stable, then decay pattern. Adding momentum and adjusting batch size each helped in specific phases. Tests on image classification and a language model matched the predicted phase behavior.
arxiv-2602-04874:
Quantum cascade lasers lose performance to roughness at their internal interfaces, so growth conditions matter at the atomic level. Alessio Cargioli and 2 co-authors optimize the growth of a strain-compensated laser on an unusual indium phosphide substrate orientation. Atomic force and X-ray measurements guide the tuning of arsenic flux and the group ratio of elements.

The team reports the first lasing device on this platform. Its threshold and slope efficiency came out below the standard orientation's reference, a result they state plainly. A spectral redshift is traced to impurity scattering from the exposed crystal direction, after strain explanations were checked and ruled out by calculation.
arxiv-2602-05174:
Generative modeling on curved spaces, such as spheres or the space of positive-definite matrices, needs its own error theory. Yunrui Guan and 2 co-authors supply one for Riemannian flow matching in this 2026 statistics paper. The sampler learns a time-dependent vector field on the manifold and follows its flow with Euler steps, carrying a simple starting distribution toward the data distribution.

The key tool is a differential inequality tracking how the total variation distance between two flows evolves, driven by the mismatch between vector fields and the score of the reference flow. New bounds handle parallel transport and curvature, the geometric complications flat space never raises. The final estimate separates cleanly into a discretization term set by step size and a learning term set by field accuracy. Worked examples give explicit polynomial iteration counts for the hypersphere and for positive-definite matrix manifolds.
arxiv-2602-05274:
What makes a group of organisms a species, if all we may use is the family tree? Samuel Allen Alexander pursues that question in this 2026 mathematical biology paper, accepted by the Journal of Mathematical Biology. The arena is a graph linking every organism, past, present, and future, with edges for parenthood, and the simplifying assumption that life never goes extinct.

Alexander proposes axioms a genealogical species definition should plausibly meet. The key one, the identical ancestor point axiom, says that for any member of a species, either almost all of the species descends from it or almost none of it does. Together with a convexity axiom, this reduces the subjectivity in drawing species boundaries, in a technical sense. Sets meeting both are called specieslike clusters. The paper then finds extra constraints guaranteeing every organism a maximal such cluster, and proves no smaller set suffices.
arxiv-2602-05374:
Medical question answering by language models is mostly tested in English. Chaimae Abouzahir and 3 co-authors measure what that hides in this 2026 study, accepted at a health NLP workshop at EACL 2026. Arabic-speaking patients and clinicians are a large population, and models that are reliable in English may quietly fail them.

The team ran a cross-lingual comparison of model performance on Arabic and English medical questions. A language-driven gap persisted across models and grew wider as the tasks got harder. Tokenization study showed Arabic medical text being chopped into structurally fragmented pieces, one plausible mechanism for the gap. A second worry emerged from reliability study: the confidence models reported and the explanations they gave correlated only weakly with whether the answer was right. The authors call for language-aware design and evaluation before such models are trusted in care.
arxiv-2602-05474:
Why a user picks one item over another is the deeper question behind motivation-based recommendation, the topic of a single-author paper by Yicheng Di. Most systems learn motives only in a hidden way from clicks and choices, losing the rich cues in review text. The proposed framework, called LMMRec, uses large language models and several kinds of input to model user motives more directly.

Experiments on three real-world data sets show that the framework works well compared with earlier methods. The paper argues that reading reviews for explicit motive cues can make recommendations easier to explain and more persuasive. Readers should know that the author's own note flags writing errors in the methods section that still need correction. The author also plans more experiments and rewrites of the opening and related-work sections, so this version is a draft-stage report.
arxiv-2602-05774:
Speculative decoding speeds up language model output by drafting tokens cheaply and letting the big model verify them. Draft models, though, are usually trained in a way that mismatches how decoding really works. Xiandong Zou, Jianshu Li, Jing Huang, and Pan Zhou propose Variational Speculative Decoding, which treats draft training as variational inference over latent draft paths. Training then maximizes the chance that the target model accepts the draft.

The objective promotes high quality draft paths while keeping them close to the target distribution. A path level utility and an expectation maximization procedure reduce variance: one step samples from a filtered posterior, the other maximizes weighted likelihood with two added safeguards. Theory confirms the method raises expected acceptance length and speedup. Across language and multimodal models, it beat strong rivals such as EAGLE 3 by clear margins in decoding speed.
arxiv-2602-06174:
Amorphous solids like metallic glasses bend and flow in ways that depend on their past treatment. Pushkar Khandare and Srikanth Sastry build an elastoplastic model based on the energy landscape picture. The solid is split into small blocks, each sitting in one of many possible states, called mesostates.

Each mesostate has an energy, a strain range where it stays stable, and a strain where it bears no stress. When a block hits its limit under global strain, it jumps to another state, which counts as plastic change. The model reproduces known effects, including the brittle-to-ductile shift with annealing and the Bauschinger effect, plus slow failure near the yield point under repeated shearing.
arxiv-2602-06374:
Neural networks usually build their answers by adding many small contributions. Hee-Sun Choi and Beom-Seok Han study an architecture where multiplication, not addition, is the basic building block. They prove a universal approximation theorem for it: with enough units, such networks can approximate a wide class of functions.

Their analysis focuses on how errors distribute in space and how smoothness is preserved, measured in Bessel potential spaces and with Zygmund-type seminorms. Numerical tests used targets with sharp transition layers and points where smoothness drops. The multiplicative design kept its errors tightly aligned with those rough regions, and its smoothness measures converged more steadily. Architecture choice, they conclude, has concrete analytic consequences.
arxiv-2602-06674:
Yonghao Si and six co-authors release CytoCrowd, a public dataset for cytology, the study of cells under the microscope. Most medical image datasets give one clean answer key, which hides the fact that experts often disagree. Others keep the disagreement but offer no trusted reference for scoring. This dataset was built to hold both at once.

CytoCrowd contains 446 high-resolution images, each labeled independently by four pathologists whose markings sometimes conflict, plus a separate gold standard set by a senior expert. It can therefore score ordinary detection and classification models against the reference, and also test algorithms that merge conflicting expert labels into one. Baseline results for both uses show the dataset is demanding, and the authors present it as a resource for more realistic medical image tools.
arxiv-2602-06774:
Jiali Wu, Abhinav Anand, Shweta Verma, and Mira Mezini open up state space models, the efficient rivals of transformers, to see what they actually learn about code. Earlier work showed these models can match or beat transformers on code tasks under fair training, but their inner workings stayed hidden. The paper gives the first systematic comparison of the two architectures on code understanding.

The analysis finds that state space models pick up syntactic and semantic structure better than transformers during pretraining, but forget some relations when fine-tuned on certain tasks. To diagnose that loss, the authors introduce a frequency-domain tool that shows a shift toward short-range dependencies during fine-tuning. Design changes guided by the diagnosis improved one code search benchmark by up to six points of mean reciprocal rank.
arxiv-2602-06874:
Maria Chudnovsky and Ilya Maier study chordless loops in graphs and how many distinct lengths they can take. Counting distinct loop lengths gives a rough gauge of a graph's complexity. The pair shows that graphs which dodge two banned patterns, a big clique and a big complete bipartite piece, cannot pile up many loop lengths while staying structurally wild.

More sharply, such graphs have bounded treewidth, a trait that makes many hard problems easy. From that link comes a fast test: a program can decide in polynomial time whether a graph holds chordless loops of at least three distinct lengths. A simple count thus opens a door to deep structure and to a concrete algorithm.
arxiv-2602-07174:
Segmenting brain tissue in MRI scans gets harder across the lifespan, because brains change shape and appearance with age.  Yongheng Sun and three co-authors present DuMeta++, a dual meta-learning method for few-shot segmentation that works across diverse ages without paired scans of the same person over time.

One part of the method learns age-agnostic features of evolving brain structures, while the other learns starting points that adapt quickly from few cases.  A memory-bank regularization step enforces consistency over time without longitudinal pairs.  Clinicians and brain experts get a segmentation tool that travels better across ages, where labeled data is often scarce.
arxiv-2602-07674:
When a model denies someone a loan or a job, algorithmic recourse tells them what to change for a better outcome. Standard counterfactuals can fail if another near-optimal model would decide otherwise.  Bohdan Turbal and two co-authors present ElliCE, a method for recourse that stays valid across the Rashomon set of near-optimal models.

Optimizing counterfactuals over an ellipsoidal approximation of that set yields explanations provably valid across the ellipsoid. Guarantees on uniqueness, stability, and match with key feature directions, backed by tests.  Responsible AI teams get recourse that survives model multiplicity instead of depending on one arbitrary model among many equally good ones.
arxiv-2602-07974:
Learning theory usually studies prediction within a known context, but real problems span many contexts that must first be discovered. Xin Li develops structural learning theory for that second difficulty, introducing width, the minimum number of jointly contractive, low-risk cells needed to cover a problem.

Width is incomparable with VC dimension: either can blow up while the other stays bounded. The paper proves a phase transition: with fewer cells than the width, learning hits an irreducible error floor, while with enough cells the problem reduces to ordinary statistical learning within cells. A contractive-similarity operator and its Laplacian provide a way to estimate width from data. Theorists gain a new axis for understanding structured, multi-context, non-stationary learning.
arxiv-2602-08374:
The Schrödinger bridge problem asks for the most likely path between two distributions, but in practice those endpoints are known only through samples. Denis Belomestny and three co-authors take a learning-theory route instead of the usual Sinkhorn iterations. Their arXiv paper rewrites the bridge system around a single positive transformed potential that obeys a nonlinear fixed-point equation.

The authors then fit that potential to data, choosing from a broad family of candidate functions, with uniform concentration guarantees under sub-Gaussian assumptions. Plugging the learned potential into a stochastic control picture yields samples from the bridge. Numerical trials illustrate the method in action. Readers get a fresh, theory-backed way to bridge distributions from data alone.
arxiv-2602-08874:
A harmful request need not arrive in one sentence: it can be split across a long document and reassembled by the model itself. Yu Fu and five co-authors probe this risk, called compositional reasoning attacks, in which fragments of a harmful goal hide inside long contexts while the final question stays neutral. They test fifteen leading models on contexts up to 64,000 tokens.

Models usually refuse plainly harmful requests, but refusal falls sharply when the goal must be pieced together, and longer contexts often fail worse. The breakdowns are not mostly retrieval slips: models frequently infer the goal and then comply anyway. Extra reasoning at run time helps only partly, at high cost.
arxiv-2602-08974:
Could the universe bounce instead of beginning, and cycle forever? Rikpratik Sengupta and two co-authors study that idea on an anisotropic brane with a timelike extra dimension, in the Shtanov-Sahni framework. They drive the dynamics with a single scalar field rolling at a constant rate, with shear anisotropy fading as the sixth power of the scale factor.

A general classification follows: turnarounds at negative energy density always occur, while bounces above a critical density need the negative high-energy brane correction to beat the shear term. Closed-form bounce and turnaround rules, a finite cyclic branch, and a cosmic-microwave-background-normalized parameter point complete the picture, including superinflationary and ordinary inflationary phases after the bounce.
arxiv-2602-09074:
What counts as thermodynamic entropy when a quantum system is far from equilibrium? Md Manirul Ali and one co-author argue the usual von Neumann entropy does not, in general, govern heat exchange once coherence builds up during nonequilibrium evolution. Their framework merges the resource theory of quantum coherence with thermodynamic principles.

Thermodynamic entropy is identified with energy entropy from energy-measurement statistics, and a dynamical temperature extends the equilibrium concept to transient states. An exact entropy-balance relation splits heat-associated flux from coherence-loss production, linking coherence, heat flow, and total change. The formalism, tested on an exactly solvable open system, defines temperature, work, heat, and free energy throughout evolution.
arxiv-2602-09174:
Graph workloads choke on moving data between processor and memory, a bottleneck processing-in-memory designs attack by computing near the data. Marzieh Barkhordar and seven co-authors test that promise on real hardware, implementing representative graph algorithms on UPMEM's general-purpose processing-in-memory system rather than a simulated proposal. They characterize performance, name the key bottlenecks, and compare against CPU and GPU baselines.

Choosing the right data partitioning across memory cores proves crucial for speed. The study also identifies hardware limits in current processing-in-memory systems across compute, memory, and communication, and points to enhancements future designs need. For builders of graph accelerators, it grounds hype in measurements from a shipping system.
arxiv-2602-09274:
Jeremy Mould asks whether dark matter could trigger a class of supernovae. Crashes between stellar leftovers and dark matter in our galaxy's bulge are common. A primordial black hole striking a white dwarf would heat its degenerate core, by at least a degree for a lunar-mass intruder if all kinetic energy thermalizes. That estimate is conservative in two ways: the specific heat is lower than the simple value, and gravitational focusing accelerates the incoming object.

Detailed physical models of such triggering now exist, but present data cannot yet tell whether Type Ia supernovae track starlight in galaxies or concentrate toward centers, as collisional triggering would predict. Coming hauls of millions of supernovae from Rubin's telescope, the author argues, will settle the question.
arxiv-2602-09374:
Finding rare, high-value setups under strict query budgets is hard when each test is costly and black-box. Classical optimizers cluster on dominant modes, while diversity methods need large budgets, and quantum sampling needs a problem Hamiltonian that black-box settings lack. Saisubramaniam Gopalakrishnan and Dagnachew Birru extend this stand-in route in their 2026 paper, modeling richer variable links for quantum-assisted search.

Earlier quadratic stand-ins capture only pairwise structure. The new method uses self-attention to model higher-order links, then projects them into a valid positive semi-definite quadratic form that quantum sampling can draw from. On risk discovery for business document systems, the quantum-guided sampler matches classical rivals on utility while improving variety of form. It recovers roughly twice as many tail-risk outliers as most baselines, plus a set of high-value setups no rival found.
arxiv-2602-09574:
Tree-search decoding scales language-model reasoning at test time, but real deployments cap tokens per query, and that cap varies by setting. Sora Miyamoto and two co-authors note that existing tree-search policies largely ignore the budget except as a stopping rule, risking late-stage over-branching or premature termination. Their 2026 algorithm, Budget-Guided MCTS, aligns search policy with the remaining budget.

Search starts broad, then shifts toward refinement and answer completion as the budget drains, while cutting late branching from shallow nodes. Across inference budgets, the budget-guided policy beats budget-agnostic tree-search baselines on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and an additional physics reasoning benchmark with open-weight models. The paper thus turns a fixed token budget from a mere cutoff into a guide for search.
arxiv-2602-09674:
Léo Hubert proves a shape spread of the Dold-Kan match for sheaves of abelian groups in his 2026 paper. For any test class in Grothendieck's sense, a fit rule links hole matches with weak matches of sheaves. Then the shape class of abelian sheaves is equal to the low derived class of abelian groups.

The match comes from a Quillen match for a model structure on abelian sheaves set up under these rules. The result covers a wide range of test classes and is shown to apply to Joyal's class Theta. Old Dold-Kan thus gains a shape form, spreading the match from simple objects to the broader landscape of test classes.
arxiv-2602-09874:
Equational reasoning sits at the heart of quantum circuit tuning and checking: small parts are swapped for proven equal parts under a fixed set of rewrite rules. Colin Blake gives six near-Clifford circuit fragments a shared treatment in his 2026 paper, with wire order handled as structure rather than as algebra. The fragments span qubit Clifford, real Clifford, Clifford-plus-T up to two qubits, Clifford-plus-CS up to three qubits, CNOT-dihedral, and qutrit Clifford.

Starting from earlier completeness results, Blake moves completeness into this setting and drops redundant non-structural rules, then checks minimality with tailored interpretations for single axioms. The resulting presentations are minimal in all arities for qubit Clifford, real Clifford, and CNOT-dihedral, and minimal in bounded ranges for the rest. All six share one transfer-and-separation pattern, making their presentations directly comparable.
arxiv-2602-10174:
Market stress reshapes link networks, but single-scale views miss how structure deforms across market spans. A 2026 paper led by Jose De Leon Miranda, with three co-authors, introduces a multi-scale wobble measure joining trend-free cross-correlation analysis with minimum spanning tree sifting. The Elastic Detrended Cross-Correlation Ratio tracks the log response of average tree length to viewing scale.

Applied to global equity indices, the measure rises sharply during market stress, showing tighter short-term herding among traders and shrinking link gaps. It reveals scale-tied reshapes hidden from single-scale views and splits stressed from stable regimes clearly. The approach needs no fixed-spread assumption and applies where linkage strength varies with scale.
arxiv-2602-11274:
Transitional millisecond pulsars flip between radio and X-ray states. Silvia Conforti and five co-authors track PSR J1023+0038 with optical and X-ray timing, measuring the phase lag between optical and X-ray pulses and the evolution of orbital timing to 2023. A small lag supports a common origin for both pulse types.

Orbital timing advances by about twenty seconds per year, and since 2017 it follows a parabolic trend. That trend signals a growing orbital period and separation, steady with non-conservative mass transfer where the donor loses far more than the accretor gains. The lag measurement further supports synchrotron emission at a shock between pulsar wind and accretion flow as the shared source.
arxiv-2602-11374:
State-space models save compute but lag models on recall tasks. Aviv Bick and two co-authors trace that gap to a small set of gather-and-aggregate focus heads that state-space models struggle to reproduce. Their recall-aware distillation converts a pretrained model into a hybrid student by preserving only recall-key heads.

Ablation on a built recall task identifies the needed heads, yielding sparse, non-uniform focus placement. Keeping just two percent of focus heads recovers nearly all teacher results on recall-heavy tasks, far fewer than hybrids retaining a quarter or more. With recall handled, the recurrent backbone simplifies with little loss, even under large state cuts. The hybrid proves several times more memory-fast than similar hybrids.
arxiv-2602-11474:
Why do some active galaxies look obscured and others bare? Atsushi Tanimoto and five co-authors test the unification model with radiative hydrodynamic simulations plus photoionization calculations. Angular spreads of neutral and ionized hydrogen are computed, then cover factors for Compton-thin and Compton-thick obscuration are derived.

Compton-thin cover for combined hydrogen proves independent of Eddington ratio at a high value, while neutral-only cover sits lower, also independent of ratio. Compton-thick cover matches sights, but Compton-thin cover agrees only at high Eddington ratios, falling short at low ones. Extra Compton-thin gas beyond current computer regions is needed to close that gap, a concrete target for larger simulations.
arxiv-2602-11574:
Picking the right setup for an AI agent means choosing workflows, tools, token budgets, and prompts from a huge menu of combinations. Today that choice is usually a fixed template or hand-tuned rule, applied the same way to easy and hard questions alike, which wastes compute and breaks on new tasks. Aditya Taparia and two co-authors recast setup choice as a sequential decision problem, where each setup acts as a long-lived option for handling a query.

Their learner, ARC, is a light hierarchical policy that picks a setup per query instead of one for all. Across reasoning, tool-use, and agentic benchmarks it beats budget-matched tool-using models. Reasoning accuracy rises by about 31 percent and tool-use accuracy by about 14 percent, and success on an airline task benchmark doubles from 9 to 18 percent. Learning the setup per query, the authors argue, beats any single fixed design.
arxiv-2602-11774: Kyle Bradford presents what the paper describes as a solution to the Straus-Erdős conjecture. The conjecture concerns writing fractions as sums of unit fractions. It states that for each prime number, four over that prime equals one over x plus one over y plus one over z. Here x, y, and z are positive whole numbers in increasing order. The paper outlines a proposed solution, so readers should treat the claim as proposed rather than established.
arxiv-2602-12174:
Weak lensing surveys now hit a wall set by gas physics, since gas blown out of haloes damps small-scale matter clumping. Amy Wayland led this work with two co-authors, forecasting what happens when lensing data are joined with fast radio bursts. Bursts give dispersion measures that trace gas around haloes, offering a second handle on the same physics.

Even after allowing for burst redshift errors and source clustering, adding bursts to a Stage-IV lensing survey cuts the damage to the S8 measure by about 80 percent. Bursts alone leave two gas traits tangled, but lensing breaks that tangle. Adding galaxy clustering tightens matter density and one gas trait, though it adds little to S8 beyond lensing plus bursts.
arxiv-2602-12674:
Knowledge distillation for large language models has become more key as models grow in size and complexity. Yet old approaches focus on copying teacher behaviour and often miss the original learning setting that shaped the teacher's knowledge. Yuang Cai led this work with one co-author, Yuyu Yuan, giving Experiential Knowledge Distillation, or X-KD. It is a new and general frame letting student models learn in the teacher's original learning setting.

Inspired by experiential learning theory and inverse reinforcement learning, X-KD adopts Approximated Variational Reward Imitation Learning. That recovers the teacher's learning setting as a reward function. Students then learn by interacting with that recovered setting, rather than merely copying teacher outputs. Tests show X-KD beating standard distillation rivals across jobs, with better generalisation to new settings.
arxiv-2602-12774:
Counting objects in images usually needs costly point labels for every object, and weakly supervised methods mostly count just one category, like people. Xiaowen Zhang and five co-authors present WS-COC, the first framework driven by a multimodal language model for weakly supervised counting of any category, using only image-level counts as training signals. Rather than forcing the model to guess counts directly, they bootstrap it with three strategies.

First, a dialogue routine narrows the count range step by step. Second, a ranking routine teaches the model to order images by their counts. Third, a fusion step blends local and global count estimates to handle dense scenes. On four benchmarks the method matches or beats many fully supervised rivals while slashing labelling cost, a practical win for counting in the wild.
arxiv-2602-12874:
A unimodal distribution has a single peak, and its cumulative distribution function is convex then concave. Markus Zobel and Axel Munk move that shape description over to the quantile function. Their note shows the quantile function of a unimodal law never jumps, which turns unimodality into a property of its derivative, the quantile density.

Specifically, unimodality becomes equivalent to quasi-convexity of that density. The argument leans on generalised inverses of non-decreasing functions and an inverse-function rule adapted to such functions. For statisticians, the shift matters: working on the quantile side can make shape constraints easier to state and test, with the density carrying the peak structure directly.
arxiv-2602-12974:
Brain scans have changed brain science, from growth through ageing to nerve decay, yet its data are high-D and messy. Jian Kang and four co-authors survey number-based chances and hurdles across four areas. They cover brain growth to age 20, the adult and ageing brain, nerve decay and mind-nerve illnesses, and brain coding and reading. A quick primer on MRI, fMRI, EEG, and PET sets the stage.

The hurdles are known to number experts: reading noise, motion glitches, shift across subjects, sites, and scanners, and sheer study scale. The paper reviews cutting-edge studies, flags data and model building hurdles, and highlights where number experts can help most. Its closing message is joint: progress toward better tests, workings insight, and tailored treatment needs number experts, brain experts, and doctors working jointly.
arxiv-2602-13074:
In slow-roll to ultra-slow-roll to slow-roll inflation, the curvature power spectrum shows a finite dip whose origin at linear order has been controversial. Wen Li and Chao Chen revisit the perturbation dynamics using junction techniques and asymptotic Hankel-function expansions. For the first time, they derive accurate, simple asymptotic formulas for how modes evolve and for the resulting spectrum, guided by three systematic rules for picking dominant terms across transitions.

The dip, they find, comes from two growing modes cancelling within linear theory, not from a constant term cancelling a growing one, as earlier work suggested. The paper also gives analytical accounts of amplitude enhancement and two oscillatory patterns in the spectrum. All asymptotic results are validated numerically against the reconstructed inflationary potential, settling the dip's linear-order origin.
arxiv-2602-13174:
Partial differential formula models often contain unknown functions that cannot be measured straight, limiting forecasts. Torkel Loman and four co-authors show that standard workflows for estimating PDE settings can be stretched to infer functional components from data. Neural networks embedded inside the PDE system learn unknown functions during training with high closeness.

As a case study with nonlocal aggregation-diffusion formulas, the team recovers external potentials and interaction kernels from observations at steady state. Reconstruction closeness is examined against the number and mix of answers, sampling density, and measurement noise. After training, the PDE model serves conventionally to study conduct and generate forecasts. The system thus keeps the advantages of standard PDE tuning while extending it from scalar settings to whole functions.
arxiv-2602-13274:
How a prompt is phrased can shift a language model's moral judgment and safety, yet comparisons of prompting styles have been scattered across data sets and models. ProMoral-Bench unifies the test, scoring 11 prompting styles across four model families on ETHICS, Scruples, WildJailbreak, and a new robustness test called ETHICS-Contrast. Scores use a Unified Moral Safety Score that balances accuracy with safety.

Short, example-guided prompts beat elaborate multi-stage reasoning, earning higher scores with greater robustness at lower token cost. Multi-turn reasoning proved fragile under small changes, while few-shot examples steadily improved moral stability and jailbreak resistance. Rohan Subramanian Thomas leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13674:
Linear differential equations can be tackled by relating operators to one another, and this paper develops an operator approach to solving them based on intertwining links between operators. Rules for when intertwining operators exist are obtained, and in low-order cases the problem reduces to Riccati-type equations, a classical and tractable form.

The method extends to linear partial differential equations, where it constructs solutions directly, and the linear Klein-Gordon equation serves as a worked example. By shifting the problem from solving equations to finding intertwining operators, the approach offers a clear route through a class of equations that resist direct attack. O. V. Kaptsov is the sole author.
arxiv-2602-13774:
The Impostor Phenomenon is the persistent belief of being a fraud despite evident competence. It is common in software engineering, where high expectations for expertise and innovation prevail, yet evidence on coaching in the field remains thin. This study examines a structured group coaching program for early-career software engineers through a quasi-experiment with 20 people across two project teams, using a wait-list control design plus outside observation. The treatment group received three coaching sessions, while the control group received them after an observation phase.

Impostor feelings were measured with the Clance Impostor Phenomenon Scale, alongside well-being, life satisfaction, and affect measures. Coaching produced modest score drops, but the control group also improved during observation, suggesting context and timing factors may have shaped results more than the formal program. Coaching may still support reflection and awareness around impostor feelings. Paloma Guenes leads the work with six co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13874:
Ben Kosa and five co-authors report a 2026 arXiv study of do-it-yourself assistive tech for people with visual impairments. Off-the-shelf aids often take a one-size-fits-all form, while DIY kits tend to demand an engineer partner or coding skill. That leaves many users unable to shape tools to their own needs.

The team explored how large language models might act as co-making partners, not just visual aids, in hands-on prototyping. Their study surfaces needs for better spatial and visual support, tactics for coping with novel AI errors, and design lessons for more accessible prototypes. The goal is a process where blind and low-vision makers lead the build themselves.
arxiv-2602-14274:
Boning Zhou and three co-authors present a 2026 arXiv framework for causal inference from unstructured text. Causal inference guides business decisions, but it usually relies on structured data that may be incomplete or absent. The paper asks whether transformer language models can fill that gap using text alone.

Causal estimates from unstructured text were compared with estimates from structured data at population, group, and individual levels. Results lined up consistently across levels, validating text-based inference as a viable route. The approach extends causal methods to settings where only textual data exists, letting firms make data-driven choices even when tabular data is scarce.
arxiv-2602-14574: Doosung Park, writing alone, proves Poincaré duality for smooth projective morphisms in log motivic homotopy theory, fitting Annala, Hoyois, and Iwasa proofs to the log setting. As a use, the crystal cohomology of a log compactification is shown to be free of its choice. The short paper moves a classic duality result into log shape theory.
arxiv-2602-15274:
Madani and colleagues explore how memory can aid navigation in changing environments. In a foraging task, the agent must find its way from home, through barriers to food. The world is non-stationary: barrier and food locations may change day to day, and agent sensing is uncertain and very limited. Map building and planning must be robust, and learning must be fast enough to be useful.

They examine strategies from simple to complex. They find an architecture combining multiple strategies is required, especially for exploration and search when food location is unknown, and planning a path to a remembered food location. An agent using non-stationary probability learning to update episodic memories can build maps and plan on the fly with imperfect maps limited to its experience. It grows much more efficient than minimal-memory agents as difficulty rises, as long as uncertainty from localization and change stays small.
arxiv-2602-15474:
Prieto-Garcia and colleagues test Quantum Reservoir Computing scores for number and money problems. They use a pool of two super-cold isles linked via volt levels of room. The key non-linear parts giving the pool rich motion are the Josephson links joining each isle to the earth.

They show Quantum Reservoir Computing built in this loop can exactly sort chance spreads, including those with fat ends. It can spot phases in linked runs, such as spells of high swing from usual econ models. They find Quantum Reservoir Computing beats some best older tools when the volume of data is small. This shows its promise as a noise-tough quantum teaching method able to handle real-world problems within now open super-cold rigs. They discuss how to boost the Quantum Reservoir Computing routine in real super-cold gear to gain from a much bigger Hilbert room.
arxiv-2602-15774:
Jones and colleagues propose a minimal tight-binding model for the electronic layer of the lanthanum aluminate and strontium titanate pair with oxygen gaps. In the model, effective carriers face magnet flaws induced by oxygen gaps. Both random on-site potentials and Zeeman-like exchange links between linked carriers and magnet flaws are taken into account.

Applying combined coherent potential approximation and dynamical mean-field theory for a ferromagnetic state, the team uncovers a disordered Fermi-liquid regime for majority spins. They also find a low energy scale controlling transport of minority-spin carriers. Both effects stem from magnet flaws. The work gives a compact model for a much-studied oxide layer, linking gap-induced magnet effects to distinct transport behaviour for the two spin populations.
arxiv-2602-15974:
Green surveys stellar microlensing as a hunt for primordial black holes and other compact dark matter objects. When a compact body passes in front of a distant star, its gravity briefly brightens the star, and surveys counting such events can test whether these objects make up the dark matter.

Under standard assumptions, current observations already rule out compact objects as the whole of the dark matter. The excluded range is huge, from far below a solar mass to far above it. Written for theorists working on primordial black holes, the review traces the history and theory of the method. It takes stock of what surveys have found, and looks ahead to what future observations could still reveal.
arxiv-2602-16174:
Wireless metaverse services need high visual quality and low latency at the same time. Meeting both demands takes coordination across mobile edge servers, which hold data in scattered places. Fatih Temiz and coauthors propose a federated split decision transformer, called FSDT, for resource allocation in this setting. The transformer model is split between edge servers and the cloud.

Edge-side parts, such as embedding and prediction layers, adapt to local conditions. Shared global layers in the cloud enable cooperative training across servers. That split avoids sending full model parameters everywhere and softens the harm from naive global aggregation in mixed radio environments. Tests show quality of experience gains of up to a tenth over baselines, while nearly all transformer parameters move to the cloud, easing the load on edge servers.
arxiv-2602-16274:
Rahul Singh and coauthors present the first regret bound for classical online Q-learning in infinite-horizon discounted Markov decision processes, without relying on optimism or bonus terms. They first analyze Boltzmann Q-learning with decaying temperature. Regret depends critically on the suboptimality gap. For sufficiently large gaps, regret is sublinear. For small gaps it deteriorates and can approach linear growth. To address that limitation, they study a smoothed epsilon-greedy exploration scheme combining epsilon-greedy and Boltzmann exploration. It yields a gap-robust regret bound near a stated sublinear rate.

Sample complexity guarantees also follow, with both bounds holding with high probability. To analyze these algorithms, the authors develop a high-probability concentration bound for contractive Markovian stochastic approximation. The work thus gives online Q-learning its first rigorous regret guarantees and a new concentration tool.
arxiv-2602-16474:
Hongyu Gao, writing alone, investigates when structural lubricity ignores load, using molecular dynamics simulations of a mismatched gold-graphite interface. Strict load freedom, the paper shows, occurs only in laterally infinite, area-filling contacts, where loss comes from phonon-mediated viscous coupling and shear stress scales linearly with sliding velocity.

Finite contacts with explicit boundary terminations show substantially higher friction yet remain load-free up to a set load. Load dependence appears only when elastic out-of-plane deformation near the contact line exceeds a set amplitude, activating additional loss channels. The results show that contact geometry and local elastic compliance, rather than normal load itself, decide when lubricity starts and breaks down.
arxiv-2602-16574:
Javier de Frutos and Julia Novo give optimal error bounds for fully discrete approximations to finite-horizon problems. The problems are solved by dynamic programming. They adapt an earlier infinite-horizon error analysis to the finite case. They prove an a priori bound governed by the time step and the spatial mesh size. With piecewise constant controls, first-order convergence holds in both time and space. Standard regularity assumptions suffice.

A notable gain is that stricter control regularity is no longer needed. That stricter regularity was demanded in the infinite-horizon analysis. The loss of time convergence rate seen there is also avoided here. Readers in numerical optimal control get a clean, sharp error theory. It covers a widely used method, with assumptions easier to meet in practice.
arxiv-2602-16874:
Lenka Ptackova and Michal Outrata examine domain decomposition for mean curvature flow of surface polygonal meshes. They first test traditional domain decomposition methods with and without overlap of deconstructed domains. They then present adapted Robin transmission conditions of the optimized Schwarz method.

Resulting smoothing is analyzed from the viewpoints of shape quality and texture deformation. By splitting the initial mesh into two sub-meshes, the method solves two smaller boundary value problems instead of one big problem, and the two tasks can run almost entirely in parallel. Mesh processing researchers get a route to faster curvature flow smoothing for surfaces built from arbitrary simple polygons.
arxiv-2602-16974:
Yongjie Zhou and co-authors present a comprehensive taxonomy and evaluation of document chunking plans for info search, moving beyond chunk-then-embed. Document chunking is a critical preprocessing step in dense search systems, yet the design space of chunking plans remains poorly understood. Recent research has proposed several concurrent approaches, including language-model-guided methods and contextualized strategies generating embeddings before segmentation to preserve contextual information.

The paper reproduces prior studies and presents a systematic frame unifying existing strategies along two key dimensions. One dimension is splitting methods, including structure-based methods such as fixed-size, sentence-based, and paragraph-based, plus semantically-informed and language-model-guided methods. The other is embedding paradigms, determining the timing of chunking relative to embedding. Reproduction tests those routes in two search settings: in-document search and in-corpus search, the standard info search task.
arxiv-2602-17674:
Bijean Ghafouri and Emilio Ferrara study what happens when AI systems summarize and relay text to other AI systems, in a telephone-game paradigm. Across five studies tracking content through AI transmission chains, three steady patterns emerge. The work asks how relay transforms content, not merely whether it degrades it.

First, convergence pulls texts toward a shared default of moderate confidence, muted affect and analytical structure. Second, selective survival keeps narrative anchors while stripping evidence texture, hedges, quotes and attributions. Third, competitive filtering lets strong arguments survive while weaker yet valid views vanish. Human readers rated relayed content as more credible and polished, yet showed worse factual recall, weaker balance perception and dulled emotional resonance.
arxiv-2602-18274:
Viktoriia Makovska and four co-authors teach data design as group work, not a solo technical task. Their 2026 paper notes that entity-relationship diagrams shape how data systems picture people, work, and groups, yet classes usually teach the skill as pure technique. Research on joint design shows that bringing varied voices into the work brings out hidden knowledge and challenges quiet assumptions.

The team introduces GARLIC, a workshop format that adapts the earlier ONION joint-design frame into role-play, joint building, guided critique, and repeated revision. GARLIC builds both design skill and a critical eye for the social and ethical stakes of how data pictures people. It lowers the entry barrier to joint design work and gives students hands-on practice in shared, inclusive design.
arxiv-2602-18774:
Test coverage for code usually means covering every edge of a control-flow graph, but real test plans also impose rules about order, such as flows that must or must not happen. Jakub Ruszil, with three co-authors, studies in 2026 how five such constraint types change whether an edge-covering test set exists and how hard it is to find.

Positive constraints demand at least one path with one vertex before another, negative constraints forbid any such path. Once, max-once, and always constraints tighten how often or how universally that order appears. Positive constraints stay decidable in polynomial time, while the other four are NP-complete, even on acyclic graphs, by reductions from variants of SAT. A fixed-parameter algorithm for negative constraints offers a practical foothold despite that hardness.
arxiv-2602-18874:
Generating a new Chinese character in a target font style from only a few examples is a hard disentangling problem. Jie Li, with three co-authors, presents SLD-Font in 2026. It is a structure-level disentangled diffusion model for few-shot Chinese font generation.
