The authors vary the choices, from smooth versus instant collapse to probabilistic versus per-halo evolution, and trace each through the two-point correlation of the deflection field. Most variations shift the signal at small scales, though spotting the gaps depends on the probe.
arxiv-2605-24274: Siahkoohi studies input-convex neural net training. Convexity demands non-negative inter-layer weights. Projected gradient descent re-crosses the boundary endlessly under mini-batch noise, so the projection never settles. Direct softplus tunes a free latent weight through a positivity map whose gradient fades for negative weights. The proposed lift swaps the latent weight for a slack plus a batch-dependent body, coupling updates to batch gradients. Where softplus stalls at the shoulder, the lift fits targets better and reaches the same reconstruction roughly three times sooner.
arxiv-2605-24674: Yan Li and others argue that video-editing diffusion transformers fail for two structural reasons. First, editing signals feed undifferentiated into every block. Second, focus patterns get only indirect supervision from pixel reconstruction. Their RVEDiT framework fixes both. It routes learnable editing tokens from a multimodal model into shallow blocks, saving native tokens for deeper blocks. It also aligns editing focus with a parameter-sharing reference branch during training. It beats leading baselines, with the clearest gains on localized and compositional edits, at no extra inference cost.
arxiv-2605-24774: Jinjin He and co-authors propose Hermite-NGP, a hash encoding for neural PDE solvers that keeps values and mixed derivatives at grid vertices. Older hash methods rely on automatic differentiation or finite differences, which bring instability or high cost. Direct storage allows fully analytic gradients, Jacobians, and Hessians through Hermite interpolation. A multi-resolution curriculum moves from coarse to fine optimization, like multigrid cycles. Across two- and three-dimensional PDE benchmarks it cuts error up to about twenty times versus prior neural methods.
arxiv-2605-24974: Yhonatan Kvich proposes lattice-based modulo sampling for multidimensional bandlimited signals. Standard modulo converters fold each signal part into a square domain, splitting recovery into separate one-dimensional problems. Kvich extends recovery guarantees to any lattice at the same sampling rate as the standard setting. Existing recovery algorithms extend to the general lattice case as well. Picking a lattice with a smaller second moment cuts reconstruction error two ways. It lowers folded signal power, trimming absolute noise at fixed signal-to-noise ratio, and it reduces quantization error.
arxiv-2605-25174: Eivinas Butkus, Kedar Garzón Gupta, and Nikolaus Kriegeskorte train a recurrent convolutional network that can grow in width, depth, and processing time, with each resource carrying a differentiable cost. Pressures on the three resources trade off against one another. Networks expand in all directions as tasks get harder, taking extra recurrent steps when inputs are partly hidden. Strikingly, the model's processing time tracks human reaction times on an object recognition task, linking resource limits to brain-like design.
arxiv-2605-25274: Andrea Ottolini and Shannon Starr prove a case of a conjecture by Soumik Pal about how the permanent of a special matrix family grows with size. The matrices come from a smooth symmetric function on the unit square, sampled at grid points. Its growth rate was already known from large-deviation theory, while its algebraic factor comes from a formula for doubly stochastic matrices. The pair settles the conjecture when the underlying function stays constant on blocks. They use a known combinatorial splitting of permutations into blocks.
arxiv-2605-25374: Kazuki Kusama and colleagues test how well language models write log statements, the notes programs leave for debugging, across languages. Most earlier tools were judged in one language only, leaving multilingual performance unknown. The team builds a benchmark of 150,000 examples across five languages and compares three specialist tools with five language models. A specialist system called UniLog performs best overall and stays strong across languages. Difficulty varies by language, with Python hardest and JavaScript easiest, a gap tied to log habits rather than model size or data volume.
arxiv-2605-25474: Yao Liu builds typed counterfactual pretraining for classifying conflicts between Chinese provisions. Given a superior and subordinate provision pair, the task predicts conflict and its doctrine type among responsibility, condition, sanction, and definition. Stage one pretrains a shared encoder on expert minimal revisions as counterfactuals, teaching a factor head to see no conflict evidence in revisions. Stage two transfers the encoder to a five-way classifier, pre-registered on 696 records. The variant improves macro-F1 over the strongest baseline on both backbones, with gains on unseen records.
arxiv-2605-25874: Ying and colleagues present WBench, a multi-turn benchmark for interactive video world model evaluation across five areas: video quality, setting fit, interaction fit, consistency and physics compliance. It holds 289 test cases and 1,058 interaction turns across varied scenes, styles, subjects and viewpoints, with navigation, subject moves, event edits and viewpoint changes. Navigation blends text, 6-DoF pose and discrete-action control. Evaluation uses 22 automatic sub-metrics validated against human judgments. Across 20 leading models, none performs strongly on all fronts.
arxiv-2605-26174: Fukui asks what orchestration does to defects no lone worker can see. Production systems split requests across hidden worker agents that recombine one report. Fukui tests cross-section defects, contradictions between distant sections, all else fixed, models varied. Ten systems span five generations from one developer, plus five providers with distinct styles. Models finding such defects alone lose most of that ability under orchestration, detection falling by two-thirds or more. Scale and longer reasoning do not close the gap. Fallen models fail differently.
arxiv-2605-26374: Armando Reyes maps the family of left modules over a semi-graded ring, rings that widen graded rings behind noncommutative projective geometry. He shows this module family holds a canonical set of free generators built from shifted twists. That gift endows it with a Grothendieck structure, hence enough injective and projective objects. It also yields a semi-graded form of Baer's injectivity test and a first step toward projective resolutions.
arxiv-2605-26474: Yingfan Liu and five colleagues widen nearest-neighbor search to ranges. Each vector carries a numeric range, like price bands or time spans. A query seeks the k closest vectors under any user range-range rule: containment both ways, overlap both ways, or a mix. Old methods fail arbitrary rules, so the team offers a multi-segment tree graph that skips nodes failing the rule. Index size and build time match the best filtered search. Real tests reach 12.5-fold speedups at same accuracy, with stronger interval and time search.
arxiv-2605-26674: Suryawanshi studies a class of maps called odometer maps on Fock spaces, vector spaces used in quantum theory. She splits each map into an upper triangular block form, with one block that preserves lengths and a second block that acts like a Toeplitz operator from complex analysis. That split lets her sort out when the map is isometric, unitary, or invertible, and she derives a direct formula for its adjoint.
arxiv-2605-26774: Tian and twelve colleagues present the first public dataset for segmenting cesarean scar defects in transvaginal ultrasound images. Scar defects are often missed because they are small and irregular, yet their outline and size guide treatment. The set holds 1,111 images and 16 videos, with 501 confirmed positive cases marked at pixel level by sonographers and trained doctoral students. It gives researchers a shared benchmark for improving automated diagnosis.
arxiv-2605-26874: Mandarapu and Kunkunuru ask how much the data layer matters for language-model agents doing industrial asset operations. Routing each question by its best answering route lifts GPT-4 on AssetOpsBench. LLM-written Cypher queries raise it from 65 percent to 82-83 percent, while native graph primitives with no language model reach 99 percent on graph-answerable cases. For answers missing from the data, generation-augmented knowledge materializes facts as tagged graph nodes, lifting answerability on flagged failure scenarios.
arxiv-2605-27174: Garcia and Reiss investigate AI integration in sound designer workflows via a survey of 76 practitioners plus interviews with 20 professionals. Five themes emerge: Context, Workflow, Potential, Risks, and Right Use. Current AI tools perform adequately in fast media work but lack story depth for high-end sound design such as films and immersive settings. Practitioners prefer assistive, task-specific tools, especially restoration and library work, over end-to-end generative systems. The authors advise sound technologists and developers to build better AI tools for sound design.
arxiv-2605-27274: Zhu and Zhu make a structural case for an eco-civilization paradigm of decentralized, modular eco-communities. They argue the planet is on a path toward a new ecological balance, breaching the 1.5-degree threshold in under seven years. Cutting direct waste heat cannot fix the imbalance, since almost all of it comes from atmospheric radiative forcing, not local heat. Legacy centralized frameworks, they argue, cannot hold, so core life support, local energy, and edge computing must be insulated from cascading macro-system failures by shifting asset valuation and industrial capacity.
arxiv-2605-27474: Eichi Uehara builds a dose-response estimator that keeps extreme events instead of suppressing them. Standard robust methods trim the tail to stabilize the bulk average, but in finance or climate losses the rare event is the target. His estimator emits tail shape, deep-tail return levels, and shortfalls beside the mean, and refuses to extrapolate when the data cannot support it.
arxiv-2605-27774: Huang and colleagues study how fine-tuning teaches a transformer to recall facts from examples given in its prompt. They define a task where the model must infer a hidden relation from sample pairs and retrieve the matching answer from stored knowledge. Theory and experiments show the model converges on a pairwise attention pattern, needing only a very small number of training examples to succeed.
arxiv-2605-28074: Jiachen Qian demonstrates a stealthy poisoning attack on retrieval-augmented generation that hijacks answers with a single fluent document per query. SilentRetrieval keeps the poisoned page retrievable while weaving in triggers, reaching high hijack rates on standard question sets. Combined defenses cut success substantially but slow the system, and human raters flagged the poisoned text far less than clumsy baselines.
arxiv-2605-28674: Amir Ali Ahmadi, Sanjeeb Dash, Yixuan Hua, and Bartolomeo Stellato present disjunctive sum of squares, a way to certify that polynomials never go negative. Unlike the standard sum-of-squares approach, which uses one algebraic identity, the disjunctive approach uses several identities that can be found in parallel. Their main result, a disjunctive Positivstellensatz, keeps each identity's degree as low as the polynomial's degree. From it they build a hierarchy of lower bounds for shrinking a polynomial over a compact basic semialgebraic set, with the largest semidefinite constraint fixed throughout.
arxiv-2605-28874: Yutong Qu and Wei Zhang explore Program-of-Thoughts prompting for chart summarization, using zero-shot learning to motivate light visual word models to reason by numbers. Python programs serve as go-betweens yielding valid summary stats for chart reading. A novel chart-to-dictionary helper task offers a more loose format than older chart-to-table methods, suiting use with the Program-of-Thought strategy. Tests show their strategy performs on par with older chart summary methods across meaning and factual metrics.
arxiv-2605-29174: Jay Yu, Amy Zhao, and Danning Sui survey DeFi investment agents, AI-driven on-chain trading projects topping 3 billion dollars in token value. From over 1,900 AI-tagged projects they curate 10 cases and analyze 11 Solana treasuries. Treasuries hold paper gains over 30 million dollars while holders lost about 192 million, with the top 1 percent taking about 81 percent. Median returns run negative, tokens fell 93 percent on average from peaks, and the authors propose a maturity framework spanning execution, profitability, and stakeholder alignment.
arxiv-2605-29574: Felix Waldherr, Lukas Möller, and Simon Stellmer report laser fluorescence spectroscopy of the intercombination transition in neutral zinc. Isotope shifts for all stable isotopes are measured with kilohertz precision, improving earlier data by about a hundredfold. For zinc-67 they resolve the excited-state hyperfine structure and extract its center-of-gravity shift and hyperfine constants. A King plot comparison against a second zinc transition yields field- and mass-shift parameters. The results ground narrow-line cooling and precision measurement with zinc, including work toward an optical clock.
arxiv-2605-29674: Taichi Kosugi and four colleagues test a sharper quantum phase estimation method on a trapped-ion machine. Their QAVG blends low-detail scans from shifted starting points to rebuild excitation spectra more finely than one scan allows. They run it end to end for carbon monoxide on an iron carbide surface, using plain circuits and error-shielded logic circuits. Even with noisy counts, rebuilt spectra beat base scan spacing by far, and smoothed cost maps cut false dips that stall tuning.
arxiv-2605-29874: Francisco León Zúñiga Bolívar extends a cooperation benchmark to four frontier language-model agents. The earlier bench, built on repeated prisoner's dilemma play, found cooperative bias in two models. Applying the same protocol across three prompting styles and four mixes, the extension finds cooperative bias, with ten of twelve pairs favouring cooperation in balanced settings. Provider spread is large: one model reaches aggressive shares when biased, another high cooperative shares when refined. Provider identity, not generation, is the strongest link to outcomes, while noise stays a challenge.
arxiv-2605-30174: Matan Levy and eight colleagues introduce LiveSVG, a zero-shot route to SVG animation from video generation. Code synthesis cannot express fine Bézier deformations, and score distillation gives noisy gradients and needs skeletons. LiveSVG generates a target video from the input SVG and a motion prompt, then fits the vector art to it by differentiable rendering. Fitting is skeleton-free, pairing per-group homographies with per-path Bézier offsets, plus a recolorization trick for colour ambiguity. It beats prior methods on AniClipart and ChallengeSVG.
arxiv-2605-30274: Yutong Wang and eight co-authors present Loong, a document translation agent with observe-and-act context selection. Document translation challenges language models, whose limited context windows impede cohesion. Loong uses a 3E memory storing summaries, sentence pairs and entities, and adaptively picks the context for guidance. It optimizes its policy through reinforcement learning, using preference data from reasoning trajectories. Evaluations show gains in English-Chinese, German and French directions, averaging 13 points across three metrics. Loong generalizes across domains, resists noise, and stays stable in ultra-long documents.
arxiv-2605-30974: Colombo and colleagues compare shape-based and process ways of judging how habitat loss threatens populations. Using a reaction-diffusion model of growth and dispersal in a viable patch in hostile surroundings, they compare shape descriptors against a process metric. That metric is built from growth near the extinction threshold. Along degradation, shape metrics overestimate persistence, suggesting moderate impacts, while process indicators show rapid approaches to extinction. The authors argue shape-only approaches are limited, and process assessments are needed for biodiversity loss.
arxiv-2605-31074: Tschernig and colleagues fix waveguide optics via Löwdin orthogonalization. The tight-binding model gives light motion through coupling between guided modes. Its guess that guided modes form a basis breaks down when guides are close or arrays grow. Non-orthogonal modes give a generalized eigenvalue problem with overlap, unlike the standard model and wave solutions. Their method builds a clean basis from modes, barely changing shape and keeping balance. The method brings back the standard problem and matches beam tests, capturing long-range coupling and odd hopping phases.
arxiv-2605-31174: Zhang, Yin and Yoshioka turn object detection into an adaptive decision process run by a multimodal language model. Their DetAS agent picks restoration tools and specialist detectors per scene instead of following a fixed pipeline, and DetAS-X adds harvested decision experience from a small labelled set. Across six hard benchmarks the experience-aware version lifts F1 score by 28.36 percent on average over rival language-model detectors, with a 37 percent gain on DarkFace.
arxiv-2605-31574: Hohnen-Ford and team present CONSIDER, a prototype one-to-one AI tool for navigating radical moral disagreements. Such disagreements are polarising topics often censored in daily life, and polarisation costs public mental health. Some propose large language models to support open debate, yet existing tools are poorly calibrated for these intense topics. Drawing on Mill's account of disagreement's value, CONSIDER seeks value clarification through set disagreement with an opposing model opinion. The paper describes its design and weighs risks to guide future development.

arxiv-2606-04274:
JooYoung Lee and colleagues report in 2026 that small fine-tuned models beat giant zero-shot language models at a sorting task. The task: label how people respond to false claims on Reddit — agree, push back, or stay neutral.

The big models looked strong at first glance. But their edge rested on test sets heavy with easy cases. Once the classes were balanced, small models trained on the task won clearly. The gap was largest on pushback replies, the class that matters most for correction work. The authors argue that zero-shot scores flatter big models when data is skewed. For narrow, high-stakes sorting, a small tuned model is the safer buy.
arxiv-2606-04374:
Bokang Wang and colleagues present DSIRM in 2026, a relevance model for e-commerce search built on discrete semantic identifiers, compact codes that group products by meaning. Such codes promise fine-grained matching, but unsupervised generation cannot decide which items deserve to share a code for a given query.

Their fix injects query-item interaction signals directly into the code-learning step, so the partitions become relevance-aware rather than purely visual or textual. On the query side, a generative model predicts item codes from the query text, rescuing vague and long-tail searches. Hierarchical matching between the two code sets then complements ordinary dense similarity scores. On production data from Tmall, the system improved offline ranking quality and delivered measurable online gains in clicks and conversions.
arxiv-2606-04474:
Ming-Hao Hsu and colleagues find why speech-based language models reason worse than text-based ones, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Comparing two speech models with their text modes, they show speech matches or beats text on spatial, syntactic, and factual tasks. The gap opens only on logic tasks requiring entity tracking, where speech accuracy falls to chance. They diagnose an entity binding failure: continuous speech features blur the links between named things and their properties during implicit reasoning.

Their fix, Entity-Aware Chain-of-Thought, is a prompt forcing the model to list entities and bind each claim to its entity before reasoning. It closed much of the gap, raising accuracy by up to 24.4 percentage points even when spoken names were misrecognized, and ablations confirmed the binding step caused the gains. The authors reframe the gap as an elicitation failure rather than a missing capability.
arxiv-2606-04774:
Hu and Ivaki prove new inequalities in centro-affine geometry, in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. They obtain weighted Bochner formulas on spherical caps associated with smooth strictly convex hypersurfaces. As consequences, they prove weighted Poincaré inequalities on caps and intersections of caps for weights depending on the hypersurface's position vector.

In the unconditional case they obtain a centro-affine Poincaré inequality with a weight, and use it to prove a Brunn-Minkowski inequality for a dual quermassintegral. Their main contribution is a flat centro-affine geometry on the positive orthant, in which a Bochner formula yields a Poincaré inequality and a new proof of a centro-affine inequality for unconditional bodies.
arxiv-2606-05274:
Nehal Afifi and colleagues detect sensor anomalies in electro-hydrostatic actuators with an LSTM autoencoder in this 2026 arXiv paper. These actuators are common in aerospace and industrial systems, and catching sensor faults early is essential, but their data arrive at high sampling rates. Classical detectors such as z-scores, isolation forests, and k-means ignore the temporal structure inside the signals and suffer false alarms.

The authors build an offline framework for univariate temperature and pressure signals from a controlled test bench. An LSTM autoencoder learns normal behavior, and its reconstruction errors, calibrated against the validation-set error distribution, flag anomalies. Across fault-injection scenarios the method averaged 99.0 percent accuracy, with precision up to 100 percent and recall above 90 percent. F1 scores ran from 93.1 to 99.8 percent, showing high sensitivity with a low false-alarm rate. Future work aims to move it online for near-real-time detection.
arxiv-2606-05574:
Lin and colleagues built a test of how well code agents clean up messy code in a 2026 arXiv paper. Coding agents now write and fix software at speed. Their output can turn bloated and hard to maintain, yet most tests check only whether code works. The team created SmellBench, a benchmark that plants flaws called code smells into clean code from real projects. Human-written fixes serve as the answer key.

SmellBench holds two hundred ninety-four cases across seven flaw types and three skill levels. It grades working code, flaw spotting, and repair quality. Two agents and six large models took the test. The best pairing scored only about fifty points out of one hundred on flaw removal. The authors trace the gap to a focus on local flaws and weak grasp of links across files. Fixes needing whole-project awareness remain out of reach.
arxiv-2606-05874:
Huiyuan Zheng and colleagues ask multimodal models to pick randomly, and watch them fail in a 2026 arXiv paper. Many tasks offer several equally good options, like rival travel plans. A fair picker should spread choices evenly when told to choose at random. RandomBench tests that neutral behavior and scores it with three bias metrics. The authors name the failure Stochastic Collapse.

Models pile onto one favorite option instead of spreading. In the worst case a single option drew ninety-seven percent of picks where a quarter was fair. One leading model's randomness index sank near zero. Extra studies changed languages and answer formats without shaking the bias. The collapse looks structural, not a quirk of wording. Deterministic habits may serve logic tasks, but they quietly skew recommendations and sampling. The benchmark gives builders a way to measure, and someday fix, that skew.
arxiv-2606-06174:
Jonathan Colen and colleagues model childhood asthma flare-ups in coastal Virginia in this 2026 arXiv paper. An exacerbation is a worsening episode that sends a child to hospital care. Pollution, weather, and neighborhood conditions all push on that risk at once, so untangling which factor does what is the hard part. The team studies Hampton Roads, seven cities holding over one and a half million people.

They assembled pollution readings, weather data, and child opportunity measures for each zip code, then tracked acute asthma visits from 2018 through 2023. Three methods were compared: generalized linear models as a baseline, neural networks as a accuracy ceiling, and a sparse dictionary learning framework that yields readable equations with interactions. Despite their different designs, the three approaches agreed on the relative risks assigned to the exposure variables. That consensus points to combined effects worth targeting in public health planning.
arxiv-2606-06474:
Paul Jünger and co-authors turn a model's discarded guesses into a search tool in this 2026 arXiv paper. Diffusion language models write by denoising: at each step they tentatively fill every blank, keep the confident tokens, and throw the rest away. The team noticed the throwaways are useful. Even shaky early tokens often name the key entities a question hinges on, long before the answer settles. Their system, SARDI, feeds those lookahead tokens into retrieval while generation is still running.

That makes retrieval dynamic: evidence arrives mid answer, aimed at the bridge facts multi hop questions need. SARDI needs no training and works with any retriever. Across five multi hop benchmarks, it beat other training free retrieval systems while running up to eight times faster. Grounding in retrieved evidence also loosens token dependence, suiting parallel decoding well.
arxiv-2606-06574:
Ziyue Li, Yang Li, and Tianyi Zhou show a language model's layers need not run once, in order, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard inference marches through every layer at fixed depth. The authors find that pretrained layers behave like reusable modules. For most inputs, a shorter program that skips or loops some layers matches or beats the standard pass. Some wrong answers from full inference are even corrected by programs using fewer layers. They call this flexibility program of layers.

To exploit it, a lightweight prediction network learns which contiguous layer segments to skip or repeat for each input, without touching the model's weights. On math reasoning benchmarks, the method improved accuracy over standard inference and earlier dynamic depth methods, often while executing fewer layers. The gains held on out of distribution tests too. Fixed depth, the authors argue, taps only a narrow slice of a model's latent reasoning capacity.
arxiv-2606-06674:
AI companies often speak of aligning models with what people want, as if people wanted one thing. Coelho and Hale test that assumption in this 2026 arXiv paper. They analyzed fifteen hundred open ended answers in the PRISM data set, gathered from people in seventy five countries, about what they actually want from AI systems.

Most wishes were shared by fewer than a quarter of respondents. Truthfulness was the lone exception, named by about forty nine percent. Yet even that word split apart on inspection. Some people meant sourced claims. Some meant expert opinion. Some meant hearing unpopular views. Other traits, such as how human like a model acts or whether it has guardrails, were openly contested, with some users demanding them and others rejecting them. Blending all of this into one reward score, the authors argue, erases real differences.
arxiv-2606-07574:
Wang accelerates a projection that neural network architectures perform, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Manifold-constrained hyper-connections mix residual streams using matrices that must be doubly stochastic, meaning rows and columns each sum to one. This is enforced by projecting onto the Birkhoff polytope, the set of all such matrices. The Sinkhorn-Knopp iteration is slow, memory-hungry in training, and loose on inputs, hurting the balance the constraint exists to protect. Wang focuses on the 4-by-4 case implementations use.

Through the dual form, the projection collapses to a 3D convex problem solvable by Newton's method with fast, accurate results. Implicit differentiation replaces unrolled backpropagation, giving exact gradients, no stored steps. A graphics processor kernel at register level exploits many cores. Against open-source baselines, the solver produced more reliable results, especially for large-magnitude inputs, and ran 20 times faster at batch sizes, with far smaller errors.
arxiv-2606-07774:
Sirker proves a negative result about many-body localisation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Many-body localisation is a proposed phase where a disordered quantum system fails to spread energy, keeping memory of its start forever. The test system is a disordered Ising chain, a line of interacting spins in random fields drawn from positive distributions.

Sirker tracks how a local operator grows under repeated commutation with the Hamiltonian, sorted by region length. Even at moderate lengths the weight grows almost factorially, the fastest rate allowed. Local operators therefore delocalise completely, ruling out the strongest form of localisation at any disorder strength. The proof also gives a crossover scale: systems shorter than the square of the disorder-to-coupling ratio show only a pre-asymptotic regime, so many numerical studies may miss the true behaviour. A counting argument about branching paths further blocks standard constructions of local integrals of motion.
arxiv-2606-07874:
Alloula and co-authors show that language models used as safety judges are stubborn about prior rules, in this 2026 arXiv paper. At scale, safety evaluation depends on model judges, since human review cannot cover the volume. Safety is contextual, though: the same content can be acceptable under one definition and banned under another. The authors test whether judges adapt when given new information, demonstrations, or a changed definition.

Evaluating many generalist models and safety-specific judges, they find judges learn from fresh in-context information when it agrees with them. But when context or definition contradicts their internal prior, they broadly refuse to adjust their verdicts. That rigidity matters, because deployers routinely need definitions differing from a model's defaults, for a product, jurisdiction, or community. An unsteerable judge silently enforces its own rules. The fix, they argue, starts with evaluation: judge benchmarks must test steerability, not just agreement with humans.
arxiv-2606-07974:
Yuhai Wang and co-authors ask a planning question most world-model research skips, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A world model imagines future states so an agent can evaluate candidate actions before committing. Imagination accuracy gets the attention. But the planner also needs good candidates to evaluate. Typical planners sample almost blindly, or borrow expert demonstrations only as a starting average, discarding the expert's confidence.

Their framework, PRISM, extracts an action prior from the world model itself. A small network attached to the model's frozen encoder predicts a distribution over good actions, learned from the same data as the model, with no separate teacher. At planning time the prior is fused into the sampling distribution with a precision-weighted product of Gaussians. The closed-form update trusts the prior where it is confident and explores where it is not. Search starts from plausible actions, with a simple architecture.
arxiv-2606-08074:
Robert Conte pins down the analytic character of a famous universal wave profile, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Gurevich-Pitaevskii solution of the Korteweg-de Vries equation describes the onset of dispersive shock waves, the oscillating transition that appears when a wave breaks in a dispersive medium. The same profile also satisfies the self-similar reduction of the next equation in the KdV hierarchy.

Conte asks whether the profile also obeys some lower-order partial differential equation of its own. The answer is restrictive: if such an equation exists, its order cannot exceed one. He supports the analysis with a local representation of the solution as a convergent Laurent series in space and time. The upshot disciplines folklore around special solutions: a profile famous for universality is tightly constrained in the equations it can satisfy.
arxiv-2606-08474:
Junjie Li tackles causal estimation when the outcome data are missing in the worst way, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Difference-in-differences is a workhorse design that compares changes over time between treated and control groups to estimate a treatment effect. Its conclusions collapse when outcomes are missing not at random, meaning the chance of missingness depends on the unobserved values themselves. Li's semiparametric framework restores identification using a shadow variable: a fully observed variable associated with how the outcome evolves but independent of the missingness process.

The paper establishes the identification conditions and gives an estimation algorithm for the average treatment effect on the treated under this weaker missingness. Finite-sample performance is evaluated through simulation studies, and a real data application demonstrates the method in practice. The work extends the credibility of difference-in-differences to panel data where nonresponse cannot be assumed benign.
arxiv-2606-08574:
Chenhan Jin and colleagues prune training data while promising, with proof, not to hurt the model, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Data pruning reduces training sets to ease heavy training burdens, striving for near-lossless performance. Existing approaches select highly informative samples. But that selection biases gradient estimation compared with full-dataset training, and analysis of the bias remained ambiguous. Their framework, OrderDP, is a plug-and-play dynamic pruning method with theoretical guarantees behind the losslessness claim.

OrderDP first randomly selects a subset, then keeps the top fraction of it ranked by importance. Because the first stage is random, unbiasedness is established with respect to a surrogate loss. The authors further establish convergence and generalization analyses, clarifying how the pruning affects optimal solutions and test performance.
arxiv-2606-08974:
Liang and colleagues argue that reasoning models improve when they think in more varied ways, not longer chains, in this 2026 arXiv paper. They define thinking schemata as two habits of a model's reasoning: how it moves between steps, and how many distinct answer candidates it explores. Across models, greater diversity in these schemata tracks better performance on mathematics. Their framework, DiScO, first teaches a model awareness of these schemata. Reinforcement learning then rewards diverse reasoning, and inference-time techniques push diversity further.

On math benchmarks, DiScO beat group relative policy optimization, the usual baseline. The 7-billion-parameter version scored 95.6 percent on MATH-500 and 70 percent on the AIME 2024 competition set, averaging 72.9 percent accuracy. Human-annotated analysis added a finding: DiScO models recovered from wrong attempts more often, backtracking instead of committing to a mistake. The authors propose diversity as an axis for scaling reasoning, alongside model size and chain length.
arxiv-2606-09274:
Sparviero and Viola build a reverse stress testing framework that starts from a financial shock and works backward to the market scenarios that would produce it, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Reverse stress testing inverts the usual question: impose a loss in one asset class, then find the joint market paths consistent with it. Their framework conditions stressed time series on a single exogenous perturbation, a shock imposed from outside.

A sampling phase generates plausible market-wide scenarios from that one shock. It comes in three variants, parametric, semiparametric, and nonparametric, sharing one conditioning logic read through empirical likelihood, weighting observed data without assuming a full probability model. Tested on real market indices, the simulated responses matched the expected magnitude of the shock. The joint behavior of fixed-income, equity, and interest-rate factors stayed economically coherent along the paths.
arxiv-2606-09774:
Matthew Ho and his co-authors wrap a stock coding agent in a thin adapter so it can run science simulators in this 2026 arXiv paper. Setting up a simulator means writing an input deck that obeys strict rules across many files. The chore eats hours to days of expert time. Rebuilding the agent loop, though, would waste its tuned habits.

Their SIGA adapter leaves the model and loop frozen. It adds lookup of past decks, a store of prior runs, checks the agent can call, and a gate that ends work only when checks pass. Old runs can even rewrite the adapter itself. On GEOS, a subsurface simulator, hard held-out tasks gained in match score, from zero point seven two to near zero point seven nine. Run spread shrank about sixteenfold, since blank or broken decks were blocked.
arxiv-2606-10174:
Hamdan and colleagues release a large open dataset for training machines to spot wildfires early, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer vision. Early fire and smoke detection helps limit spread and damage to the environment and infrastructure. Their Global Wildfire Prevention Dataset gathers geographically diverse images and videos of flames, smoke, fog-like conditions, near-infrared scenes, and embers, plus challenging negative samples that resemble fire without being fire.

To test robustness and cross-domain generalization, the team benchmarks multiple convolutional and transformer architectures in both in-domain and cross-dataset settings. They also explore a lightweight frequency-spatial feature design using Hadamard-enhanced residual connections to probe representation robustness under domain shift. The dataset and source code are slated for public release, giving wildfire detection researchers a shared, diverse benchmark beyond the small private collections typical in this field.
arxiv-2606-10274:
Ablikim and the BESIII collaboration measure a rare electromagnetic decay of a charmed meson with improved precision, in a 2026 arXiv paper on particle physics. The decay is a Dalitz decay, where an excited Ds meson sheds energy through a virtual photon that converts into an electron-positron pair, leaving a ground-state Ds meson. The data come from electron-positron collisions recorded by the BESIII detector in Beijing at energies between about four point one and four point two gigaelectronvolts.

The measured branching fraction is just over seven thousandths, with statistical and systematic uncertainties both well under one thousandth. The result agrees with the previous measurement while improving precision by a factor of about two and a half. It provides important input for constraining theoretical models and for determining, by a relative method, the absolute branching fractions of the meson's pion and photon decay modes.
arxiv-2606-10474:
Kumar, Mishra, and Chaudhuri study flocking particles in this 2026 arXiv paper on active matter, systems whose units move under their own power. Their model is Vicsek-like: particles travel at fixed speed and turn toward the average heading of their neighbours. The twist is finite-time orientational relaxation, meaning each particle adjusts toward that local average at a limited rate rather than instantly. Large simulations map how the behaviour changes with activity and alignment rate.

Raising the alignment rate drives an ordered sequence of states: a disordered gas, moving polar bands, a cross-sea pattern of intersecting bands, a uniform polar flock, and finally micro-clusters. The first step is strongly first order, with gas-like and liquid-like regions coexisting. Band width grows with activity following a square-root power law, but varies non-monotonically with alignment rate. Finite relaxation time thus restructures the whole phase diagram.
arxiv-2606-10574:
Alves presents a method for filling gaps in children's records in this 2026 arXiv paper on health data methods. Longitudinal studies weigh and measure children repeatedly, but values go missing, and combined studies may index measurements against different growth references, such as WHO or CDC charts. The method first interpolates linearly within each child across visit dates, filling interior gaps only. Whatever remains is imputed from an age- and sex-specific growth reference, carrying each child's estimated centile forward.

The reference standard is an explicit setting per data source, and every imputed value keeps a label saying where it came from. In a synthetic test with sixty subjects and 288 visits, thirty percent missing, the method restored full completeness. Masked-value checks gave a mean absolute error of 1.78 kilograms for weight and 2.84 centimetres for height. Interpolation proved more accurate than reference-based filling, supporting the chosen order of the two stages.
arxiv-2606-10774:
Hewa Kaluannakkage fixes two failure modes of learning over links in this 2026 arXiv paper. In decentralised federated learning, devices train a model by gossiping parameters with neighbours, no server involved. Over lossy wireless links, retransmission is too slow, so nodes must aggregate updates. Classical gossip then fails twice: selection bias, since updates from poor links arrive less often and are under-weighted, and staleness, since asynchronous nodes contribute outdated models. The author proves this bias is irreducible for classical gossip and grows with the link-loss rate.

The DFL-AA algorithm corrects both. Inverse probability weighting, fed by channel estimates, cancels the link-quality distortion in expectation, while age-of-information decay discounts stale updates with no shared clock. On EMNIST and CIFAR-10, across networks of 20, 40, and 80 nodes. With loss rates from 10 to 50 percent, DFL-AA beats the best baselines, with the largest gains where loss and heterogeneity are worst.
arxiv-2606-10874:
Ana-Maria Pangeva and colleagues shrink the circuits needed to load images into quantum states in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard encodings such as FRQI, QPIE, and NEQR can demand many gates and deep circuits, a poor fit for today's noisy quantum hardware. Their tool is low-rank approximation via Schmidt decomposition, which keeps only the strongest parts of a state's entanglement structure.

Across all three encodings, circuit depth falls by up to 97 percent and CNOT counts by up to 96 percent, while reconstruction error stays near an MSE of 0.27. FRQI gains the most. Most visual information sits in a few Schmidt components, so exact preparation is often wasted effort.
arxiv-2606-11074:
Jia and five co-authors study personality in multimodal large language models in a 2026 arXiv paper. These models read images and text together. They increasingly serve in social roles like companionship, where a set personality shapes every reply. The team adds explicit personality conditioning, instructing the model to adopt stated traits, and builds an evaluation framework around it.

The framework covers single-personality induction, multi-persona blending, and switching persona mid-conversation. Experiments show a split result. Conditioning improves image captioning, where a fitting voice helps describe a scene. It impairs tasks needing precise reasoning, such as visual question answering. During blending and switching, earlier traits leave residual effects, coloring behavior after a new personality takes over. Prompt methods built for text models also transfer poorly to multimodal settings. The authors conclude that personality here is dynamic and layered, needing tailored induction methods and evaluations of its own.
arxiv-2606-11174:
Cambie and Freschi settle a Ramsey theory problem of Erdős and co-authors in a 2026 arXiv paper. The Ramsey number of two graphs is the smallest board size forcing a pattern. Color every edge of the complete graph red or blue. A red copy of the first graph or a blue copy of the second must appear. Here the first graph is a cycle of length k, the second any graph H with m edges and no isolated vertices.

They prove the Ramsey number is at most (k minus one) times m plus one, hence at most k times m. That confirms the constant in the Erdős question equals k. The bound is tight in key cases. It recovers the known triangle result, where trees and matchings attain equality. A single-edge H attains it for every k. It stood as problem thirty-four in the standard collection.
arxiv-2606-11374:
Marziani, Dalla Barba, and Foschini argue a quasar framework can flag the most extreme accretors in a 2026 arXiv conference paper. The quasar Eigenvector-1 Main Sequence organizes the spectral diversity of type 1 active galactic nuclei. In its optical plane, the width of the hydrogen-beta line and the iron strength ratio define a sequence driven mainly by Eddington ratio. Extreme Population A sources at its end are the likely super-Eddington accretors.

The authors discuss why the framework suits searching for super-Eddington sources among jetted, gamma-ray-emitting AGN. Some candidate super-Eddington accretors show radio properties, like high brightness temperature cores or lobes, consistent with genuine jet activity. A subset of low-redshift gamma-ray narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies shows spectra consistent with extreme Population A type. Super-Eddington accretion and relativistic jets can coexist, they conclude, even if uncommon and subject to selection effects.
arxiv-2606-11574:
Jiang, Wu, Schroeder, and Webb, of Princeton University, reframe design optimization around ranges in a 2026 arXiv paper. In many design problems, good candidates have values inside an acceptable window rather than at a single optimum. Recovering several distinct valid designs matters, since cost or robustness may favor one over another. Their range-aware Bayesian optimization scores candidates directly by the posterior chance of satisfying a target range.

It extends naturally to several distinct specs pursued in parallel over one candidate space. Its closed-form Tolerance Ball acquisition is sampling-free and analytically tractable. Across benchmarks it recovers larger, more diverse sets of valid designs than standard baselines and recent goal-seeking methods, with high target fidelity. Two case studies show the utility. One chooses reaction conditions for polymer synthesis with prescribed molecular weight distributions; another discovers sequence-defined oligomers for prescribed optical absorption bands, backed by quantum chemical calculations.
arxiv-2606-11674:
Anton Firc leads a team simplifying a deepfake audio detector in this 2026 arXiv paper. The detector's back end, AASIST, is a widely used graph-based module that pools speech features to decide whether audio is genuine or spoofed. Public versions carry redundant operations, so the team replaces learned pooling and attention steps with explicit, lightweight choices.

Their system, SpAArSIST, uses separate pooling ratios for training and inference, scores graph nodes by simple magnitude, and averages nodes instead of attending over them. The best configuration cuts back-end computing by about one fifth and slightly shrinks the model. Out-of-domain accuracy on the In-the-Wild collection improves markedly: the equal error rate falls from over four and a half percent to under three percent. Results on the ASVspoof 5 benchmark stay competitive. A combined scoring rule weighing accuracy, calibration and compute helps practitioners pick a balanced version for deployment.
arxiv-2606-11974:
Malte Baumecker and three colleagues speed up a basic network task on sparse graphs in this 2026 arXiv paper. A ruling set is a set of nodes, no two adjacent, such that every node lies within a few steps of a chosen one. The case of distance two is a sweet spot between cost and coverage. The setting is the LOCAL model of distributed computing, where nodes communicate in synchronous rounds with neighbours.

Their randomised algorithm finds a two-ruling set on low-arboricity graphs, networks that are locally sparse, in a doubly logarithmic number of rounds. That is an exponential improvement over previous state-of-the-art results, and nearly matches the known lower bound. Distance two is provably the right target: distance one, the maximal independent set, needs far more rounds even on very sparse graphs. For general arboricity the authors give further improved algorithms.
arxiv-2606-12074:
Semih Vazgecen and three colleagues recognise faces from awkward angles on tiny hardware in this 2026 arXiv paper. Face recognition worsens sharply for non-frontal views, and drones or edge devices cannot run heavyweight models. Their framework pairs two lightweight parts: a network that frontalises a profile face, and a classifier built on memristors, memory-resistors whose physics computes efficiently.

Tests on two datasets show pose remains the dominant accuracy factor: without correction, accuracy collapses from about thirty-five percent at fifteen degrees of head turn to about seven percent at ninety degrees. That stage recovers much of the loss, and the full system reaches ninety-six percent accuracy. To evaluate honestly, the team combined design simulation with empirical modelling of the classifier. The approach targets in-situ recognition on resource-constrained platforms, where conventional deep learning costs too much to run.
arxiv-2606-12274:
Leon and co-authors compress how flat metals screen electric fields into a handful of moving modes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The dielectric response describes how electrons answer an applied field, underlying spectra and correlation energies. In flat metals the response varies richly with momentum, and first-principles data are bulky and hard to reuse. Multipole-Padé approximants instead summarize a response by a few modes, like notes standing in for a chord.

The team extends that idea across the full Brillouin zone, the complete map of allowed momenta, with a symmetry-conserving anisotropic form. They build compact versions for seven flat metals in distinct electronic regimes. A small set of dispersive plasmonic modes, charge waves shifting frequency with momentum, reproduces the response accurately. Correlation energies computed from the compact forms also stay accurate. The result bridges heavy first-principles output and light analytic models.
arxiv-2606-12474:
Shi and co-authors rehearse attacks on AI agent teams in simulation, so real attacks can be intercepted before they land, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-agent systems collaborate through messages, and that chatter is an attack surface: poisoned messages spread and cascade. Most defenses react after execution, isolating harmful agents once damage may be irreversible. SAIGuard instead simulates the message state over the interaction graph before messages spread.

It estimates each incoming message's impact on the receiving agent and on the whole system. Risky messages stand out as deviations from benign message patterns. Rather than isolating agents, SAIGuard sanitizes or regenerates flagged messages in place. Across diverse topologies, chain, tree, star, and random, and multiple attack scenarios, it lowers attack success rates while preserving the team's usefulness. It outperforms reactive defenses, and holds up as talks lengthen over many turns.
arxiv-2606-12674:
Bhandari and colleagues introduce Evoflux, a search method that helps small language models use external tools reliably, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tool-using agents must discover tools from live catalogues, fill in required inputs correctly, and chain outputs across steps. Compact models often produce workflow plans that look plausible yet fail when actually run. Training on a few hundred example traces, the authors argue, rarely teaches recovery from such failures.

Evoflux instead repairs plans at inference time, while the task is being attempted. It treats a plan as a typed workflow graph and evolves it through structured edits, real execution feedback, and pruning that preserves variety. On held-out MCP-Bench tasks spanning 28 live servers and 250 tools, it lifts the share of executable workflows from about 3 percent to between 17 and 24 percent across small planners. Fine-tuning on the same data matched, lagged, or fell below the untrained baseline.
arxiv-2606-13374:
Avila, Dell, and Lapinskas generalise a classic result about opinion spread on changing networks in this 2026 arXiv paper. In the voter model, each node in a network repeatedly adopts the opinion of a random neighbour, until everyone agrees. Stronger connectivity should mean faster consensus. A known result ties the consensus time to the network's conductance, a measure of how easily flow escapes any subset. For dynamic networks, where edges appear and disappear, applying that measure snapshot by snapshot fails, because one disconnected snapshot makes the conductance collapse to zero.

The authors introduce temporal conductance, a connectivity measure that credits edges appearing at different times. It captures paths that unfold over time, not just within one instant. With it they extend the earlier consensus bound to dynamic networks with changing degrees and structure. The expected consensus time is governed by the temporal conductance together with the network's size and minimum degree.
arxiv-2606-13474:
Carlucci and colleagues apply safety methods to the risk of losing control of AI agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Frontier laboratories deploy agentic systems internally for coding and research. The authors define loss of control: the inability to reliably constrain, audit, reverse, or halt AI-mediated changes to code, infrastructure, or deployment in time to prevent harm. This is a sociotechnical problem, wider than model behaviour alone. They ask whether systems-thinking methods can surface risks that model-level evaluations miss.

Working from a frontier-lab coding-agent scenario reconstructed from public materials, they apply three analysis frameworks. The analyses surface complementary findings. Governance frameworks can leave responsibilities and feedback loops externally unverifiable. Delays in monitoring and intervention can make valid control actions arrive too late. Routine variability can erode the calibration and independence of safeguards. The authors argue frontier risk management should adopt systems methods.
arxiv-2606-13574:
Liang and colleagues refine a generative method for modelling the Sun's spectrum in this 2026 arXiv paper, part of the hunt for Earth-like planets. Extreme-precision radial velocity measurements detect planets by the wobble they induce in their star's light. The method is limited by the star: activity, absorption in Earth's atmosphere, and instrument effects distort the spectrum. The authors apply a framework, Æstra, to Sun-as-a-star observations from the NEID instrument. The framework decomposes spectra into stellar line-shape changes, micro-telluric absorption, and continuum changes, without templates.

After removing the telluric and continuum parts, a low-dimensional summary of the spectrum is trained to infer activity-driven velocities with planet signals. The method is stress-tested with 500 injected fake planets spanning periods from a few days to over a year and small amplitudes. The detection rule is set to yield 0 false detections.
arxiv-2606-13674:
Wang and colleagues present RepWAM in this 2026 arXiv paper, a world action model for robot control built on a new kind of tokeniser. World action models predict how the world will look after actions, bridging prediction and control. Existing models inherit video tokenisers from generation systems, which are trained for pixel reconstruction. Reconstruction preserves visual fidelity but gives limited guidance for learning the dynamics that connect future prediction to action. The authors instead train a representation visual-action tokeniser that compresses input into aligned visual tokens and latent action tokens, a shared semantic space.

Their model is pretrained to predict future visual states and the latent actions linking them, under language instructions. It is then adapted on robot trajectories for closed-loop manipulation. Experiments span real-world manipulation tasks and simulation benchmarks. The design aims at tokenisers that encode what matters for acting, not merely for redrawing pixels.
arxiv-2606-13874:
Matas and Romao hunt for materials where light can create strong magnetic fields through vibrating atoms. When atoms move in circles, their charges form tiny currents, an effect called dynamical multiferroicity. Framework materials, open crystal structures including metal-organic frameworks, might amplify this because their light atoms can swing widely. Their 2026 arXiv paper computes the effect from first principles across inorganic and organic frameworks.

Nineteen materials were surveyed. The metal-organic framework Zn(NH4)(formate)3 stood out, with vibration modes carrying magnetic moments almost twice those of strontium titanate, a standard reference. Its largest moment reached zero point three one six nuclear magnetons. The cause is circular motion of hydrogen ions in the ammonium groups, which have high gyromagnetic ratios. A second material, BPO4, reached zero point two zero four. Frameworks also allow larger magnetization before the crystal melts, and many host useful modes in the mid-infrared.
arxiv-2606-14474:
Ma and co-authors outline a tutorial on user simulation in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is aimed at search and recommendation researchers. Language-model simulators now stand in for human users in tests. They help judge search engines and recommender systems. Yet most simulators are opaque. Nobody can tell why a fake user chose as it did. Nor whether the choice fits its set profile.

The proposed framework treats a simulator as a checkable artifact. It has seven parts that can each be audited. They run from a structured persona to a refinement loop. Two hands-on mini-labs are included. One covers recommendation list scoring. The other covers search query writing. Participants learn to tell diagnosis apart from proof by statistics. They also run checks for fidelity and bias. Bias matters because fake users can treat minority groups unfairly.
arxiv-2606-14574:
Lu, Zhang, and Zhang introduce SIMMER, a benchmark for hidden planning failures, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Language models increasingly plan household tasks for autonomous agents. Existing benchmarks check whether plans execute, but latent failures slip through: the plan runs on while silently ruining the goal, sometimes irreversibly.

SIMMER tests plans against a human-curated symbolic world model of a kitchen with seventy-seven actions, two hundred sixty-two objects, and roughly forty-six thousand eight hundred possible interactions drawn from real cooking scripts. A state-machine executor flags precondition violations, latent hazards, and irreversible failures. Across six language models, even the frontier systems produced at most seventeen percent error-free plans, and up to fifty-six percent of plans contained latent failures. Adding counterfactual foresight simulation, explicitly reasoning ahead about states, cut latent failures by up to seventy-two percent.
arxiv-2606-14674:
Jixuan Chen and a large team take apart how embodied AI agents are built in a 2026 arXiv paper. Modern agents are scaffolded systems. They mix reasoning, memory, self-checks, action, and learning parts. But the parts are often welded into one pipeline. That hides what each part adds. Their scheme, AgentSpec, writes agents as typed builds. The parts are reusable blocks with standard links.

The team built AgentSpec agents for four embodied test suites. The suites cover home tasks and grid-world tasks. They swapped reasoning, memory, self-check, and learning blocks across model cores. Scores were set by how well blocks fit and worked together. Single-block strength mattered less. Rich, layered memory helped track state over long tasks. Self-checks traded fixes against cost. Learned blocks worked best when trained inside the setup used at run time. Code and a play tool are public.
arxiv-2606-14874:
Emmons and co-authors improve isotope identification in gamma-ray spectra with machine learning in a 2026 arXiv paper. High-purity germanium detectors record gamma spectra from radioactive samples. Experts fit the peaks in each spectrum to name the nuclides present. That work is slow, and amending the software's isotope list is awkward. The team trained models to map analyst-fitted peaks to identification results.

The spectra covered mixtures drawn from a library of sixty-five isotopes. The best model reached an F1 score of zero point nine seven. Traditional software scored zero point eight four on the same library. Gradient-boosted trees beat deep neural networks here. The team then used SHAP values to see which peaks drove each call. The models relied on physically relevant peaks, not spurious ones. That makes their suggestions easier for analysts to trust.
arxiv-2606-15374:
Harris and coauthor count special numbers inside cyclotomic fields in a 2026 number theory note. Cyclotomic fields are built by adjoining a root of unity, a complex number that multiplies to one after a fixed number of steps. The note fixes a bound on height, a measure of a number's arithmetic size, and asks how many algebraic integers and units fit under it as the field grows through prime powers.

The main theorem bounds the count of cyclotomic units by a subexponential function of the field index, once conjectures about class numbers hold. A second result bounds all algebraic integers exponentially in the field degree, while polynomial lower bounds show the counts cannot shrink too far. Most counting results fix the field and grow the height; reversing the roles exposes how arithmetic complexity accumulates as fields expand, a question tied to deep conjectures about class numbers.
arxiv-2606-15474:
Li tackles a monitoring puzzle for AI-judged products in a 2026 statistics paper. Teams score interactions with a cheap model, sample a judge, and page someone when scores drift. But the judge is a hosted model: a silent version bump or prompt change can shift its scoring. Each alarm is then ambiguous: worse product, or changed judge. The fix: a fixed anchor set of human-labeled items the judge re-scores on schedule.

An anytime-valid process watches the judge-versus-human gap on the anchors, and a guard rule returns three verdicts: none, system, or judge. On two judge changes it names a silent version bump as judge drift in every run, never blaming the system, and attributes a strict-prompt change correctly almost always. The default rolling z-test false-alarms on most drift-free streams. Attribution is cheap if anchors out-run the stream they guard.
arxiv-2606-15674:
Ai and colleagues report in 2026 that the nearby narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy Mrk 382 switches X-ray states, using fifteen years of observations from Swift, Chandra, XMM-Newton, and eROSITA. Its soft X-ray flux swings nearly tenfold, with repeated moves between bright and faint states. Ultraviolet, optical, and infrared data complete the picture.

The galaxy brightened tenfold from 2010 to 2011, faded six or sevenfold into a low state by 2019, and has since brightened again in Swift monitoring. Its spectrum hardens as it fades, and the faint state shows a narrow iron line and reflection-dominated light. Reflection modelling points to a compact corona under strong light bending near the black hole. The ultraviolet varies with the X-rays but more mildly, and the galaxy never drops into an extreme X-ray-weak state or changes optical type. Such a nearby, transitioning Seyfert is a rare laboratory for changing coronal geometry.
arxiv-2606-16074:
Fodeh and colleagues present PVminerLLM2 in 2026, models for turning patient-written text into structured research data. Patients describe lived experience and care engagement in free text, but unstructured notes are hard to use in outcomes research. An earlier benchmark and model began this task. Supervised fine-tuning alone struggles with rare, fine-grained, and unevenly spread errors.

PVminerLLM2 adds preference optimization, training that favors better outputs over worse ones, aimed at token-critical mistakes. A gated term stops training from degrading basic token likelihoods while preferences shift. Confusion-aware pairs target distinctions the model most often mixes up. Importance weighting and frequency reweighting counter token imbalance and class skew. Across model sizes, the new models beat their predecessor and DPO baselines in the reported tests. Gains are strongest on rare sub-codes, and run variance falls.
arxiv-2606-16174:
Chen proves new harmonic analysis estimates in 2026 for exponential sums tied to dispersive equations on the torus. Discrete Strichartz estimates, also called discrete restriction bounds, limit how wave-like sums spread. The paper treats two-dimensional sums whose phases are fractional powers or perturbed polynomials. Three curve classes are covered, including the fractional Schrödinger-type curve and the fully fractional curve.

For each class, Chen obtains weighted Lp bounds with decoupling-type form at each scale, in both low and high exponent regimes. The proofs rest on finite-type decoupling, splitting frequency ranges into nearly flat pieces. Localization and rescaling steps handle curvature degeneracy, anisotropic scaling, and bounded phase perturbations. Arithmetic results from congruencing serve only as benchmarks. Sharp dispersive bounds feed into well-posedness theory for nonlinear wave and Schrödinger models.
arxiv-2606-16574:
Teixeira builds in 2026 a class of dark sector models where dark matter and dark energy interact through entropy itself, hiding the interaction from the universe's expansion history. The intrinsic entropy of the dark matter fluid couples to a scalar field playing dark energy, inside a covariant Lagrangian framework. Algebraic and derivative entropy couplings both appear. Their net effect is pure momentum exchange between the two dark components.

The background cosmology is unchanged: the models match the standard Lambda-CDM or uncoupled quintessence. The fingerprints live in the small ripples. The dark matter Euler equation gains scale-dependent contributions, while its continuity equation stays unmodified. Entropy perturbations act as non-dynamical, spatially varying sources for it. The models pass current cosmic microwave background constraints and could leave visible signs in large-scale structure. Much coupling can hide in plain sight, visible only in how structure grows.
arxiv-2606-16674:
Dong and Lee study a metal placed on hexagonal boron nitride in a 2026 condensed matter paper. The nitride hosts a hyperbolic photon mode, where light occupies a hugely expanded range of momenta in a narrow frequency window. The question is whether that trapped light can strongly change the electrons in a metal laid directly on top.

The coupling resembles electron-phonon coupling, but with a key twist: it is driven by time-dependent charge fluctuations and grows steeply with the energy gap between electron states. Dong and Lee compute the electron self-energy and find strong frequency and momentum dependence, plus a clear dimensionless coupling constant. The mode suppresses quasiparticle weight, yet the leading correction to velocity cancels exactly. A side band appears in the spectral function, which experiments could measure. Hopes for induced pairing fade, since the leading attractive terms also cancel, for reasons the authors explain.
arxiv-2606-17574:
Li and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on DeepInsight, a single evaluation system for a whole physical AI stack. It spans one decoding step of a foundation model to thousands of physics ticks of body control. Today each layer is tested by its own harness, with no shared runtime or scoring, so faults that cross layers are hard to trace. DeepInsight keeps the layers' differences but unifies them behind three narrow abstractions for tasks, resources, and results.

One episode driver, one resource-handle protocol, and one trace identity scheme are shared by every subsystem in the design. Deployed across all three layers of an embodied humanoid stack, new benchmarks join mostly by configuration alone. It matches peer frameworks' readings at the model end while running the same suites faster. Its real payoff is diagnosis: cross-layer regressions stay findable in one trace.
arxiv-2606-17774:
Abeyaratne and colleagues examine in a 2026 mechanics paper how growing solids add material, either throughout their volume or only at their surfaces. Working in a recent optimization-driven framework for elastic solids, they do not prescribe a growth law in advance. Instead, the growth pattern is whatever distribution best satisfies a constrained optimization problem.

For growth driven by minimizing the work of external loads, the authors derive explicit solutions in one-dimensional and axisymmetric settings. Although growth starts as a spread-out volumetric process described by a strain field, the optimal patterns turn out singular. They concentrate on boundaries or internal interfaces, and for a simple bar the growth collapses to a single point where the axial force is smallest. The results give a variational explanation for surface growth emerging on its own.
arxiv-2606-17974:
Bo and colleagues bound how many flips it takes to turn one orientation of a graph into another, in a 2026 combinatorics paper. An inversion picks a set of vertices and reverses every arc inside it. All orientations of a graph form an inversion graph, where neighbors differ by one flip, and its diameter is the worst-case number of flips between two orientations.

Answering a question of Havet, Hörsch, and Rambaud, the authors prove the diameter is at most twice the square root of the number of edges. A counting view of the inversion graph as a Cayley graph yields a matching-flavored lower bound from the edge to vertex ratio. For bipartite graphs they refine the upper bound using the top degrees on each side, and constructions show the refinement is tight up to a factor of two.
arxiv-2606-18274:
Preti and colleagues shrink hypergraphs without losing a single fact, in a 2026 data management paper. A hypergraph links groups of items at once, not just pairs, which makes it rich but bulky to store and query. Compact summaries exist for plain graphs. For hypergraphs, no lossless method was known. Their framework, HyDRA, stores a summary as a smaller weighted hypergraph built from supernodes and superedges, plus a correction table that makes rebuilding exact.

The key move ties the task to co-clustering: nodes and edges are grouped together. A greedy algorithm with no tuning knobs merges clusters to cut a storage-aware cost, updating the table step by step rather than redoing it. On real data, HyDRA cut storage by eighty to ninety-three percent in some cases, beating random, spectral, and prototype rivals. Since summaries stay hypergraphs, they answer connectivity and centrality queries directly.
arxiv-2606-18474:
Ducourtial asks when ordered tuples can be coded as sets built from pure projections, in a 2026 mathematical logic paper. Starting from an infinite domain, each new layer consists of finite nonempty sets of the previous one; the classical Kuratowski coding of an ordered pair is the famous low-level example.

An injection at a given stage would give a definition of tuples of a length as sets at that level. Ducourtial calls the length and level pairs where this succeeds good. He recasts the question as the study of a certain integer function, then develops its basic theory with qualitative results, computed values for small arguments, and quantitative bounds. Variants close the paper, including a Kuratowski-style coding valid at one low level for tuples of distinct entries of any length, and a multiset version where an easy counting argument succeeds.
arxiv-2606-18774:
Lai, Hu, and Ye build an evaluation platform that judges language-model routers by real user preference, not answer keys, in a 2026 paper on AI infrastructure. Routing systems pick which model from a heterogeneous pool should answer a query, balancing quality against cost and latency. But existing evaluations rely on static benchmarks and automated scores. Those impose one notion of quality, and ignore the preferences of users.

RouteJudge runs pairwise comparisons. For the same query, different routing strategies each select a model, under pool and budget constraints. Users anonymously compare the responses. The preference is credited to the strategy behind each answer, with cost, latency, and task metadata logged for analysis. Its companion toolbox ORBIT standardizes router development, offline benchmarking, and submission. So methods can be integrated and tested under consistent protocols. Early results show offline and online evaluations give complementary signals about router quality.
arxiv-2606-19474:
Shakya and colleagues introduce secure coding drift in 2026, a socio-technical risk model for post-quantum cryptography development with language model help. The move to post-quantum cryptography is demanding. Code must keep constant-time execution, resist side channels, and set parameters precisely. At the same time, language models are deeply embedded in development workflows. They boost productivity but often generate insecure or suboptimal code.

Secure coding drift names the gradual decay of secure practice from sustained reliance on model-generated code. Unlike prior work on static code flaws, the model treats risk as a longitudinal behavior shaped by human-AI interaction. To counter it, the team proposes a gamified, model-augmented framework. It embeds adversarial evaluation, behavior feedback, and security scoring into the coding loop. Catching drift as a habit problem, not just a code problem, reframes how teams should govern AI help on cryptographic work.
arxiv-2606-19574:
Chengwei Zhou and seven colleagues present FrequencyFormer in 2026, a sensor-to-processor pipeline for vision transformers. Edge cameras running vision transformers choke less on compute than on sending image data onward. Moving raw pixels from sensor to processor burns energy and bandwidth.

FrequencyFormer squeezes images at the sensor using the frequency domain, where visual data packs tightly. A multi-scale discrete cosine transform tokenizer turns a standard image into compact frequency tokens. Off-chip data volume falls by up to 128 times with modest accuracy loss. A look-up table chip near the sensor runs the tokenizer without multipliers, saving area and power. A tweaked low-power link standard then cuts energy per bit for the smaller stream. The pipeline swaps in for the usual patch embedding and keeps pretrained backbones usable. Communication energy drops about 230-fold in the full design.
arxiv-2606-19674:
Pratishtha Agnihotri, Priyank Kalla, and Steve Blair compare phase modulation routes for photonic chips in 2026. Silicon photonic circuits steer light for fast links, and testing them leans on good phase modulators. Co-packaged optics raise the stakes for built-in test and calibration.

Two families face off: thermally induced phase shifts and carrier-based electrical modulation. Both are studied in Mach-Zehnder and microring modulator designs. Extinction ratio, tuning efficiency, power use, and modulation bandwidth form the scorecard. Trade-offs emerge between speed, energy cost, and tuning control. Thermal and electrical routes each win in distinct operating regimes. The authors distil practical guidance for picking a strategy in scalable photonic systems. Designers adding test signal generation can match the modulator to its calibration job rather than defaulting to one habit.
arxiv-2606-19974:
Kyle Janse van Rensburg and Herman Kamper interpret what factorized speech representations actually encode in 2026. Self-supervised speech features mix what was said with who said it, and a recent matrix factorization splits them into a shared content part and speaker-specific transforms. The authors correlate each dimension of the WavLM-based split with pitch, intensity, voicing, and formants to see where each trait lives.

Early content dimensions carry intensity, higher formants, and voicing, while pitch sits in a later one. The top speaker dimension tracks pitch and gender strongly, with later dimensions holding high-frequency detail. Editing chosen dimensions steers synthesis in targeted ways, and joint edits give fine control over pitch and loudness. Voice conversion and synthesis gain an interpretable control panel.
arxiv-2606-20174:
Nicko Starkey, Marcin Wojewodzic, and Krzysztof Rzecki review computational methods for detecting many cancers early from a single blood draw. Their 2026 paper surveys work from 2022 to 2025 on cell-free DNA, the fragments of DNA that cells shed into the blood. Because tumors release distinctive fragments, analyzing their sizes, patterns, and chemical marks could flag several cancers at once, including types with no established screening today. The review explains the biology behind these signals before turning to the algorithms.

The authors compare classical statistics and machine learning with deep learning frameworks, including autoencoder models, weighing interpretability, validation strategy, and readiness for clinical use. Challenges are sorted into technical, computational, and methodological groups, with open problems named for each. Multimodal ensembles that combine several signal types look closest to clinical integration. Still, the field needs standardized evaluation and reporting before future methods can be compared fairly side by side.
arxiv-2606-20774:
Seunghyun Shin and four colleagues present TriMotion in 2026, a framework for camera control in generated video that accepts many input forms. Camera motion guides how a viewpoint changes. Older methods usually take one input type, such as a pose path or a reference video. Users, however, may describe the same move in words, poses, or clips. TriMotion maps video, pose, and text inputs into one shared motion embedding space.

Learning that space needs synchronized examples across forms. The team builds a Motion Triplet Dataset from a multi-camera video set. Geometry-based motion descriptions are derived from camera positions. A latent motion consistency objective pushes generated video to follow the target path in latent space. That avoids costly pixel decoding during training. Tests show high-quality videos that follow target motion well, suggesting flexible control need not mean weaker control.
arxiv-2606-21174:
Xiangyu Li and Ran Su present HERO in 2026, a method that uses omics data as a testable hypothesis to guide evidence retrieval in breast cancer slide analysis. Matched multi-omics can improve biomarker and prognosis prediction from whole-slide images. Most pipelines treat omics as a side feature stream or text context.
