Custom firmware on the chip captures and injects wireless frames for common test attacks such as beacon flooding and forced disconnects. A handheld case design makes the tool standalone.

The work builds on an earlier popular tester with stronger hardware and usability. Frame level access lets learners see real protocol weaknesses firsthand. Portability suits field audits where laptops draw attention. Cost stays low enough for classroom sets. Network defenders gain an open tool that narrows the gap between beginner and professional kits.
pmc-13260974:
Meraj Sharifi and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study of non-glaucomatous optic atrophy, wasting of the optic nerve not caused by glaucoma, at a referral center in southeastern Iran. All 155 patients had a confirmed cause established through clinical evaluation, additional tests, and record review. Causes were grouped into categories including ischemic, meaning reduced blood flow, traumatic, toxic, inflammatory, compressive, and hereditary. The team also analyzed which factors predicted current visual sharpness.

Ischemic causes were most common, in forty-six patients or 29.7 percent, almost all from one condition called non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. Trauma was second, in thirty-seven patients. Nearly half the patients had vision of counting fingers or worse. Toxic optic neuropathy had the poorest outcomes, with five of six cases at that severe level. Longer time since symptom onset was the only independent predictor of worse vision.
pmc-13261474:
Xie Ma, Lingjian Ye, and Zhiqiang Ge proposed in 2026 a random attention method for predicting product quality in chemical plants from process data. Quality measures are hard to sense directly, so software models infer them from easier readings. Deep latent variable models do this well, yet picking which hidden features to trust stayed murky.

Their method draws many random attention picks from the hidden features pooled across the deep model's layers. Each pick trains its own submodel for the same quality target. A fusion step then blends the submodels' answers into one prediction. On a debutanizer column, the method cut average prediction error by about a fifth against regular approaches. On a carbon dioxide absorption column, the cut reached about a third. The authors present the randomness as a feature, not noise, since varied views stabilize the estimate.
pmc-13261974:
Sak Lee and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2026 the role of metadherin, a cancer-promoting protein, in head and neck cancer. The protein appears at high levels in many cancers, but its head and neck profile was scattered. Their search of four databases gathered thirty-three studies under standard review guidelines.

Across tumor subtypes, metadherin ran high and tracked with advanced features and poor prognosis. Laboratory studies showed it pushing migration, invasion, spread, blood vessel growth, and resistance to chemotherapy. It switches on several growth pathways and is in turn reined in by nine small regulatory RNAs. The review also notes head-and-neck-specific links, including a macrophage signaling loop and effects on radiation sensitivity through a cell death route. The authors nominate the protein as both a warning marker and a treatment target.
pmc-13262174:
Martin Černý and co-authors compared in 2026 two automated ways to grade pituitary tumors from MRI scans against human experts. The Knosp grade describes how far a tumor reaches toward the cavernous sinus, guiding surgery expectations. Human grading, though, varies between raters.

One method rebuilt the original geometric rule from tumor and artery outlines, by hand or by machine. The other was a deep learning classifier trained on 394 annotated scans. On 99 fresh scans, two human experts scored in the low sixties for accuracy. Both automated methods landed in the forties, below the humans. Higher automated grades still predicted sinus invasion and lower chances of full removal in the right direction. The authors judge the tools helpful for support but not ready to grade alone.
pmc-13262574:
Hang-Yu Zhao and colleagues map chest infections in Shenyang children after pandemic rules lifted. Nearly twenty-seven thousand children in hospital with acute lower respiratory infections were tested for twelve pathogens. Their 2026 study covers three years of stays at two hospitals in northeast China.

By gene testing, rhinovirus led, trailed by influenza A and respiratory syncytial virus. Antibody testing instead crowned Mycoplasma pneumoniae, which sat mostly in six to fourteen-year-olds. Infants carried the RSV burden, and several pathogens struck girls more often. Age, season, and sex each on its own shaped infection odds. Their atlas guides local testing and timing of preventive care.
pmc-13262674:
Edson Munanura and colleagues audit how three Ugandan referral hospitals use a workhorse antibiotic. Ceftriaxone treats infections and guards surgical patients, but misuse breeds resistance. Their 2026 study reviews seven hundred fifty-three patients across the three hospitals, plus talks with staff.

About two-thirds of use matched national rules, mostly as surgical prevention in once-daily doses. Blood cultures, the test that should steer therapy, happened in barely one percent of cases. Long treatment courses hurt fit, while surgery wards helped it. Staff blamed missing limits, stockouts, crushing workloads, and patchy checking. A national use plan is the authors' call.
pmc-13263274:
Fatema Mohamed Ali Abdulla Aljufairi leads the first Gulf region study of thyroid eye disease in children in a 2026 journal article. Graves' disease is an immune condition that overactivates the thyroid; its eye form inflames tissues around the eye. Doctors in Bahrain screened all known child Graves' patients in late 2025 and compared those with eye disease to an adult group.

Among 22 children, half had thyroid eye disease, most of it mild and often affecting both eyes. None had sight-threatening disease or double vision. Eye bulging or swelling was the most common symptom, and lid retraction the leading sign. Children had milder disease than the 81 adults, who more often showed lid lag. Parents being blood relatives was more common in children with eye disease.
pmc-13263574:
Bashar Jawich and colleagues used in 2026 a nationwide research network to ask whether diabetic nerve damage worsens the long arc after lower back decompression surgery. Diabetes already shadows spine outcomes, yet the specific mark of neuropathy was unmapped. Matching balanced 19,265 patients with the complication against the same number without it.

Across one, five, and ten years, the neuropathy group suffered more sepsis, clots, heart attacks, and strokes. Their emergency department use stayed elevated at every horizon. Repeat lumbar surgery also came more often, starting early and persisting across the decade. Survival free of revision ran significantly lower in the neuropathy group. A stricter comparison group without any diabetic complications told the same story. The authors frame neuropathy as a sign of lasting vulnerability worth flagging before surgery.
pmc-13263674:
Stacy Schmidt and colleagues write the missing rulebook for obesity medicine fellowship training in the United States. Programs existed without shared rules, unlike other fields. Their 2026 project drafts standards for adult and children's programs through an expert council process.

Drafts went through many rounds of expert edits, with input from the specialty's board and every known program's leaders. All thirty-one programs then voted section by section, with a section kept only on three-quarters of votes. Every single item cleared the bar for both adult and pediatric tracks. The agreed rules give a young field shared standards for curriculum and bedside training.
pmc-13263974:
Lawrence W. Wu and Ryan H. Moy offer a 2026 review that questions an older anatomy-based system for cancers where the esophagus meets the stomach. The Siewert system groups tumors by their center above or below the gastric cardia and has long guided surgical choices. Modern care now also uses systemic drugs, biomarkers, targeted treatments and immunotherapy, which the original system did not reflect.

The review sets Siewert types beside molecular subtypes described by large cancer genome projects, including chromosomal instability and microsatellite instability groups. Evidence from a major cancer center suggests molecular type predicts survival apart from tumor location. Readers see why future classification may need to combine anatomy with tumor biology rather than rely on location alone.
pmc-13264074:
R Tume and a large team examine links between gut permeability, lifestyle and brain health by sex in a 2026 cohort study. Eight hundred twenty-seven middle-aged adults from a Barcelona brain health study had cognitive testing, brain scans and a blood marker of nerve injury. Gut leakiness was estimated from three blood proteins tied to bacterial products and barrier control.

Single markers showed only small links with brain outcomes after full adjustment. Combined patterns differed for women and men, joining permeability markers with age and vascular risks in distinct ways. In women that pattern related to smaller brain volumes and higher nerve injury marker levels. The authors stress sex-specific analysis when studying the gut and brain connection in midlife.
pmc-13264174:
Dania El Rahal and colleagues stress-test an automated aorta outlining tool for CT scans in a 2026 study. Accurate aorta maps guide diagnosis and surgery, and deep learning promises fast results without manual tracing. Sixty angiography scans from one center covered young and older patients, aneurysms, dissections and scans taken in different contrast phases, giving the system normal and difficult anatomy to handle.

Two radiologists rated hundreds of segments for quality. Most ratings were good or excellent, with the best results in young patients. Performance fell notably in dissections and aneurysms, where torn or bulging walls confuse the model. The authors conclude the tool is dependable for normal anatomy but needs caution and human review in diseased aortas.
pmc-13264274:
Nastaran Ansari and colleagues published a 2026 study of gut viruses in the water supply of Hamadan, Iran. Such viruses spread through water and can harm health, yet local data were scarce. The team checked raw source water, treated water, and well water across the city system.

They took 100 samples in summer and autumn and tested each with five methods. Adenoviruses, one virus group, showed up in 24 percent of samples. Source water was much more polluted than well water, and summer samples were worse than autumn ones. The authors say virus traces in treated water call for more checks on amount, spread risk, and public exposure.
pmc-13264374:
Haonan He and colleagues compare two cholesterol strategies for preventing heart procedures in a 2026 Hong Kong cohort study. Patients with established artery disease already on moderate statins either added ezetimibe, a cholesterol absorption blocker, or switched to a high-intensity statin alone. Hospital system records from 2014 to 2023 were matched on baseline traits to balance the groups, then followed for first stent procedures or bypass surgery as the combined outcome of interest.

After matching, the combination group was far smaller than the statin-only group. Combination patients showed a substantially lower hazard of needing a procedure during follow-up. Results align with other outcomes favoring the pairing. Observational matching cannot fully remove prescribing bias, so randomized confirmation for this endpoint would strengthen the case.
pmc-13264574:
Eleni Papachristodoulou and a large team wrote a 2026 study on stress before diagnosis in systemic lupus erythematosus, an illness where the immune system attacks the body. Stress has been tied to such diseases, but its link to later lupus course was unclear. The team measured major life stress in the two years before diagnosis.

They studied 140 patients at one large hospital, most of them women, with a median diagnosis age of 35.5 years. About 46 percent reported moderate to high stress before diagnosis. The high stress group had more depression, high blood pressure, obesity, and fatigue than the low stress group. High stress also linked to a clotting syndrome tied to lupus and to fewer long quiet periods of disease. The authors call for studies that follow patients forward in time.
pmc-13264974:
Remzi Çetinkaya and colleagues published a 2026 study of the HALP score as a death warning in pneumonia caught outside hospital. The score blends four routine blood values: haemoglobin, albumin, lymphocytes, and platelets. Older pneumonia scores have limits, so the team tested whether this simple blend predicts death within 30 days.

They reviewed 467 adults admitted with pneumonia at one center. The 30-day death rate was 21.4 percent. Patients who died were older, more often male, and had lower HALP scores. The score predicted death well on standard tests. Further analysis showed its link to death ran largely through illness severity: standard severity scores, confusion, oxygen levels, and scan findings carried much of the effect. The authors offer HALP as a support tool beside the standard scores, not a replacement.
pmc-13265174:
Gunnar Wichmann, Theresa Wald, and Andreas Dietz discuss neck cancer with no found primary tumour, in a 2026 article. In this rare condition, cancer appears in neck nodes while the original site stays hidden. Better scans and standardised surgery now find many hidden primaries in the tonsils or tongue base. Randomised trial evidence for treatment remains missing.

The article reviews a study comparing standard care with gentler trial treatments for virus-linked cases. Standard work-up found the primary in most patients. Register data show that structured assessment by a specialist board improves survival. The authors stress careful diagnosis before any move to reduce treatment intensity.
pmc-13265674:
Bernhard Thalhamer and the team develop a proof test for plant saponins in poultry feed (2026). Quillaja saponin is added to thousands of tonnes of feed each year. No test confirmed its presence, and cheaper Madhuca saponin often adulterates extracts. Advanced chromatography and mass reading were combined.

Pelleted feed samples were analysed for marker compounds of each saponin type. Quillaja presence was proved for the first time in such feed. Madhuca was unexpectedly found in some samples, proving the fake mix. The test gives makers and state staff a practical tool where additive contents are often kept secret.
pmc-13266174:
Achla Bharti and colleagues benchmark deep learning models for classifying mouth tissue images, published in 2026. Separating normal lining, precancerous change, and cancer by eye is slow and variable. A curated set held more than two thousand images across the three classes. Seven model architectures trained under standard conditions.

Augmentation expanded training data to handle class imbalance. One model, EfficientNet-B0, reached the highest validation accuracy and best test scores. Three other models performed nearly as well. Errors clustered at transition zones between normal, precancer, and early cancer. The authors support automated classification as a diagnostic aid.
pmc-13266474:
Ece Bayram wrote a 2026 commentary arguing that sleep deserves more focus in Alzheimer's disease in women. Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia, and women carry the higher risk. Poor sleep is common in the disease yet is left out of its formal diagnostic rules.

Bayram discusses a study of women over 65 with mild memory loss and high genetic risk. In the higher-risk group, worse sleep was linked to weaker visual memory and more tau protein build-up in limb regions of the brain. No such links appeared for word memory. Bayram urges more research and better sleep care for women at risk.
pmc-13266774:
Zhimin Xu and co-authors present in 2026 a model that predicts whether a lung nodule will grow, using only its first CT scan. Growth over a year helps signal possible cancer, yet waiting for a second scan delays decisions. Their study drew on 1,387 nodules from patients who had at least two scans between 2021 and 2024.

The model fused two kinds of image features: measured radiomics traits and deep features from a transformer network. Combined, they beat either approach alone at separating growing from stable nodules. Decision and calibration checks also favored the combined model. Such a tool could let clinicians tailor follow-up timing to each nodule's risk instead of using one schedule.
pmc-13266874:
Yuyu Dai and co-authors rate in 2026 the quality of Chinese TikTok and Bilibili short videos that deal with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Social platforms now serve as major health information sources, so errors can spread widely. The team assessed 275 videos with several standard scoring tools for quality, reliability, and presentation.

Bilibili videos scored higher on quality and reliability, while TikTok videos drew more engagement despite being shorter. Videos by medical practitioners and science communicators beat those by general users on most measures. Popularity did not track quality well: more likes and shares sometimes went with lower scores. The authors call for more expert creators and stronger platform oversight of health content.
pmc-13267574:
Sheng Huang and colleagues wrote a 2026 study of steel for bridge cables under fast loading. Bridge cables face shaking from wind, traffic, and quakes, so their steel must behave in a known way when stretched quickly. The steel studied is a pearlitic type with added vanadium, shaped by rolling that varies across its thickness.

Tests pulled the steel at speeds from very slow to moderately fast. Added vanadium and the varied rolling together gave very high yield and breaking strengths. The steel still stretched well, though faster pulls cut its stretch and changed its break surface from dimpled to flatter. The team built an improved math model of this behavior. They offer it for safety checks and design of advanced bridge cable systems.
pmc-13267774:
José Ignacio Quesada-Márquez and co-authors show in 2026 how yeast cells use the length of fat chains to sense whether nutrients are plentiful. Ceramides, a family of membrane lipids, vary in chain length and head chemistry. A signaling hub called TORC2 watches membrane state and adjusts growth, and the team asked which lipid features it actually reads.

Making the longest chains, at twenty-six carbons, proved essential for TORC2 to quiet down when food ran short. Cells unable to extend chains kept signaling and failed to shrink. Swapping in mammal enzymes that build other chain lengths restored sensing only for some lengths. A separate head modification mattered not for sensing but for physically carrying out the size change, splitting the pathway into a sensor step and an execution step.
pmc-13268174:
Jinghui Hou and Xiaogang Guo present a 2026 study of a rock asphalt additive for road binder. Normal asphalt ruts in heat and ages in air. Their additive mixes natural rock asphalt with treated titanium dioxide particles. The team tested binders with doses from none to about a third additive, using standard bend, shear, and thickness tests plus chemical scans.

The additive stiffened the binder and cut its sensitivity to temperature. Chemical scans suggested the change is mostly physical blending, helped by new polar groups. A grey relational analysis, a ranking method for linked factors, found aging resistance was the additive's strongest gift, then stiffness, ahead of stretch. High doses hurt cold-weather relaxation, though. Balancing gains and losses, the authors recommend a dose of about 22 percent, which met road specifications in their tests.
pmc-13270874:
Caroline Rometsch wrote a 2026 commentary on how to judge psychosocial help, support for mental and social needs, after mass casualty incidents such as attacks or disasters. Such events cause wide distress, and support services are now built into response plans, yet systems lack a structured way to check whether that help works.

Rometsch notes that symptom questionnaires exist, but no checked tools are built to capture how people actually used care, its quality, or trust in it after a disaster. The commentary sets out time-based indicators, measures that change with the phase after an event, as a proposed framework. It calls for planned, long-term studies to build models that can scale.
pmc-13271274:
Jiaqi Liu is lead author of a 2026 journal article screening varieties of Pseudostellaria heterophylla. That plant is used as a functional food ingredient in East Asian cooking. It is valued for its sugars and saponins, soap-like plant compounds. Few diverse, locally suited varieties exist, so the team combined crop traits with electrical measures of plant tissue to rank 13 varieties.

Varieties differed clearly in water handling, nutrient movement, and metabolic activity. One variety, Zheshen I, gave the highest fresh and dry weights, while Zheshen II had the most polysaccharide, the valued sugar fraction, at 49.27 percent, and Zheshen IV the most saponin at 2.83 percent. A combined ranking named six varieties, including the current main local variety, as best for promotion in Guizhou.
pmc-13271674:
Vinícius Silva Junqueira and coauthors derive in 2026 formulas for prediction error in genomic selection when some candidates have no DNA test results. Breeders use DNA markers to predict the merit of plants and animals, yet testing every candidate costs too much. Programs must choose whom to test without a firm measure of the risk involved.

The authors work out exact expressions for prediction uncertainty in untested candidates under pedigree, genomic, and combined relationship models. Computer simulations with populations up to 15,500 matched the formulas against direct calculation. Breeders can now judge testing plans in advance and spend genotyping budgets where they cut uncertainty most.
pmc-13271974:
Gang Ji and Zheng-min Mo test in 2026 whether plain CT measurements of eye socket tissues can judge activity in thyroid eye disease. Active inflammation and quiet scarred phases need different treatment, but scoring activity usually leans on clinical signs. Precise tissue numbers from scans could give a more objective read.

The team studied 31 patients with active disease, 46 with inactive disease, and 46 healthy controls, measuring muscles, fat, and the tear gland in three dimensions. Eyes were grouped as active, inactive, or normal for comparison. Several size and density measures separated the groups, suggesting scan-based numbers could support activity grading.
pmc-13272074:
Vasundra V and coauthors review in 2026 how pre-cancerous mouth lesions turn into oral squamous cell carcinoma. These lesions carry widely varying risk, and grading tissue under the microscope predicts that risk poorly. A clearer molecular picture could help doctors watch the right patients closely.

The review traces gene instability, chemical gene switches, chronic inflammation, and changes in surrounding tissue as joint drivers. Several growth signaling pathways recur across studies, feeding cell flexibility and immune escape. One condition, oral submucous fibrosis, is treated as a high-risk model where stiffened tissue itself pushes cells toward cancer. The authors call for marker-based risk assessment.
pmc-13272274:
Miguel González is lead author of a 2026 mathematics journal article proving a scaling limit theorem for controlled branching processes. Those are models of populations where each individual produces a random number of offspring. A control rule adjusts the population. The work sets broad conditions under which a sequence of such processes settles toward a continuous limit.

The authors study controls split into two separate parts: an immigration term depending on current population size, and a size-divisible term built from each member's share. This covers common control laws based on Poisson, binomial, and negative binomial distributions. The limit is a continuous-state branching process with dependent immigration, proved through tightness arguments and a martingale problem, with a classic diffusion as a special case.
pmc-13272674:
Rui Wang and co-authors used multi-omics data to classify liver cancer linked to hepatitis B in a 2026 study. This cancer varies widely between patients and often has a poor outlook. Finer grouping could point to better treatment choices.

Working from a large cancer atlas cohort, they found two subtypes. One had a better outlook and an immune rich tumor setting, while the other looked more aggressive with a quiet immune setting. They built a machine learning risk score from many model combinations, and it beat ten earlier scores. A drug search flagged a compound that killed high risk cancer cells in lab tests and shrank tumors in mice. They also report a gene that may suppress tumors through a known growth pathway.
pmc-13272874:
Omolbanin Izadi leads a 2026 study of what predicts whether nurses in Iran report medical errors. Reporting is seen as a sign of commitment to patient safety and a mirror of workplace culture. Using the theory of planned behavior, the team surveyed 280 nurses in teaching hospitals linked to Shiraz University in 2024.

All parts of the model linked to reporting behavior, and the model fit was fairly strong. Perceived control over reporting and intention to report had the strongest direct links. Beliefs about control had the greatest indirect effect. The authors advise easier access to reporting systems, steady feedback, rewards for timely reports, and a supportive workplace that builds positive attitudes.
pmc-13273774:
Gorter and colleagues report a pilot trial of an e-health app that helps youth with brain-based disabilities move into adult care. Their 2026 journal article describes a randomized trial run in Canada. The app teaches skills for managing health and services.

The full trial planned to enroll 264 young people. Recruitment reached only 43 participants. Engagement with the app was modest. Fewer than a third of the teaching units were completed. The team stopped the full trial. They reshaped the study as a pilot instead. The authors share lessons on recruitment and app design. Their experience may guide future transition tools for disabled youth.
pmc-13274074:
Henrik W Schytz and co-authors present 2026 results from the RESOLUTION trial of a migraine prevention drug. Participants had chronic migraine plus medication-overuse headache, a cycle where pain drugs used too often worsen head pain. All received brief education about overuse, then half got eptinezumab infusions and half a placebo for twelve weeks.

After that first phase, everyone received the drug for twelve more weeks, and 584 of 608 participants finished the trial. Gains in migraine days, severity, and quality of life held up for the early treatment group. Those switched from placebo caught up to similar levels. Side effect rates were close between groups, with no new safety signals.
pmc-13274574:
Shinsuke Otagiri and colleagues report a 2026 case report of two migrated medical stents locking together inside a patient's small bowel. The patient was a seventy-eight-year-old woman with pancreatic head cancer. She had received a plastic bile duct stent for jaundice and a metal mesh stent to hold open her blocked duodenum, the first stretch of intestine.

Four months into chemotherapy her tumor shrank and the blockage eased, but both stents had slipped down into the ileum, the bowel's final section. There they interlocked mechanically and jammed, and a scope procedure could not free them. Surgeons removed the affected bowel segment, and tissue study showed deep inflammation with an abscess, pockets of infected fluid.
pmc-13274974:
Sascha Riaz and colleagues present a 2026 journal article testing the heat-and-aggression link on the football pitch. Earlier evidence came mostly from labs and crime records, which may not reflect everyday social life. The team analyzed about one million amateur football matches across Germany, comparing games at the same venue in the same league and season.

Referee cards, their measure of aggression, followed an inverted U against temperature. Cards rose as it warmed up to about thirteen degrees Celsius, then fell away. Matches in extreme heat drew fifteen percent fewer disciplinary actions than the average match. The authors read this as moderate warmth raising irritability, while severe heat saps the physical energy aggression needs.
pmc-13275674:
Nuraly S Akimbekov and co-authors review vitamin D and antimicrobial peptides in defence against fungi, in a 2026 article. These peptides are short proteins the body makes as a first barrier against invading microbes. Unlike standard antibiotics, they rarely drive resistance, which makes them attractive as drug options fade.

Healthy vitamin D levels help switch on peptide pathways that act against Candida, Aspergillus, and Cryptococcus. The authors separate this immune-support role from direct antifungal use of vitamin D itself. Direct use would need unsafe doses that raise calcium to harmful levels. Species differences, such as a primate-only gene switch, also limit how far rodent findings carry to people.
pmc-13275774:
Iason-Spyridon Patergiannakis and Ioannis Pappas wrote a 2026 review on plant-based compounds for mammary cancer in dogs and cats. Breast tumors are among the most common cancers in both pets. Surgery is the main treatment, but advanced cases often return and resist standard drugs.

The review gathers early lab evidence on extracts and plant chemicals as possible add-on treatments. Some, including an extract from a spurge plant and two named compounds, strongly slowed dog mammary tumor cells in dishes and in mouse models. Evidence for cats is still scarce. The authors stress that safety and benefit depend on the compound, dose, and species. How each pet's body handles these substances differs, so more work is needed before clinic use.
pmc-13275974:
Annie Bjäreback and co-authors report a 2026 first-in-human study of radiation doses from a cancer imaging tracer. The tracer targets a receptor called GRPR, found in large amounts on many tumors but scarce in healthy organs. Knowing where its radiation lands in the body is required before wider use.

Twelve patients, six women with breast cancer and six men with prostate cancer, received the tracer and had scans at six time points. The pancreas absorbed the highest dose, followed by the bladder wall and the kidneys. More than half the tracer left the body in urine within four hours. A standard injection gave a total body dose the authors describe as low, in line with similar tracers already in use.
pmc-13276074:
Mohammed Alqahtani and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on tuning fuel cell models with a nature-inspired computer method. Proton exchange membrane fuel cells make clean power, but their math models contain unknown values that must be fit to real data. Good values improve design, simulation, and fault detection.

Their method, a modified Draco lizard optimizer, mimics how gliding lizards search, balancing wide exploration with fine local search. They ran it fifty-five times on three commercial fuel cell systems. It was compared with the original lizard method and three other recent optimizers. The modified version reached the lowest errors, settled fastest, and stayed most consistent across runs. The authors say its fitted values matched measured voltage behavior closely for all three systems.
pmc-13277274:
Marcella Tazzari and a large team hunt for features that predict response to a dendritic cell vaccine in metastatic melanoma, in a 2026 study. The vaccine trains immune cells on tumour material, yet clinical benefit is patchy and poorly explained. Samples of the vaccine product itself were profiled in depth.

An unexpected population of antibody-producing B cells turned up inside the finished vaccine products. These cells were more abundant in patients who later responded to treatment. Their tumours also showed mature immune clusters before treatment began. Dendritic cells from responders switched on heat-shock genes tied to antigen handling. The authors propose that B cells help load and tune the vaccine during manufacture.
pmc-13278474:
Yanru Jia and Longsheng Wei present a 2026 study of a computer method that judges image quality the way humans see it, without needing a clean reference image. Images degrade during sending, compression, and storage, so automatic quality scoring matters. Their framework combines meta-learning, graph-based learning, and feature fusion across image scales.

A graph module maps relationships among distortion types, distortion levels, and image content, trained under two kinds of supervision. Tests on four benchmark datasets beat hand-crafted methods by wide margins and edged out other deep learning approaches. Removing parts of the system weakened it, confirming each part helps. The result is a more discriminating, generalizable way to score distorted images, the authors say.
pmc-13278774:
Santhi P Bhavanam leads a 2026 greenhouse study of how herbivore warning cues affect sugar maple seedlings, young trees of a long-lived species. Plants can raise defenses from damage signals or from mere signs of herbivore presence. Four-week-old seedlings were exposed to a plant hormone spray used as a damage signal, or to the slime trail of a slug, across one growing season.

The hormone cue slowed seedling growth and raised total phenolics, defensive chemicals, but did not change growth of spongy moth caterpillars feeding on them. The slug slime cue changed neither growth nor phenolics. Responses depended on cue type, and some faded over time while others persisted, the team found.
pmc-13278974:
Gwendoline Hoslett and a large team uncover how cancer cells clear a drug-trapped enzyme to resist treatment, in a 2026 study. PARP inhibitors kill repair-deficient cancers by trapping the PARP1 enzyme on DNA. Cells that clear the trapped enzyme survive, blunting the therapy.

The clearance route proved to be nucleophagy, a selective self-eating process inside the nucleus. A receptor protein, TEX264, grabs trapped PARP1 and hands it to the degradation machinery with help from the p97 segregase. Blocking that pathway, chemically or genetically, left more enzyme trapped and restored drug sensitivity in resistant cells. Damage and cell death rose accordingly. The authors name nucleophagy a protective shield worth targeting.
pmc-13279574:
Mats Jonas Karlsfeld and colleagues report a 2026 lab study of shoulder steadiness with torn cuff muscles. The rotator cuff is a group of shoulder muscles that press the ball in its socket. The socket depth also helps hold the joint. Tears were simulated in eight donor shoulders mounted in a robot test rig. Muscle loads mimed whole cuff, part tears, mass tears and full tears with deltoid loss.

A load and shift test pushed the joint toward front dislocation, and peak force marked steadiness. Tears of the front tendon and of the back tendon each cut the force needed to shift the joint. Shallow sockets, scored by a bone ratio, held less well than deep ones. Cuff pull and socket depth work as a pair, so repair plans should weigh both.
pmc-13279774:
John Sharp and colleagues report a 2026 letter on bispecific antibody care after CAR T cell care in follicular lymphoma. Follicular lymphoma is the second most common non Hodgkin lymphoma, with about fourteen thousand new United States cases a year. First care can give long calm spells, yet up to half of patients need many care lines. The letter gives real world results for one sequence.

Eighteen patients got a bispecific antibody, a dual target immune drug, after CAR T care failed. Most got mosunetuzumab, and the rest got epcoritamab. Median past care lines were five. Overall response rate was sixty one percent, with full response in thirty nine percent. Best response came at a median near two and a half months. Prior CAR T response in the same group was seventy two percent. Later line immune care can still work after cell care.
pmc-13279874:
Mostafa Kamandi and colleagues report a 2026 case of testicular seminoma in a man with suspected Lynch syndrome. Lynch syndrome is a family cancer syndrome from faults in DNA mismatch repair genes. Germ cell tumours, most of them seminomas, arise most in younger men on their own. A link with Lynch syndrome is rare. Their patient was a fifty six year old man with low back pain and a testicle mass.

CT scans showed swollen nodes behind the belly, which fit testicular cancer. The right testicle was removed and tests proved a classic seminoma. Four cycles of VIP chemotherapy followed, since cancer had spread to the lungs. Node surgery after chemo found no cancer left in the nodes. Later checks for anemia, a low red blood count, found colon cancer as well. Tissue stain checks backed the Lynch suspicion. Two cancers in one man can flag a family syndrome.
pmc-13280774:
Hayeon Hwang and colleagues published a 2026 genomics study of organelle evolution in Ishigeales, an early-diverging order of brown algae whose members range from filaments to leafy forms. Only one species in the order had organelle genomes available, limiting inference. The team assembled the chloroplast and mitochondrial genomes of four species, from the filamentous Pilinia rimosa to two leafy Ishige species. They rebuilt the group's family tree with two approaches.

The trees agreed that evolution ran from simple ancestors toward the complex Ishige body plans, though one placement conflicted between analyses, hinting at a tangled history. Both showed rearrangement. Two species carried expanded mitochondrial genomes, and one had duplicated a respiratory gene. The authors attribute the growth to spreading tandem repeats now decaying. Several chloroplast genes evolved fast between the sister Ishige species, including a gene family tied to their differing shapes.
pmc-13280874:
Caroliny Oliveira Cavalcante and colleagues published a 2026 study adding gallic acid, a plant phenolic, to a printable hydrogel for bone tissue repair. The base gel combines oxidized alginate with gelatin, a pairing already used for scaffolds. Three loadings of the acid were tested. Spectroscopy confirmed it entered the network, thermal checks showed the polymer framework survived, and images found rougher surfaces after the addition.

The acid lifted the films' antioxidant power to about 96 percent on a standard scavenging test without changing how they swell or degrade, so structure stayed intact. At the two lower loadings, flow properties improved enough for clean 3D printing of scaffolds with pores near 0.6 millimeters. Bone precursor cells grew happily on the printed scaffolds, and the films killed Staphylococcus aureus, a bacterium notorious in chronic bone infections. The authors present the combined material as a printable, bioactive candidate for regenerating infected or damaged bone.
pmc-13280974:
Tingting Li and colleagues published a 2026 feeding study of letrozole, a drug that blocks estrogen production, in weaned lambs of the Turpan black sheep breed. Sixty two-month-old lambs were split into a control group and two dose groups fed the drug for 75 days. The team tracked growth, rumen fermentation, blood hormones and metabolites, and gut microbes.

The higher dose improved weight gain, body length, and chest girth, and it sharply raised growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. Blood chemistry shifted by dose: the lower dose group showed changes centered on bile acid metabolism, while the higher dose altered cholesterol handling. Rumen fermentation products rose in both treated groups, and the microbial balance tilted toward fiber-digesting Firmicutes families, with different marker bacteria enriched at each dose. The authors conclude letrozole reshapes hormones, rumen function, and microbes, while noting the endocrine manipulation needs care.
pmc-13281674:
Victoria Tweedie-Pitre and colleagues published a 2026 neuroanatomy study mapping which neurons in the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis make octopamine, a signaling chemical playing norepinephrine's role in invertebrates. Earlier maps disagreed with each other. The team combined an RNA labeling technique with antibody staining to trace three things at once in the snail's central nervous system. They traced the RNA for the enzyme that builds octopamine, the enzyme itself, and the finished chemical.

About forty neurons lit up on all three measures and are true octopamine producers, including cells already known from electrical recordings to use the chemical. Roughly forty more showed the RNA and enzyme but no transmitter, while a handful showed only the transmitter. The authors weigh causes from antibody cross-reactivity to enzyme variants and blocks on enzyme activity. Their moral: single-label maps of chemical identity in the brain should be read with suspicion.
pmc-13281874:
Zhe Jiang and colleagues reviewed immune signals that steer kidney scarring in a 2026 paper. Chronic kidney disease creeps forward as swelling grinds the organ down. Macrophages, roving immune cells, can fan or calm that swelling. Signals called interleukins flip them between attack and repair modes. The team searched two databases for work from 2015 onward. They kept one hundred eighty-six studies in people and animals.

Attack signals push macrophages into a sugar-burning attack mode that harms tissue. Their output recruits yet more attackers, locking in a loop. Calm signals flip cells to repair mode and guard the kidney. But in chronic disease the repair mode can twist, pumping out scarring factors instead. The review maps drugs that nudge the balance, from signal blockers to plant compounds and diabetes pills. The authors say the flip system is a rich drug frontier.
pmc-13282174:
Kai Yu and co-authors wrote a 2026 scoping review on deep learning tools that support decisions in epilepsy surgery. Deep learning is a form of artificial intelligence that learns patterns from large data sets. Surgery can help some people whose seizures resist drugs, but choices at each stage are complex. The team mapped one hundred forty-five studies published between January 2018 and May 2025.

Nearly all work sat in the planning stage before surgery. No included studies covered support during the operation itself, and few covered care after it. Most used small, single-centre, private data sets and a common image-based model type. Testing on outside data and use inside real clinic routines were rare. Only a minority reported even partly integrated workflows. The authors call for shared multi-centre data, stricter outside testing, and outcomes that matter to patients, before such tools can be adopted safely and fairly.
pmc-13282474:
Saeid Safiri and colleagues reported global estimates in 2026 for aortic aneurysm, a dangerous widening of the main artery that can burst. Drawing on Global Burden of Disease 2021 data, the report tracked deaths and years of life lost to illness from 1990 to 2021, plus the share tied to known risk factors.

World death and disability rates fell by about a quarter over the period, yet national rates varied widely. Armenia, Montenegro, and Nauru showed the highest rates, while Georgia and Uzbekistan rose sharply. Smoking, high blood pressure, and high body weight were the leading linked factors. The authors call for stronger prevention and vascular care where services are thin.
pmc-13282674:
Ani Misirian and co-authors present a 2026 case where treating a parasitic worm infection cleared a returning lymph cancer, without chemotherapy. Their patient was a healthy sixty-four-year-old man from Peru. He had earlier been treated for a slow-growing MALT lymphoma, a cancer of immune tissue in the gut lining, with antibody therapy and radiation. Two years later his symptoms returned and tests confirmed the lymphoma was back.

Tests then found a Strongyloides infection, a threadworm that lives in the small bowel and can persist for decades. Instead of full-body drug treatment, doctors gave oral ivermectin, a standard worm treatment. The lymphoma responded completely. MALT lymphomas are often driven by underlying infections, best known with a stomach bacterium. The authors urge clinicians to hunt broadly for infectious drivers, especially in immigrant patients, before stepping up cancer treatment.
pmc-13282774:
Devon J Hensel and co-authors present a 2026 diary study on how daily bladder and bowel leakage relates to emotional functioning in young adults with spina bifida. Spina bifida is a birth condition affecting the spine, often causing lifelong incontinence. Twenty-three adults aged eighteen to twenty-six, all with recent leakage, completed end-of-day assessments for thirty days, totalling six hundred forty-three entries.

Urinary leakage was reported on about fifty-four percent of days, bowel leakage on about twenty-one percent. On worse urinary days, with more frequent or larger leaks, shorter dry spells, or avoided activities, mood was lower and leakage anxiety higher. Bowel leakage showed the same pattern, worsened by needing help with management. Daily burdens also tracked with poorer quality of life at month's end. The authors say day-level variability, not just average severity, matters for rehabilitation assessment.
pmc-13282874:
Nepali secondary schools hosted HASHTAG, the teen mental health program evaluated in 2026 by a team under Nagendra Prasad Luitel. The program is called HASHTAG and serves teens aged 13 to 16 years. Schools can reach many teens, but proof from low-income settings is still limited.

A trial ran in four secondary schools in Morang district. Surveys at the start and after three months tracked well-being, behavior, support, and school climate. The program paired a three-month school climate part with six weekly group sessions. Interviews and group talks added views on fit and acceptability. The design tests whether a broad school approach can work in Nepal.
pmc-13283174:
Cotton-field soils on Turkiye's Seyhan Plain carry boron well above natural background, Yakup Kenan Koca's 2026 sampling shows. Boron helps crops at low levels but harms them when slightly too high. Close tracking is needed for safe soil and food production.

A total of 51 surface samples came from cotton fields under standard farming. Lab tests gave a mean boron level well above natural crust background. Index scores pointed to moderate enrichment and moderate contamination of the soils. Health risk scores stayed below concern levels for children and adults. Boron levels also varied by soil class in the survey. Ongoing checks are advised for farm planning.
pmc-13283374:
Poor sleep before chemotherapy foreshadows heavier side effects, Fang Zhao's two-center cohort of 300 women shows in 2026. Past work on drug side effects often ignored sleep quality and mental strain. The team tracked all three across chemotherapy cycles.

A total of 300 women from two centers joined the cohort study. Sleep and distress were checked before and after each of six chemo cycles. Patients with poor sleep at the start had more side effects in most types. Baseline distress tracked closely with total side effect scores in the data. Adjusted models kept distress as a separate predictor of side effects.
pmc-13284574:
Chang Seok Bang led a 64-expert panel in 2026 to revise Korea's national guidelines for Helicobacter pylori infection, the fourth edition since the series began. Much had changed since 2020: clarithromycin resistance climbed from about eighteen to thirty-three percent, gene-guided tailored therapy spread, and a new class of acid blockers arrived. Twelve recommendations passed on the first vote. The headline shift is a two-pillar strategy pairing tailored therapy with empirical four-drug therapy, while plain clarithromycin triple therapy is now restricted to set conditions. Sequential therapy was dropped. The stronger acid blockers are endorsed as alternatives, and treatment indications widened to include cancer prevention in inflamed stomachs and shrinking certain small polyps.
pmc-13285174:
Zhe Li and co-authors test whether prior use of common blood pressure drugs links to delirium in intensive care in a 2026 record study. Data came from a large United States critical care database for 2008 to 2022, covering 15,666 patients split by prior use of ACE inhibitors, related blockers, or neither. Delirium within thirty days was the main outcome.

Both drug groups showed far lower adjusted delirium risk than non-users in the models reported here. ACE inhibitor use also linked to lower kidney injury risk, and both groups needed kidney replacement therapy less often. The authors urge caution, since record studies cannot prove the drugs caused the lower rates, and trials would be needed.
pmc-13285674:
Resting defender T cells wear a sugar-rich coat that sheds once they wake, Laxmi Prasad Adhikari and co-authors show in a 2026 study. Hyaluronan, a slick sugar chain in body gels, was long thought a product of support cells alone. Naive helper T cells build their own coat, paired with a partner protein, versican, the team found by imaging and gel reads.

As cells split into fighter types, the coat vanished from the surface and the sugar moved inside. One making enzyme, HAS3, ruled in resting cells: cells lacking it bore bare surfaces and multiplied wildly when triggered. The authors frame coat turnover as a brake and release system for T cell growth.
pmc-13286074:
Marvin Guth and colleagues test phone location data as an early warning for mood episodes in bipolar disorder in a 2026 quantitative study. Shifts in where a person goes each day may whisper that depression or mania is on its way. Using a factory-born method that flags drift from a personal baseline, the team checked GPS trails against recorded episodes.

Data covered 28 patients and more than ten thousand days, spanning 26 depressive and 20 high episodes. Time spent at each haunt flagged episode days better than the count of new places visited, which showed no firm link at all. Tuned settings sharpened the flags, yet no single measure cleared the set bar for both catching episodes and sparing calm days. Some charts did show drift before episodes began, a hint the authors say deserves finer tools and larger tests.
pmc-13286174:
Yunkyeong Hwang and co-authors test cheap blood ratios as death predictors in kidney disease in a 2026 retrospective cohort analysis. Two ratios built from routine blood counts promise a quick read on body-wide inflammation, while a third measure tracks how uneven red cell sizes have become. The team asked whether the ratios still warn once that red cell measure enters the picture.

Charts held 2,654 adults with kidney disease who were not on dialysis, followed for years at one large hospital. Across the whole group, the red cell measure alone kept a firm link with death after full adjustment. Split by that measure, though, one white cell ratio did predict death among patients whose red cells stayed even. The other ratio failed everywhere, which argues for judging such markers inside red cell bands rather than as blanket rules.
pmc-13286574:
William Cabral-Miranda and colleagues map child pneumonia against neighborhood conditions across São Paulo in a 2026 ecological study. Records from 2010 to 2020 covered all 96 districts of the huge city, counting deaths and hospital stays for residents up to age 19. District scores for wealth, housing quality, and road layout were tested for ties to the disease burden, with spatial models hunting for clusters.

Deaths totaled 1,486 over the decade, falling more on boys and bunching in particular districts rather than spreading evenly. Mortality sank as the share of high-standard homes and a composite social index rose, and climbed near fast roadways. Hospital admissions, far more numerous, traced wealth more weakly. The authors urge prevention aimed by map, pairing vaccines with housing and planning fixes where the risk concentrates.
pmc-13286874:
Nabil Saleem and colleagues describe a stomach tumor unmasked by severe anemia in a toddler in a 2026 case report and literature review. Yolk sac tumors usually grow in ovaries or testes of adolescents; the stomach is a rare address, and a pure form there rarer still.

She remains tumor-free three years later, with the marker back to undetectable. The authors' review found only twelve prior reports of pure gastric yolk sac tumors, just one in a child, making hers the first in a young girl.
pmc-13286974:
Alberto Fernández-Bernaldez and colleagues compare gene activity in the skin and blood of eczema patients to find blood markers that mirror skin inflammation. Their 2026 study analyzes gene readings from lesions and from circulating T cells, then checks candidate proteins in blood from patients with moderate-to-severe disease. A blood test for activity would spare patients repeated skin sampling.

One protein, S100A8, rose with disease severity in blood, while another, SOCS3, moved the other way. Two further candidates trended in the same directions. Monitoring eczema from a blood draw looks plausible, the authors conclude.
pmc-13287174:
Xiaohuan Li and co-authors evaluated advanced magnetic resonance scanning in 2026. Their aim was to spot dangerous swollen veins in the food pipe of people with liver scarring, without first using a camera scope. Fifty-eight patients had both the scan and endoscopy for comparison.

Blood speed and pressure measures in several abdominal veins ran higher in the high-risk group of 25 patients. Spleen vein peak speed performed best among single scan measures. Combining that value with spleen size and a spleen stiffness-related measure gave stronger accuracy, reported as 0.945. The authors present combined scanning as a possible way to reduce unneeded scope checks.
pmc-13287274:
Christoph Sandmann and colleagues reported in 2026 the first girl known to develop heart and brain disease from a change in AIFM1, a gene carried on the X chromosome. The variant usually affects boys. Genetic testing found one altered copy, with the healthy copy switched off in almost all cells tested.

Heart scans at eight months showed a thickened main pumping chamber with normal squeezing. By age two and a half the chamber had stretched and weakened, and heart failure treatment began. The authors reviewed earlier heart cases in this condition. They urge early heart checks for carriers, including girls and women.
pmc-13287474:
Sydney K Wheatley and co-authors propose in 2026 growing hard-to-culture gut bacteria one cell at a time inside tiny gel beads made with microfluidic chips. Standard dishes favour fast growers, leaving much of gut diversity unstudied. The beads use a four-arm polymer that the team found friendly to gut microbes.

By varying polymer strength and adding a short attachment peptide, the authors tuned bead stiffness and pore size. They then checked survival, growth, and colony formation for oxygen-shunning gut species. Beads supported strong growth under air-free conditions. The authors present the system as a handle for isolating rare gut bacteria and testing them one strain at a time.
pmc-13287974:
Jiawei Chen and co-authors review in 2026 the growing evidence that bacteria live inside tumours themselves, not only in the gut, and take part in how cancers start, spread, and answer treatment. Inside, bacteria can damage DNA, stir long-term inflammation, and help cancer cells break away and seed new sites. Effects on immunity cut both ways: some bacteria help tumours hide, others sharpen attack. Detection methods from sequencing to imaging are surveyed. The authors weigh bacteria as diagnostic clues and as targets for sharper cancer care.
pmc-13288174:
Burgert Muller and a large team tracked in 2026 the spread of a pollen-feeding hoverfly, native to the Americas, across Africa after its arrival there. Records came from field collecting, museum holdings, and citizen science sightings, then fed climate matching models for present and future worlds.

The models proved accurate on both home and invaded ranges. The fly largely kept its home climate tastes, with modest expansion into new conditions. Host plants were not modelled, a gap the authors note.
pmc-13288774:
F Kumara Mastrorosa and a large team read the center of chromosome 21 in 2026. Their paper deals with Down syndrome families. The center repeats a lot of DNA. Long tries at assembly failed there. Small centers were blamed for faulty division. Eight affected families gave long-read data.

The team weighed 24 proband centers. Controls held 287 chromosomes. Small centers were not more common in cases. That undercut the old suspicion. Two cases did show extreme size mismatch. The mother's two copies split widely there. They rank among the smallest female centers on record. Chromosome 21 seems prone to such lopsided centers.
pmc-13288874:
Mehrdad Amir-Behghadami and Seifollah Heidarabadi present a 2026 protocol on child voice checks. The planned work is a scoping review. Babies and toddlers are hard to assess often. Cheap checks are also hard to run. AI reading voice traits might flag delay early. No invasive tests would be needed.

Motor, thinking, language, and social delays all count. Two reviewers will screen on their own. Voice capture and model types will be charted. Blocks to real-world use will be logged.
pmc-13288974:
Anjali K Henders and colleagues profile a large ALS cohort in Australia. Their 2026 report describes the SALSA-SGC group. The group links all major ALS clinics there. It pairs health data with stored samples. Recruitment ran from 2016 to 2024.

Gene screens found known risk changes in some cases. One gene change, in C9orf72, led the list. An open data tool lets others explore the set.
pmc-13289074:
Melissa D McCradden and colleagues put forward a 2026 plan to test an AI scribe in Australia. The test sits in a child development clinic. The tool drafts visit notes from talk. Doctors still write notes as usual. The AI works in silence beside them.

The team will weigh note quality for both paths. Review time will also be compared. Fairness checks are built into the audit frame. Notes will be read for gaps and risks. Two ethics boards have approved the plan. Results will guide a larger trial later. A plain summary will be posted for the public.
pmc-13289374:
Konstantinos Triantafyllias led a 2026 follow-up study on artery stiffness as a heart risk marker in autoimmune rheumatic diseases. The test, carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity, times how fast a pressure wave travels and reflects aortic stiffness. The authors asked whether it predicts heart events better than the standard SCORE2 risk calculator in these patients.

The cohort held 143 patients with rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis, or spondyloarthritis who had baseline testing between 2012 and 2017. Over a median of seven years, 20 heart events occurred in follow-up. Stiffness ran higher in those who later had events, while SCORE2 scores did not differ between groups. Stiffness separated future cases far better and stayed predictive after age adjustment.
pmc-13289774:
Wenchen Zhao and Xinxia Li offer a 2026 narrative review on how digital health literacy links to quality of life through middle factors. Guided by a World Health Organization digital strategy, the authors searched three databases for studies naming mediators between literacy and life quality.

Only seven studies passed screening, and all used cross-sectional designs that snapshot one point in time. Five middle factors stood out: social support, confidence in self-care, self-management skill, life satisfaction, and fear of disease worsening. Each helped carry the link from literacy to better life quality in the studies. Future programs should build those middle strengths, not just tech skill.
pmc-13289874:
Emily R. Jakob and colleagues propose a 2026 scoping review protocol on what shapes physical activity programs for people with multiple sclerosis. Moderation evidence, meaning clues about who benefits most in which settings, could guide smarter tailoring, but that evidence has never been mapped as a whole.

The review will search eight databases, hand-check reference lists, and chase citations for all included work. One reviewer will screen titles and abstracts, with full-text checks done independently in pairs. Charts will display which sclerosis groups and methods dominate the field. Results on moderation will then be summarized to steer program design.
pmc-13290774:
Old and new ideas about having children coexist in Shandong women's minds, Zihan Zhou and colleagues report in a survey study from 2026. Under China's universal two-child policy, they asked married women of reproductive age what pulls their fertility attitudes in each direction.

A total of 1,782 valid questionnaires came back from women aged 18 to 45. Traditional attitudes clustered with lower education, family health risks, household economic standing, and strong expectations voiced by husbands, parents, in-laws, and society, plus community support. Emerging attitudes, by contrast, weakened where eldercare and childcare costs ran high and where policy reimbursement and community support felt inadequate. Zhou and colleagues read the split as expectations feeding tradition while money pressure and thin support feed the new outlook, a map for policy aimed at either.
pmc-13291274:
How older adults use the web shapes their social lives. Nicole Memmer leads a 2026 study of adults in their late sixties to nineties. Web use splits into social, facts, and fun domains. Each domain may link to company in a different way.

Data came from 648 adults living at home. Feelings and thoughts about tech were both measured. Warm feelings toward tech tied to all use domains. Clear thinking about tech showed no such tie. Younger age also meant more use overall. Social use linked to less loneliness. Fact use linked to more social activity. Fun use linked to less activity, a warning sign.
pmc-13291374:
Maria Carelli, Nelson Nazzicari, Massimo Confalonieri, and Carla Scotti mine alfalfa lines for genes behind forage quality, in 2026.
