The model species gave its own variant sets for flowering and stem traits. Gene classes covered transcription control, DNA and RNA handling, and sugar and fat pathways. Two pentatricopeptide repeat genes stood out as candidates, one for flowering time and one for stem form. The authors offer them as leads for breeding better forage.
pmc-13291474:
Diabetes may raise risks after knee ligament surgery. Fardis Vosoughi leads a 2026 review of reconstruction outcomes. More older and less healthy patients now get this surgery. Past data on diabetes risk was scattered.

Four databases were searched through March 2025. Studies compared patients with and without diabetes. Main focus fell on repeat surgery rates. Infection, readmission, and blood clots were also pooled. Set rules guided study choice and math. The authors expected more overall problems with diabetes. They expected no rise in repeat surgery, though. Pooled numbers give surgeons a firmer base for consent talks.
pmc-13292374:
Sybren Slimmen and colleagues treat student wellbeing as a web of connected processes in a 2026 Dutch study. Surveys reached 497 students at a university of applied sciences in late 2023, with 207 answering again the next June. Measures covered wellbeing, study stressors, self-beliefs, coping styles, and social surroundings. A statistical network mapped cross-links at the start, and follow-up models traced which factors predicted later ones.

Links inside the network were mostly modest, and wellbeing connected directly to few other factors. Wellbeing and social support still sat centrally, tying the web together. Over the year, most measures predicted mainly themselves, showing strong stability. Few cross-factor effects survived to the second wave. The authors warn that snapshot networks can mislead when concepts overlap and links run weak. Wellbeing looks less like a lever to pull and more like one strand in a steady system. Support services may need system-wide thinking.
pmc-13292474:
Xusheng Zhang and co-authors chart fifteen years of research linking gut microbes to bile duct cancer, in a 2026 bibliometric study. Cholangiocarcinoma research touching the microbiota has grown fast, yet its shape was unmapped. The team mined the Web of Science for work published from 2009 through 2025. Software tools traced publication trends, key authors, institutions, and hot topics. One hundred twenty-four papers made the final set.

Nearly nine hundred researchers at 278 institutions across thirty-seven countries contributed. Output climbed steadily and peaked in 2024. China led in papers and citations, with Italy and the United States behind. Oslo, Khon Kaen, and Palermo universities anchored the institutional map. The freshest frontier centers on metabolism, hunting disease mechanisms and treatment ideas through microbial chemistry. The authors caution that one database skews coverage by region and language. Even so, the map shows newcomers where the field's weight sits.
pmc-13292574:
Yongyong Wang and a large team settle a 2026 practical question in chronic hepatitis B. When standard tests say the virus is gone but sensitive ones still whisper, should patients switch drugs or stay? They enrolled 557 people on first-line nucleos(t)ide therapy for over 48 weeks with negative conventional DNA results, then retested everyone with high-sensitivity assays.

Low-level viremia hid in 35.9 percent of these apparently clear patients, while 64.1 percent were truly suppressed. Older age and longer treatment cut the odds of lingering virus; higher surface antigen, e-antigen positivity, and ALT raised them. After 48 more weeks, complete response hit 81.63 percent in switchers and 86.36 percent in stayers, a meaningless gap. Other markers matched too. The authors say either strategy works for most such patients.
pmc-13292674:
Xiaoqiu Shu and colleagues offer a 2026 review of how the innate immune system helps drive amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal dementia. These two disorders overlap in symptoms, genetics, and the clumped proteins found in nerve cells. The authors argue that immune activation inside the brain is an active cause of decline rather than a side effect of injury.

Attention centers on three connected pathways known as cGAS-STING, the NLRP3 inflammasome, and TREM2-DAP12 signaling. The review traces how disease-linked proteins and gene changes switch these pathways on, and how the pathways can reinforce one another. One loop may even strip a protective receptor from microglia, the brain immune cells that clear debris. Understanding these links could guide combined treatments and new markers for sorting patients into subtypes.
pmc-13292774:
Pouya Navidifar and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study on breeding timing in Holstein dairy cows. The work tested whether a hormone step given before the Heat Synch protocol could lift fertility in cows of different parity.

Cows pre-treated with GnRH or hCG showed stronger signs of heat than cows without that step, based on the study highlights. The hCG group also had higher progesterone levels in blood. Responses looked alike across younger and older cows in the trial. Better heat signs can help farmers time insemination well, which supports the goal of a calf every 12 to 13 months. Larger trials would be needed to confirm the gains.
pmc-13293974:
Yelin Shen and coauthors tell a 2026 nursing case story about repeated breathing tube removal failure after colon surgery. Their patient was an 18-year-old man with Alström syndrome, a rare multi-system genetic disorder. Emergency surgery for a twisted colon included partial sigmoid removal and a stoma, followed by intensive care.

Twice the tube was removed and twice the patient needed it back. Blocked airways, weak cough effort, retained secretions, aspiration risk, and lung infection all played a role. Coordinated care added airway cleaning by scope, drugs to cut secretions, infection checks, and a structured weaning plan. The third removal succeeded, and the patient left hospital stable.
pmc-13294174:
Matheus M. A. Salles and Fabricius M. C. B. Domingos ask how fast lizard mitochondrial DNA changes, and how much the answer depends on method choices, in a 2026 study. Substitution rates anchor estimates of when species diverged, yet they are often borrowed from a few genes or model organisms. The pair used nearly complete mitochondrial genomes from twenty-seven pleurodontan lizard species and tested how data partitioning, calibration, and model settings shift the numbers.

Rates varied sharply across the genome, differing between codon positions and between coding and non-coding stretches. Commonly borrowed rates matched the fastest-evolving sites most closely, suggesting the field's defaults lean on quick-changing signals. Calibrated analyses gave somewhat lower rates with tighter ranges, though intervals overlapped broadly. The authors supply partition-specific rates and urge judging model complexity by how well parameters resolve, not by how many there are.
pmc-13294874:
Maria Eleni Katsanou and co-authors test whether the coatings on sunscreen nanoparticles make them safer for skin cells, in a 2026 laboratory study. Titanium dioxide particles block ultraviolet light well, but sunlight can also excite them into producing reactive oxygen species that damage cells. The group compared uncoated particles with versions wrapped in silica or in an alumina-silica mix, exposing human skin cells called keratinocytes to ultraviolet A light.

Uncoated particles broke down a test dye fastest, showing the strongest light-driven activity, while the alumina-silica coating cut that activity to roughly a third. Cell survival fell with dose and time when ultraviolet light met the particles, and the doubly coated version harmed cells least. Oxidative stress rose in all exposed cells, and a laser-based check revealed damage inside cells, hinting at membrane injury. Coating chemistry, the authors argue, belongs at the center of sunscreen safety testing.
pmc-13294974:
Yang Li and co-authors review a workhorse cell protein that moonlights across a surprising range of diseases, in a 2026 survey of GRP78. Also called BiP, the protein lives mainly in the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's folding workshop, where it keeps new proteins folding correctly and manages the stress response when folding fails. Chemical tweaks such as phosphorylation tune its activity, and under stress it can relocate to the cell surface or nucleus for other jobs.

Misbehavior of GRP78 shows up in cancer, brain degeneration, infections, heart and blood vessel disease, inflammation, and metabolic disorders, sometimes helping and sometimes harming depending on tissue and stage. The review catalogs attempts to drug it, from small molecules to antibodies and gene-based tools, noting strong preclinical promise but weak specificity and slow progress to the clinic. Sharper tools and precision strategies, the authors argue, decide whether the target pays off.
pmc-13295074:
Yuxin Xiong and a large team examine how much activity protects muscle in dialysis patients in a 2026 study. People on peritoneal dialysis move little and often lose muscle strength and mass, a state called sarcopenia. The helpful dose of activity for this group was unknown.

In all, 881 patients from two large Chinese hospitals were assessed for activity, grip, walking function, and muscle amount. Links between activity and muscle loss bent rather than running straight, suggesting a sweet spot exists. Protection appeared once weekly activity passed a stated threshold, and walking function gains levelled off at higher doses, arguing for targeted, not endless, activity goals.
pmc-13295874:
Alberte Laura Oest Müllertz and colleagues report findings in 2026 from the Happy Healthy Active Children project in two poorer Copenhagen neighbourhoods. Seven kindergartens ran weekly outdoor days built around play, nature and cooking, and children wore movement sensors to compare those days with ordinary ones.

Fifty-one children aged three to five gave usable data, acting as their own comparison. On project days they spent more time in brisk activity and less time sitting, with play days showing the biggest gains. Nature and cooking days showed no clear difference. The authors say playful outdoor sessions can lift activity where need is greatest.
pmc-13295974:
Qian Lai and colleagues sort the phenolic compounds of Penthorum chinense leaves by strength of alcohol wash and compare what each share can do, in a 2026 study. The plant, known in China as Gan-Huang-Cao, is rich in protective plant compounds. A macroporous resin split the extract into four shares, washed off at twenty, forty, sixty, and eighty percent ethanol.

Chemistry found eighty-five compounds across the shares, among them phenolic acids, flavonoids, tannins, and anthocyanins. The weakest wash held the most total polyphenols and fought oxidation best, while the forty percent share led on flavonoids. The sixty percent share most strongly blocked a sugar-splitting enzyme tied to blood sugar. The authors match shares to aims, from liver guarding to glucose control.
pmc-13296074:
Junnan Ding and Xin Li study, in 2026, soil fungi in a degraded salty wetland reserve in northeast China and nearby converted farmland. They compare four habitat types at two depths to see how damage, farming and depth reshape fungal life below ground.

Degraded salty patches had the harshest soil, with more salt and alkali but less water and nutrient content. Fungal variety peaked in surface farmland soil and bottomed out deep in degraded patches. One fungal phylum dominated the stressed soils, and most kinds were specialists tied to narrow conditions. The authors say depth and salt together steer these communities, informing wetland repair.
pmc-13296474:
Erin Tsai and colleagues show how mixing two precisely built peptoid polymers creates adjustable micelles, in a 2026 materials study. Peptoids are synthetic chains whose monomer order can be set exactly. The question was whether chains with different charge patterns would mix into shared assemblies or sort themselves apart.

Energy-transfer experiments confirmed that the different chains co-assembled into hybrid micelles in water. X-ray scattering showed that micelle size and the number of chains per micelle shifted with the mixing ratio. Surface water-repellence could also be tuned by changing that ratio, a dye-binding test confirmed. Mixing a small set of sequences thus opens a wider design space for carriers such as drug delivery particles.
pmc-13296774:
Romina-Christiana Pavlovici and a large team review how cytokines, the immune system's signal proteins, drive a destructive tooth condition in a 2026 article. In this condition, cells much like bone-eating cells dissolve tooth root tissue amid lasting swelling. Blows, infection, and dental work can start it, yet they cannot explain why some patients fare far worse than others.

The signal proteins sit at the centre of the team's account. One bone-control pathway, gene variants, and markers in local fluids all shape how fast the root is eaten away. Tests of saliva and gum fluid may one day allow early warning and live tracking. The authors call for shared test rules so the markers can serve precise dental care.
pmc-13297274:
Jamil Haider and co-authors starve, in 2026, vessel-lining cells of glutamine, a fuel amino acid, to see how shortage ages them. The human cell line was watched for an ageing marker plus growth, shape and helper functions, including in a zebrafish graft model.

Starved cells showed more ageing-marker activity, grew poorly and built misshapen networks. They stuck more to passing blood cells and supported host tissue growth less in the fish model. The authors conclude that steady glutamine supply is essential for keeping vessel linings intact, healthy and functionally competent.
pmc-13297474:
Heart muscle diseases are often blamed on genes or on wear and tear. A 2026 review by Antonio Lattanzio and his team makes the case that immune attack plays a core role too. They pulled proof from five diseases, from thick-heart and loose-heart forms to Fabry disease and amyloid buildup.

Each disease starts with a unlike trigger: stored fats, misfolded protein, strain, or bits of virus. All of them switch on the same immune paths, through Toll-like receptors, NF-κB, and the NLRP3 inflammasome. The immune fire then drives scar tissue and stiff walls. If that shared path holds, drugs that calm the immune system could help across all five diseases.
pmc-13297574:
Md Manirujjaman and a large team ask how a Western diet reshapes the fat pad around the mouse breast, in a 2026 study. Obesity raises breast cancer risk, yet its effects on the tissue cradle of the breast stay little studied. Female mice with working immune systems were fed the fat- and sugar-rich diet, and their tissues were weighed and profiled.

The diet raised body, liver, and belly fat weight and drew in myeloid immune cells. Breast fat pads switched on gene programmes for complement, innate defence, cell eating, and immune fuel use. Helper and killer T cells, by contrast, barely changed in the tissues checked. How these shifts feed breast cancer growth needs direct tests, the authors say.
pmc-13297674:
Artificial smarts have barely reached the rooms where sick kids get image-guided care. Abdulaziz Mohammad Al-Sharydah maps that gap in a 2026 review of pediatric interventional radiology, based on papers and society statements through early 2026.

The tools could help at each step of care. They could cut scan dose, read images, plan the path of a needle in 3D, and flag risk after the case ends. Kids bring hard limits, though: they are more prone to harm from scans, their bodies change as they grow, rules are strict, and big labeled data sets are rare. The author points to clear-design AI and shared-data learning as the next steps, with strong rules to keep kids safe.
pmc-13297774:
Diana-Ivette Rivera-Reza and colleagues review markers that might warn when mouth lining changes are turning toward cancer, in a 2026 survey. Abnormal mouth lining, called oral epithelial dysplasia, behaves unpredictably: some lesions progress and many do not. The team gathered studies that stained tissue for signs of a shift in which cells loosen their epithelial nature, a step tied to invasion.

Twenty-one studies covered fifty-seven markers in all. Just twelve studies carried a low risk of bias. Among the sound, conclusive ones, two markers stood out: falling E-cadherin, the glue protein of epithelium, and rising vimentin, a marker of the looser state. Thin statistical backing still tempers the claim, the authors warn.
pmc-13297874:
Ion Lingenheil and colleagues review operations that rebuild the breast from a patient's own tissue while also repairing lymph drainage, in a 2026 survey. Breast cancer care can leave arm swelling when lymph nodes are lost, and reconstruction is often a separate second surgery. Twenty-seven studies covering 499 patients, followed about two years, met the entry rules.

The usual pairing moved lower belly tissue with its lymph nodes to the chest, rebuilding the breast and easing drainage at once. Arm swelling fell, infections grew rarer, and quality of life rose. Problems were uncommon, mostly small fluid pockets, and loss of the moved tissue was very rare. Longer, more uniform studies still need to follow.
pmc-13298274:
Sebastian Contreras leads a 2026 laboratory study on heat generated during implant drilling in bone. Excess heat can harm healing and implant integration, so drill system, motor, and irrigation choices matter. Osteotomies in bovine rib blocks compared two drill kits, two motors, and rinsing conditions, with temperatures captured by thermal camera and probe.

Drilling without rinsing consistently gave higher bone temperatures. Regression analysis found one motor lowered temperature significantly, while a lance drill without added irrigation raised it. Final temperatures stayed near room range when rinsing was used. The authors conclude rinsing, above all paired with the cooler motor, protects bone during osteotomy preparation.
pmc-13298374:
Nearly three in ten Kazakh adults sleep poorly, finds a 2026 national survey led by Yerlan Ismoldayev. Interviewers collected Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index data from 5,872 adults aged 18 to 69 during the first survey wave after the country adopted a single time zone.

The weighted share with poor sleep was 28.1%, driven mainly by trouble falling asleep and disturbed nights rather than medication use. Odds ran higher for women, older adults, city dwellers, smokers, heavy drinkers, and people with diabetes. Depressive symptoms carried the strongest link, an adjusted odds ratio of 4.26. Rural residents slept better, and several regions fared worse than the North. The authors frame the results as a baseline for sleep health policy.
pmc-13299074:
Fragments of DNA floating in the blood might help sort psychiatric patients by inflammation, propose Chiara Galbiati and colleagues in a 2026 review. Cell-free DNA, shed by damaged and dying cells, can itself provoke immune signaling, and its mitochondrial portion is especially reactive.

The authors gather evidence across depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia, linking altered levels to stress exposure, childhood trauma, mitochondrial strain, and hormone axis disruption. Findings remain mixed and methods unstandardized, which they acknowledge plainly. Even so, they argue these fragments could eventually stratify patients for personalized treatment, especially if combined with other omics data and methylation patterns that reveal which tissue shed the DNA.
pmc-13299374:
Which proteins cling to a long noncoding RNA can betray where in the cell it lives, demonstrates Hidenori Tani in a 2026 computational study. Localization decides what these RNAs do, and most predictors read only the sequence itself.

Crosslinking data for 139 RNA-binding proteins in K562 cells predicted nuclear versus cytoplasmic residence better than transcript size or total binding alone, with an AUC of 0.73. Proteins tied to splicing and other nuclear jobs pulled predictions toward the nucleus, while translation-related proteins pulled toward the cytoplasm, a pattern that transferred to a second cell line. The author offers the occupancy approach as an interpretable companion to sequence-based tools.
pmc-13299474:
Men in long-term treatment for cybersex addiction share early starts and fragile self-esteem, describe Luís Lorente-Corral and colleagues in a 2026 clinical profile study. Their cohort held 27 people, twenty-six men and one woman, enrolled in therapeutic support programs and assessed with standardized screening and self-esteem scales.

Pornography use showed high intensity and early onset, and 48.1% of participants scored low on self-esteem. Neither starting age nor self-esteem tracked with how severe the disorder currently was. One pattern stood out: patients with longer time in therapy showed fewer impulse-control difficulties. The authors suggest sustained, nursing-led support may stabilize this patient group.
pmc-13300474:
Gabriel Fiakpornu and Naoto Kamata study what shapes fungus-carrying pits on a beetle that spreads Japanese oak wilt, in a 2026 paper. Female Platypus quercivorus beetles transport the wilt fungus in small pits on the thorax, called mycangia, so pit number may influence how widely the disease travels. The team raised beetles at different controlled temperatures and compared daughters of mothers with many pits against daughters of mothers with few.

Cooler rearing produced larger beetles carrying more pits, while warmer conditions gave smaller beetles with fewer pits. Maternal influence also showed through, since daughters of high-pit mothers tended to develop more pits themselves. The authors conclude that both environment and inheritance set this trait. They argue that forest managers forecasting oak wilt spread should weigh warming climates alongside the beetle's genetics.
pmc-13300774:
E Simsek and co-authors describe left sided sympathetic ganglion block for recurrent ventricular tachycardia in patients living on left ventricular assist devices, in a 2026 case series. These patients face shocks, decompensation, and high mortality when the rhythm keeps returning despite drugs. The retrospective review covered nine recipients at one center who received the radiofrequency block after repeated defibrillator shocks, all while on beta-blockers and other antiarrhythmic medicines.

Over a median follow-up of eight months, about forty-four percent had no recurrence at all, and seventy-seven percent stayed free of tachycardia beyond the first week after the block. Two patients died and one received a transplant during follow-up. No permanent complications occurred, although every patient had a temporary drooping eyelid on the treated side that resolved. The authors offer the block as a useful adjunct for selected assist device patients.
pmc-13301074:
M Velescu and co-authors search for what drives atrial fibrillation recurrence in the year after radiofrequency ablation, in a 2026 study built on two tissue markers. Low voltage areas on atrial maps and P wave dispersion on the electrocardiogram both hint at fibrotic, slow conducting tissue. The team split 196 patients treated between 2021 and 2024 into four groups by whether each marker ran high or low, then weighed common cofactors against recurrence.

The combined high group, carrying both low voltage tissue and wide P wave dispersion, showed the strongest association with recurrence, and the marker pairing overall reached statistical significance with a medium effect. Individual comorbidities such as hypertension, lung disease, and heart failure raised concern clinically. Yet none acted as an independent predictor in the best fitting model, which still classified about seventy-one percent of outcomes correctly. The authors call for prospective confirmation.
pmc-13301174:
Removing a small lung segment instead of a whole lobe demands a map of one patient's private anatomy, Victor A. Shahen and Cheng-Hon Yap argue in a 2026 narrative review. Three-dimensional bronchovascular modelling rebuilds segmental arteries, veins, and airways from CT scans, replacing the mental guesswork that flat images impose on thoracic surgeons.

Segmental branching varies widely between people, and missing a variant can mean bleeding or wrong margins during sublobar resection for early lung cancer. Patient-specific models sharpen planning before surgery and decisions inside it, especially through keyhole approaches with limited view and feel. The authors weigh present limits and foresee modelling woven into routine personalised thoracic care.
pmc-13301374:
C Mages and co-authors compare how much vein isolation hurts afterward under two single shot techniques in a 2026 prospective study. One hundred one patients with paroxysmal or persistent atrial fibrillation received either cryoballoon or pulsed field ablation under a deep sedation mix of propofol, midazolam, and fentanyl. Pain scores were recorded right after the procedure, at six to eight hours, and between eight and twenty-four hours.

Pulsed field cases ran shorter, a median thirty-six minutes against sixty-one, yet needed significantly more of every sedative per kilogram. Reported pain, though, refused to separate. Twelve percent of patients hurt immediately, about a third by the middle check, and three quarters by the last. The pain was mostly mild groin discomfort rating two out of ten, with extra painkillers rarely requested. The authors conclude the experience is tolerable under both, which matters as same day discharge becomes the goal.
pmc-13301474:
Elisabeth M. Mandler and co-authors map where a foot surgeon can cut during plantar release in a 2026 anatomical study. The operation frees the plantar aponeurosis and neighboring tissues for heel pain and high arched cavovarus feet, but nerves and vessels thread through the crowded territory with variation. Forty-one cadaver feet were dissected, measuring distances between the muscle's origins and each nearby nerve.

Two of the muscle's four origins appeared in every specimen, while the middle two varied. The tightest squeezes: the medial calcaneal nerve passed about three millimeters from the first origin, and both plantar nerves ran within roughly three to five millimeters of the second. The authors chart high risk zones around those spots and low risk zones at the back of the heel bone and near the ankle. Their message is humility: the anatomy varies enough that a patient specific plan beats a standard map.
pmc-13301674:
Maria Concetta Torrione and co-authors examine how often ductal carcinoma in situ comes back in a 2026 study. The group covered 403 patients with non invasive disease at one center between 2016 and 2023, 417 lesions. Care was breast conserving surgery or mastectomy. With overtreatment a debate, the team compared returning and non returning patients across imaging, tissue findings, and treatment choices.

Only twenty-one returns, about five percent, appeared. Over half were non invasive, though about thirty-eight percent had turned invasive. Most returns followed breast conserving surgery. About half of these patients had skipped radiotherapy. None had received hormone therapy, despite every returning case being estrogen receptor positive at diagnosis. Neither grade nor size separated the groups. No distant spread or deaths were recorded. The authors argue that clinical factors cannot sort risk. They favor combined assessment to spare low risk patients treatment.
pmc-13302374:
M A R Desouki and co-authors report, in a 2026 registry study, paroxysmal atrial fibrillation ablation with a catheter that can deliver two energy types. The Sphere-9 tool mixes pulsed field and radiofrequency energy and had been tested mainly in persistent cases. The team compared it against a pulsed-field-only catheter and standard radiofrequency tools.

The cohort held 139 patients treated between October 2024 and June 2025, including first and repeat procedures. The dual-energy catheter achieved full procedural efficacy in every case, ahead of both comparators, and finished fastest at a median of eighty-four minutes. Early major adverse events were fewest in that group, though three-month rhythm recurrence rates were similar across all three. Longer follow-up in more patients is still needed.
pmc-13302774:
Hunting gene pairs that act together across the whole genome just became a browser task, Lars Wienbrandt and colleagues announce in a 2026 software paper. Their free service, GWAIS-Web, screens pairwise and three-way SNP interactions in large case-control datasets, work that once demanded years of computing. Tasks run on graphics processors and FPGA hardware hosted by the service, keeping user data privacy-compliant.

Speedups top a thousandfold over established CPU tools, cutting runtimes from years to days. Supported methods include PLINK's logistic regression test and BOOST, with linkage-based SNP filtering and region-restricted runs. Standalone code is public, so groups can also run the accelerated pipeline on their own machines.
pmc-13303574:
Hongjie Li heads a 2026 materials study on protective nickel-boron coatings strengthened with tiny lanthanum oxide particles. The coatings were placed on N80 carbon steel by electroless plating, a chemical method that needs no electric current.

Changing the particle dose in the bath altered coating shape, makeup, and resistance to corrosion. Microscopy and related tests showed a dense layer about 10 micrometers thick with particles spread evenly. The best dose refined the crystal grains, helped a steady protective film form, and blocked corrosive fluids more effectively. The work offers a route to longer-lasting steel parts in harsh settings.
pmc-13303974:
Abdur-Rahman Ridwan leads a 2026 trial protocol testing what draws people into a phone-based well-being study with repeated short check-ins. Such moment-by-moment tracking reveals daily life well, but the burden of frequent prompts keeps many groups from using it.

About 4,809 users of a community platform for the King's Cross area of London will be assigned by chance to one of three invitations. One offers entry into a prize draw for shopping vouchers, one invites people to a feedback event, and one offers nothing extra. Reasons for refusal and preferred rewards will also be gathered.
pmc-13304574:
Melissa Huynh Mabry and colleagues report a 2026 single-center look at brain stimulation for epilepsy left after viral brain infection. Seizures that resist drugs often start at several spots after such infections, blocking removal surgery.

Nine patients received a responsive stimulator that senses and answers seizure activity. Four met the responder bar with at least half fewer seizures after about three years of follow-up. Responders had lived fewer years with drug-resistant seizures before the device went in. Seizure types that spread across the whole brain stopped in all responders. Early, tiny numbers call for caution.
pmc-13305074:
Ui-Bin Baek and Hack-Youn Kim test high-pressure processing for raw beef meant for pet food in a 2026 study. Squeezing food at great pressure can kill germs without heat, but effects on meat quality during storage need checking.

Beef loin was treated at four pressure levels for varied times, then refrigerated for two weeks. Counts of five harmful germ types fell as pressure and time rose, and the strongest treatment pushed one germ below detection for the whole storage span. Color lightened and yellowness rose, firmness and water holding climbed, and fat oxidation markers increased with pressure.
pmc-13306174:
Jakub Niestępski and colleagues review in 2026 what illnesses children and teens bring back to Europe after travel abroad. Thirty-one studies issued since 2010 were brought together under standard review guidance. Special focus went to malaria groups, other illnesses, and syndrome-based reports.

Malaria was the illness logged again and again, usually Plasmodium falciparum caught in sub-Saharan Africa. Trips to see friends and kin led travel reasons in malaria reports. Gut illnesses led many mixed groups, with other bacterial and parasitic illnesses beside them. Study designs and write-ups varied so much that pooling results was not possible. The authors call for shared, child-focused tracking after travel. Doctors are urged to weigh travel history, place visited, and symptoms as one when naming the illness.
pmc-13306474:
Juro Živičnjak introduced a digital imaging method for judging surface fuzz on fabrics in a 2026 textile study. Loose surface fibres roughen cloth during wear, yet the standard eye test suits stronger damage such as pilling better than fine fuzz.

A new viewing device images fuzz separately from pilling on the same cloth sample by refining the viewing angle, and companion software returns numeric measures. Six single-fibre woven fabrics in cotton, wool, viscose and synthetics supplied test material. The authors present objective counts as a fairer base for comparing how cloth surfaces age.
pmc-13307874:
Jiannan Li and colleagues engineer a vaccine in 2026 that uses Pseudomonas aeruginosa's own membrane bubbles to deliver one of its proteins, PcrV. Bubbles carrying the protein were compared in mice with free protein and with simple mixtures. The bacterium resists many antibiotics and threatens intensive care and burn patients, so vaccine options matter.

Microscopy confirmed round nanoscale bubbles of the expected size carrying the cargo. After challenge, bubble-based groups reached complete protection against skin-route infection. The engineered bubble group cleared lung colonisation better and caused less inflammatory injury than controls. T cell counts and several antibody classes also rose higher with bubble delivery. Making the bacterium produce its own delivery vehicle beat simply mixing parts together. The authors present the construct as experimental support for a Pseudomonas vaccine programme.
pmc-13308674:
Elisio Pereira, Grant Taylor, and Kylie N Johnston study in 2026 what South Australian providers need before a physio led heart and lung service joins a hospital at home scheme. They spoke with one manager and seven private physiotherapists in semi structured talks and sorted the replies by shared themes.

Staff felt unsure who should be sent, what physio would do, and how risk at home would be held in the new scheme. Few had fresh hands on work in home based heart and lung care, yet most saw the patients as stable overall. Training, clear rules, gear access, oversight, and lean notes topped the need list. Fit with private work loads will make or break uptake.
pmc-13309674:
Mohamed M G Mohamed and colleagues report a hard diagnostic case of stubborn pneumonia after a stem cell transplant in a 2026 article. The patient, a 63-year-old woman with leukemia, kept coughing with a lung patch that standard drugs barely improved. Tests pointed to Mycoplasma, a germ that can resist the usual first drug in its class.

Blood tests also flagged a fungal infection common in dry regions, which led to antifungal treatment. Deeper confirmatory tests came back negative, and the patient had no exposure risk for that fungus, so the antifungal was stopped. A different antibiotic plus antibody replacement brought clear improvement, with oxygen needs ending. The authors warn that stray positive tests can divert care in fragile hosts.
pmc-13310374:
Peter Lodemann tracks iron and ferritin in blood after combined COVID and flu shots in a 2026 case report. Both measures swing during inflammation, yet their week-by-week course after vaccination was poorly charted. One patient agreed to a set sampling timeline around the shots.

Blood was drawn from vaccination through six weeks after, with pre-shot values as the personal baseline. The shots triggered a sharp drop in blood iron alongside a rise in ferritin, the iron storage marker. Ferritin returned to baseline within six weeks, while iron climbed steadily back. Past flu shots alone had caused this patient no such reaction. The author offers the timeline as a template for larger vaccine response studies.
pmc-13310774:
Yanlin Zhong and colleagues test eyelid lump care guided by a smart risk model in a 2026 study. Chalazion lumps often return after treatment, and doctors lack a firm way to pick who needs stronger care. Care options include a steroid shot, light therapy, or both together.

Care covered 366 patients followed for return of lumps. Combined care cleared the most cases at three months and had the lowest return rate. Age, mite infection, long duration, and gland trouble raised return risk. A hybrid smart model sorted risk better than a standard model alone. High risk patients still relapsed often, even on combined care, so close watch matters.
pmc-13311074:
Mingyu Zhang and colleagues review smart fusion of many data types for breast cancer care in a 2026 paper. Breast cancer varies widely in genes, images, and tumor surroundings, so single source tests miss key traits. Deep learning can now join scan traits, tissue images, gene data, blood markers, and clinic facts in one model.

Joined models beat single source tools at diagnosis, subtype calls, drug response forecasts, and outlook grading in past studies. New paths include patient digital twins, tiny leftover disease tracking, and large multimodal language models. Shared data rules, clear model logic, and multi center proof still block routine clinic use.
pmc-13311174:
Junxiong Yu and colleagues optimize salt shock steps for ectoine making in salt loving germs in a 2026 study. Halomonas elongata can ferment cheaply in open, non sterile tanks, yet pushing ectoine yield past its ceiling is hard. Graded salt jumps were designed and tuned with flux maps and learning models.

Stepwise salt stress shifted carbon flow from energy making toward product building, boosting key paths and precursor supply. A joint learning model plus a genetic search found a best five stage salt plan. Scale up reached record yield, speed, and cell mass in 28 hours of ferment time. The frame may guide other salt germ processes.
pmc-13311274:
Mano Harshadan and co-authors, in 2026, describe a case of lymph-node-first Kawasaki disease hidden behind a deep neck infection in an infant. The picture at first looked like a pus-forming infection of the neck and chest.

The child had fever, swollen glands, and abscesses near the throat and chest that only partly answered antibiotics. Heart scans then showed widened coronary arteries with an aneurysm, pointing to Kawasaki disease. Drainage of the abscess plus immune globulin treatment led to full recovery. The case urges doctors to think of Kawasaki disease when fever and gland swelling persist despite antibiotics.
pmc-13311374:
Valentin Quemard and colleagues give their 2026 systematic review on whether ankylosing spondylitis, a spine inflammation illness, travels with periodontitis, a gum disease. Both are long-term inflammatory conditions.

Searches of four databases followed PRISMA 2020 rules and screened 255 records down to 18 sound studies. Gum disease rates in spine patients gave mixed answers across studies. Gum measures such as bleeding and pocket depth often tracked with spine disease activity scores, though not always clearly. Anti-TNF drugs seemed to ease some gum measures. The review shows a link worth probing, not a settled one.
pmc-13311574:
Robert Klaus Uhrich, Craig Beringer, and Louis Chadinha survey emergency doctors in Johannesburg on nerve-block pain relief for hip fractures in a 2026 study. Blocks can ease pain well, yet use varies.

Eighty doctors at three university-linked hospitals answered the survey. Only 39 percent had had hip-fracture-specific block training, and half of those felt ready to do the blocks. Knowledge scores were middling on technique and side effects but stronger on when not to use a block. Views were warm, with 93 percent calling the method safe and effective. Training gaps, not attitudes, look like the main brake.
pmc-13311974:
Alan Shaun Wilkinson and co-authors present their 2026 integrity assessment of two needle-free closed transfer devices used as end closures for syringes and IV bags holding chemotherapy drugs. British guidance demands proof the seal holds in storage and transit.

Both physical dye tests and a fourteen-day microbial challenge with Brevundimonas diminuta were run on syringe adapters and vented bag spikes from the ChemoClave and ChemoLock lines. A vibration challenge mimicked a typical transport trip, logged on three axes. Positive and negative controls anchored the readouts. Pharmacy services need such data before preparing doses in advance.
pmc-13312074:
José Francisco López-Gil and co-authors argue, in a 2026 policy article, that Latin America's rules on food labels and child-directed advertising are not enough to improve child nutrition. Warning labels and marketing limits have spread across the region, Ecuador included, yet childhood overweight and obesity keep climbing because ultra-processed foods still dominate shops, screens, and schools.

The authors contend that labels only help when healthier food is present, affordable, and competitive where people buy. They propose added steps: healthier school food settings, price incentives for minimally processed foods, rules for digital marketing, and closer ties to local food systems. Their framework also calls for guarding policy against industry capture, so that the default diet children face actually changes.
pmc-13312174:
Farzad Rostami and colleagues report a 2026 study of how frontal brain injury changes risky decision-making when the outcome affects the patient or someone else. The study enrolled twenty patients with frontal damage and 20 matched controls. Each accepted or rejected mixed gambles, choosing either for themselves or for an anonymous other person.

Patients accepted more bad gambles than controls when choosing for themselves, yet turned more cautious when choosing for another, while controls showed no such split. A four-parameter prospect theory model fit best, and patients showed nearly straight probability weighting, steeper utility curvature, and weaker loss aversion. Modeling pointed to reduced loss aversion as the main driver of the extra risky acceptances. Damage overlapped most in ventral and medial prefrontal areas, giving a mechanism for the split behavior.
pmc-13312274:
Elizabeth Randell and co-authors report a 2026 feasibility study of Watch Me Play!, a play-based program for young children delivered remotely to families referred to United Kingdom services. The intervention builds child development and emotional resilience through child-led play with a caregiver, at a time when children's mental health problems are rising and waiting lists are long.

Families and providers found the program acceptable, reported adherence was 80 percent, and mixing online with face-to-face sessions worked. Average cost came to £209 per family. Limited staff capacity was the main barrier. The authors judge the core approach feasible and recommend a randomized feasibility trial next.
pmc-13312574:
Bilal Hamamra and co-authors present a 2026 qualitative study of what war and displacement have done to elderly people in Gaza. Older adults face frailty, chronic illness, and the collapse of the community networks that once held them. The team asked how repeated forced displacement, deprivation, and lost dignity feel from inside that experience.

The team held long interviews with forty elderly men and women living in shelters in Rafah. They showed displacement shattering any sense of home and safety, feeding chronic anxiety, grief, and disorientation. Collapsed health services and blocked access to medicines deepened physical suffering and helplessness, while crowded, unsanitary shelters stripped privacy and autonomy. Many held on through faith, the cultural value of sumud, or steadfastness, and mutual help, though the authors warn those resources are stretched to breaking and plead for age-sensitive aid.
pmc-13314574:
Takamichi Sugimoto and colleagues compare two ways of catching muscle twitches in ALS in a study appearing in 2026. Fasciculations, small involuntary twitches, can be seen on muscle ultrasound and heard as signals on needle electromyography, but how the two views line up was not known.

The team recorded both methods at the same time in up to three muscles per patient, for 3 minutes each, in adults later proven to have amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Ten patients were included, and 472 ultrasound twitch events were checked one by one against the needle record, as counted in the report. They also timed each twitch by M-mode imaging. Matched records let the authors judge whether ultrasound alone can stand in for the needle test when hunting this disease sign.
pmc-13314674:
Yutaro Sakamoto and Ryuichi Kumagai propose a simple way to size group bias in a whole test, in a paper from 2026. Differential test functioning checks whether a test favors a group beyond real skill gaps, and its size reads best in raw score points.

Most gauges rest on item response theory models, which many users lack. Their Index S sorts test takers by a clean anchor score built from items not flagged for bias. It then averages the score gaps within each band, weighted by how many takers sit there. Sparse bands are merged to keep each group big enough, and a standardized form is also given. Fake-data tests with a two-parameter model, varying group size and other settings, checked how the index behaves. The tool brings bias checks within reach of plain sum scores.
pmc-13314874:
Ling Zou, Feng Li, Hongyu Li, and Zhihong Su hunt a blood sign for seizure return in sick toddlers, in a study from 2026. Benign convulsions with mild stomach flu are common in young children, yet doctors lack a quick test for which child will seize again within two days.

The team reviewed children aged 6 months to 6 years treated from 2020 to 2026. Of 86 children, with a median age of 14.5 months as stated in the report, a total of 23 seized again, a share of 26.7 percent in the figures given. Blood total carbon dioxide at admission ran higher in those who relapsed, at median values of 17.4 against 15.1 mmol per liter as reported. Adjusted models kept the link, and younger age also raised risk. A routine blood value may help wards watch the right children closer.
pmc-13315974:
Siti Azyyati Nur Shadrina and a large team pooled studies in 2026 on a simple blood ratio as a marker for erythema nodosum leprosum. That is a severe leprosy reaction that recurs and can damage nerves. Diagnosis still leans on clinical judgment and tests that are often missing in low-resource settings.

The neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio comes from a routine blood count and costs little, making it attractive where leprosy care runs. Following standard review rules, the team searched four databases to late November 2025 for studies comparing the ratio in reaction versus non-reaction leprosy. They graded quality and pooled mean differences, with checks for study variation.
pmc-13316274:
Ran Ao and colleagues built an automated detector in 2026 for sharp epileptic discharges between seizures on scalp EEG, a key diagnostic sign that human reading finds slowly and unevenly. Their Epilepsy-IEDs model learned from 141 recordings holding 2,597 discharges and 4,633 non-discharge segments.

Four algorithms were compared, with a separate daytime check to control for sleep effects. The gradient boosting model won, reaching sensitivity of 84.6 percent on the full set and 87.1 percent on daytime data, with strong area under the curve values in both tests. A slim ten-feature version kept strong performance for clinic use.
pmc-13316674:
George Ladas, Joseph Cascone and Ahmed H. Badawi report, in 2026, blistering pellagra in a woman with alcohol use disorder and a prior gastric bypass. Pellagra comes from lack of niacin, also called vitamin B3, or poor use of tryptophan. It classically causes skin rash, diarrhoea and confusion, and untreated disease can be fatal.

The 31-year-old arrived with a painful burning erosive rash that began on one arm and spread to both legs after sun exposure. She had nausea and vomiting and a history of alcoholic pancreatitis. Another hospital had first treated her for erythema multiforme with an antiviral and steroids, based on a biopsy showing dead surface skin. Recognition of pellagra redirected care toward replacing the missing vitamin.
pmc-13316874:
Friday Ogbu Edeh and Nurul Mohammad Zayed wrote a 2026 editorial introducing a research collection on ethical leadership and workplace fairness. Its theme is the emotional labor staff perform when they must display feelings they do not hold. Service workers, for instance, stay polite while frustrated inside.

The editors frame fair leadership as behavior that models right conduct, explains decisions clearly, and cuts perceived bias, building cultures where dignity is respected. They trace three routes by which such leadership may lift wellbeing: felt support from the organization, safety to speak up, and related work conditions. Studies in the collection test the middle steps and boundary conditions of those routes. The issue aims to guide fairer management of emotionally demanding jobs.
pmc-13317774:
Maisaa Hassan Abd-Alkareem, Hussam Eddin Mohammed Shibli, and Faizeh Ali Alquobaili test, in a 2026 Syrian study, a variant in the apelin gene. They ask whether it tracks with coronary artery disease; the gene makes a vessel-relaxing hormone. The variant sits in the gene's promoter, the dimmer switch region.

The case-control study enrolled 108 patients and 114 healthy controls, measuring blood apelin and gene type. Patients carried far lower apelin levels on average. Among women only, the mixed TC gene form and the C variant appeared much more often in patients, tripling odds in the reported figures, while men showed no pattern. Gene type did not clearly move blood levels. A sex-specific genetic risk, the authors suggest, deserves wider testing.
pmc-13318574:
Ming Li and Guoyi Gao review a 2026 diagnostic problem in brain imaging. Enlarged ventricles on scans can mean hydrocephalus, where fluid dynamics are disturbed. They can also mean harmless widening from brain shrinkage. Mixing the two up can cause needless shunt surgery or missed treatment.

The authors weigh imaging signs such as the Evans index and callosal angle. They also cover scans that track fluid movement and tissue structure. Fluid pressure testing and spinal infusion studies add another angle. Fluid proteins like tau and amyloid may help separate causes. Symptoms alone overlap too much to settle the question. They propose combining imaging, fluid tests, markers, and symptoms into one framework.
pmc-13318774:
Fangfang Zhou and colleagues present a 2026 prospective study of a new ultrasound method for breast lesions. Microvascular flow imaging shows tiny tumour vessels better than standard colour Doppler. The team also built machine learning models using the new measures. Their goal was sharper separation of benign and malignant lumps.

The sample held 101 lesions from 79 patients. Flow imaging found blood flow in 16 lesions that Doppler had missed. Reader agreement was also higher with the new method. A vascular index ran much higher in cancers, at a median of 20.25 against 3.10 for benign lesions in their data. Among eight models, a nearest-neighbour model scored best, with 0.927 accuracy on test data. Age and imaging category were the top predictors.
pmc-13318874:
Haini He and colleagues describe a 2026 case of a severe drug-alcohol reaction in a four-year-old boy. He was in hospital with bronchopneumonia, receiving the antibiotic cefoperazone-sulbactam. Treatment had worked well for seven days. On day eight he accidentally drank a small amount of an alcoholic cocktail.

About ten minutes later, during his antibiotic infusion, he collapsed into shock. Signs included widespread rash, flushing, breathing trouble, and blood pressure of 70/50 mmHg in the reported episode. His heart rate hit 180 beats per minute. Doctors first suspected allergy, then learned of the drink. Stopping the drug, oxygen, fluids, and a steroid brought recovery within hours. He went home two days later, fully well at two weeks.
pmc-13318974:
Bing Zhai leads a large team reporting a 2026 feasibility study of sleep trackers for predicting next-day fatigue. Participants had neurodegenerative or immune-mediated inflammatory diseases, plus healthy controls. In total, 134 people across four European centres wore three trackers at home. They logged fatigue and sleepiness daily over 3,062 nights.

Trackers agreed moderately with laboratory sleep studies in a validation subgroup. Prediction worked best for physical fatigue in healthy adults, reaching an AUC of 0.75 in their models. Breathing rate and REM sleep duration drove that result. In disease groups, accuracy was weaker, near 0.62 to 0.66 across outcomes in the analyses. pmc-13319674:
Eliane de Morais Machado and co-authors revisit trial data on knee pain tests in a 2026 study of pain around the kneecap. The ache hits about one in four young people and adults and often lasts for years. Clinics use tasks such as stepping and squatting to provoke the pain and track change, while patients also rate pain and life quality on forms.

Whether scores on the tasks move with what patients report was the core check. A stepping test that sets a pain threshold tracked most closely with patient forms on pain, life quality, and sport. A squat test tracked with none of the forms. Stepping scores may thus help clinics follow progress alongside patient reports.
pmc-13319974:
Rachel Hor and co-authors lay out a review plan in a 2026 protocol on openness steps and trust in smart software at work. Firms increasingly show staff how smart tools reach calls, by sharing rules, steps, or leader notes. Such openness may shift two kinds of trust at once, trust in the tool aided call and trust in the human who owns it, a pairing past reviews have not joined.

Counts from number based studies will be pooled, while word based findings will be grouped by theme, then the two strands will be read together. The aim is to show which openness steps build or drain each kind of trust.
pmc-13321374:
Hillary M Topazian, Camille E Morgan, and Varun Goel map links between animal ownership and malaria across Africa in a 2026 study. Keeping animals near homes has long been proposed to divert mosquitoes, yet past findings were mixed. Simple models tied ownership of cattle, poultry, goats, and other stock to higher infection odds, between 1.55 and 1.67 in the report. Finer models flipped the picture by area, with effects ranging from protective to harmful. Vector type, herd size, and land cover did not explain the swings, pointing to local culture and ecology.
pmc-13322174:
Saalwirth and co-authors study how climate emotions relate to wellbeing and green behaviour in this 2026 paper. Many people now report eco worry and eco hopelessness, meaning dread that nothing can be done. The team asked whether these feelings differ when aimed at one's own life or at society as a whole. They ran two surveys with adults in Germany.

The first study had 339 participants and the second had 313, and both gave the same pattern. Hopelessness went with lower emotional wellbeing and life satisfaction, while worry showed no such link. Worry, not hopelessness, was the feeling tied to environmentally friendly behaviour. Hopelessness about one's own situation hurt wellbeing most, while worry about society drove action most. Saalwirth argues the two emotions should never be lumped together.
pmc-13322874:
Nitesh Kumar Yadav and co-authors feed rohu fish a plant extract diet under winter cold stress, in a 2026 feeding trial. Fingerlings received Wolffia globosa extract at four levels for 75 days in outdoor tanks, where water stayed near 18 to 22 degrees during the season.

Fish on the extract showed stronger non-specific immune measures, better antioxidant defence and healthier blood and liver markers than controls, alongside improved body protein and lipid content. Serum glucose fell while total protein and albumin rose, and liver stress markers declined. Gene activity linked to immunity and defence also changed. The authors present the extract as a feed addition that may help farmed rohu cope with winter conditions.
pmc-13324274:
Valtteri Peitso and a large team review cell therapy products for osteoarthritis, in a 2026 article on next-generation care. Joint injections such as hyaluronic acid, platelet-rich plasma and anti-inflammatory drugs ease symptoms briefly but do not change disease course, leaving a gap for early to moderate disease.

Cell products aim to calm joint inflammation, slow senescence-linked paths and support cartilage matrix through signals they release. Trial signals encourage, yet only a few products hold approval worldwide. Wide variation in cell source and strength, short survival inside joints, small trials and factory and regulatory hurdles slow progress. The authors ask for proof of edge over simpler joint preparations, clear redosing plans and long-term data.
pmc-13324474:
Michaela Caboňová and colleagues question how new fungal species get introduced in print, in a 2026 analysis of taxonomy papers. Fungi may number in the millions, yet only a small share are formally named, and habitat loss makes the naming work urgent.

The authors reviewed species descriptions from 2020 to 2024 in six large genera, covering 591 new basidiomycete and 322 new ascomycete species. Most appeared in papers on a few close relatives, but multi-species release papers are growing. Introductions in single-lineage papers often gave only genus-level background, and just 25 percent scored above half the expected detail. Most new species claims rest on DNA alone. The authors argue for fuller context so readers can judge each claim.
pmc-13324674:
Shanza Ashraf and colleagues study amla fruit as a possible aid against urinary tract infections in a 2026 paper that also develops a functional tea. Such infections strike nearly 40 percent of women in their lifetime, and drug resistance keeps shrinking antibiotic options.

The team profiles those chemicals with LC-ESI-MS/MS methods as part of judging the fruit for infection care. Their work answers calls for plant-based options where standard drugs fail more often, above all in South Asia. A tea format would make any benefit easy to take daily.
pmc-13325874:
Tymofii Sokolskyi and David Baum test whether simple fatty bubbles can evolve without genes in a 2026 experiment. Fatty acid vesicles grow and split on their own, making them a stand-in for the first cell-like systems.

The team ran 192 separate vesicle populations through daily feeding and transfer rounds. Half the lines were bred from the cloudiest tubes, and half at random as drift controls. Across three runs of at least ten generations, selected lines grew consistently cloudier than controls. Follow-up tests ruled out simple carryover soup as the cause. Instead, a few surviving parent vesicles seemed to coach new material into shared structures, a cooperative inheritance without DNA.
pmc-13326974:
Rémy Masson and colleagues published a brain-imaging study in 2026 on attention problems in migraine. They asked whether people with episodic migraine without aura handle distraction differently between attacks. Brain activity was recorded with magnetoencephalography, a method that tracks fast magnetic signals from the cortex.

Nineteen patients and nineteen healthy adults did a task with visual cues, sounds to attend to, and distracting sounds. Patients showed a weaker rise in alpha activity over visual areas while waiting for a target sound, which points to poorer blocking of sight-related input that did not matter. Other measures did not differ between groups. Weak top-down blocking could help explain why distraction and sensory overload are common in migraine.
pmc-13327074:

Their 2026 look-back multi-site study covered 127 people aged 65 or older with AO/OTA 23-C1 or C2 wrist breaks and later slip during follow-up. Of these, 78 stayed with watchful care while 49 had late surgery. Bone and use results were checked at three and twelve months.

Surgery gave better short-term bone and use results, but by twelve months no clear gaps stayed in either area. The team holds that care should fit the break type, line-up steadiness, and each person's own factors, since long-term results meet.
pmc-13327874:
Shen Dongxing and colleagues assess focused radiation for brain spread of HER2-positive breast cancer in a 2026 hospital review. Kinase inhibitor drugs help many such patients, but the brain can still worsen at a few spots. The review covered 40 patients treated with stereotactic radiotherapy for limited brain progression between January 2020 and January 2025.

Median time without brain progression after radiation was 6.4 months, and overall survival came to a median of 9.5 months at a median follow-up of 10.7 months across the group. Patients whose scans had been stable before progression fared better, at 7.9 months against 5.5 months for those already progressing. Severe side effects included diarrhea and anemia at 20 percent each.
pmc-13328174:
Xinyan Chen and a large team compile best evidence on digital health for coronary artery disease self-care in a 2026 summary. Following Joanna Briggs Institute methods, they searched major English and Chinese databases through November 2025 and graded evidence with the GRADE approach. From 5,312 records, 38 studies qualified.

The kept sources held six guidelines, thirteen systematic reviews, fifteen randomized trials, and four quasi-experimental studies. They yielded 36 evidence statements across five domains covering delivery modes, support strategies, lifestyle management, medication adherence, and outcomes. Digital tools backed by this graded base can guide nurses building self-management programs, rather than each clinic improvising its own app-based advice.
pmc-13328374:
Olivia N Julian and co-authors trace the past and future of radiosensitization in cervical cancer in a 2026 review. The disease claims about 348,000 lives a year worldwide, and locally advanced cases survive five years only about half the time despite combined radiation and cisplatin. That drug pairing, set by four trials in the 1990s, has barely changed since.

Radiation hardware has leapt ahead in twenty-five years, so the authors look to antibody-drug conjugates, which have already improved survival in spread disease, as sharper radiation partners for local disease. Immune checkpoint drugs also help in both settings, and they propose layering them onto conjugate-guided radiation. Trials of the triple approach are the clear next step, they argue.
pmc-13328474:
Kaihuan Zhou and co-authors compare nine blood-count indices for forecasting sepsis death in a 2026 multicenter study. Ratios built from routine counts are cheap and quick, but their relative worth was untested. The development set drew 26,512 intensive care patients from the MIMIC-IV database, with a Guangxi hospital cohort for outside checking.

Within 28 days, 2,669 patients in the development cohort died, and all nine indices tied significantly to mortality after the first-day landmark. Four stood out after full adjustment, led by the monocyte-to-lymphocyte and neutrophil-to-platelet ratios among the strongest in the model. Pairing the best ratios with standard organ scores may sharpen early triage, the authors propose.
pmc-13329074:
Sung Jun Ma and team report dodging a jaw bone gap with a high slant sagittal split cut in redo surgery. Their 2026 case report and literature review notes that a jaw bone gap knots redo jaw surgery, lifting risks of bad breaks and nerve harm. The high slant method gives a planned swap for the usual two-sided sagittal split.

The case was a 31-year-old Chinese woman with bone relapse twelve years after first two-jaw surgery. Scans found a 1.5 by 1.5 centimeter round gap in the right jaw body joining the nerve canal. Surgeons did a one-sided high slant cut on the right and a standard sagittal split on the left. Six-month checks showed fair face profile gains and steady bite, with no nerve feeling loss or bad breaks. The team stresses full before-surgery scans, calling the method safe and strong for dodging local disease.
pmc-13330674:
Maria Inez Dacoregio and colleagues pool safety data on immune checkpoint drugs in early breast cancer in a 2026 review and meta-analysis. Such drugs aid cure aims but add immune side effects beside chemotherapy. Searches covered major databases and meeting sources for trials reporting harm outcomes.

Thirteen studies with 3,977 patients entered the pool in the reported counts. Hair loss and low white cells were the most common overall side effects in treated arms. Severe drops in neutrophils led the high-grade list. The most common immune side effect was low thyroid action, while severe adrenal failure led the severe immune list. Most harms were mild, yet gland watch is vital, the authors stress.
pmc-13331174:
Matija Zupan and Senta Frol studied no-reflow in stroke, where recanalization does not mean reperfusion. The CHOICE 2 trial showed a 15% increase in top daily-life results, 57.5% versus 42.9%, with alteplase in the artery and reduced low flow on imaging. Brain bleeds with symptoms were not much more common, although deaths were slightly higher in the lytic arm. Larger phase III trials with standard plans and long-term safety data are required before changing guidelines.
pmc-13332474:
Pia AW Görts and co-authors built an automatic cleaning tool in 2026 for the hand-drawn tumor outlines used to train tracking models for MRI-guided radiotherapy. Drawing errors are common in such labels and quietly degrade the models trained on them, yet manual checking of moving scans is slow.

Their tool uses the Segment Anything 2 foundation model, which can follow objects across frames, to flag suspect outlines in two-dimensional cine-MRI and propose corrected contours. Two radiation oncologists who reviewed the output preferred the corrected contours over the original manual ones. On a set labeled by five observers, corrected contours scored a Dice value of 0.95 against 0.88 for agreement between human observers. The authors present the method as a way to cut the manual effort of dataset cleaning while raising label quality.
pmc-13333374:
Xiaobin Huang and colleagues built targeted delivery bubbles for curcumin in a 2026 Alzheimer's study, aiming the anti-inflammatory compound straight at microglia, the brain's immune cells. Natural exosomes can cross into the brain, but they wander without a homing signal, wasting their cargo.

In inflamed microglia-like cells, treatment suppressed the hostile M1 state and cut the release of inflammatory messengers. In 5xFAD mice, a standard Alzheimer's model, the therapy eased the microglia-linked brain damage and slowed cognitive decline, with no notable side effects. The authors present the platform as a non-invasive route for anti-inflammatory drugs against brain inflammation.
pmc-13333474:

WTAP's m6A tagging proved to destabilize SOX2's message, which quieted Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and curbed malignant behavior. The authors present WTAP-guided editing of SOX2 as a candidate drug target. They note animal studies are still needed before the mechanism can be trusted beyond the dish.
pmc-13335874:
Xiaolong Wang and colleagues study 2026 targeting KDM3B to elicit anti-tumor immunity by easing SHP1 STING blocking in triple-negative breast cancer. The authors identify KDM3B as a key driver of immune evasion in this cancer.

In detail, KDM3B targets SHP1 by reducing H3K9me2 levels at its switch. Weakening KDM3B weakens SHP1 STING blocking, sparking strong type I immune responses. pmc-13336374:
Xinyi Li, Ning Zhang, and Zijie Jin built SPADE, a deep learning framework for spatial transcriptomics, in a 2026 computing study. Spatial platforms map gene activity across tissue but read thinly and cannot name single cells directly, so single-cell data must be aligned onto the map.

It jointly models expression similarity between single-cell and spatial data and the agreement between spot distances and communication patterns, and it measures cell-cell communication across regions. Across 55 mock and real datasets it recovered region-specific cell patterns and sharpened expression maps. pmc-13336874: A 2026 correction notice fixes Figure 3G of a 2023 spinal cord injury paper in Advanced Science on a magnetic miR-26a therapy meant to regrow nerves and guide axons. Two Western blot images, labeled GSK-3β and GAPDH, were placed wrongly while the figure was assembled. The notice supplies the corrected figure, and the authors state that, after checking their original records, the error does not change the paper's findings or conclusions. The item is only this brief correction, not a full research report.
pmc-13336974:
