pmc-13386174:
Genovefa A. Papanicolaou and a large team study stubborn herpes infections after stem cell transplant in a 2026 multicenter review. Records from seven United States centers covered adults whose mouth or skin herpes failed a week of standard antiviral therapy. Resistance testing, healing times, side effects, and recurrence over one year were tracked.

Among those tested, over four in five infections proved resistant to the standard drug acyclovir. Most patients needed second-line therapy, led by foscarnet, whose courses often harmed the kidneys. Just over half the patients healed fully, at a median of 38 days from treatment start, which underlines the need for better options.
pmc-13386774:
Ruchir Rastogi's team tested whether extra training on personal genome and transcriptome data improves gene-expression models, in a 2026 paper. Sequence-to-expression models predict gene expression from DNA, but perform poorly on variation across people when used as shipped. The team fine-tuned Enformer, a pretrained model, on paired personal genome and expression data, testing several fine-tuning strategies.

Fine-tuning improved predictions for held-out people, even from held-out populations, for genes seen during training, matching variant-based linear models used in transcriptome-wide association studies. It did not improve transfer to held-out genes with unseen sequences and variants. The paper argues that individual genetic variation and paired expression data should shape future model design.
pmc-13387174:
Shen and colleagues compared nerve harm from two forms of the cancer drug irinotecan in 2026, the standard form and a liposomal form packed in fat bubbles. Reports hinted the two differ in neurotoxicity, harm to nerves, but the reason was unknown. The team joined computer toxicity forecasts, a national side-effect database, and molecular modeling to test whether the parent drug itself harms nerves.

Computer checks flagged high nerve risk for both irinotecan and its breakdown product SN-38. Database patterns split cleanly: the standard form linked to both brain and spinal effects and peripheral nerve effects, while the liposomal form linked only to peripheral ones. Modeling found eight nerve-related targets the drug binds tightly, with a stress-signaling cascade at the center. The authors argue the parent drug drives brain effects when it can reach the brain, which should shape safer formulation choices.
pmc-13387974:
Yuan Ding's team merged genetics and blood-protein data to hunt for early warning signs of multiple sclerosis, a disease that begins years before its first symptoms. They tested model levels of 2,545 plasma proteins against disease risk. The comparison covered nearly fifteen thousand cases and twenty-seven thousand controls, using inherited gene variants as stand-ins for protein levels.

Thirty-nine proteins linked to risk, most forming an immune network centred on B and T cell signals, and eight of them also flagged later diagnosis in UK Biobank samples taken years beforehand. One protein, DKKL1, looked protective across risk, timing, and severity, pointing to blood tests that might one day flag the disease early.
pmc-13388574:
Jing Wang's team traced how an overactive gene-switching off enzyme drives colorectal cancer by switching off HOXD11, a gene that normally restrains tumours. They compared thirty tumour samples with matched healthy tissue, screened the three main DNA methyltransferase enzymes, and tested the effect in cancer cells and in mice.

Only switching off DNMT1 restored HOXD11, and restoring HOXD11 slowed cell growth, movement, and invasion while triggering cell death. A demethylating drug had the same restraining effect, and blocking DNMT1 curbed tumour growth in mice. The DNMT1-HOXD11 axis thus emerges as a lead drug target in colorectal cancer.
pmc-13388974:
Ziyan Zhao's team solved the structure of a malaria drug-defence protein bound to a lead drug, aiming to outflank the parasite's defence against front-line antimalarials. The protein, PfMDR1, helps the parasite Plasmodium falciparum resist mefloquine and chloroquine, while ACT-451840, a phase-one lead, lacked a clear account.

Cryo-electron microscopy at 3.42 angstroms showed the drug wedged in the protein's central cavity, locking it open and blocking its pumping activity. Set against the mefloquine-bound form, this state explained why defence mutations to the new drug can resensitise parasites to mefloquine, and contrast with the human counterpart clarified its selectivity.
pmc-13391474:
Sanskruti Shrenik Patil's team joint carboplatin-loaded solid lipid nano bits with tumour-aimed immune drugs for oral cancer therapy in an early study. Mice primed with KB oral cancer cells made antigen-specific immune drugs, and spleen cells fused with marrow-cancer cells yielded hybrids, with the third fusion attempt optimal.

Lipid nano bits near 145 nm with good charge killed oral flat-cell cancer cells in time- and dose-linked fashion, outperforming free carboplatin. The dual immune-drug-plus-nano-bit strategy shows promise for targeted oral cancer drug delivery, though the work remains early-stage and pre-human.
pmc-13392074:
Zhaofeng Ouyang's team reports a stack-punching method for high-throughput micro battery making, swapping slow bottom-up build out that yields uneven devices and weak power. Micro batteries power built-in circuits, wear tech, implants, and microrobots, but making has limited their use.

An initially anode-free design with a woven-in electrode-electrolyte fusion layer survived high-speed punching at 1,800 units per hour. It gave uniform devices with a maximum per-volume energy density of 1,306 milliwatt-hours per cubic centimetre. Joined with tiny sensors and mounted on ants and bees, the batteries point toward bio-hybrid micro systems for wildlife data collection.
pmc-13392174:
Manon J A P Evers, Bastiaan P Krom, and Caroline A de Jongh build, in 2026, a step-by-step account linking mouth microbes to Alzheimer's disease through brain inflammation. Alzheimer's is the most common dementia. It brings brain inflammation with build-ups of amyloid and tau. Mouth bacteria and fungi have been found in patient brains more than once.

The review gathers proof on two named germs found in Alzheimer's brains after death. In mice, mouth germs can cross into the brain. There they sit with roused guard cells and amyloid loads. Neurology and dentistry readers gain a testable route from gum health to brain disease.
pmc-13392474:
Daniela Fava and many co-authors tackled a common clinic puzzle: telling true early puberty driven by the brain from breast development that will not progress, in girls who are also gaining weight. Extra fat can speed growth and bone ageing on its own, which blurs the usual physical clues. Their group covered one hundred girls plus sixteen prepubertal controls with obesity.

Height measures and bone age looked much the same across the two main groups, so they could not separate them. Hormone measures could, with luteinising hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone, oestradiol, and IGF-1 all clearly apart between groups. Body scans added one contrast, a higher waist-to-hip fat ratio in the nonprogressive group. Among heavier girls the growth clues blurred further, leaving blood tests as the dependable route.
pmc-13392574:
Aid, development, and peace work are often urged to join up in fragile places under the label of the triple nexus, yet a decade of policy talk has produced patchy practice. The article under review builds a typology of how that joining-up actually happens, moving attention from single project designs to organisational strategy, institutional mandates, and the trade-offs each setting forces. No byline appears with the text.

Current strains frame the argument, among them shrinking aid budgets and the merging of climate and displacement work into nexus plans. Rather than endorsing one universal model, the author holds that workable practice grows from negotiation as mandates and priorities shift. The typology is offered as a guide for choices fitted to each context, not as a template to copy.
pmc-13393674:
Martin Šrámek and colleagues compare long-term survival of Czech divers with the general population in a 2026 cohort study. Diving brings hyperbaric stress, oxidative strain, and accident risk, but divers also tend to be fit and resilient, so the net effect on lifespan was uncertain.

Data from 1,076 divers in the DIVE-PFO Registry from 2005 to 2024 were linked to national health records, yielding over 10,000 person-years of follow-up. Only 15 deaths occurred, four possibly diving-related, and none from cardiovascular causes. The paper gives divers and doctors a reassuring first picture of survival in this group.
pmc-13393774:
Helene Louise Elliott-Button and colleagues examine United Kingdom policy on social homecare at the end of life in a 2026 document analysis. Homecare workers are crucial for people who wish to die at home, yet their training and support in policy documents had not been mapped.

The team reviewed current UK policy documents shaping homecare practice, counting and analyzing passages on end-of-life care, the workforce, and training. Extracted passages were examined for what support and training they actually promised. Policymakers gain a gap analysis showing where homecare workers are named but left unsupported.
pmc-13393874:
Anuradha Ganesan, Vinu B Priya, Krithika Chandrasekar Lakshmi, and Yesoda Aniyan present a 35-year-old South Asian man whose month of recurring mouth ulcers announced pemphigus vulgaris. The autoimmune blistering disease can threaten the airway when it spreads through the throat. His skin examination added blisters across chest and back. Antibodies in this disease attack the glue proteins holding skin cells together, and mouth lesions are the opening sign in most patients.

Scrapings from the ulcers showed the rounded, detached cells typical of the condition, and a biopsy with immune studies confirmed the diagnosis. Steroids remain the backbone of treatment despite limited options in some settings, backed by supportive care and steroid-sparing drugs where available. The authors stress that careful tissue and immune work separates this disease from look-alike blistering disorders, and that several specialties must coordinate when the upper airway is involved.
pmc-13394074:
Kugiyama and co-authors search, in 2026, for bile-based biomarkers of biliary tract cancer, a hard-to-detect cancer of the bile ducts and gallbladder. Because bile touches the tumor directly, they sequenced the microRNAs inside exosomes, tiny released particles, from bile of 10 cancer patients and 10 controls. Candidates were then validated in a larger group of 50 patients and 53 controls, and checked against standard blood markers.

Two microRNAs, miR-196a and miR-196b, were specifically elevated in patients' bile, and miR-196a was already raised in early-stage disease. MiR-196a alone reached a diagnostic accuracy score, the area under the curve, of 0.79 in the validation cohort. Adding the blood marker CA19-9 lifted that score to 0.86, and adding CEA reached 0.88 with the combined panel. Laboratory assays showed both microRNAs also drive cancer cell growth and invasion, linking them to tumor progression itself.
pmc-13394974:
Khurram Jahangir Toor and co-authors test, in 2026, how fat-rich diets in rat parents shape their pups. Mothers and fathers ate a control diet or a high-fat, high-sugar diet for five weeks before mating. Four pairings mixed lean and heavy parents. The team weighed pups at birth and weaning and checked survival, body length, belly fat, and a fullness hormone.

Pups of heavy mothers were born lighter, and heavy fathers worsened the drop for sons. Pairings with two heavy parents had shorter pups and more newborn deaths. By weaning, pups from heavy mothers were often heavier with more fat. The authors urge health work for both parents before conception.
pmc-13395374:
Asra Moslemipour, Ali Salmasnia, and Hadi Mokhtari model, in 2026, cloud manufacturing systems that rent out factory capacity online. Orders are custom, and plants sit far apart, so scheduling, shipping, pricing, and quality choices tangle. Most past work treats each choice alone. Their model joins all four and adds customer happiness and fairness among customers as goals.

Profit, happiness, and fairness pull in different ways, so the model blends them into one score. Exact solving worked for small and mid cases, and a genetic search handled the big ones fast. Dropping shipping, happiness, or lateness fines gave worse plans. The authors present the frame as a scalable guide for platform managers.
pmc-13395574:
Claire Orth and colleagues follow, in 2026, patients treated for stones in the jaw saliva gland over five to ten years. Care either removes the gland or keeps it, using a scope to clear the stone. Eighty-two patients of one surgeon were traced, and thirty-six answered a survey in 2024. Dry mouth was the main long-term measure.

Every gland removal patient had symptom relief after the first round. In the keeping group, about seven in ten were clear after one round, and some later lost the gland. Final success ran high in both groups. Dry mouth rates were alike, which dents a key claim for keeping the gland. The authors weigh durability against repeat work.
pmc-13396674:
Clare Mills and co-authors studied febrile babies whose spinal fluid carried virus but, puzzlingly, no rise in white blood cells. Their 2026 study uses a prospective multicenter cohort of young infants checked for meningitis, where enterovirus and parechovirus are frequent finds.

A missing cell rise, called absent pleocytosis, is often blamed on early testing or an immature immune system. Blood protein profiling told a sharper story: infants without the cell rise showed signs of lymphocyte depletion alongside switched-on cytokine signals. In other words, the flat spinal fluid reflected a real biological state in the blood, not a timing artifact or a stray virus.
pmc-13397474:
Minori Takada and co-authors ask whether planned cesarean birth at 38 weeks, rather than at 36 or 37 weeks, helps babies when the placenta covers the cervix. Their 2026 study uses records from one large hospital covering 2015 to 2024. Placenta previa can cause heavy bleeding, so timing the birth means balancing risk to the mother against gains for the newborn.

Among 204 women with single pregnancies, 29 gave birth in the later group and 81 in the earlier group after set rules were applied. Blood loss, operating time and severe problems for mothers looked much the same in both groups. Babies born at 38 weeks weighed more and needed hospital care and treatment for low blood sugar less often, which supports more study of later planned delivery.
pmc-13397574:
Han Li and a large team present a data-driven way to rebuild three-dimensional views of tiny structures from electron microscope images. Their 2026 paper tackles electron tomography, a method held back by missing angles, heavy radiation dose and shallow focus. Learning-based fixes had stalled because real training data are scarce.

Rather than hunt for rare datasets, the group built large training sets from random high-entropy projections, folding in real shape patterns and depth effects. The proof case mapped a platinum particle just 13 nm wide, placing 52,138 atoms with very small position error. Match between images and model also improved, stretching how deep the method can see at atomic scale.
pmc-13397674:
Tetiana Zolotarova, Areesha Moiz, Audrey Lelièvre and Mark J Eisenberg review trials of ways to help people quit vaping. Their 2026 narrative review responds to fast growth in e-cigarette use, above all among the young. Quitting aids proven for smoking may not map neatly onto vaping, so the trial record needed gathering.

Searches of PubMed, Google Scholar and ClinicalTrials.gov through 27 April 2025 found 11 randomised trials with 8,182 people in total. Four tested tailored text-message support, three nicotine replacement, three the drug varenicline and one cytisine. Follow-up ran from one month to two years, and text programmes showed early promise for keeping people off vapes.
pmc-13398474:
Milad Ibrahim and colleagues investigated a protein called AMBRA1 in melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer. Their 2026 paper asks what AMBRA1 does beyond its known role in autophagy, the cell process that clears damaged parts. Melanoma resists many therapies and spreads aggressively, so mapping new control proteins could open fresh treatment angles.

Using gene activity data from AMBRA1 overexpression and knockdown, the team found broad disruption across cancer pathways, including MAPK growth signaling, blood vessel growth, tissue growth factor signaling, and Wnt signaling. Yeast tests also revealed new binding partners for AMBRA1. Loss of AMBRA1 raised metastatic genes and proteins, leading the authors to call it a tumor suppressor in melanoma. The work is mainly cell-based, so clinical relevance still needs patient and animal confirmation.
pmc-13398774:
Bas Janssen and co-authors publish a recipe for purifying a plant hormone switch so its clumping behaviour can be studied in a test tube. Their 2026 methods paper handles MpARF2, an auxin response factor from the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha, which forms assemblies inside living nuclei. Whether those assemblies arise by phase separation, the droplet-forming process behind many cell compartments, is unknown.

Pure protein is the entry ticket for such tests, and the paper walks through producing and preparing MpARF2 for in-vitro phase assays. Auxin response factors steer gene activity in answer to the growth hormone auxin, so their physical state may tune plant responses. The protocol serves anyone probing whether transcription factors work as droplets, clusters or lone molecules.
pmc-13398974:
Jiaqiang Chen and colleagues define a forgiving entry zone for screws that brace the hip socket from below. Their 2026 study rebuilds pelvis models from 100 patients in three dimensions. Infra-acetabular screws strengthen broken socket repairs, but the classic single ideal entry point and narrow corridor slow surgery and limit choice.

The entry zone proved quasi-elliptical, with its centre sitting inward and forward of the classic ideal point. A clinical comparison in 20 fracture patients then pitted the central entry technique against the ideal point method. Central entry cut operating time and X-ray exposures significantly, while screw length and success held level, evidence the wider target is also the kinder one.
pmc-13400474:
Justin Chong Meng Chua and colleagues ask, in 2026, whether a rare vessel disease called ANCA-associated vasculitis clusters in families with other immune diseases. The condition involves antibodies that drive inflammation of small blood vessels. Shared family patterns could hint at common inherited susceptibility.

The team matched 145 patients with 145 controls who had no immune-mediated inflammatory disease. Nearly half the patients reported such a disease in a close relative, against about one in six controls. After adjustment, patients were about seven times more likely to have that family history. Among relatives themselves, immune disease was also far more common on the patient side, and female relatives carried double the risk of male relatives.
pmc-13401574:
Ryan J McCarty and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of obsessive-compulsive disorder in three groups that research has historically neglected. The groups are Latino and Latin American people, Black and African American people, and sexual and gender minority individuals. The review gathers what is actually known about OCD in these populations.

Core symptoms look broadly similar across groups, the authors find. What differs is everything around them: discrimination, minority stress, stigma, family context, and spirituality shape how symptoms appear. Access to care shapes how severe they become and whether people reach treatment. Recent work has tested assessment tools in these groups and supports exposure and response prevention therapy, while stressing culturally responsive assessment and care. Large initiatives are improving representation in OCD research too, and closing long-standing knowledge gaps.
pmc-13401674:
Kailey Paterson, Kay Franks, Janet Wallace, and Dileep Sharma carried out a 2026 scoping review of dietary advice for type 2 diabetes delivered in dental settings. Diabetes and gum disease are both inflammatory conditions, and diet messages could improve both, yet dentists rarely feature in diabetes lifestyle care.

Following Joanna Briggs Institute methods, the team searched MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL. Scopus in May 2024 and again in June 2025 for English-language evidence on dietary counselling of diabetes patients by dental practitioners. From 394 initial studies, only seven qualified. Two combined dental treatment with dietary advice, and four developed or implemented combined diabetes-periodontal approaches, a sign of how young this field is. The review maps what exists for practitioners considering diet conversations during periodontal treatment and maintenance visits.
pmc-13401874:
Xulin Hu, Yangyan Liu, and Bo Li built a screening model for congenital heart disease in children living at high altitude, in a 2026 study. Standard screening criteria were designed for the plains, and thin plateau air raises both missed diagnoses and false alarms.

Data came from 7,315 school-age children screened in high-altitude areas. A logistic regression model, built by stepwise selection, predicted heart disease detection and was checked with ROC curves, calibration, and decision curve analysis, while random forest plots ranked variable importance. Medication use and respiratory infections carried the strongest independent associations with a diagnosis, followed by age and smoking exposure variables. Discrimination was strong, with an area under the curve just under nine-tenths. Three screening strategies were also costed in a Markov model to weigh accuracy against expense.
pmc-13402074:
Jawaher Ibrahim Alahadeb models where the crop fungus Fusarium incarnatum could spread as the climate warms, using occurrence records and weather layers in a MaxEnt mapping exercise. The fungus already causes heavy crop losses, yet its future range is poorly mapped. Alahadeb drew 112 cleaned records from the Global Biodiversity Information Facility and kept five climate drivers, led by annual mean temperature.

Model skill looked strong, with an AUC of 0.88 and a true skill score of 0.80 recorded in the results. Warming pushed suitable ground northward: wide parts of Canada, northern Europe, and Siberia shifted toward medium or high suitability by 2050 and 2070. The high-emission path opened far more new ground than the low-emission one. Farm planners get an early warning map for surveillance and for breeding or quarantine choices ahead of the fungus.
pmc-13403374:
Anna V. Leopold and Vladislav V. Verkhusha presented in 2026 a way to switch immune sensors on and off with far-red light. Normal sensors of this kind spot germ parts and start the body's first defense lines. The team swapped the outer sensing part of three sensors for a light-sensing part from a bacterium.

The rebuilt sensors fired key defense pathways in mammal cells only when far-red light was present. One pathway was also rewired so it triggered cell death signals instead of alarm chemicals. Such light control could let researchers probe immune action in set places and times, without flooding the whole body with drugs.
pmc-13404874:
Mao Chen and team review how bacterial chromosomes fold into three-dimensional shapes and how that folding is steered. Their 2026 review covers packed bacterial genomes that underpin copying, transcription, and segregation, joining chromosome conformation capture and imaging studies. Fine folding rules had stayed partly unknown, despite their weight for cell function.

The review shows how genome shape shifts with environmental cues and how structural layout sways gene activity and genome steadiness. It also probes synthetic biology uses, where built folding could tune microbe systems and open novel therapies. The synthesis gives a frame for bacterial genomic balance and adaptation, guiding researchers who want to design or perturb bacterial genomes with structural insight.
pmc-13405074:
Xiaolei Shi proposes a new control method for permanent magnet motors in a 2026 engineering paper. Standard predictive controllers lose quality when motor parameters drift from their assumed values. The design here drops the fixed model and learns behaviour from data instead.

A nonlinear autoregressive model with outside inputs tracks the motor, updated by an adaptive learning rule with a variable forgetting factor. Simulations compare it with conventional predictive control under wrong inductance and flux values. Current distortion fell by 28.3 percent against the standard method in one mismatch test in the reported results. Load changes and sensor noise were also simulated, with the new controller holding steadier performance.
pmc-13405174:
Christelle Ndjali and co-authors report a rare growth on a newborn's head treated in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo, in 2026. An 18-day-old girl arrived with a mass at the back of her skull present since birth. Hamartomas are disorganised but benign growths of normal tissue, and they are uncommon in newborn brains.

The mass measured 10 by 6 centimetres, firm in the middle and softer at the edges, and it pulsed. Scans suggested a teratoma, but full surgical removal and tissue analysis confirmed a hamartoma growing both outside and inside the skull. A wound infection after surgery cleared with broad antibiotics, and the three-month follow-up was favourable.
pmc-13406874:
Jose Cuenca-Alcocel and co-authors compared blood fat particles in children with excess weight against normal-weight children in a 2026 study. Rather than stopping at a standard cholesterol panel, the team used a nuclear magnetic resonance test that counts lipoprotein particles by subclass, size, and number, along with their fat makeup.

Children carrying extra weight showed higher levels of several fat measures tied to very-low-density and intermediate particles, plus more remnant cholesterol. Their low-density particles were also smaller on average. Because the children were prepubertal, the differences point to metabolic change starting early in life. Detailed particle profiling, the authors argue, can reveal risk that routine lipid tests miss.
pmc-13407174:
Sean Goodwin and Leo Goldsmith map, in 2026, how far national climate adaptation plans include sexual and gender minorities, groups hit disproportionately by climate harm. No worldwide count existed, so the pair reviewed adaptation plans, or stand-in documents where plans were missing, for 256 territories and states.

Of 198 United Nations framework member states, only 23 mentioned these minorities at all. Among those, about 65 percent acknowledged unequal impacts, 26 percent planned action on them, and 9 percent addressed the deeper drivers of vulnerability. Inclusion tracked with stronger legal protections and warmer public opinion in a country. The authors call for local, place-based engagement with affected communities so adaptation reflects lived vulnerability rather than assumptions.
pmc-13407474:
Yalong Xie and co-authors tackle, in 2026, the timing of construction vehicles inside long road tunnels, where crossing paths, head-on meetings, and congestion can turn dangerous. Earlier work often planned routes apart from timetables or handled conflicts loosely. The team therefore built one model joining path choice, departure timing, and three conflict types.

Their method blends a pedestrian-style movement model with a road-capacity formula to plan paths, then searches departure intervals and routes together with an improved search algorithm. A repair step measures disorder at each node as conflict entropy and fixes clashes by ranking priority and delaying selected vehicles. On a test network of 30 nodes and 41 links, the best setup finished scheduling in 136 minutes with only two conflicts, avoiding every head-on and congestion clash.
pmc-13407574:
Esteban Ramirez-Ferrer and co-authors review, in 2026, the non-motor symptoms of brain tumours on the right side of the brain. Right-side gliomas are often treated as less critical than left-sided ones. Speech sits mainly on the left. Yet these tumours disturb thinking, behaviour, and social life in ways that shape quality of life.

Searching three databases under standard review rules, the team gathered 372 patients from 88 studies. Before surgery, problems with cognition and executive function led at 43 percent, followed by vision and spatial deficits and then language trouble. After surgery, language deficits topped the list at 46 percent. Reporting on tumour removal extent was patchy, limiting firm conclusions. The authors urge wider functional testing and surgical planning that respects right-side networks.
pmc-13408874:
Yasir Taha and co-authors package a potent but poorly delivered cancer drug candidate onto gold nanoparticles in 2026 and test it against lung cancer cells. The drug, quinalizarin, blocks an enzyme that cancer cells lean on for survival, yet the body handles it badly. Linking it to gold particles was meant to carry more of it into tumours and release it where conditions turn acidic.

The finished complex measured around eighty-five nanometres, carried a negative surface charge, and let go of far more drug at tumour-like acidity than at blood pH. In dishes of A549 lung cancer cells it killed at lower doses than the free drug, and microscope images confirmed the particles were taken inside the cells. The authors present the system as a promising, pH-responsive carrier for this drug class in non-small cell lung cancer.
pmc-13411474:
Pedro Melo and colleagues assess in 2026 readiness in an Azores island health unit for a new surveillance system tracking nursing diagnoses in the population. Nursing problems like tobacco use and drug dependence rarely appear in health statistics, which hides nurses' contribution. The study used a community empowerment model to diagnose local conditions.

Three priority problems framed the work: smoking, drug dependence, and teenage decision-making around sexuality and life plans. Community leadership for the change rated weak, participation limited, and coping capacity short. Strengthening leadership, communication, and training are the levers named. Done well, the system could make nursing-sensitive problems visible in island health planning for the first time.
pmc-13411974:
Sahar Elnajjar and colleagues revised and validated a pneumonia medicine checklist for hospitals in the United Arab Emirates in 2026. The Norwegian original no longer matched current treatment guidelines or local drug resistance, so the team rebuilt its criteria, tested them with ten experts, and checked them against 30 real cases.

The revised tool holds 13 criteria covering drug choice, lab testing, dosing, switching from drip to pills, and course length, with near-perfect expert agreement on drug choice. Stewardship teams gain a local, tested checklist for judging whether pneumonia antibiotics are truly appropriate.
pmc-13412174:
Alon Yehoshua and colleagues tracked 67358 Americans aged 65 and older after a COVID-19 hospital stay in late 2023 to early 2024. The burden of COVID-19 does not end at discharge for older adults, so the team used Medicare records to follow care needs and deaths for six months.

Over half of patients who had lived at home with self-care needed more help after discharge, fewer than half returned home fully independent, and about 17 percent died within six months. The paper gives planners a stark post-hospital picture for staffing home care, rehab, and follow-up after COVID-19.
pmc-13413274:
Ioana Manea and colleagues ask in 2026 whether the length of DNA fragments floating in blood can sharpen liver cancer detection. The standard marker, alpha-fetoprotein, misses many early tumours in people with chronic liver disease. In a prospective cohort of 125 such patients, the team measured fragment size by chip electrophoresis and tested it alone and inside multi-marker panels against the reference marker.

Fragments ran significantly shorter in patients whose cirrhosis had turned cancerous than in cirrhosis alone. Added to a panel of alpha-fetoprotein, age, and liver reserve, though, fragment size brought no significant gain in their analysis. Age and platelet count proved the strongest independent predictors in this exploratory cohort. The authors want larger validation before judging the marker's true worth.
pmc-13413874:
Seung Hun Lee and colleagues run a 2026 crossover trial on how tilting the foot platform changes a split squat. Wedges are common in clinics and gyms to steer ankle alignment, yet their whole-leg effects during single-leg exercise were murky. Thirty healthy young adults performed split squats on no wedge, an inward-tilting medial wedge, and an outward lateral wedge, in random order, while motion cameras, force plates, and muscle sensors recorded everything.

The lateral wedge fired up the outer calf and inner thigh muscles and widened motion at ankle, knee, and pelvis in their measurements. The medial wedge instead recruited the shin and outer thigh muscles and trimmed hip motion. Vertical force rose under the lateral wedge, while side-to-side forces never budged. The authors warn against generalizing from a rigid platform to clinical shoe inserts.
pmc-13414174:
Konstantinos Tigkiropoulos and colleagues report in 2026 eight years of experience with the Ankura stent graft for repairing abdominal aortic aneurysms from inside the vessel. Long-term proof for this graft, introduced in Europe in 2015, had stayed thin. Their single-centre review covered 220 patients treated electively between 2015 and 2023, nearly all men, with aneurysms averaging 59 millimetres across, followed by scans first and ultrasound later.

Technical success reached 97.3 percent at the first attempt and 100 percent with touch-ups, and no patient died within thirty days. Freedom from reintervention held at 95.9 percent by six years in their follow-up, and the iliac limb stayed open in 99.5 percent of patients. Aneurysm-related death during follow-up was 2.2 percent.
pmc-13415274:
María Razo-González and co-authors describe a new caddisfly species from Oaxaca, Mexico, in a 2026 taxonomy study. The insect belongs to Caenocentron, a small genus of net-tube caddisflies found in the southern Nearctic and Neotropics. Only two species were previously known from Mexico.

The new species, Caenocentron chinantecum, differs from a Costa Rican relative in the shape and spines of its lower appendages. DNA barcodes showed gaps near five percent between species in the genus. Of four computer delimitation methods, only one matched the anatomy based grouping. An updated identification key for the whole genus closes the work.
pmc-13415774:
A 2026 interview feature examines why viral hepatitis still kills over a million people a year despite vaccines and cures. Hepatitis B can be prevented by vaccine and controlled by treatment, while hepatitis C can be cured outright. The discussion centers on India's national control program and lessons from countries that reached control status.

Silent infection is the core problem: most carriers feel well for years and learn their status only after liver damage. Delayed confirmation testing loses patients before care starts. Same day test and treat models, decentralized molecular testing, and public awareness are presented as fixes. The 2030 elimination goal set by the World Health Organization frames the conversation.
pmc-13415974:
Mina Soryal and co-authors report acute myeloid leukemia arising in a patient with xeroderma pigmentosum, in a 2026 case report. Xeroderma pigmentosum is a rare inherited failure of DNA repair after ultraviolet damage, causing extreme sun sensitivity and early skin cancers. Blood cancers occur in such patients only occasionally.

Leukemia in this setting may arrive younger, carry complex chromosome changes, and respond poorly to treatment, the authors note from this case and prior reports. Regular blood monitoring for patients with the condition is their central recommendation. The report reviews the repair genes behind the disorder and its wide geographic variation in frequency.
pmc-13417174:
Jiashan Mi and colleagues pin down the structure of a drug salt forced into a new crystal form by pressure, in a 2026 study. Pressing during tablet making can flip a medicine into a different solid form with different behaviour. The material here, a tosylate salt called GDC-0022, changed under 250 megapascals of pressure.

Nuclear magnetic resonance measures on three atomic types showed old and new forms sitting side by side as separate domains. Computer crystal prediction then matched a dense new form to the measured signals. The salt nature survived the change, with one nitrogen still holding its extra hydrogen. The method suits messy mixed powders.
pmc-13417474:
Yanyan Bai and co-authors write in 2026 to critique a study linking gene variants in ticagrelor metabolism to side effects in heart attack patients. Ticagrelor is a blood-thinning drug, and the original study tied one CYP3A5 variant to breathlessness. This comment accepts the finding's interest but disputes its statistical strength.

First, the comment notes the study tested two gene variants against several outcomes without correcting for multiple comparisons, so borderline results might be chance findings, and no independent group confirmed them. Second, it argues the breathlessness endpoint was too broad: counting even the mildest grade mixes trivial, short-lived symptoms with the moderate-to-severe breathlessness that actually makes patients stop treatment. The authors urge caution until the results are validated with tighter definitions.
pmc-13418274:
Mengting Yin and colleagues engineer a two faced microneedle patch for infected diabetic wounds, in a 2026 study. Such wounds stall in a cycle of bacteria, oxidative stress, and inflammation fuelled by high blood sugar. The patch base holds iron based nanozymes that, under near infrared light, release reactive oxygen to kill bacteria fast.

The needle tips carry propolis extract, an antioxidant bee product, deep into the wound bed. In lab tests the patch calmed inflammation and shielded fibroblasts and their energy centres from oxidative harm. In infected diabetic mice, light activated patches closed wounds faster, with better vessel growth and collagen rebuilding.
pmc-13418474:
Cheng-Kai Chiang and co-authors review how gut bacteria remove methyl groups from drugs, a reaction called O-demethylation, in a 2026 mini review. Many medicines carry methoxy groups, and gut microbes can clip them before or after absorption. This microbial chemistry sits alongside liver metabolism and varies between people, contributing to uneven drug responses.

Clipping can lower active drug levels or create products with their own effects, shifting benefit and toxicity. The review covers the chemical logic, which microbes perform it, and likely clinical consequences. Measuring or steering this activity could become a biomarker or treatment lever in microbiome aware prescribing.
pmc-13418774:
Hakimeh Mostafavi and colleagues mapped hospital staffing inequality across Iran's 31 provinces in 2026, covering 383 districts. Staff distribution shapes care quality and deaths, yet planners lacked a national picture of where doctors, nurses, and other hospital workers cluster or run thin.

Physician density averaged 0.34 per bed and nurse density 1.28 per bed, with moderate inequality for doctors and lower inequality for nurses, though some provinces showed far sharper doctor gaps. The paper gives health officials a province-by-province staffing map for fairer hiring and placement, especially for provinces where doctor shortages bite hardest.
pmc-13420074:
Zhang Qi and colleagues report a patient whose muscle breakdown followed a double lung infection with Legionella and influenza A at once. Muscle breakdown floods the blood with cell contents, harming kidneys and other organs in its wake. Each infection alone can strain the body hard; together they deepened the injury in this case.

High fever, inflammation, and direct infection damage are among the routes that can destroy muscle fibers. Released muscle proteins then clog and injure the kidneys, pushing the patient toward failure of several organs. The authors present the case as the first of its kind they can fill into the record. Clinicians facing severe combined pneumonia gain a warning to watch muscle enzymes early, before kidney damage locks in.
pmc-13420174:
Javaheri‐Tafti and colleagues tracked in 2026 how diet quality relates to survival in patients with liver cirrhosis. Cirrhosis is late-stage scarring of the liver that limits life. They followed 121 newly diagnosed patients for sixty months and scored the quality of carbohydrate, fat, and protein in their diets.

Patients with the best overall diet quality had a far lower risk of death over the follow-up. Their risk was about two-thirds lower than that of patients with the poorest scores, after other factors were taken into account. Better carbohydrate quality and better fat quality each linked to lower risk on their own. Protein quality showed a similar trend, but it was not firm enough to count as proven. They back diet counselling as part of routine care.
pmc-13420674:
Robbe Knapen and colleagues report a young patient with multiple myeloma whose heart was stiffened by amyloid deposits, guided through stem cell transplant by an implanted pressure sensor in the lung artery. Cardiac amyloidosis makes fluid balance a knife-edge, since the stiff heart tolerates neither overload nor depletion. The sensor let the team steer water pills toward a set pressure target before transplant.

His marrow showed 62 percent plasma cells in the biopsy reported, with gene changes confirming the myeloma diagnosis. Blood and urine markers showed heavy kidney involvement beside the heart disease. He finished transplant without heart failure collapse and reached complete remission of the blood cancer. The case argues that live pressure data can beat bedside guessing in cardio-oncology care this complex.
pmc-13421474:
Lucio Zugliani leads a fourteen-author team showing, in a 2026 paper, single-photon detectors carved from a superconductor just atoms thick. Such detectors catch single photons one by one. Reaching from near-infrared toward terahertz waves needs materials that are even, thin and easy to build in.

The team patterned niobium diselenide, a layered superconductor, into wires under 100 nanometres wide. The devices detected single photons at two telecom-relevant wavelengths, kept false counts below one per second, and timed arrivals within fifty picoseconds. Models suggest the material could in principle reach millimetre wavelengths. The authors present the result as a route to detectors built straight into quantum photonic circuits.
pmc-13421674:
Im and colleagues present a 2026 review of programmable nanomedicine built with bioorthogonal chemistry, reactions designed to run inside the body without disturbing its own chemistry.  Bioorthogonal tools let builders attach working parts to a particle's surface after it is made, and control when and where a drug load switches on.

The review covers three levels of control: fitting surfaces with targeting or shielding modules. It also covers gating drug release in space and time, and higher-order tricks such as particles clumping at a disease site or linking directly to cells. Together these give medicines that activate more selectively in diseased tissue than plain formulations can. The authors close with open problems: safety, scale-up, and patient proof.
pmc-13422274:
Yanjun Yu, Liurong Xu and Tianlin Chen survey 527 nurses across twenty Chinese hospitals, in a 2026 study, on the emotional acting their job demands and the exhaustion that follows. Nurses either fake the feelings they show — surface acting — or genuinely summon them, deep acting, and the two strategies carry opposite costs.

Surface acting came with more emotional exhaustion, fitting a resource-loss spiral, while deep acting came with less, fitting a resource-gain pattern. Psychological resilience softened surface acting's harm substantially, buffering that link by well over half. Its protection on the deep-acting side behaved differently, giving the moderation an asymmetric shape. The authors argue resilience training should be aimed where the strain actually forms.
pmc-13423074:
Xianghong Zhou leads a large case–control study of environmental exposures and prostate cancer in older men from western China, drawn from the WeEndPd cohort. The team measured hormone-disrupting chemicals in urine and estimated air pollution at home addresses, asking whether single exposures or mixtures track with localised disease.

Cases were 580 men who had prostate surgery between May 2021 and June 2023, matched with 1,160 cancer-free controls on age and sampling date. Urine tests covered nine bisphenols and nine phthalate breakdown products. Men in the highest quarter of five-year sulphur dioxide exposure showed a clear rise in cancer odds. The authors present the work as preliminary, a first map of combined chemical and air exposures in this population.
pmc-13423174:
Chi Zhang and nine colleagues track how an RNA chemical mark called m1A shifts after spinal cord injury, cell type by cell type. Because direct measurement is hard, the team scored injury samples by the activity of genes that write, erase, and read the mark, treating that score as a stand-in for mark levels.

The score rose within a day of injury, then fell below starting levels by days three and seven. Immune cells called microglia showed falling scores at every time point, while neurons showed rising scores throughout. Lab and animal checks tied the microglial pattern to changes in cell state and the neuronal pattern to energy use, suggesting the mark helps coordinate the injury response.
pmc-13424274:
Takafumi Fujita leads an eighteen-author registry study of a drug-coated balloon strategy for narrowed thigh and knee arteries. The aim is to leave nothing behind. Between 2021 and 2022 the registry enrolled 310 limbs in 277 patients; 273 limbs entered the main analysis. Groups covered balloon alone, drug-eluting stent, and the combination of both. The primary measure was primary patency at one year, with repeat treatment driven by symptoms among the secondary measures. The authors set the selective approach against the simpler balloon-only route.
pmc-13424574:
Lise Graversen and colleagues present four unrelated Danish and Australian patients whose Lynch syndrome picture traces to a rare switch-off of the MLH1 gene. Two showed patchy marking that hints at mosaicism, where only some cells carry it. The series argues for steady testing of possible carriers, since looks alone cannot separate these patients from other Lynch cases.
pmc-13424774:

pmc-13425574:
Mukul S. Tambe and coauthors tested oral safety of an Ayurvedic herbo-mineral preparation in rats in a 2026 toxicology study. The mixture combines Tinospora cordifolia, Withania somnifera, and Kukkutandatvak bhasma, an eggshell-derived mineral ingredient. No deaths or clinical signs followed the single large dose, and weight gain plus food intake during repeated dosing matched control animals in the reported results. Preclinical readers gain a first safety check for a formulation intended for repeated use. The rats were watched with care for signs of pain, weight loss, poor feeding, and harm to key organs through the whole test.
pmc-13426074:
Samuel Obiosa Onyekweli and coauthors review engineering of CAR-T cells for solid tumors in a 2026 article spanning design and clinical translation. Integrated design aims to repeat such wins more broadly.
pmc-13427074:

In experiments, gloomy emojis also nudged people toward preventive health steps. The nudge worked best when emoji and text told the same story. Mismatched pairs lost much of their power to persuade readers. Health teams should match emoji mood to message mood with care.
pmc-13427374:
Chung and Park tracked depressive symptoms in 2026 among Korean adults using a phone app that asked about twenty symptoms once a day for two weeks. The study compared those recalls with daily reports from 695 adults who completed at least seven daily sessions.

Average severity scores fell slightly in week two by both methods. Yet the estimated chance of reporting any symptom rose, a contrast recall scales alone would miss. The team also grouped participants by average severity, day-to-day swings, and how often suicidal thoughts appeared, to profile subgroups at higher risk for depression and suicidal thinking.
pmc-13427474:

Standardized isolation and checking should improve comparability across the fast-growing vesicle literature. Blood can be drawn in a plain ward visit, so vesicles from it can be run in large groups with no cut and no scan at the start. The steps use gear found in most labs, so the way can spread with ease from lab to lab in time.
pmc-13427574:

pmc-13427674:

pmc-13427774:

Mast cells are immune cells that can turn cancerous in skin. Special stains and a protein marker test confirmed the tumor type firmly. The report gives zoo vets a first reference case for the species. Wildlife vets may now watch for this tumor in related species.
pmc-13428374:

pmc-13428774:
Tarishi Parmar and colleagues ask whether common blood pressure drugs change outcomes after total shoulder replacement. Both groups instead had higher 90-day rates of emergency visits, readmission, heart attack, and acute kidney failure, plus higher one-year rates of joint infection, loosening, and revision surgery. The authors stress the link is associative, since patients taking these drugs often carry more other illnesses.
pmc-13429574:
Raucher and colleagues report in 2026 how low-income pregnant patients with diabetes experienced SweetMama, a web-based phone app built to support them. The highest marks went to ease of learning, which matters for patients learning diabetes skills fast during pregnancy. Most users identified as Black or Hispanic, the groups the app was built for. pmc-13430174:

Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans grows slowly from the skin's deep layer and can reach large sizes before it is noticed. MRI mapped a contained lesion under the skin. Surgeons removed it with a wide margin of healthy tissue, and pathology confirmed the diagnosis with tumor-free edges. Checks every three months found no return over the first year. Whether trauma truly seeds this cancer is unsettled, and the authors present the timing without claiming proof. Non-healing lumps at scar sites deserve biopsy, the case reminds clinicians.
pmc-13430474:

The authors found a gap between board advice and what teams could act on, shaped by limits in funds, staff, and support systems.

Their board now asks researchers to share context before and after each talk, covering limits that shape what a study can do. That steady exchange helps the board shape advice that fits each team's real capacity. It also keeps shared goals in view. The authors present the approach as a way to make board input more useful for health research in local communities.
pmc-13430574:
Darko and colleagues explore treatment for people with combined mental illness and substance use disorders in Ghana in this 2026 qualitative study. Users described care as discontinuous, with repeated relapse and re-engagement, while workers pointed to inadequate staffing, transport difficulties, and inconsistent outreach. Both groups agreed on the system-level problems, and the authors call for integrated, person-centered services.
pmc-13431374:
Lei Chen and co-authors tested in 2026 whether a bundle of heart scan measures can sort risk for people with diabetes whose heart arteries show no hard block. A scan of the heart arteries can read far more than tightness alone.

The bundle joins plaque load, signs that a plaque may tear, weak flow past deposits, and swelling in fat that hugs the vessels. Joining these reads forecast bad events better than any one alone. The authors say the full bundle could help clinics flag higher-risk patients for closer watch and earlier guard steps. They also warn that the diabetes-linked claims remain early and need fresh proof.
pmc-13433874:
Lihua Zeng and colleagues reveal a core gene network, switched on by epigenetic marks, that drives leukaemia signalling in acute myeloid leukaemia. Core hubs were checked for single-cell location and subtype patterns in a blood-cancer database, with perturbation analysis expanding the network. The study hands leukaemia researchers a compact, epigenetically activated circuit to test as a drug target.
pmc-13434374:
Jonah A Schneider and colleagues hunt for kin of a rare wasp in 2026. The known species is the only one in its family with two rows of spines on the female belly plate. The team checked more wasps with that trait using form study and public DNA barcodes.

At least five more likely species turned up around the world. Two are named and described here, while the rest wait for more material. pmc-13434474:

Plants with one working copy and one lost copy hit the best balance of height, stems, and nitrogen uptake. Those mixed plants out yield both pure forms, a gain breeders call hybrid vigor. Elite hybrid lines in farms already carry the mixed state. One amino change, favored since early farming, softens hormone output.
pmc-13434574:

A guard protein blocks faulty pairing, while a pause in the process can restore matches. Faulty pairing also links to egg cell death. Fast repeat change may thus limit which groups can breed.
pmc-13434774:

A two part active motif drives the odd path, bench work proves. Breeding rounds sharpened both speed and shape choice. Runs at gram scale made chiral alcohols and diols for later use. Green chemists gain a new trick: remote control of shape without harsh reagents. The scope survey shows which starting alcohols fit best.
pmc-13435374:
Moore and colleagues ask whether a weaker heart pump speeds brain shrinkage in people who carry the APOE ε4 gene variant, the strongest common genetic risk for Alzheimer's disease. Cardiac output, the blood volume pumped each minute, can sit low without frank heart disease. Low output tied to smaller brain volumes only in gene carriers, not in non carriers. Over time the pattern sharpened. Carriers with lower starting output showed faster growth of a fluid filled brain cavity, a standard sign of tissue loss. Non carriers showed no such link. The authors urge caution and replication, but the split suggests heart health may matter most for brains already at genetic risk, a case for watching cardiac function in carriers.
pmc-13435474:
Mianqun Zhang's team tested pyrroloquinoline quinone, or PQQ, in 2026 to protect pig eggs from heat stress, a major drag on female fertility. PQQ restored key maturation steps, cut reactive oxygen, steadied membrane charge and energy stores, eased DNA damage and cell death, and kept spindle and cytoplasm structures in order. Embryos from treated eggs cleaved and reached blastocyst stage more often. Animal breeders get a promising lab lead for hot climates, with human relevance still untested.
pmc-13435674:
Janis Timoshenko and coauthors teach a machine learner to split blended X ray spectra by species in 2026. Catalysts under work hold many atom forms at once, and their spectra blur together. Training used vast sets of computed spectra across many compounds.

The learner spots shared patterns and pulls blended signals apart. It also reports how unsure each split is, a rare bonus. Copper oxide under carbon dioxide conversion gave a live test. Charge split oddly there, forming copper oxalate plus metal even with no current applied. Operando studies gain a sharper eye for the active few atoms.
pmc-13436674:
Abagayle Bierowski and coauthors survey junior emergency faculty on the unwritten rules of academic life in 2026. Every respondent felt the unwritten curriculum shape their growth. Mentorship and peer backing stand out as unspoken must haves in the themes. Informal norms govern who gets chances, credit, and cover in daily work. Schlossberg transition theory frames how newcomers read those norms. Naming the hidden rules may ease the rocky move from trainee to faculty.
pmc-13437074:

A donor filtration rate at the low mark hurt most strongly, and donors aged one year or younger drew refusals. The child's age, dialysis status, and donor infection history did not shift choices in a clear way. The authors suggest shared, evidence-based rules for accepting offers could steady such decisions.
pmc-13437274:

The study asks what happens to craft training when smart tools enter writing, recording, release, and rights handling.

AI now touches each stage of the music chain, the study finds, pushing jobs toward digital, team-based, and data-guided work. Yet the groups see the change unevenly, and their ability to adapt varies widely. That mismatch leaves the talent pipeline out of balance, with schools, firms, and officials pulling in different directions. Wang proposes a four-part plan built on stronger institutions, reformed teaching, engaged employers, and community support. The goal is a workforce that can keep pace with the tools.
pmc-13438774:

Mining single-cell datasets from human livers, their 2026 study spotted a distinct stellate subgroup marked by a gene called AREL1, raised only in this disease.

The authors present AREL1 as a fresh, druggable address. The study hands drug hunters a mechanism and a delivery route.
pmc-13439074:

The integrated model beat baselines and partial variants on precision, recall, and ranking quality at various cutoffs. pmc-13439374:

pmc-13439474:

pmc-13441374:
