A three-part result held, reflecting Kernberg's model, but the full fifty-seven-item form lacked stability across samples, prompting a fourteen-item version that did hold stability. Self-other swings tracked character illness, while goal and behavior swings marked immature shields. Clinicians get a shorter, cross-sample Czech tool for edge assessment, with defense patterns as a useful tag.
pmc-13441774:
Jiyan Xu and colleagues examine how college students' views of their own bodies, thinking and feeling alike, translate into physical activity, reporting a 2026 survey study. Many students know exercise matters yet fail to act, a knowing-doing gap. A survey of 2,016 students used standard questionnaires for body-self relations, sport motivation, and activity levels. Models tested how cognitive body assessment and affective body assessment combine and whether motivation carries their effects.

No sex gap appeared in either body assessment, though motivation and activity differed by sex. The two assessments worked synergistically: positive feeling compensated when thinking appraisal ran low, yet feeling alone added little when thinking already ran high. Motivation carried much of the effect, with inner motivation far stronger than outer pressure. Feeling also amplified the path from thinking to activity through motivation. The authors recommend dual-track programs that build body knowledge and body warmth together.
pmc-13441974:
Baopeng Song's team shared fine Cambrian fossils in 2026 that settle a long debate: bryozoans, colony filter feeders, arose in the Cambrian burst like other major animal groups. An earlier fossil find lacked clear soft tissue and bone detail, leaving its ties debated. New specimens from China's Xiannudong Formation preserve stone-filled soft tissues inside block frames, including styles, ring muscles, thin sacs, and septa.

These traits place the fossils firmly in Bryozoa as crown members, proving Cambrian origin and showing early diversity in colony build. The deep crown position also means an even deeper stem origin. Paleontologists get a resolved phylum origin and a richer picture of Cambrian colonial life.
pmc-13442374:
Robin C Anderson and colleagues test whether a tungsten compound can stop nitrate from fattening Salmonella in cattle rumen fluid, reporting work in 2026. Nitrate feeding in ruminants may enrich nitrate-breathing Salmonella, an unwelcome trade. Tungstate blocks the nitrate reductase enzyme, so it might cut that enrichment. Rumen microbes were incubated for twenty-six hours under rumen-like conditions with nitrate, tungstate, both, or neither, half the vessels seeded with Salmonella Newport.

Tungstate did slow nitrate use and nearly erased nitrite build-up, as the enzyme logic predicts. Salmonella grew more under tungstate, alone or with nitrate, than in control or nitrate-only vessels, the opposite of the hoped-for protection. Coliform bacteria surged under the additives, especially in seeded vessels. The authors conclude that blocking nitrate reduction does not restrain Salmonella in this system and may free room for it, a caution for feed additive design.
pmc-13442874:
Wanzhuo Shi and colleagues design carbon rings that act as tiny electromagnets in a 2026 paper. Charge through a loop makes a magnetic field, yet single-molecule loops make weak fields. Round carbon hoops with ring-shared electrons can carry currents around the whole hoop.

Two math frames mapped currents in hoop junctions wired through one hoop unit. Near twin energy peaks, wave clash could flip ring current and swell it far past the through current. The same trick held in C60 ball junctions, where gate volts reach the key peaks with ease. Fields hit 14.2 mT under a bias of 100 mV in the fullerene runs. The authors offer clash-led design as a route to molecule-scale magnets for future circuits.
pmc-13443074:
Lulu Du and colleagues model spine bone safety when cancer-eaten vertebrae get radiation seeds plus cement in a 2026 study. A 3D computer spine, built from scans of a healthy adult, held fake eaten zones in the L4 bone at three size grades. Each grade faced seed-only care or seeds plus bone cement, called vertebroplasty.

Heat, dose wear, and load stress fed one joint model under a 500 N load with a twist. For small zones at or below a 30 percent share of the bone, seeds alone barely moved stress marks. Cement raised bend shift to 7.12 mm and peak stress to 36.29 MPa in that grade. Large zones gained little from seeds alone. The authors use the model to weigh when cement helps or hurts bone strength.
pmc-13443174:
Tingting Wu and Bing Liu present a 2026 framework for high-fidelity processing of colorless images. These grayscale pictures are common in posters, branding, and photo art, where older tools blur edges and mismatch color. Their dual-channel pipeline for color-plus-depth images adds a weighted Laplacian step for cross-modal consistency, a three-level feature hierarchy, and brightness-guided edge protection.

On standard benchmarks, the method cut color reconstruction error by 60 percent against the Welsh method, lifted matching recall from 62.3 percent to 91.4 percent, and reached strong sharpness scores on a photo editing set. It also ran faster than diffusion rivals while beating them on picture quality. The authors offer the pipeline as a transparent, reproducible benchmark for graphic design work, with broader image sets still to test.
pmc-13443674:
Yang Wang and coauthors present a 2026 geochemistry study of metals in sediment and pore water from an intermountain basin in the Northwest Pacific. The region is far less studied than the eastern Pacific or Atlantic. The team traced ten metals through the sediment-water boundary zone, where early chemical change concentrates and dissolves metals.

In this nutrient-poor region the oxygen boundary sat deeper than in richer seas, and weaker biology plus scarcer clay carriers left both solid and dissolved metals lower. Above the boundary, solid enrichment and scant dissolved metal varied in step, pointing to shared redox controls at each depth. The findings sharpen models of seafloor mineral growth and the fate of metals near nodule exploration blocks.
pmc-13444374:
Allaham reviewed how well AI models reading structural brain MRI can split Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment from cognitively normal controls. Searching five databases to February 2026 yielded seven qualifying studies. Most were deep learning systems trained on the ADNI research cohorts.

For Alzheimer's versus normal controls across five studies, pooled sensitivity reached 0.96 and pooled specificity 0.95 in the pooled analysis. That shows top discrimination in the meta-analysis. The two mild impairment head-to-heads told a murkier story. Sensitivity stayed high, between 0.91 at the low end and 0.93 at the high end. But specificity swung widely, spanning 0.54 at the bottom to 0.98 at the top between the studies. That spread makes pooled figures for early impairment hard to read, in the author's view. The review concludes MRI-based AI performs strongly for full Alzheimer's. It needs larger studies, tested outside their home data in diverse groups, for early stages.
pmc-13444474:
Taher Babaee and colleagues compare two braces for teen spine curves with high chest peaks in a 2026 study. The Chêneau brace sculpts curves in 3D, yet guides cap its use at peaks below the T7/T8 line. Their trial put 52 teens with peaks above that line in either a Milwaukee or a Chêneau brace, each with matched exercises.

The pool held 12 boys and 40 girls in all. Both arms cut the Cobb angle, chest hump, trunk shift, and peak bone drift against pre-brace marks, each at p below 0.05 in the checks. Head-to-head reads found no clear gap between the braces on in-brace X-ray marks. The authors say the Chêneau cap may sit too low for high curves. Fit and wear time may matter more than brace brand here.
pmc-13445774:
Georgia Vayena and coauthors show a 2026 study that magnetite rescues biogas output in sulfate-rich air-free tanks, where sulfate eaters compete with methane makers and sulfide poisons the system. The team ran magnetite-amended reactors under sulfate stress, mapping germs by genome-centered gene surveys and energy models.

Magnetite cut sulfide poison by settling and lifted methane output by 19 percent, while methane makers grew without squashing sulfate eaters or partner guilds. The stronger teamwork network moved carbon and charge better despite sulfate stress. Tank crews gain a group-level fix, though cost and scale trials remain.
pmc-13446074:
Wahia Tasnim and M. Rubaiyat Hossain Mondal mine gene data for shared signals between chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and rheumatoid arthritis, in a 2026 computing study. The two diseases often travel together, yet their shared molecular roots stay murky. The pair layered several analysis and learning methods in the R language.

Comparing gene activity across datasets gave ninety genes changed in both diseases. Network analysis pulled hub genes from that set, while a penalized learning method, the strongest of those tried, named its own key genes. The overlap left four candidates: ETS1, YY1, CREBP5, and GTF2H1. Each sorted patients from controls well in checks, and the paper maps partner factors and drugs tied to them, as leads for lab follow-up.
pmc-13446874:
Margot J. A. van de Sande and colleagues track fetal growth in twin anemia polycythemia sequence, where slow blood drift between shared-placenta twins leaves one anemic and the other overloaded, in a 2026 study. Donor twins often arrive small, yet growth paths in the womb were poorly drawn. Records covered forty-five spontaneous cases at Leiden from 2002 to 2024.

Donor weight estimates trailed the recipient's at every check. Growth restriction, by a set weight line, hit over four in ten donors at twenty weeks and none of the recipients, and no recipient crossed the line before twenty-four weeks. At birth about three in four donors were small for their age, against one in five recipients, even though donors often held the larger placenta share.
pmc-13447074:
Zhiheng Wang and colleagues ask how three liver enzymes measured early in pregnancy relate to gestational diabetes, in a 2026 cohort of 9,077 single pregnancies. The enzymes, ALT, AST, and GGT, are routine blood marks of liver strain, which travels with sugar trouble. The team tested each mark alone and in each other's company.

GGT carried the strongest tie to later diabetes in every model. ALT's tie, clear on its own, faded once GGT entered the model, and math checks showed GGT accounted for most of ALT's signal. AST flipped sign under joint modeling, showing a negative direct tie against a positive path through GGT, a split that sharpened in women with higher ALT. Body weight and sampling week bent the links further.
pmc-13447274:
Jebum Kim, Lina Wen and Sangyoon Lim study how restored face-to-face cues shape medical service quality in South Korea in a 2026 survey. Mask rules during the pandemic hid smiles and expressions that build trust between patients and staff. With mandates lifted, the authors ask whether visible nonverbal cues now lift satisfaction and loyalty beyond a simple return to normal.

Four hundred eight people who visited medical facilities after mandates ended answered an online survey. Quick, helpful responses and easy access most raised how useful care felt, while physical setting also shaped how easy care felt. A sense of flow, meaning smooth absorbed engagement, carried quality gains into satisfaction and loyalty. The authors advise clinics to treat nonverbal skill as a core part of quality, not a soft extra.
pmc-13447974:
Roya Paridar and Babak Mohammadzadeh Asl offer a 2026 simple sound beam shaping weight that preserves background speckle while crisping detail. Minimum variance imaging clears well but costs too much compute, while null minus imaging loses speckle, so the team derived weights from minus between two transmit sub-array images.

Mock and lab tests showed the method beating both rivals on detail, alone lifting detail, contrast, and speckle keeping at once. Low computing burden suits real-time use. Doctors gain sharper built opening images without losing the speckle texture that aids spotting.
pmc-13448074:
ZhiDi Liu and colleagues apply a 2026 machine learning approach to pinpoint fracturing sweet spots in deep coal rock gas in the Daning-Jixian block on the Ordos Basin edge. Facing strong reservoir heterogeneity, the team built a graded evaluation model from ten geological and engineering factors using a particle-swarm-optimized extreme learning machine.

Predictions for two coal seams in Well X-11 topped 85 percent accuracy, with top-grade sweet spots predominating, and block-wide mapping confirmed abundant high-quality resources. Later perforation and fracturing data validated the picks. Operators gain reliable logging-based guidance for interval selection and stimulation design.
pmc-13448174:
Hyeon Ju Lee and colleagues review imaging of traumatic aortic injury and blood around the heart in a 2026 article. Both conditions rank among the deadliest in chest trauma, and many victims die before reaching hospital. CT angiography, a contrast-enhanced vessel scan, anchors diagnosis, triage and treatment planning when patients are stable enough to reach the scanner.

Key scan signs for aortic injury include a torn inner flap, blood inside the wall, a bulging pouch and leaking contrast, which together feed a standard grading system that guides care. For blood around the heart, scan density, pressure signs on the heart and associated heart injuries set urgency. Look-alike pitfalls such as a normal duct bump, nearby blood without aortic injury and motion blur are catalogued to prevent errors.
pmc-13448474:
Guorui Zhou, Yana Li and Beihai Wang build a two-layer freshness indicator film for minced pork in a 2026 packaging study. Smart films that change colour as food spoils can replace guesswork from dates, yet common film materials swell, tear or block gases poorly. A biodegradable plastic base plus a pigment coating from purple tomatoes offered a sturdier pairing, with plasma treatment helping the layers bond.

Rising pigment content stretched the film further before breaking, cut water vapour and oxygen passage, and sharpened the pH-driven colour shift. Migration into food simulants rose with pigment load yet stayed part of the reported profile. On pork mince packs, films at higher pigment levels shifted from pale purple toward green as the meat went off. Real-time spoilage signalling plus better barrier performance broaden the base plastic's packaging prospects.
pmc-13448874:
Hong Sang Choi and co-authors investigate in 2026 whether a diabetes drug class that lowers uric acid also lowers the chance of developing gout. They drew on Korea's national health insurance database from 2015 to 2020, comparing new users of SGLT2 inhibitors with new users of DPP-4 inhibitors, a similar diabetes treatment. After matching, 20,866 pairs were analyzed.

Gout appeared less often in the SGLT2 group, at 2,792.6 cases per 100,000 person-years against 3,346.7, giving a hazard ratio of 0.80. The pattern held across several sensitivity checks. A genetic analysis using variants in the drug's target gene as a stand-in for lifelong inhibition also pointed to lower gout risk. The authors counsel caution, since records-based studies cannot fully rule out hidden differences between groups.
pmc-13448974:
Rodolfo Nunes and co-authors describe in 2026 a way to make unusually concentrated silver nanoparticle suspensions and lock them into cellulose films for reuse. Most water-based recipes yield weak, short-lived colloids. Their method reduced a silver salt with a borohydride reagent in the presence of a polymer stabilizer. It reached concentrations up to 100 millimolar, with mostly round, evenly sized particles that stayed stable for at least a month.

The particles were then set into regenerated cellulose films holding up to 5 percent silver by weight, keeping the cellulose's own crystal form. The films sped up a standard test reaction, the reduction of 4-nitrophenol, and survived at least five reuse cycles with little loss of performance. Against bacteria, the films acted on both Escherichia coli and Staphylococcus aureus, with stronger, dose-dependent effects on the latter.
pmc-13449474:
Xue-Jing Yang and coauthors built an explainable machine-learning model to predict death in children with sepsis, publishing in 2026. Sepsis remains the leading cause of in-hospital death among children, yet precise early prediction tools are scarce. The team used the 2024 Phoenix criteria to define cases at a Nanjing children's hospital.

From hundreds of thousands of screened admissions, 2,477 children with sepsis were identified, and three feature-selection methods narrowed the inputs to twelve. Eight algorithms were trained on seventy percent of the data and tested on the rest, with the best model chosen by test accuracy and discrimination. Because the model explains its predictions, clinicians can see which factors drive a high-risk flag and act on them sooner.
pmc-13449574:
Liya Bida and Khalil Kashkush compared wild emmer wheat with bread wheat in 2026 to trace large genome rearrangements. Wild emmer is the direct ancestor of domesticated wheat and holds diversity that breeding may need, but its large, complex genome has kept big structural changes poorly explored. The team looked for changes linked to jumping genes called transposable elements.

Seventeen large genome-specific changes, from one thousand to one million base pairs, were found, many tied to Gypsy and Copia retrotransposons. Genotyping across sixty-eight wild emmer lines from seven regions confirmed the changes as highly variable, with several showing strong regional patterns. Most changes covered genes, including disease-resistance and metabolic genes. Breeders gain a map of variation that may carry useful traits.
pmc-13451174:
Kanchan Kushwaha and others built a half-auto solid target rig in 2026 to make med isotopes with an old PETtrace-800 cyclotron in India. Scan work needs isotopes like copper-64 and indium-111, whose making needs rich solid targets for good yields. The two-decade-old rig at the Radiation Medicine Centre had run only liquid and gas targets.

A home-made solid target rig was built and fit to the med cyclotron site. Day-to-day making of pharma-grade copper-64 and indium-111 then went ahead, with yields per beam that back clinic use. The refit stretches an old rig to new isotope work with no need for a new cyclotron. Scan centres gain a plan for a like refit of their own old rigs.
pmc-13451874:
Thanh-Cong Truong sets out in 2026 a protocol that welds strict review rules into design science work on applied tech. Such studies often rest on reviews no one can retrace and end with gadgets that yield no shared design lessons. The protocol runs seven phases, from problem framing to pulling design knowledge out of the built thing.

A known review frame, PRISMA 2020, sits inside the mapping phase. Six worksheets log each phase, and three tracing rules bind them: each need traces to proof, each part to a need, each claim to a test. A worked case on AI choice for small firms fills every sheet, and two short cases show the frame fits other fields.
pmc-13452274:
Dalia Diaz-Delgado, Katlijn De Meulenaere, and Anna Rosanas-Urgell test in 2026 whether a rare Duffy blood variant shields red cells from a monkey malaria now spilling into people. The Duffy dock on red cells is the germ's main door, and the FY*X variant thins that dock. Blood came from seven donors whose Duffy types were set by clumping tests and gene reads.

One donor carried the variant on both copies. In a single invasion run, germ growth in that donor's cells reached only a fraction of the fold seen in standard cells. The authors say the variant curbs this malaria in the dish, and they urge exact Duffy typing in lab host studies.
pmc-13452574:
Vanshika Gupta and five co-authors give tumor model balls of cells a new way to glow under electric control, with no lamp needed. The glow method, called electrochemiluminescence, pairs a ruthenium dye with a helper amine that soaks into the cell balls first. Their 2026 study swaps this pair in for an older, weaker chemistry based on luminol and peroxide.

Soaking the balls in the amine first sharpened the glow image and kept imaging going for over three hours. The balls even kept glowing for minutes after the voltage stopped, a first for a living system. Balls grown from cancer cells glowed at a different strength than balls from healthy cells, likely since they soaked up more of the amine. The gap hints at a simple lab test to tell tumor like growths from harmless ones.
pmc-13452874:
Pickel and Rabern ask whether Venn diagrams, the overlapping-circle figures of logic classes, possess a compositional semantics like language, where each syntactic rule pairs with a rule for building meaning. Diagrams are often cast as the opposite of language, so a successful compositional treatment would redraw the boundary between linguistic and visual representation.

They develop two syntaxes for the diagrams: a region-first approach that builds from spatial regions, and a cell-first approach that builds from the smallest enclosed cells of the figure. For each syntax they construct a matching compositional semantics, so the meaning of any whole diagram derives systematically from its parts and their arrangement. No earlier work had supplied such a semantics, despite the diagrams' clear formal structure and correctness conditions known since Venn. The authors suggest the two approaches open new routes for analyzing other visual representation systems compositionally.
pmc-13453774:
Laima Okunevičiūtė Neverauskienė and Dalia Bagdžiūnienė survey how techno overload, the flood of digital demands at work, feeds insecurity among Lithuanian employees. Their 2026 study covers 754 workers from public and private employers, with an average age of 41.9 years. Phone and web surveys fed a model built on two work psychology theories.

Techno overload tracked higher worry about both the current job and the wider occupation's future. Job insecurity sat in the middle of the chain, carrying overload's effect into plans to quit and into occupation worry. The authors argue that digital change thus harms staff through felt risk, not only through workload itself. They call for fuller studies of occupation insecurity, a less explored form of work worry, and for designs that pace new tools.
pmc-13454074:
Sen Tong, Jiaxin Chen, Yan Li, and Wei Zhao review how to design water rich gels that copy real blood vessels, for grafts and for tissues that need their own blood supply. Their 2026 review pulls lessons from native vessels into four design dimensions and tests them against two fields that rarely talk. Hydrogels appeal since they hold water like tissue and can be tuned in stiffness and chemistry.

The four dimensions are layer by layer sizing from artery to capillary, multi layer walls, a chemical setting that invites vessel growth, and stretch that matches the body's demands. Uses range from small artery grafts to bone repair, wound healing, and heart tissue patches. The authors warn that copy fidelity is not the goal: gels rot on one clock, vessels mature on another, and joins to the host often fail. Smart, stimulus aware builds are the way forward.
pmc-13454174:
Yucheng Zhao and fifteen co-authors uncover the full recipe that iris family plants use to build isoflavones, prized plant compounds with drug like effects. That recipe was well mapped in beans and their kin, yet a mystery in other families. Their 2026 study finds the iris route runs on an uncharted enzyme family member as its synthase, plus a hydroxylase that is not of the usual class.

Two further enzymes add methyl groups, and a newly found family member adds the final hydroxyl touch. Family tree analysis suggests the iris path is ancient and widely conserved, perhaps the original route in land plants. Soybean, by contrast, runs a specialized path found only in its own family. The find closes a long gap and shows two plant lines solved the same chemistry in their own ways.
pmc-13454574:
Chieh-Yu Liang and twelve colleagues test, in 2026, how to coax fresh antibodies against new coronavirus variants in mice whose immune systems were trained on the original strain. Prior exposure creates imprinting, a bias that can crowd out responses to updated vaccines. Female mice were primed with one of two Wuhan-strain vaccines, then boosted with Omicron-matched shots.

Moving the shot to a new muscle site barely changed variant-specific responses. Larger doses and repeat boosters helped. The nose route helped most: a nasal booster raised variant-specific antibodies in blood, lung wash fluid, and nearby lymph nodes above the muscle route. Blocking the new variant rested mainly on antibodies that ignored the old strain. The authors conclude that route and repetition can break imprinting's grip, at least in mice.
pmc-13455474:
Sandra Díaz-Torres and colleagues warn that high iron stores in pregnancy may slow fetal growth in a 2026 cohort study. Low iron and anaemia have long been tied to small babies, yet the effect of high ferritin without anaemia during pregnancy was less studied. The ECLIPSES study followed 713 mother-child pairs, measuring ferritin in the first and third trimesters and tracking fetal size through pregnancy to birth.

High ferritin at either time linked with smaller fetal weight, thigh bone length and head size late in pregnancy. A persistently high ferritin path more than doubled the risk of a short thigh bone and tripled the risk of low birth weight in one estimate. Low ferritin without anaemia, by contrast, linked with slightly larger fetal weight and no birth harm. The findings question blanket iron supplements for women who already store plenty of iron.
pmc-13457374:
Huimin Wu and a ten-author team test prunetin, a flavonoid, against the inflammatory cell death that worsens heart damage after a heart attack. Network pharmacology flagged TNF-alpha as a likely target, and binding simulations plus resonance assays backed the pairing. Their 2026 study then used a mouse heart-attack model, measuring heart function, tissue scarring, and blood injury markers, RNA sequencing and protein assays tracing the mechanism.

Prunetin-treated mice pumped better, carried less blood injury, and showed reduced fibrosis and inflammatory signals. The treatment lowered pyroptosis proteins such as NLRP3 and active gasdermin D, by damping the TNF-alpha/p38 MAPK/ERK signaling chain. A drug that forces TNF-alpha back up erased prunetin's protection, supporting the proposed route. Results in glucose-and-oxygen-starved heart cells and human cardiac organoids lined up with the mouse data, a basis, the authors suggest, for developing prunetin toward therapy.
pmc-13457674:
Ito‐Naito and colleagues catalog genetic variation in three lesser-known immune genes in the Japanese population in this 2026 study. The genes HLA-E, HLA-F, and HLA-G guide immune recognition. They vary far less than their famous classical relatives. Their full-length sequences, including control regions, were poorly charted in East Asia. The team used long-read sequencing on samples from 531 healthy Japanese individuals.

They identified 24 HLA-E versions, 30 HLA-F versions, and 19 HLA-G versions, including 36 entirely new variants and 16 extensions of known ones. Despite this hidden variety in non-coding regions, the actual protein diversity stayed narrow, with one HLA-F version carried by 96.7 percent of participants in the sample set. Related genes HLA-F and HLA-G showed linked inheritance patterns, while HLA-E varied independently, giving transplant and disease researchers a detailed reference.
pmc-13458674:
Hanyue Li and colleagues patch a blind spot in the international grading system for lung adenocarcinoma, which currently excludes the mucinous variant entirely. Invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma behaves distinctly, so leaving it ungraded limits prognosis. Their 2026 study folds mucinous and mixed tumors into an expanded three-grade scheme, classing mucinous-predominant tumors with under 20 percent high-grade patterns as grade 2.

The team built the system on 692 stage I to III patients from Shanghai Chest Hospital, then validated it in 7,862 patients from the American SEER registry. Prognostic accuracy improved in both, with C-index values near 0.71 in both cohorts. Survival separated cleanly by grade: five-year rates of 87.5 percent for grade 1, 73.1 for grade 2, and 55.5 for grade 3 in the training cohort, and a similar spread in validation. The expanded scheme outperformed the current system head to head, giving clinicians a standardized risk tool for a tumor type that fell outside the framework.
pmc-13458774:
Hai-Shun Ni and colleagues shrink penile prosthesis surgery down to local anesthesia and a two-centimeter cut. Three-piece inflatable implants are the standard fix for severe erectile dysfunction that ignores pills. Standard surgery needs general or spinal anesthesia and a longer incision, barring many older or medically fragile men. Their 2026 retrospective study compares 220 implant patients: 118 conventional against 102 done through the scrotal opening the team calls Wang's incision, under local block.

The modified group was faster throughout: quicker cylinder placement, shorter operating time, and a shorter incision. Pain stayed bearable, peaking at 4.51 on a ten-point scale during reservoir placement, and nobody needed conversion to deeper anesthesia or suffered a serious complication. Erectile function gains matched the standard group, and patients were just as pleased. The authors recommend the technique for men unfit for general anesthesia, trading nothing in outcome for a smaller wound and quicker recovery.
pmc-13459174:
Wei Duan and co-authors built a forecasting system for influenza in Baoshan City, China, by blending several data streams into a deep learning model. Their 2026 study gathered confirmed flu cases, flu-like illness reports from clinics, symptom monitoring, weather records, and search-engine trend data from January 2022 to June 2025. They used a Long Short-Term Memory network, a model designed for time-pattern data, and tested which combination of inputs predicted case counts best.

Clinic reports of flu-like illness correlated most strongly with confirmed cases among all sources examined. The model using those reports alone performed best, reaching a fit score of 0.79 on held-out test data. Adding one search keyword about flu-shot necessity matched that accuracy with a more practical model, while weather and symptom data added little. The team also derived an early-warning threshold for outbreak alerts.
pmc-13459274:
Cecilie von Bülow and co-authors ran a pilot trial of group based occupational therapy for adults whose chronic conditions limit daily activities. The group program, called ADAPT, teaches structured problem solving and adaptive strategies, and was compared with usual one to one therapy in a Danish municipality. Their 2026 feasibility study randomized a small group of clients. It checked recruitment, retention, staff impact, completion of outcome measures, and how faithfully therapists delivered the manual, against preset criteria for proceeding to a full trial.

Twelve clients and four trained occupational therapists took part. The group program was delivered with high fidelity and full dose, and most progression criteria were met. Recruitment ran slower than hoped, and the one to one group completed fewer follow up evaluations and reported receiving limited trial information. The authors judge a full scale trial feasible after minor procedural fixes.
pmc-13459374:
Koffi Romiald Kouame and co-authors examined what insecticides do to malaria mosquitoes that survive exposure, focusing on reproduction rather than death. Their 2026 study worked with a resistant Anopheles gambiae population from Tiassalé, Côte d'Ivoire, plus a susceptible lab strain. Females were exposed to doses of three insecticides set to kill only twenty percent. Afterward they tracked lifespan, blood feeding success, viable egg production, and the share of females laying viable eggs, using standard World Health Organization bottle tests.

Sublethal effects differed by insecticide and strain. Broflanilide shortened life in the resistant field population, while the other two compounds hit the susceptible strain harder. Deltamethrin cut blood feeding success by 25.5 percent in the susceptible strain and 19.5 percent in the resistant one. Chlorfenapyr and broflanilide reduced viable egg output in both strains; after chlorfenapyr, only 41.5 percent of resistant females produced viable eggs against a 65 percent comparison level.
pmc-13459774:
Mohd Tarequl Islam and co-authors hunted for a drug weakness specific to colorectal cancers missing the chromatin protein PBRM1, lost in many tumors and leaving cells stressed by DNA damage. The strategy, synthetic lethality, kills only cells with the defect by blocking the backup repair pathway they depend on. In their 2026 study, the team engineered matched colorectal cancer cells with and without PBRM1, screened four drugs including two PARP inhibitors, and checked colony growth and cell cycle behavior.

The PARP inhibitors selectively suppressed the cells lacking PBRM1 in the dose response and twelve day colony assays reported. The mechanism involved arrest at the G2/M checkpoint, the last quality control stop before cell division, where damaged cells stalled instead of dividing. Broader chromatin targeting drugs from the same screen showed no such selective profile. PARP inhibition is a precision option for this group, the authors propose.
pmc-13461574:
Tansheng Lu and Zihan Cheng build a 2026 theory framework about what happens to thinking and skills when artificial intelligence surrounds a job. A key idea is occupational exposure: how much a job's tasks overlap with what AI can do. Some workers offload thinking to AI, while others watch and steer their own thought more carefully. The authors link these habits to a narrowing effect they call an information bubble.

Drawing on ideas about shared thinking across people and tools, the framework tries to explain why the same AI setting helps one worker grow and leaves another weaker. Offloading routine steps can free attention for harder work, yet heavy reliance may dull memory and judgment over time. Self-checking habits sit between exposure and outcome in their model. The piece is theory only, with no new data, and it maps questions for later studies of skill change as AI use deepens.
pmc-13462274:
Fassio and colleagues surveyed apple orchards in northwestern Italy over three years to track the woolly apple aphid and its enemy, the parasitoid wasp Aphelinus mali. The aphid, a North American import, attacks roots, trunks, and branches and has grown harder to control as key insecticides were withdrawn. The team followed five orchards under organic and integrated management to see how pest and parasitoid move together through the seasons.

Infestations rose in spring, peaked in summer, and faded toward autumn, but pressure varied by year and orchard and ran higher under organic management. The wasp's numbers broadly mirrored the aphid's, and its parasitism rate climbed after pest peaks. Analysis showed the wasp answers rising host density up to a threshold, past which control shows as a higher kill rate rather than more wasps. The numbers, they say, can base spray thresholds that use the parasitoid's work.
pmc-13462774:

pmc-13463274:

pmc-13463374:

pmc-13463574:

pmc-13463774:

pmc-13464874:

pmc-13465274:

pmc-13465674:

pmc-13466074:
Syed Sameer Aga and colleagues reviewed pancreatic cancer cases in 2026 from Jeddah, asking how often diabetes travels with the disease and which blood groups appear. Pancreatic cancer ranks seventh for cancer deaths worldwide, and diabetes roughly doubles its risk, with the link running both ways. pmc-13466274:

A full twelve-lead ECG recorded before arrival can be transmitted ahead, letting teams spot a blocked artery early and prepare the catheter lab. The review also covers how tracings get read, by machine or by clinician, and the network design behind regional heart attack systems. Current European and American guidelines anchor the recommendations.
pmc-13466774:
Lileikyte and colleagues analysed a 2026 retrospective cohort on handgrip strength in the hand on the same side as a stroke, called the ipsilesional hand. The authors back grip as a simple recovery indicator, while noting the models need outside validation.
pmc-13466974:
Lee-Fong Lin and colleagues pair lab-made curcumin relatives with blue light to calm psoriasis-like skin cell growth, in a 2026 study. Psoriasis speeds skin cell production into red, scaly plaques that hurt and wear on daily life. The authors frame the pairing as a candidate light-activated therapy whose mechanism now needs mapping in living skin.
pmc-13467174:

Four source databases supplied reviews, population studies, and guidelines for the synthesis. The drug families blamed most often span seizure and migraine medicines, antidepressants, allergy-style blockers, and decongestants.

Sulfur-based drugs such as topiramate typically strike both eyes at once by swelling tissue behind the iris and pushing the lens forward, even shifting focus toward nearsightedness. Other families work through pupil widening instead. The authors list typical timing after a dose starts and give practical steps to cut risk when prescribing to vulnerable eyes.
pmc-13467774:
Yu and co-authors build an admission-time forecast for stroke recovery after clot treatment. Instead of the usual three-month disability score alone, the team measured change in that score, counting a gain of at least two points as significant improvement.

pmc-13467874:

pmc-13467974:

pmc-13468374:

pmc-13468574:

pmc-13468774:

pmc-13469374:

pmc-13470174:

pmc-13471074:

pmc-13471174:

pmc-13471274:

pmc-13471374:

pmc-13471474:

pmc-13471674:

pmc-13472174:

pmc-13472874:

pmc-13472974:

pmc-13473074:

pmc-13473274:

pmc-13473374:

pmc-13473474:

pmc-13473674:

pmc-13474474:

pmc-13474674:

pmc-13474774:

pmc-13476874:

pmc-13478574:

pmc-13479574:

pmc-13479974:

pmc-13480074:

pmc-13482474:

Thinking-only training lifted MoCA scores but not the Mini-Mental scores, a split favoring the added movement component. Brain scans agreed, with the dual-task group showing stronger growth in connections between prefrontal thinking regions and motor regions, and the authors back remote dual-task practice as a practical early intervention.
pmc-13482574:
Fathima and colleagues pool the genetic evidence in 2026 on whether variants in estrogen receptor genes predict poor ovarian response, the disappointing egg yield that undermines fertility treatment. Poor response affects roughly 9 to 24 percent of women in assisted reproduction, and two receptor genes, ESR1 and ESR2, have been suspects for years. The meta-analysis gathered 11 eligible studies and focused on three specific single-letter gene variants.

One variant stood out clearly, since women carrying the C version of ESR1 rs2234693 had 2.69 times the odds of poor response in the heterozygote comparison across studies. Under the dominant model the odds climbed to 5.41 times, and the signal was consistent in European populations within the pooled data analyzed. The other two variants gave mixed, highly variable results, so the authors back the first variant as a candidate screening marker while demanding larger, better-designed studies.
pmc-13482874:
Yang and co-authors followed middle-aged and older adults in China to see how frailty and social isolation, alone and together, relate to new depression. Their 2026 cohort study enrolled 7,330 people aged 45 and older who had no depression at the start. Frailty was scored with a 30-item index counting health problems, and isolation was scored from living alone, contact with children, and social activity.

Over follow-up, 2,007 people developed depressive symptoms on a standard ten-question scale. Frail participants faced notably higher risk than sturdy ones, and isolated participants also fared worse than connected ones. People who were both frail and isolated sat in the highest-risk group of all. Yang argues that clinics should pair physical support, like strength and nutrition help, with social programs rather than treating the two problems separately.
pmc-13483174:
Qiang Meng and others review how team find the gut germs that matter most, despite their small numbers. In 2026, the review defines keystone germs as highly connected species whose removal can sharply shift the whole germ community, even when they are not abundant. It compares the test and computational methods used to spot them.

The authors weigh network analysis, multi-omics data, and lab testing, noting that inferred networks often miss real ecological interactions. They then link identification methods to diet-based plans for restoring gut balance, describing how aimed foods could support helpful keystone species. Readers working on digestion, immunity, or microbiota-linked disease get a practical plan for moving from naming influential germs to designing programs around them.
pmc-13483574:
Zihao Wang and co-workers follow dialysis patients to see what drives good fluid control. Their 2026 study enrolled 184 people on long-term dialysis at two large hospitals. At the start, patients rated their plans, their self-control, and their daily habits. One week later, the team checked how well each patient had kept fluid in bounds.

Habit proved the best guide to later acts, ahead of stated plans. All the rated traits put together explained a large share of the gap between patients. Self-control scores showed no clear effect on their own. Plans helped most in patients whose habits were weak. For care teams, the lesson is plain: steady daily routines beat fresh resolve.
pmc-13484474:
Gonzalez-Rubio and team tested whether a classic law of perception holds while people walk, not just when they sit still judging lights or sounds. Weber's law says the smallest change a person can notice grows in proportion to the background level. Their 2026 study had healthy young adults walk at slow, comfortable, and fast speeds on split treadmills, judging which leg moved faster in forced-choice trials.

Sensitivity to leg speed differences followed the proportional pattern at slow and fast speeds, matching the law's prediction. Near comfortable speed, the pattern broke, suggesting the brain treats its preferred pace specially. A decision model using only reaction times reproduced the same scaling pattern, backing the behavioral result. Gonzalez-Rubio says the findings extend sensory scaling into the multi-sense, moving situations of daily life.
pmc-13486174:
Bechara wrote in 2026 a review of a hybrid endoscope method for Zenker's diverticulum, a pouch that forms in the throat wall of mostly older adults. The pouch stems from a stiff throat muscle that will not relax on swallowing. Food then sticks, spills back, or slips toward the lungs. Care aims to cut the wall, called the septum, between pouch and food pipe. Older scope methods cut fast but can miss the deep end of the wall.

The new method, short named SING, starts like the classic cut for the upper two thirds of the wall. Dye fluid is then puffed under the lining at the deep third, so the muscle stands out for a clean, full cut. In 102 patients at three Italian centers, the method worked in every case. Near all patients ate well at three months, with a median stay of one day and few bleeds.
pmc-13486474:
Yu-Xiang Wang builds a deep learning tool that predicts where a folded protein can be cut and rejoined without falling apart. Published in 2026, SplitSeek-Pro scores every amino acid position for splittability by fusing sequence data with three-dimensional structure. Two-stage training first learns broad patterns at scale, then refines on high-quality examples.

Tests on three distinct proteins confirmed stronger prediction than existing methods offer. Beyond single cut points, the model flags whole segments that behave as cohesive building blocks, echoing classic super-secondary motifs in protein architecture. Splitting proteins underpins circular permutation and split-reporter designs used across biotechnology, yet choosing cut sites has long been trial and error. A free web server puts residue-level guidance in any protein engineer's hands.
pmc-13487174:
Ghasemian and colleagues asked eighteen Iranian experts to validate a diabetes care model redesigned for a warming, dust-storm-prone climate. Heatwaves and storms interrupt medicine supply and clinic access, which endangers people with type 2 diabetes. Their 2026 study ran a two-round Delphi process, where experts anonymously rate statements until consensus firms up, scoring 51 statements across six health-system domains from governance to supply chains.

In round one, 46 of the 51 statements already passed the seventy percent agreement bar set by the team. The five revised statements all cleared eighty percent agreement in round two, completing full consensus. The validated model spans climate-aware governance, resilient services, workforce readiness, early-warning data systems, and protected supply chains. Ghasemian presents it as a blueprint other climate-vulnerable health systems can adapt.
pmc-13487274:
Molly E Klug traces an impulse-control wire from the ventral hippocampus to the reward hub, then shows it works in male rats only. Published in 2026, rats learn a patience task where pressing a lever too early forfeits a tasty reward, waiting twenty seconds instead. Live calcium recordings watch the pathway during choices, and targeted silencing tests cause.

In males, pathway activity rose in the five seconds before a patient, rewarded response compared with an impulsive one. Silencing the hippocampus-to-accumbens projection increased impulsive presses in males while leaving hunger, motivation, choice style, and anxiety untouched. Females showed neither the activity pattern nor the silencing effect. Sex-specific wiring for impulse control matters for disorders from addiction to obesity, where male-female differences are often treated as noise.
pmc-13487974:
Yanli Wang, Shouhui Qu, and Yapei Yang report a 2026 case of severe bleeding ten days after childbirth in a 34-year-old woman with Takayasu arteritis, a disease that inflames large arteries. Imaging of the blood vessels showed that a rare aneurysm, a weakened bulge in the uterine artery, had burst on the right side. The bleeding was heavy vaginal bleeding without bleeding inside the abdomen.

Doctors blocked the artery from inside with a catheter procedure called selective embolization, which stopped the hemorrhage. The uterus was saved, along with the patient's chance of future pregnancy. The authors warn clinicians to consider this rare cause when late bleeding after birth occurs in women with vessel disease.
pmc-13488074:
Ashaq Hussain, Marc Tatar, and Rujun Gong review cellular senescence, the state where stressed cells stop dividing yet stay alive and active, in a 2026 article. Triggers include worn chromosome ends, harmful oxygen byproducts, damage to DNA, and cancer genes switched on at the wrong time. Cells counter some threats with antioxidant defenses, which the review describes alongside the shape and metabolism changes that mark the senescent state.

Two control circuits, built around the proteins p53 and p16, lock in the growth arrest. Senescent cells also release a mix of signals that inflame nearby tissue, known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. The authors trace gene control at several levels to show why this state matters in aging and disease.
pmc-13491374:
Kursat Dikmen and colleagues compare two central line dressings in intensive care after abdominal surgery in a 2026 randomized study. Central venous catheters carry a risk of bloodstream infection, and dressings soaked in chlorhexidine, an antiseptic, may cut that risk. One hundred two patients had neck or collarbone vein lines expected to stay at least two days. They were assigned evenly to antiseptic dressings changed weekly or standard clear dressings changed every two to three days.

Bloodstream infection struck about six percent of the antiseptic group against about twenty-six percent of the standard group, a significant gap in the reported analysis. Standard dressing use stood out as a strong independent risk factor after adjustment, and each extra catheter day added risk. Skin reactions ran higher with standard dressings here.
pmc-13491574:
Mary Curnutte and others test whether rural schools differ from other schools in children's fruit and vegetable choices at lunch. In 2026, the secondary analysis uses baseline data from a cluster-randomized trial in thirty-seven Arizona schools between 2017 and 2019, weighing selected, eaten, and wasted produce to the nearest two grams. Rural schools enroll more children in the national lunch program.

On average, rural and non-rural schools did not differ in selection, consumption, or waste. Interactions told a subtler story: in non-rural schools, girls chose produce more often than boys, and slower eaters chose it more often than fast eaters, while neither pattern appeared in rural schools. The authors call for research into why sociodemographic and eating-style effects vanish in rural settings.
pmc-13491874:
Vanutsarin Anakerit leads an eleven-author team field-testing in 2026 mosquito traps across urban and rural Thailand, where surveillance programs need tools that work for many species without heavy labor. Over 270 trap-days, standard CDC light traps competed with two configurations of the BG-Pro trap, all baited, in a rotating design at sites in Bangkok, Nakhon Pathom, and a malaria-endemic rural district.

Crews collected 54,054 mosquitoes, dominated by Culex species. The upright BG-Pro caught the most insects in both city and countryside, beating the light trap several-fold, while its inverted version caught the fewest. An automated counter attached to one trap counted accurately in the city but badly underperformed in the countryside, mostly by overcounting. The authors recommend pairing traps by setting rather than crowning one device.
pmc-13493874:
Gan and Xiao tackle control problems in a hybrid system that carries offshore wind power to shore as high-voltage direct current. Their 2026 design chains a simple diode rectifier together with a modular multilevel converter in series, a flexible converter built from many switching blocks. The pair is cheaper than a full converter station but awkward to start up and prone to voltage wobble when wind output swings. The authors test three ways of running the offshore unit in simulations of a two-thousand-megawatt system.

A plain fixed-voltage scheme failed badly, letting the converter's direct voltage ripple reach well into double digits. Their proposed strategy, which controls the direct voltage directly, held that ripple to a small fraction of the failed case and kept bus voltage swings narrow. A coordinated start-up method also energised the system smoothly.
pmc-13495174:
Xin Chen, Shaomin Cheng, and Delin Zhang pool, in a 2026 meta-analysis, trials of ginger supplements in type 2 diabetes. Ginger has shown metabolic promise in lab and early clinical work, yet its net effect on sugar, blood pressure, and blood fats needed an updated tally. The team searched four databases through mid-2025 for randomized trials that set ginger against a placebo.

Thirteen trials qualified. Ginger lowered fasting blood sugar and long-term sugar control, trimmed systolic blood pressure, and cut triglycerides, a blood fat, while raising the protective cholesterol fraction. The gains, though real on paper, were small enough that the authors doubt their weight in daily care. Insulin resistance, diastolic pressure, total and harmful cholesterol, and body mass did not move. Wide spread between trial results also tempers the reading. The authors conclude ginger may help modestly, not that it can stand in for standard treatment.
pmc-13495274:
Zhenpeng Xiao and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether a simple blood ratio flags death risk in intensive care patients with protein-energy malnutrition. The ratio sets lactate, a stress marker, against albumin, a nutrition and health marker. The team drew 2,750 such patients from a large United States hospital database and split them into quarters by the ratio.

Patients in the top quarter died far more often within twenty-eight days and across the intensive care stay than those in the bottom quarter. The link held after wide adjustment for other factors, though it bent rather than rising in a straight line. Checks across patient subgroups backed the pattern. The authors propose the ratio as a cheap risk-sorting tool for this fragile group, while noting the data are backward-looking and from one database.
pmc-13495474:
Lasi Wu and colleagues count, in a 2026 study, eye changes among pregnant women in China who have HELLP syndrome, a grave pregnancy condition of blood breakdown, liver strain, and low platelets. Eye harm in this syndrome is under-recognized, though it can threaten sight. The team reviewed thirteen years of records at a Wenzhou hospital for women with the syndrome who delivered there.

Seventy cases were found, and forty-nine had an eye consult. Over half of those checked showed retinal changes, split between vessel changes and fluid lifting the retina. Higher diastolic blood pressure at diagnosis went with both kinds of change. Women given steroid drugs showed more of the fluid type, a link the authors flag with care. They urge eye checks as part of HELLP care and closer study of the steroid tie.
pmc-13495974:
Madison R Bullock and colleagues describe in 2026 a cheaper way to prepare plant DNA samples for targeted sequencing, which reads selected genes rather than a whole genome. Working with flowering plants, they shrank the usual lab reaction to one tenth of its normal size. Smaller reactions could let conservation studies include many more plants for the same budget.

The team processed 768 samples at two reaction sizes, using a standard gene set for flowering plants and robot liquid handling. Tenth-size libraries cost much less and mostly matched the larger ones in read quality. Some tenth-size libraries gave shorter inserts and fewer recovered genes overall, yet repeat samples performed as well or better, including material from old herbarium sheets.
pmc-13496074:
Di Wu and others launch a 3D printing plan that builds ordered tiny shapes inside printed plastics. In 2026, the method, called PIANO, splits tiny-scale lining up from network making, solving a kinetic mismatch in vat light-setting where rapid linking often traps mixed plastics in jumbled states. Ethylene glycol acts as a flow helper.

Boosted chain flow enables rapid in-place lining up into tunable layered and six-sided packed tube patterns with spacings of twenty to sixty billionths of a meter. During post-print heating, ethylene glycol becomes a latent linker, locking order while firming the matter. The platform enables layered, nature-like working systems from a standard printing process.
pmc-13498774:
Bollina and colleagues tested how microbes living inside mussel shells relate to survival and stress responses when mussels face heat exposure out of water. It was a 2026 marine ecology study. Such endolithic microbes, literally rock-boring organisms, can shift between helping and harming their hosts depending on conditions, and coastal heat stress is intensifying with climate change.

Bollina found mussels with corroded, microbe-bearing shells consistently survived heat stress better than clean-shelled mussels. Heat impaired everyone's movement and reduced the anchoring threads mussels spin, but mussels with endoliths were partly buffered against both losses. Their molecular responses differed: they raised two heat-shock proteins less after stress, suggesting less damage to repair, while keeping two others higher at baseline, as if pre-armed. The authors conclude these shell communities may bolster mussel resilience as marine heatwaves grow, a reminder that species' neighbors shape their climate tolerance.
pmc-13499574:
Wu and colleagues followed 205 teenagers with severe short-sightedness for ten years, in a 2026 imaging study from the Zhongshan High Myopia cohort. They tracked how a crescent of exposed tissue beside the optic nerve, the parapapillary gamma zone, grows as the eyeball lengthens. They built an algorithm for eye scans that measures the gamma zone's area, spread, and depth in three dimensions.

Wu found gamma zone area tracking with eyeball length and prescription strength, and the relationship was not a steady slope. Young people in the largest gamma zone quarter lengthened their eyes faster than everyone below them. The acceleration kicked in once the zone crossed a critical size, as if the membrane anchoring the optic nerve opening had lost its counterforce against stretching. The team argues that watching gamma zone growth offers a prognostic marker for spotting eyes headed for rapid, irreversible myopia progression, when intervention matters most.
pmc-13499674:
Ikhlas Jarrar reviews captopril kin as blockers of New Delhi metallo beta-lactamase 1, a zinc-needing enzyme that destroys most beta-lactam germ drugs including last-line drugs. In 2026, the full paper review selects studies giving blocking doses in vitro, reading them by theme because test setups varied too much for direct counted match-up.

Action rested on a free thiol group, with masking cutting potency. Shape set best binding angles, water-shy groups helped only within steric limits, and an acid end served as a second anchor. In vivo data remain limited, but captopril emerges as a hopeful scaffold with a reasoned plan for tuning future blockers.
pmc-13500374:
Yuichi Miyagawa and others compare kidney markers in Shiba Inu dogs with other breeds. In 2026, the study tests symmetric dimethylarginine, kidney marker, and cystatin C in blood from twenty-three healthy Shiba Inu and thirty-six dogs of other breeds. Symmetric dimethylarginine is promoted as an early kidney marker supposedly unaffected by muscle mass, yet breed gaps are poorly studied.

Shiba Inu showed clearly higher symmetric dimethylarginine, with a median of 12.3 versus 9.5 micrograms per decilitre and a higher reference interval, plus higher kidney marker, while cystatin C showed no consistent difference after partial weight matching. Veterinarians should interpret these two markers cautiously in Shiba Inu and with other medical assessments.
pmc-13500474:
Hongyi Chen and others build a knowledge-driven multi-modal fusion plan for diagnosing sepsis-induced acute breathing distress syndrome and predicting death. In 2026, the model joins CT images, CT reports, and lab indicators with a disease-specific knowledge graph. Sepsis-induced ARDS kills about forty percent of patients and is often missed by doctors.

The plan predicted syndrome incidence with a rightness score of 0.930 and twenty-eight-day mortality with a score of 0.843, outperforming simpler models. Error analysis and ablation studies showed each modality and the knowledge graph contributed. The interpretable system offers doctors an early warning tool to trigger program sooner.
pmc-13501074:
Ju and colleagues designed a new family of tyrosinase inhibitors, compounds that block the enzyme starting melanin production, as candidate skin-lightening agents, in a 2026 chemistry and biology study. Starting from a known copper-grabbing scaffold, they built thirteen benzamide derivatives carrying a sulfur group meant to chelate the copper at the enzyme's heart. They then tested them against mushroom enzyme, mouse melanoma cells, and zebrafish larvae.

Ju found one derivative beat the standard inhibitor kojic acid twofold against the mushroom enzyme, and kinetic studies clarified how three derivatives inhibit it. Strikingly, every derivative suppressed melanin production in the mammalian cells more potently than kojic acid, in step with blocking the cells' own tyrosinase. One compound inhibited zebrafish larval pigmentation hundreds of times more potently than the standard. The authors warn that mushroom enzyme results poorly predict performance in vertebrates, a trap for the many inhibitor programs screened that way.
pmc-13501274:
Zhao and colleagues published a 2026 review on a traditional Chinese exercise for older adults. Baduanjin is a gentle mind-body routine of eight flowing movements. The team pooled eighteen randomized trials with 1,527 adults aged 60 and older. They asked whether the practice helps sleep, mood, life quality, and body shape.

Sleep quality improved clearly in the pooled results across trials. Depressive symptoms eased by a large margin as well in the analysis. Life quality and handgrip strength also rose with regular practice. Waist and hip measures shrank modestly over the study periods. The authors flag uneven trial quality and urge bigger, stricter trials. Benefits held across the trials despite differing practice schedules used. Seven databases fed the search for trials used in the review.
pmc-13501574:
Yanmei Huang leads an eight-author team with a 2026 case of a four-pathogen infection in a 67-year-old man with diabetes. He arrived with cough, sputum, and bone pain, and a chest CT scan showed a cavity in the left lower lung lobe. Biopsy confirmed pulmonary cryptococcosis, a fungal infection, and antifungal therapy improved his breathing at first. Bone pain persisted, however, and after he stopped treatment his symptoms returned with fever and breathing failure, alongside bone-destroying lesions.

Sputum culture grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a common hospital bacterium. Sequencing of fluid washed from his airways revealed two more culprits, the fungus Aspergillus fumigatus and Mycobacterium abscessus, a fast-growing relative of tuberculosis bacteria. With therapy retargeted at all four germs he recovered and went home. The authors stress that single-pathogen thinking fails in such mixed infections, and they credit repeated review plus sequencing for the full picture.
pmc-13501774:
Hamideh Ebrahimi leads a four-author team presenting a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of restless legs syndrome prevalence across Pakistan. The disorder brings an irresistible urge to move the legs at rest, wrecking sleep and quality of life. Following PRISMA 2020 guidance, the team searched six databases, including the regional PakMediNet, up to February 2026 for observational studies using validated tools. Quality was graded with a Joanna Briggs Institute checklist, and a random-effects model pooled the estimates.

Sixty-one studies with 65 separate reports entered the analysis. Pooled prevalence was high, though the studies disagreed a lot. The heaviest burdens appeared in predictable high-risk groups: pregnant women, dialysis patients, people with diabetes, and students. Most studies used the international study group criteria, yet variation persisted. Coverage was also uneven, with no data at all from Baluchistan Province. The authors call the condition common but under-recognized in Pakistan.
pmc-13502574:
Shanshan Zhou leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 materials strategy that finally disperses carbon nanotubes properly for flexible thermoelectric films. Single-walled nanotubes conduct electricity beautifully and bend without breaking, yet they clump into bundles that wreck performance, and ordinary dispersants barely help. The team designed a small molecule, OTN, with two gripping systems. A donor-acceptor conjugated backbone hugs the nanotube surface through pi interactions, and dangling free-radical ends repel neighbouring tubes through radical-radical interactions.

Films of the hybrid reached a power factor of 30.1 microwatts per centimetre per kelvin squared, far beyond earlier reports, while staying free-standing and flexible. A nine-leg device built from the films delivered normalized power density of 0.653 on the reported scale, among the best results yet for nanotube thermoelectrics. The authors present radical-mediated dispersion as a general escape from the aggregation ceiling that has capped carbon thermoelectrics.
pmc-13503674:
Maria Michelina Raso leads a team testing a new way to build a vaccine against Klebsiella pneumoniae, in a 2026 paper. The germ causes many hospital infections and newborn sepsis, and it often resists drugs. No licensed vaccine for it exists yet.

The team used GMMA, small bubbles shed by altered germ cells, to carry two sugar coats from the germ surface at once. Mice given the bubbles made strong antibody replies to both coats. Adding the coat from the capsule did not blunt the reply to the coat from the outer film. The result backs a mix of several GMMA types to cover many strains of the germ in one shot.
pmc-13503774:
Jamin Ali leads a team studying why a major crop pest, the peach-potato aphid, comes in green and red forms, in a 2026 study. The pest feeds on more than 400 plant types and spreads many plant viruses. Colour form may change how the pest grows, moves, and faces its foes.

Lab tests tracked growth, breeding, settling, and movement in both forms, plus attacks by ladybird young and a parasitic wasp. Green aphids bred more on older plants but grew slowly; red ones grew fast and did better on young plants. Green forms settled more and roamed less. Red forms were caught by predators more often, while the wasp showed no colour bias. The authors note the work used one clone in the lab.
pmc-13505174:
Yosra Gassara and others analyze genetic polymorphisms and gene levels of DRD3 and HTR2A in bruxism. In 2026, the case-control study covers eighty-two bruxism patients and eighty-seven controls, genotyping two variants and testing peripheral blood messenger RNA. Bruxism, involuntary grinding or clenching, reflects genetic, mental, and environmental influences.

The HTR2A rs6313 variant linked clearly with bruxism, with the C allele raising risk about 1.89-fold, and HTR2A levels was upregulated in patients. DRD3 genotype did not differ clearly, though its C allele appeared to raise sleep bruxism susceptibility and its levels was downregulated. Mood signal and drive signal pathways thus appear involved in bruxism, aiding early finding and aimed treatment research.
pmc-13507074:
Changrong Wu and colleagues examine, in 2026 work, why giant Late Permian reef and shoal belts line one trough edge in the Sichuan Basin of China. Their case is the Damaoping Block at the trough end, home to major gas fields. Improved seismic reading let them pick out single reef mounds and small gas stores in quiet zones.

Sponge reefs sat in deeper calm water, fed by rising cold currents rich in food and oxygen. Rear mounds lined up along the trough direction and faded toward the platform interior. Those currents likely steered both reef growth and the dolomite caps that hold gas. The method aids hunting for small reef-top gas stores elsewhere.
pmc-13507174:
Mansour Ghaderpoori and colleagues optimize, in 2026 work, light-driven removal of the antibiotic ciprofloxacin from water using a titanium and iron oxide nanomaterial under ultraviolet light. The drug resists breakdown and reaches rivers and groundwater widely. Batch tests in a three-liter reactor varied acidity, time, drug level, and particle dose by a structured design.

Particles were round, under 100 nanometers wide, and evenly spread, which signals clean synthesis. Best settings removed about 95 percent of the drug, and the fitted model matched data closely. Treated water also proved less toxic to test bacteria than raw drug solution, with a clear statistical gap. Scale-up and by-product safety still need work before field use.
pmc-13507274:
Yuxin Zheng leads a 2026 team that solves nineteen structures of transthyretin amyloid fibrils taken from living patients with hereditary amyloidosis. In this inherited disease, mutated transthyretin protein clumps into fibrils that damage nerves and heart. More than 130 mutations exist, but how each shapes fibrils was unclear. Tiny muscle biopsies and eye fluid supplied the material.

Frozen electron microscopy resolved fibril folds at near-atomic sharpness for ten patients with nine mutations. Deep learning read whether mutant or normal protein dominated each fibril. Patterns linked the species that starts clumping with age of disease onset. Biopsy-based structure work could extend to many inherited amyloid diseases.
pmc-13508074:
Seonmo Yang and a large team report a battery study, published in 2026. It aims to make rechargeable magnesium batteries last longer. Amine-based liquid electrolytes help magnesium ions move at the metal surface. But their uncontrolled reactivity shortens battery life. The team searched for a better solvent molecule.

The group screened a family of related amine solvents. They identified one compound, shortened to ADMA. Its electron-donating strength balanced ion transport well. Its molecular bulk helped chemical stability. Cells using it cycled stably for hundreds of hours. Rest periods were built into the cycling. Full cells also kept working well. They were paired with two different cathode materials.
pmc-13508274:
Jiangyue Tian leads a fourteen-author team testing a heart failure drug in patients whose blood pressure already runs low, in 2026 work. The drug, vericiguat, helps weakened hearts, but low pressure often makes doctors wary of adding medicines. The study enrolled 164 patients with reduced heart pumping strength and no symptoms from their low pressure. Patients chose whether to take the drug, and matching methods balanced the groups. The main goal was a deep drop in a blood marker of heart strain during follow-up.

Among those who finished the study, the marker fell by at least 30 percent in about seven in ten treated patients. That compares with under half of the control group. Adjusted models kept the drug as an independent predictor of the improvement. The findings suggest low pressure alone need not rule out this drug, though the choice-based design limits certainty.
pmc-13508374:
Jad Fadlallah leads a fifteen-author reply to critics of their study on kidney size and quality of life in polycystic kidney disease, in 2026 correspondence. The critics had raised nutrition, muscle loss, and sex-specific body image as extra routes to poor quality of life. The authors used their patient survey data to test one of those ideas directly. They asked whether being able to eat a full meal without discomfort tracks with quality of life scores. It did, and strongly for physical scores.

Patients who could eat a full meal comfortably scored about 6.6 points higher on the physical scale than those who could not. That gap beat the one tied to kidney pain in their earlier work. The meal measure did not clearly track mental scores, where kidney pain stayed dominant. Meal discomfort also showed no link to kidney size itself, suggesting a broader belly and nutrition burden.
pmc-13509174:
Chatziathanasiadou introduces a 2026 special issue on gliomas, the brain tumors that account for eighty percent of malignant central nervous system cancers, and on the search for better treatments. Standard care, surgery followed by radiation and chemotherapy, has barely improved in over a decade, and glioblastoma, the most aggressive type, has a five-year survival of only about seven percent. The issue gathers work on the molecular mechanisms driving these tumors and on new therapeutic ideas.

One highlighted study found that glioblastoma cells overexpress NOD2, an innate immune receptor. That signal drives invasion programs and supports the treatment-resistant stem cell niche, tracking with the stemness markers CD44 and CD133. Knocking NOD2 down reduced invasion and lowered those markers in the experiments reported. The editorial argues that mapping such mechanisms is essential for breaking the long plateau in glioma therapy.
pmc-13509274:
Wang and colleagues report a 2026 study of a carrier-free nanoparticle for treating acute pharyngitis. The condition is a sudden, painful throat inflammation, and the particles are made from two plant compounds, baicalin and chlorogenic acid. Baicalin fights inflammation but dissolves poorly in water and absorbs badly. So the team let the two compounds assemble into nanoparticles by themselves, an idea drawn from a traditional Chinese formula.

In immune cells provoked with bacterial toxin, the particles lowered nitric oxide, reactive oxygen species, and two inflammatory signals. In rats with sore throats, the oral particles raised baicalin levels in the body more than the plain compounds did. Throat tissue also looked healthier, and inflammatory signals fell in blood and tissue. The effect was tied to calming a key inflammatory pathway in cells.
pmc-13509574:
Toranbeki and colleagues compared in 2026 four local treatments for bacteria tied to pericoronitis, the painful infection around a partly erupted tooth. Each option faced three standard bacterial species in tubes, with counts read after a day of contact.

Toranbeki found chlorhexidine the most consistent killer, cutting one species to a single surviving colony unit per millilitre and the others to low counts. The plain fibrin gel did no better than salt water. The antibiotic-loaded gel hit one species hard but left the other two at high levels, and laser light gave partial, uneven effects. The authors note the winners in this glass-tube model may differ in a real mouth with biofilms.
pmc-13509674:
Hassan Barakat and Mohamed Ghonimy review camel milk and date fruits as foods that may ease oxidative stress and support metabolic health, in 2026 work. Metabolic syndrome links belly obesity, blood sugar trouble, poor blood fats, and high blood pressure, and it raises the risk of diabetes and heart disease. The authors searched several databases for studies from 2008 onward covering either food or its active parts.

Trials suggest camel milk may help blood sugar control, with lower long-term sugar scores and lower insulin needs in some reports. Dates, despite their sweetness, generally did not worsen sugar control and sometimes improved blood fats and stress markers. Study designs, doses, and fruit types varied widely, and no study tested the two foods taken together. The authors call for standard human trials before firm claims can be made.
pmc-13510374:
Mercedes A. Terry and six co-authors compare machine learning models that sort people with Parkinson disease from healthy controls using brain and eye signals recorded during thinking tasks, in 2026 work. Participants performed a working memory task and a sustained attention task while scalp electrodes tracked brain waves and a camera tracked pupil size. Behavior alone often fails to expose early thinking change in this disease, so the team aligned signal features to task moments.

The combined signal pipeline separated the groups more accurately than standard behavior scores did. Seven features carried most of the sorting power, including frontal brain rhythm markers, rhythm ratios, and pupil responses. The telling features clustered in the hardest task stretches, with heavier memory loads, longer waits, and wrong answers. The authors offer the setup as a readable platform for hunting early markers, pending larger proof studies.
pmc-13515074:
Mariotti and colleagues wrote a 2026 narrative review on visceral obesity, the deep belly fat wrapped around organs, and a simple electrical test used in longevity medicine. This fat acts like a hormone and immune organ, and its overgrowth drives insulin resistance and artery disease. The review links that damage to inflammaging, the slow sterile inflammation of ageing.

Searching three databases for work up to April 2025, Mariotti weighed how visceral fat speeds cell ageing through unstable DNA, failing mitochondria, and exhausted repair systems. Bioelectrical impedance analysis passes a weak current through the body, and its phase angle reflects cell membrane health. Low phase angle in visceral obesity matches values seen in frail older people, which the authors read as a marker of biological age.
pmc-13515274:
Agnieszka Urbańska and nine colleagues test, in a 2026 lab study, whether the glow bacteria give off under violet light can track how cultures change over time. Twenty-eight reference strains grew on agar plates, eight colonies each. Every day or so for a week, the team shone a 405 nanometre laser on the same colonies and photographed them with a phone camera through a yellow filter. Software then extracted the hue, the dominant colour tone, from each image.

Hue values shifted over time and differed between strains, with clear interactions between the two. A few strains, among them Staphylococcus aureus and Proteus mirabilis, showed visible change. Yet the hue ranges overlapped heavily, blurring the line between strains. Urbańska's team concludes that hue tracking can follow fluorescence change inside one dataset, but it cannot name a bacterium on its own. Camera limits add to that caution.
pmc-13515474:
Maochen Luo and six colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how gut and tumour microbes may help colorectal cancer spread. Spread, or metastasis, is what makes this cancer so hard to cure. Microbes can breach gut and vessel walls, reshape the immune setting around tumours, and change the chemistry of bile acids, short-chain fatty acids, and tryptophan. The review follows these routes into the liver, lung, lymph nodes, and belly lining.

Distinct microbial patterns also track how patients respond to chemotherapy, radiation, immune therapy, and targeted drugs. That raises the hope of using microbe profiles to sort patients and forecast outcomes. Treatments aimed at microbes, from diet to transplants, appear as possible add-ons. Luo's team keeps the brakes on, though: they ask for standard methods and long-term studies that prove mechanisms before any of this enters routine care.
pmc-13515974:
Jiashuang Ji leads a ten-author team designing a multi-part vaccine against H9N2 bird flu on the computer, in a 2026 immunoinformatics study. The virus keeps mutating, and standard killed vaccines raise mostly antibody defence with weak cross-protection. The team mined two viral proteins, HA2 and M1, for stretches that stay constant across strains. From those stretches they picked pieces that B cells, killer T cells, and helper T cells can each recognise.

Three candidate designs were compared for shape and stability, and one, named HM1, won. It carries three B-cell pieces, two killer T-cell pieces, and three helper pieces, bookended by an immune-boosting chicken defensin and a targeting peptide. Modelling showed HM1 docking stably onto chicken immune sensors and presentation molecules. Simulated vaccination produced antibodies and activated the desired cell types.
pmc-13516774:
Denis Shevchuk and five colleagues test how handling blood cells changes inflammation readings in ALS research, in a 2026 study. The NLRP3 inflammasome, an internal alarm complex, is suspected in the nerve decay of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Blood immune cells could carry a readable trace of it.
