The team compared fresh cells with cells kept in culture, from twenty-three patients and twenty healthy controls, measuring gene and protein levels plus two alarm cytokines.

Culturing the cells lowered the gene activity of alarm parts and cytokines, though protein levels held. One alarm gene, NLRP3 itself, read higher in patient cells after culture. The cytokine IL-18 appeared in blood plasma, while IL-1β showed only in cultured-cell fluid. Shevchuk's team warns that the choice to culture or not can decide what a study sees. Handling rules therefore belong in the design of any blood-based inflammasome study.
pmc-13518874:
K N Arun Kumar and three colleagues analyze wear in aluminum hybrid composites in 2026 using the Taguchi statistical method. Their material mixes AL6061 alloy with 13 percent silicon carbide plus graphite at 1, 2, or 3 percent, cast by a bottom-pouring stir process. Engineers want such light, stiff composites to resist sliding wear.

Specimens with and without cryogenic treatment, deep cooling that refines the internal structure, were compared through analysis of variance and regression models. Cold treatment reduced wear scar depth and friction under the tested settings. Among all combinations, the mix with 2 percent graphite performed best. Kumar and co-authors show how statistical design can pinpoint a winning recipe without testing every possibility.
pmc-13519274:
Abed and St John-Smith presented an evolutionary psychiatry framework arguing that several recognized mental disorders are best understood as malfunctions of the human mating system. Their 2026 paper contends that pair-bonding with two-parent investment is a species-typical human trait. It is supported by a bundle of evolved psychological adaptations, just as other biological systems are shaped by natural selection to serve survival and reproduction.

Abed proposes that because functional systems can fail in characteristic ways, disorders rooted in pair-bonding should show patterns that this framework predicts. They should not appear in closely related species using different mating systems. The authors argue the approach explains both why such disorders exist and why they take the forms they do, rather than merely cataloguing symptoms. They offer the functional, family-tree-based reasoning as a template that evolutionary psychiatry can apply to other groups of mental disorders beyond mating.
pmc-13519474:
Pranav D Patil and colleagues tested fiber-reinforced fillings for teeth left fragile after root canal treatment. Published in 2026, the lab study assigned ninety extracted premolars at random to three groups and ran them through a chewing simulator at set force for half a million cycles. Root-treated teeth lose pulp and dentin, leaving them prone to fracture under normal biting.

Fiber-reinforced composite withstood far higher breaking force than standard composite, while matching metal-ceramic crowns on edge fit. The fibers blunt crack growth by deflecting breaks and soaking up energy where fiber meets resin. The authors present the material as a strong, tooth-colored option for back teeth under heavy load. Readers get lab evidence for a kinder restoration, still awaiting long-term trials in living patients.
pmc-13519874:
Fatema Nserat, Chahed Manssour, and Taghrid Hammoud measure osteoporosis in 2026 among 158 adults sent for bone density scanning at the National Hospital in Damascus, Syria. Weak bones raise fracture risk worldwide, yet Syrian referral data were thin. Density results were classed by World Health Organization T-score cutoffs at spine and hip.

Osteoporosis was the commonest finding at 53.2 percent, with low bone mass in another 36.7 percent and only a tenth of patients normal. Women, who made up 86.7 percent of the group, were significantly more likely to have osteoporosis, as were patients with overactive thyroid. Higher body mass index correlated with lower hip scores. Age, smoking, and diabetes showed no significant links.
pmc-13520174:
Sean Fletcher, Esther E Biswas-Fiss, and Subhasis B Biswas run a computer-only analysis in 2026 of the human papillomavirus replication machinery, focusing on how the E1 and E2 proteins grip each other. That grip drives viral genome copying, and its strength might separate high-risk cancer-causing types from low-risk ones. Sequences from a public database were aligned, and AlphaFold3 models supplied structures for energy calculations.

The catalytic core of E1 proved nearly identical across types, while the regulatory end varied. Low-risk complexes were predicted to bind more stably than high-risk ones, with an energy gap significant in their tests. Binding energy alone distinguished the risk groups with an area under the curve of 0.875. Wet-lab kinetic checks come next.
pmc-13522474:
Yang and colleagues examine how chromosomes line up in the middle of a dividing cell before they are pulled apart. The work appeared in 2026 on the machinery of mitosis, which is how one cell splits into two. A motor protein named CENP-E walks along microtubules, the cell's internal rails, and drags chromosomes into position. The study focuses on MATCAP, an enzyme that trims tyrosine from tubulin, the protein those rails are built from.

MATCAP clumps into droplets on microtubules through a process called liquid-liquid phase separation, meaning it condenses much like oil beading in water. Those droplets gather both tubulin and CENP-E in one place, which steadies the grip between chromosomes and microtubules. When Yang's team used MATCAP versions unable to form droplets, live imaging showed chromosome alignment faltering. The picture that emerges links droplet formation and tyrosine trimming in time and space, keeping chromosome sorting accurate.
pmc-13523274:
Daniel Hendry Ruma and co-authors assess nutrition and quality of life among very old grant recipients in Kampala, Uganda, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. One hundred fifty-nine people aged eighty or older on a national social assistance program gave a one-day diet recall, completed a quality of life questionnaire, and had body measurements taken during 2025.

Participants ate on average just under two meals daily, with low intake of meat, fruit, and eggs. Underweight affected nearly one fifth, while overweight and obesity together affected nearly one third, a double burden in one group. Eating at least three meals strongly protected against underweight. Only about one quarter reported good quality of life, with education and extra income protecting against poor scores. The authors link the pattern to sex, economic, and dietary inequalities in the program.
pmc-13523374:
Xiaojie Ding and co-authors test a plant compound against a fungal leaf disease of a medicinal plant in a 2026 study. Magnolol, drawn from magnolia bark, was applied to Alternaria tenuissima, the fungus behind leaf blight on Schisandra chinensis. Laboratory assays measured fungal growth across doses, field plots checked disease control, and gene profiling plus enzyme assays probed the mechanism.

Growth inhibition rose with dose and reached above ninety percent at the highest concentration, while field control after two weeks exceeded three quarters. The compound damaged fungal cell membranes and disturbed protective enzyme activity over time. Thousands of genes changed expression, with toxin production, energy generation, and membrane building pathways broadly suppressed. The authors offer the work as a foundation for plant-derived fungicides against this blight.
pmc-13523474:
Sophie Elisa Gibbs Ludbrook, Andrew James Robert Waters, and Justin Conrad Rosen Wormald set out a 2026 protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis. Their topic is dropout rates in hand and wrist trauma trials. Such injuries are increasingly common and can limit work and daily life. Trial participants often disengage from follow-up for logistical and social reasons, weakening the results.

The planned review will search Embase, PubMed, and CENTRAL for prospective randomized trials in hand or wrist trauma. Two reviewers will screen records independently, and dropout will be compared at 30 days, 90 days, six months, and twelve months. Analyses will consider patient demographics, injury and treatment types, and stated reasons for leaving. A standard Cochrane tool will judge bias risk. The team aims to build a toolkit that improves follow-up in future trials.
pmc-13523574:
Fauchier, Bisson, and Lenormand model a health-system trade-off in treating persistent atrial fibrillation, the stubborn form of the common heart rhythm disorder. Ablation can isolate the pulmonary veins alone, a quicker operation, or add extra lesion sets that modestly cut recurrence for that patient but consume scarce laboratory hours. Their 2026 analysis fixes capacity at a thousand lab hours a year and asks which strategy leaves the whole waiting population better off.

The simpler strategy won at population level in every scenario modelled: it treated more patients. The extra recurrences it allowed were outweighed by avoiding both the waiting-list harm and the new fast rhythms that extra ablation itself provokes, a cost the authors nickname the AT tax. Patients left on drugs because capacity ran out contributed disproportionately to hospitalisations.
pmc-13524374:
Fisher and co-authors report a 2026 case of Kounis syndrome, a heart attack triggered by a severe allergic reaction. Their patient was a fifty-eight-year-old man who developed anaphylaxis, a whole-body allergic emergency, after eating seafood. Alongside the allergic collapse he showed signs of a major heart attack, an unusual pairing that can mislead emergency teams focused on only one problem.

Heart imaging showed a ruptured plaque with a clot in the middle of the left anterior descending artery. That vessel supplies the front of the heart, confirming a type II Kounis syndrome event. In this type, allergic chemicals destabilize existing fatty plaque rather than only causing vessel spasm. The team treated both the allergy and the blocked artery in this one patient. They stress that chest pain during anaphylaxis deserves a heart workup, since the two emergencies can arrive together.
pmc-13524474:
Shifei Wei and colleagues test, in a 2026 prospective study, a stepwise atropine strategy for slowing myopia in children. Low-dose atropine drops can slow worsening eyesight, yet a single starting dose helps some children more than others. The plan began everyone on the weakest strength, then raised the dose only for children whose eyes kept worsening.

The study enrolled 150 children aged 8 to 14 with moderate myopia. After six months on 0.01 percent drops, children were grouped by progression and either stayed on that strength or switched to 0.02 or 0.04 percent for twelve more months. Children moved to stronger drops slowed markedly compared with their first six months. Overall progression and eye elongation over the switch period were similar across groups, which the authors read as early support for response-guided dosing.
pmc-13525174:
Pawid and Bandaay studied in 2026 what drives breastfeeding failure and confidence after caesarean delivery in Mountain Province, Philippines. Post-caesarean mothers often struggle to breastfeed, and confidence, called self-efficacy, varies widely. The case-control study enrolled 181 mothers from two municipalities between October 2023 and January 2024.

Older, more experienced mothers who visited health facilities more often, and whose babies had normal birth weight, were more confident and fed to six months. Young first-time mothers had low self-efficacy and needed the most support. Failure clustered in mothers under twenty-four, working mothers, and those with low confidence. The authors direct nurses' attention to those three groups first. Their instructional materials aim to help nurses promote breastfeeding where the risk of early failure is highest.
pmc-13525874:
Lisa Eleni Chionis Buhler and colleagues compared two needle biopsy methods for lumps of the parotid salivary gland. Published in 2026, the retrospective study reviewed 485 patients at a tertiary academic center from 2018 through 2023, with permanent tissue diagnosis as the reference. Fine needle aspiration is cheap and gentle but often yields too little tissue, while core needle biopsy takes a larger sample.

Core biopsy beat fine needle sampling on cancer detection sensitivity, overall accuracy, and predictive value, and it cut inconclusive results from one fifth to about one twentieth. Accuracy rose further with at least three needle passes and thicker 17- to 18-gauge needles. Complication rates stayed low and similar, without facial nerve damage or tumor spill, and time to surgery did not differ. The authors back core biopsy when cancer is suspected or tissue detail will guide surgery.
pmc-13527074:
Magdalena Julita Krystkiewicz-Orzechowska leads a large team in a 2026 protocol paper on isolating cell nuclei from prostate cancer tissue preserved in RNAlater. The reagent protects RNA but usually blocks single cell work. Their method enables single nucleus RNA sequencing from resections already stored this way, opening more usable medical archives.

The lean procedure uses bead mill grinding and a high salt lysis step, skipping sorting and gradient cleanup. Reads reached high quality scores with little contaminating ambient RNA. Work on 3,365 nuclei found eight cell compartments, keeping the full mix of luminal, stromal, and immune lineages expected in prostate tumors. The authors argue analysis of stored samples can now be routine, opening single cell genomics in translational prostate cancer research.
pmc-13527274:
Renée-Claude Bider and colleagues improve, in a 2026 methods study, a multiparametric MRI technique that maps fat and water properties separately in mixed tissue. Fat DESPOT estimates relaxation rates and fat fraction in one session, useful for liver, pancreas, and tumor work. The upgrade adds sensitivity to the phase of the signals and tests two ways to seed the fitting.

Experiments at three tesla used fat emulsion phantoms, then legs and abdomens of healthy volunteers. Two seeding strategies gave similar estimates and precision, though one drifted at a fifty percent fat mixture. Models fitting the full complex signal performed best, matching reference fat fraction within about a percentage point on average and giving the tightest precision across parameters. The authors recommend the complex, graph-cut seeded version.
pmc-13528374:
Jiang wrote a 2026 editorial setting a global course for the journal Eco-Environment and Health. Climate change, species loss, and pollution now converge as one crisis family. The journal aims to carry local governance lessons to a world audience. Jiang frames its mission around one shared Earth and common destiny.

Future work, Jiang writes, should raise sharp questions, not chase metrics alone. Strong methods and open scholarly dialogue define a world-class journal here. The journal will prize academic reputation and international reach above volume. Green, low-carbon, and circular growth paths anchor its topic choices. The editorial invites researchers worldwide to publish environment-health work there. Raising the journal's scholarly standing is the stated central task ahead.
pmc-13529074:
Kopac and colleagues surveyed the anesthesia workforce of Türkiye about burnout, in a 2026 cross-sectional study run between September and December 2024. Burnout was measured with the Maslach survey, which scores emotional exhaustion, detachment from patients, and sense of achievement at work. The team gathered 921 responses from senior doctors and residents across the country, with workplace and home-life details.

Kopac found about seven in ten at high risk for burnout and more than one in three fully meeting the signs of burnout syndrome. Residents fared worse than attending physicians on both measures, and being a female resident carried extra risk in combined analysis. Younger age, unhappiness at work, perceived understaffing, and weak support at home each on its own predicted burnout syndrome. The authors call for system-level reforms in pay, staffing, and leadership plus ongoing national monitoring to protect both clinician well-being and patient safety.
pmc-13529174:
Bany Ateah and colleagues surveyed nurses at a military hospital in Saudi Arabia about what keeps them in their jobs, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Nurse turnover drains expertise and continuity of care worldwide. The team collected online questionnaires over three months in 2025 covering personal background, perceived career growth, and intention to leave.

Bany Ateah received 350 completed surveys, a response rate above ninety percent. Most nurses viewed their career growth positively, reporting better emotional control, growing competence, and rising professional prestige, with promotions seen as timely. Intention to leave was low: about two thirds strongly rejected the idea of quitting. Career growth and turnover intention were strongly linked in opposite directions, so nurses who saw their careers advancing wanted to leave far less. the authors say makes career development a practical retention lever for military hospitals.
pmc-13529774:
Tingting Huo, Qiang Sun, and Rui Ding pick better test data for neural networks in a 2026 paper. Weak test sets let faulty models slip through, which is risky in safety fields. Their method, SAKCL, first weighs feature parts by self-attention. That step lifts the informative patterns in each sample. Clustering then groups the polished samples by shape.

Picks from the clusters balance fault-finding power with variety. Four standard image sets and three network designs hosted the trials. The method raised the share of error-revealing cases by over twelve percent on average. Diversity scores rose more than six percent. Retraining on the picked data gained about three points of accuracy. Math checks backed the gains as real. The authors offer the method as a practical quality gate for model testing.
pmc-13530474:
Droz and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 165, laboratory work toward off-the-shelf cartilage-bone grafts. The grafts are made by stripping donor tissue of its cells and then reseeding it with fresh ones. Cartilage barely regenerates, and current grafts are costly and logistically hard.

Working with pig joint tissue cut into small cubes, the team compared three decellularization recipes. The first cleaned thoroughly but wrecked the bone architecture; the second cleaned poorly. The third, freeze-thaw cycles with a low-salt solution, detergent, and DNA-chewing enzymes, removed the donor DNA adequately while preserving mechanical strength. On reseeding, placental-derived cells outgrew fat-derived stem cells, and the third protocol's plugs repopulated best. The authors conclude that protocol offers the balance of cleaning and structural preservation a human graft needs.
pmc-13530874:
Elham Afkhami and colleagues weighed the two faces of extracellular vesicles in fertility treatment. Published in 2026, the editorial letter notes that these tiny cell-derived sacs carry proteins, fats, and genetic material between eggs, nurse cells, uterine cells, and sperm. In assisted reproduction they can boost egg maturation, fertilization, and early embryo growth, and uterine vesicles can aid implantation.

Harm follows when vesicles carry damaged cargo from stressed follicles, inflammatory signals in endometriosis, or aged nurse cells, lowering egg quality and implantation odds. Technical hurdles compound the picture: isolation methods yield varied purity and amounts, standards lag, and dose comparisons across studies prove difficult. The authors urge careful, context-aware use rather than blanket enthusiasm. Readers get a balanced primer on a promising but unruly tool.
pmc-13531074:
Daisuke Ueshima and colleagues describe in 2026 a controlled way to fish out a heart closure device that slipped into the aortic arch. A 67-year-old man had received the device to seal a small heart pouch that can harbor clots during irregular heartbeat. The device broke loose soon after placement despite a good initial position.

A wire threaded through an open strut and caught by a snare let operators steer the device angle during pulling. The device entered a wide sheath and came out without harm. A second device then seated successfully, showing retrieval need not end the treatment plan.
pmc-13531874:
Lu Xu and colleagues examine in 2026 how chemotherapy nerve damage feeds social anxiety in breast cancer patients. A total of 285 patients at a central China hospital answered structured questionnaires during 2025 on nerve symptoms, arm and hand disability, and social interaction anxiety. Statistical pathway models tested how the pieces connect.

Nerve damage and arm disability each correlated with higher social anxiety. Arm disability carried part of the nerve damage effect onward, explaining about 18 percent of the total link. A blood inflammation ratio slightly weakened the first step. Managing nerve and arm problems may ease social recovery.
pmc-13532874:
Dachan Kim and colleagues searched blood proteins for systemic signs of chronic sinus inflammation. Published in 2026, the study analyzed plasma proteomics from 44,344 United Kingdom Biobank participants, including 725 people with chronic rhinosinusitis. Local nose tissue studies had mapped inflammation, but whether blood carries the same signals at population scale was unclear.

Forty-six proteins differed, nearly all raised, led by tissue-remodeling and eosinophil-linked markers such as MMP10, PRG2, PRG3, and periostin, with one protein lowered. Routine blood markers added little beyond eosinophil counts. Classification models gained from proteomic features over clinical data alone. The authors present blood proteomics as a window onto sinus inflammation beyond standard labs, with clinical use still to prove.
pmc-13532974:
Rebecca L Brady and colleagues study in 2026 thyroid antibody presence in pregnancy using Lewis rats. Such antibodies are common in women of child-bearing age and link to miscarriage and pregnancy diabetes, even when thyroid hormone levels stay normal. Antibodies were induced before pregnancy, and mothers and fetuses were checked late in pregnancy.

Glucose tolerance did not change, yet cycle length before pregnancy rose and key reproductive hormones shifted. Placentas grew larger, with more glucose transporters and swelling signals, and litters held fewer males. Readers see placenta function as a likely route for harm apart from thyroid hormone levels.
pmc-13536574:
Zibo Yin and colleagues present in 2026 an improved three-dimensional reconstruction method for seedlings based on the DIFIX3D+ framework. Thin branches and heavy occlusion often produce false geometry and artefacts in seedling models. The method cleans the input first, using smart segmentation tools to remove background clutter.

Restored and rendered images are then matched inside a diffusion model latent space, adding representation-level checks beside pixel checks. On their own dataset the method raised image quality scores clearly and cut perceptual error versus the base methods. It offers a low-cost route to faithful seedling models for growth studies.
pmc-13536874:
Jin Li and Jin Cheng model paths to blood pressure self-care among older adults in Chongqing, China, in a 2026 survey of 264 adults with high blood pressure. Daily habits such as taking medicine, checking pressure at home, and eating carefully prevent complications, yet drivers span personal, service, and family levels. Structured interviews in spring 2026 fed a theory-guided path model linking knowledge, confidence, teaching, access, and family support.

Confidence and disease knowledge each linked directly to stronger self-care. Access to care and services linked both directly and through knowledge and confidence. Family support linked directly and through several indirect routes. Teaching showed a surprising negative indirect link through knowledge, hinting at poorly matched content or timing. The authors advise pairing skills practice with reachable services and family involvement.
pmc-13538374:
Prabhdeep Singh, Akash Sharma, and Romesh Kumar Salgotra survey flower traits across wild bael trees in the northwestern Himalayan plains in a 2026 study. Bael is a valued medicinal fruit tree usually grown from seed, creating wide natural variation. Eighty wild types plus two commercial varieties were measured for flower, bud, petal, stalk, and reproductive organ sizes. Combined statistical tools summarized variation and grouped similar types.

One wild selection led on most flower measures, from bud size to stigma size. Five combined components captured nearly three quarters of total variation, each tied to a distinct trait set. Clustering split all entries into two major groups with smaller subgroups inside. The authors offer the diversity map for breeding and germplasm improvement, while cautioning that branch-level sampling may inflate genetic estimates.
pmc-13538674:
Galana Abay Kebede and colleagues pair experiments with simulation to guide flame line heating of thin steel sheets in a 2026 study. Heating along a path bends sheet metal into curves cheaply, yet judging where and how much to heat remains craft knowledge. A three-dimensional model computed surface temperatures for varied heat inputs, while bench trials on small square sheets used an infrared thermometer to control surface temperature along straight, rectangular, and parallel paths.

Simulated and measured temperatures agreed closely, with errors under seven percent across the tested paths. The match held for different heat flux levels from the gas torch. The authors present the validated model as a scientific basis for planning heating paths and doses when shaping thin steel sheets.
pmc-13540874:
David Flood leads a 2026 protocol for judging Guatemala's rollout of the HEARTS model, a World Health Organization package for managing high blood pressure and diabetes in primary care. A national scale-up begun in 2024 now reaches about a tenth of the country.

The prospective study compares districts receiving HEARTS with those not yet covered, across periods before, during, and after rollout. Six strategies carry the model, from staff training and standard treatment protocols to task sharing with non-physician workers and community outreach. Main outcomes are treatment rates for hypertension and diabetes drawn from ministry data, judged inside the RE-AIM framework alongside control, uptake, and durability measures.
pmc-13541574:
Shankar Baskar and Jeremy P Moore review, in a 2026 article, catheter ablation for the scar-driven atrial rhythm circuits that plague adults born with heart defects. More than half of patients with severe congenital disease develop atrial arrhythmias by age sixty-five, and these rhythms are often poorly tolerated.

Intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia, circling around surgical incision scars in remodelled atria, is the dominant mechanism. Medicines disappoint often enough that ablation has become the mainstay of rhythm control. The review proposes a mapping and ablation strategy for these complex substrates, with worked examples showing the pitfalls. Earlier, more assertive treatment may slow the atrial remodelling that breeds further arrhythmia.
pmc-13541774:
Qian Gao, George Fu Gao, and Jun Liu review, in a 2026 article, the protective immunogens of the world's priority pathogens, the molecular parts that vaccines and antibody drugs must target. In 2024 the World Health Organization listed thirty-two such pathogens as most likely to spark a global emergency.

Walking pathogen by pathogen, the authors catalogue the representative protective targets and their shared traits. Viruses from the same family tend to carry look-alike protective immunogens, opening the door to cross-reactive designs. Internal viral proteins, which change little between strains, emerge as favourite candidates for universal vaccines. The authors frame this catalogue as the first key for preparedness.
pmc-13542274:
Hayato Yokoyama and colleagues describe a 2026 device that turns a flat printed sheet of paper into a rolled power generator. Thermoelectric generators harvest waste heat and convert a temperature difference into electricity, but flat printed versions pack few generating junctions into a given area. Silver ink printed the wiring on paper, while a conductive polymer formed the active legs, and the sheet then folded itself into a cylinder without hands-on assembly.

Rolling placed the junctions on the inner wall of the tube, crowding far more of them into the same footprint while keeping each leg its proper length. Per unit of installation area, the rolled device produced 28.1 times more power than its flat counterpart. Careful tuning of printing conditions and electrode layout controlled internal resistance. The work shows self-folding paper as a cheap route to compact heat-harvesting devices for small electronics.
pmc-13543374:
Han-Sang Baek and colleagues published a 2026 study of complementary and alternative medicine use among thyroid cancer patients in South Korea. The patients came from the MASTER trial cohort, all treated with lobectomy, removal of half the thyroid. Surveys at surgery and at three, six, and twelve months captured which therapies 1,166 patients used and what they spent. The analysis also tested whether taking levothyroxine, the standard thyroid hormone replacement, changed the pattern.

Fifty-eight percent reported some complementary therapy. Dietary nutritional products led at baseline, while exercise and physical therapies rose over the year. Monthly spending on dietary products held steady, whereas exercise costs doubled across follow-up. Patients taking levothyroxine were less likely to use complementary therapies overall, yet those who did used more kinds at once early on. Clinicians, the authors argue, should ask about such therapies openly and guide patients on safety.
pmc-13543474:
Mohammad Basheer Alameer and colleagues published a 2026 retrospective analysis of diabetic ketoacidosis, the dangerous acid build-up that follows insulin failure, in Syrian patients at Damascus Hospital. The team reviewed charts and kept 533 admissions for analysis, roughly half of them first episodes. About twenty-seven percent of the first-episode patients learned they had diabetes only at that admission. Profiles of type 1 and type 2 patients were compared, along with what triggered each episode.

Type 2 patients died in hospital far more often, at sixteen percent against about four percent for type 1, and they stayed longer. Blood acidity, bicarbonate, and kidney markers differed measurably between the diabetes types. Skipped insulin and unknown triggers were common drivers, especially in repeat episodes. The authors argue that treatment and prevention in Syria should be tailored by diabetes type and aimed squarely at insulin adherence.
pmc-13544174:
Daniel Martins' team redrew the map of antidepressant drugs in 2026 by what they bind, rather than by the class labels history gave them. Binding strength data for twenty-five common antidepressants were pooled across serotonin, dopamine, histamine, cholinergic, and adrenaline targets, forming an affinity fingerprint for each drug. Grouping and dimension-reduction methods then sorted the drugs without any regard to their official classes.

The result was an unbroken landscape, not neat boxes. Drugs sharing a class label often sat far apart in fingerprint space, while strangers grouped together. A graded axis ran from selective transporter blockers to broad, many-target agents, with histamine, muscarinic, and adrenaline receptors doing much of the sorting. Class names, the authors argue, hide the polypharmacology that shapes both gains and side effects, and binding maps describe a drug more truly.
pmc-13547174:
Shogo Nishikawa and eight colleagues published this 2026 natural products study on the fruit of Forsythia suspensa, an herbal medicine listed in Japan's official drug book as Forsythia Fruit. The fruit's extract blocked β-glucuronidase, an enzyme tied to inflammation and the revival of toxins in the gut. The team separated the alcohol extract into its compounds, identified a new one, and measured how strongly each compound inhibited the enzyme.

They isolated a new diterpene, rengyonoic acid, plus 19 known compounds including lignans and flavonoids, pinning down the new compound's full structure with spectroscopy. Four isolates matched or beat the reference inhibitor: forsythiaside A was strongest, with an IC50 of 18.6 micromolar, ahead of pinoresinol and suspensaside A in the same tests. Rengyonoic acid itself was weaker. Weighing potency against abundance, the authors judge the phenylethanoid glycosides the main drivers of the extract's effect.
pmc-13547274:
Yeshe M Kway and a large team used MRI scans in 2026 to ask whether where belly fat sits explains metabolic risk before menopause. The question was not just how much fat a woman carries, but where it sits. They separated abdominal fat into four compartments. These ran from shallow and deep fat under the skin to fat packed around and behind the internal organs. They then built distribution profiles for Asian women and compared metabolic health across them.

Women whose fat leaned toward the internal compartment and away from the deep under-skin layer had more metabolic syndrome, more liver fat, and higher inflammation markers. Their odds of gestational diabetes were more than five times higher. Women with the opposite pattern fared best, even though total fat, body mass index, and waist size looked alike across groups.
pmc-13548474:
Alp Abidin Ateşçi and colleagues compared in 2026 four ready-made crown systems for children's back baby teeth in the laboratory. Two zirconia brands faced a flexible polymer crown called BioFlx and the traditional stainless steel crown. Eighty crowns on identical printed tooth forms were heat-cycled ten thousand times, then split between a chewing simulator for wear and a press that loaded crowns until they broke.

Zirconia crowns wore least, with steel in the middle and BioFlx wearing most. Strength rankings nearly reversed: BioFlx and steel crowns withstood by far the highest loads before fracturing, well above both zirconia brands. The authors caution that bench rankings alone should not drive clinical choices and ask for long-term studies in children.
pmc-13548574:
Bhagawaty Kalikotay and colleagues profile the health and daily habits of older adults in a hilly municipality of Dhankuta, Nepal, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Aging populations in poorer countries face growing illness with thin services nearby. Interviewers surveyed 275 adults in 2023 using structured schedules and a standard scale for independence in daily activities, most participants being unable to read or write.

Nearly half reported at least one chronic health problem, and almost as many had moderate to severe difficulty with daily tasks. Being unmarried or widowed and smoking each raised the odds of chronic illness, while light to moderate physical activity lowered them sharply. Difficulty with daily tasks rose with age past seventy-five and was tied very strongly to having chronic illness. The authors call for community screening and behavior programs aimed at older residents.
pmc-13549974:
Xiaoqing Yu and colleagues formulate repair coatings for airport concrete runways whose grip has been worn away by repeated high-pressure water cleaning, in a 2026 laboratory study. Losing surface texture cuts skid resistance and endangers aircraft. Three composite systems, built on styrene-acrylic emulsion, water-based epoxy, or a plain water-based mix, were tested for adhesion, texture rebuilding, friction, and freeze-thaw endurance.

Adhesion peaked at a three millimeter thickness, with the epoxy system gripping concrete hardest. The acrylic system rebuilt texture best, deepening the surface profile by about eighty-four percent and lifting the pendulum friction score by nearly forty percent, closely tracking profile depth. After a hundred freeze-thaw cycles the epoxy coatings survived best, keeping up to ninety-eight percent coverage. The authors divide the honors: acrylic for grip, epoxy for durability.
pmc-13551374:
Jamie Lucarelli, with six colleagues, reported exploratory measurements of isotope variants in iodate, a form of iodine important in oceans, the atmosphere, and tracking radioactive iodine. Clumped isotopes, where rare heavy atoms sit together, can reveal formation temperatures, yet iodate had not been explored this way. The team dissolved sodium iodate in water or in water enriched with heavy oxygen and sprayed samples into a mass spectrometer.

The instrument resolved single and clumped variants, and their shares shifted steadily as the solvent's heavy oxygen content rose from zero to 97 percent in the reported runs. A natural sample matched the pattern expected from random isotope placement, suggesting unbiased measurement. The authors discuss what extending the method to natural samples would require.
pmc-13551574:
Stefania Maloccu's team hunted for drugs that block a coronavirus enzyme called Nsp15, in a 2026 report. Nsp15 helps the virus hide from host defences by cutting viral RNA, so blocking it could restore the body's early antiviral alarm, known as interferon signalling. The team tuned a light-based lab test for the enzyme, confirmed it was robust, and screened a library of 1,280 known compounds.

Three compounds blocked the enzyme at low micromolar levels. The most promising, Reactive Blue 2, also slowed SARS-CoV-2 growth in cells at a low dose with little harm to the cells themselves. Crucially, the virus was held back only where the cell's interferon defences were intact, not where they were absent. That pattern backs Nsp15 as a drug target that works by letting natural defences act.
pmc-13551674:
Mathieu Nacher, leading fourteen colleagues, published a 2026 modeling study of HIV trends and diagnostic delay in French Guiana from 2000 to 2023. Treatment rules have widened, and since 2017 most patients start antiretroviral therapy regardless of immune cell counts. Using a quality-controlled cohort and a modeling platform, the team estimated infection years from CD4 decline and tracked incidence, undiagnosed share, and deaths.

Every headline indicator improved: incidence fell, delay shortened, undiagnosed cases shrank, and deaths declined. Delay still ran about two years longer in men than women and about three years longer among Surinamese or Brazilian immigrants. With roughly five percent of people with HIV undiagnosed, the authors see a residual transmission source to shrink.
pmc-13553674:
John D Arena leads a large surgical team studying loose pelvic screws after major spine repair in adults. Their 2026 review covers 152 patients who had long spine fusions fixed to the pelvis for adult deformity. Follow-up X-rays were checked for signs that pelvic screws had worked loose. The team also tracked who later needed fresh surgery on the hardware.

Loose screws showed in twenty-five cases, about one in six, often more than a year after surgery. Loose pelvic screws tripled the odds of later hardware surgery, and raised the odds even more for repair of the pelvic fix itself. Pain and function scores were worse for patients who needed new surgery. Scores did not differ simply because screws had loosened, so X-ray watchfulness still matters.
pmc-13554274:
Hillary N Patton and colleagues mapped cognitive subgroups in people experiencing a first episode of psychosis before any antipsychotic treatment, publishing the study in 2026. Thinking problems are central to psychosis, but patients differ widely, and brain-network data may help explain that spread. Participants completed a standard neuropsychological battery, and clustering of their scores revealed two subgroups within first-episode psychosis, one impaired and one intact.

Both groups had started from average estimated premorbid ability, suggesting the impaired group had deteriorated. At baseline the impaired group showed weaker connectivity than healthy controls in attention and executive-control networks, and over 16 weeks the two subgroups changed differently across networks. The results argue for treating cognitive and neural variety as real features of early psychosis, not noise.
pmc-13554874:
Sharnvir S Chattha leads a five-author team reporting a chemotherapy drug that threw a woman's heart arteries into spasm in a 2026 case report. The fifty-eight-year-old was receiving her first paclitaxel infusion for returning cervical cancer. Within minutes she felt chest discomfort and fainted on standing. Her heart tracing mimicked a major heart attack in the lower heart wall.

The tracing nearly settled, yet her instability pushed doctors to image the arteries at once. They found severe, widespread spasm with no fixed blockage. Nitroglycerin shot straight into the artery relaxed the spasm promptly, normalised the tracing, and steadied her blood pressure. Heart scans showed preserved pumping. The authors stress fast imaging when instability follows this drug.
pmc-13555074:
Liam M Crowley and Mark G Telfer present the genome of the brown tree ant in a 2026 Darwin Tree of Life report. A single female ant supplied the sample for sequencing. The assembled genome runs to about 265 million letters, with nearly all of it arranged into fifteen chromosome-like pieces. The small mitochondrial genome was assembled alongside the main set.

Annotation found more than fifteen thousand protein-coding genes in the sequence. The ant lives mainly in trees, tending aphids in bark crevices for their sweet honeydew. First recorded in Britain in 1923, it was likely introduced early last century and now thrives locally in the south-east and parts of Wales. Old oaks with damaged bark are its favoured British home.
pmc-13555874:
Jurgita Gammall leads an eight-author team building a model that predicts who will develop high blood pressure within five years in a 2026 English study. Records came from GP practices in Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. More than half a million adults without existing pressure or heart disease were followed. Fifty-four candidate signs were winnowed to thirty-nine predictors.

About one patient in ten developed hypertension during the five-year window. A plain logistic model slightly beat tree-based rivals, scoring well in both building and test groups. It caught about three quarters of future cases while clearing a similar share of healthy patients. Rebuilt on London practices, the model held its accuracy, suggesting it travels across regions.
pmc-13557574:
Kathryn Duschean and colleagues tested whether a small skin device can replace needle blood draws for measuring C-peptide, publishing the study in 2026. C-peptide tracks how much insulin the pancreas still makes, a key measure in diabetes research and care, but repeated venipuncture burdens participants and limits sampling. Healthy volunteers gave both device samples and standard blood draws, with eleven fasted device samples put through varied handling conditions.

Device readings matched the blood-draw results closely, and delayed spinning for up to 72 hours at refrigerator temperature caused no meaningful loss. Volunteers rated the device acceptable and comfortable. The authors conclude mailed micro-samples could widen trial recruitment, cut participant burden, and make biomarker tracking easier in decentralised studies.
pmc-13558074:
Tanyel Zubarioglu and six colleagues reported in 2026 that children and adults with maple syrup urine disease run low on an important omega-3 fat despite eating similar amounts to their siblings. The inherited disorder forces a strict low-protein diet that limits animal foods, a natural source of long-chain fats. The single-centre study compared 16 patients with 22 unaffected siblings who shared the same household environment, recording diets and measuring blood fatty acids.

Patients ate less total fat and cholesterol, and their blood carried clearly less DHA, the omega-3 fat vital for brain and eye development, while two other fatty acids ran high. Diet records alone did not explain the blood gap in the final models. Within the patient group, DHA tracked with intake of one amino acid the diet restricts. The authors suggest that altered fat metabolism, not intake alone, drives the deficiency.
pmc-13558574:
Cherif M Azzaz and two colleagues reported in 2026 a one-step way to spin flexible fibres that sense pressure and motion by generating their own voltage. The material PVDF becomes piezoelectric when its crystals line up in the right phase, and carbon nanotubes can serve as a built-in electrode. Their electrospinning method uses the surface energy gap between the two materials so that the fibre assembles itself, plastic shell outside and nanotube core inside, from a single nozzle.

The fibres measure about eighty nanometres across, far thinner than spider silk, and X-ray analysis showed a fivefold jump in the active crystal phase. The device displayed both direct and reverse piezoelectric effects without the electrical conditioning step such materials usually need. Voltage output matched fully treated bulk films. The authors point to self-powered sensors, smart clothing, and artificial skin as natural uses.
pmc-13558874:
Simone Ribero and six colleagues tested in 2026 a skin cream built around a compound from oats in one thousand people with chronic itching of many causes. Itch erodes quality of life through a tangle of nerve and immune signals plus a leaky skin barrier. The cream pairs the oat-derived molecule, which blocks an itch receptor, with barrier-repair ingredients. Patients applied it twice daily for two weeks and rated severity on a standard scale, while twenty volunteers gave skin samples before and after.

Average itch scores fell by about half over the fortnight, and more than half of the participants at least halved their severity, with gains consistent across causes. In the biopsy subgroup, gene activity for itch-driving molecules shifted in step with the clinical relief. The single-arm design has no comparison group, so the authors frame the work as real-world effectiveness evidence with molecular support.
pmc-13559374:
Jiafang Zhang and colleagues asked whether exercise habits before surgery predict recovery in early-stage non-small cell lung cancer. Their 2026 retrospective cohort covered 252 patients with stage IA tumors treated at Mount Sinai between 2016 and 2024. Each patient had filled in a leisure-time exercise questionnaire before resection, and the team split them into active and sedentary halves of 126.

Complications followed surgery in 29 percent of patients overall, with active patients showing a slightly higher rate that did not reach significance. After adjustment, neither disease-free survival nor lung-cancer-specific survival differed clearly between the two groups. Median follow-up ran to 32 months. Being older, male, or Black or Hispanic carried higher complication risk in the models. The authors argue that self-reported activity is too blunt a measure here, and they call for studies using objective exercise tracking in larger groups.
pmc-13559674:
Xiaoxiao He and four colleagues test whether a gut bacterium can undo resistance to apatinib, a targeted drug for liver cancer, in a mouse model. Their 2026 study used Hepa1-6 tumors grown in mice, defining resistance as continued growth under drug pressure plus a shift in drug sensitivity measured in cells. Gut microbes were profiled by gene sequencing of fecal samples.

Resistant mice carried a disturbed gut community with sharply depleted Akkermansia muciniphila, a mucus-dwelling bacterium. Their tumors also held fewer attack-ready M1 macrophages and more of the calming M2 type, with quieter NF-κB signaling. Feeding live bacteria restored gut levels, shrank tumors, and revived both the M1 pattern and the signaling pathway. Pasteurized bacteria and their culture fluid partly reproduced the effect on macrophages grown in dishes. The authors suggest microbe-based support could accompany targeted therapy, pending work in more realistic models.
pmc-13559974:
Yusra Murad's team tested whether community-crafted counter-stories can shift public views on American health care, in a 2026 mixed-methods study. Organisers use story strategy to challenge dominant accounts of the health system, but the mechanisms were rarely tested with research. Working with a power-building group, the team interviewed organisers, built two counter-stories about complexity and unaffordability, and ran a randomised trial with 1,587 people.

The dominant story pushed blame onto individuals and dampened willingness to act. Counter-stories rooted in the lived experience of those harmed most shifted blame toward outside forces and spurred some forms of joint action. The study backs pairing grassroots organisers with researchers to craft messages that move policy beliefs, not just sympathy.
pmc-13560274:
Qiurong Xie and colleagues test Tai Ji as an add-on to stroke rehabilitation, measuring both arm function and the brain-muscle conversation behind it. Their 2026 randomized trial assigned eighty-four stroke patients evenly to conventional rehabilitation alone or with an eight-form Tai Ji program, sixty minutes five times weekly for four weeks. A healthy reference group of thirty supplied baseline synergy patterns.

The Tai Ji group improved more on upper-limb motor scores and daily living independence than controls. Brain and muscle recordings showed strengthened downward drive from the motor cortex to key arm muscles, plus richer upward sensory feedback to the cortex. Muscle synergy patterns shifted toward the healthy reference. Exploratory links tied hand and wrist gains to the specific pathways that changed. The authors read the benefit as a two-way retuning of cortico-muscular coupling, pairing stronger commands with better feedback.
pmc-13562574:
Ji Young Kim and three colleagues examine how sleep quality relates to depressive symptoms in older South Koreans living in the community. The two problems often arrive together in later life, yet Korean data on the link is thin. The 2026 analysis draws on 924 people aged 55 to 80 from an ageing and cognition cohort. Sleep was scored with the Pittsburgh index, a standard questionnaire, and mood with a 30-item geriatric depression scale. Regression, subgroup, and network methods probed the connection from several angles.

Poor sleep quality went with clearly higher depression scores, and the tie survived adjustment for other factors. How people functioned in the daytime mattered most, followed by trouble falling asleep and by how they rated their own sleep. The link ran stronger past age 65, in women, and in married participants. The authors suggest that depression checks in later life should always ask about sleep.
pmc-13563274:
Michał Pers and four colleagues pit two ways of teaching medical students to centre the patient: acting scenes with classmates, or working through a linear virtual patient on screen. Patient-centred attitudes shape trust and outcomes, yet course time is scarce. The 2026 mixed-method study randomised third-year students in a communication course, 122 in all, to one method or the other. Attitudes were measured before and after with a standard orientation scale, satisfaction with a seven-point questionnaire, and six students sat for interviews.

Attitude gains matched so closely that formal testing declared the methods equivalent within half a scale point. Satisfaction, though, favoured role-play, at a median of 5.65 against 5.06. Interviews explained the split: live partners felt real and engaging, while virtual patients lowered stress and left room to reflect. The authors suggest blending the two, using screens for safe rehearsal and role-play for the human spark.
pmc-13564174:
Kylie E. Van Meter leads a 2026 materials study that merges a phase-separation trick with 3D printing to build epoxy parts with structure at many scales. As the epoxy cures, its ingredients separate into tiny domains whose size can be tuned, while a two-step curing printer lays down the overall shape.

Additives had to be balanced carefully so the ink would print and hold its shape. Microscope mapping showed woven nano- to micro-scale domains that shifted strength and heat behavior, and graded parts even showed shape-memory effects. Designers of printed parts gain a way to set internal texture and outer form in a single build.
pmc-13566374:
Anja Bernaerts and co-authors present, in a 2026 case report, magnetic resonance imaging findings in a 68-year-old woman with DFNA9. This is an inherited late-onset hearing loss caused by a change in the COCH gene. She had long-standing, worsening hearing loss in both ears and arrived urgently after sudden further loss in the left ear.

Special delayed imaging sequences also revealed secondary endolymphatic hydrops, a swelling of one inner ear fluid space, which the team links to the sudden loss. Such sequences were already known to show raised protein in the inner ear fluid of these patients. Ear specialists get a reminder that this inherited condition can hide a second, image-detectable cause of sudden deafness.
pmc-13569374:
Tianxue Hou's team reviewed interventions aimed at easing loneliness in unpaid carers of people with dementia, in a 2026 systematic review. Dementia care falls mostly on family and friends, and the isolation of that role harms carers' mental and physical health. The team searched six databases through January 2024 and found only eight eligible studies, three of them randomised trials, all testing psychosocial approaches.

Just one study significantly reduced loneliness, though several remote and online formats, including social networking, therapy, and peer support, showed promise. Four studies eased carer stress, and single pilots improved depression, anxiety, or burden. The findings are too thin for firm conclusions, but the review points to tailored remote support as the most promising direction for future trials.
pmc-13570774:
Marie-Christine Fritzsche and Charlotte Franziska Unruh explore, in a 2026 article, what harm means in medical ethics, a word that drives case deliberations and harm-benefit balancing yet is rarely defined in practice. Three philosophical accounts, comparing against what would have happened, locating harm in time, and treating some harms as non-comparative, are applied to ethics consultations and data-heavy medical innovations.

Each account sorts real cases differently, so unspoken disagreements about harm can steer recommendations, communication, and judgments about quality of life. Making each party's concept explicit, the authors argue, keeps stakeholders from talking past one another. Ethicists gain a practical case for conceptual homework before weighing outcomes.
pmc-13570974:
Hanna Feige, Timothy J. Luke, and Karl Ask map, in a 2026 mixed-methods study, how people picture intimate partner violence across four gender pairings of victim and perpetrator. One hundred sixty-one adults in the United States and United Kingdom wrote open descriptions of each scenario, and the coded features were modeled as networks showing which assumptions connect.

The overall structure of the four mental pictures looked surprisingly alike. What differed was how shared features were wired together in each pairing. Gendered assumptions, the authors argue, live less in separate stories and more in how the same pieces are combined. The reframing helps researchers and trainers target the links that bias judgments about less typical cases.
pmc-13571574:
Verónica Mäki-Marttunen and co-authors combine, in a 2026 study of UK Biobank data, brain scans from nearly forty-six thousand adults with genetic analysis. Their question is how loneliness relates to the thalamus, the brain's sensory relay station. Volumes of thalamic subregions were compared by self-reported loneliness and social isolation.

Lonely participants had smaller whole thalamus volumes and smaller medial, lateral, and rear subregions. Being isolated without feeling lonely showed no such shrinkage, separating the feeling from the circumstance. Genetic analysis found shared genetic locations between thalamus size and loneliness in the wider biobank population. The results support a real role for this relay structure in social experience.
pmc-13572474:
Sha Lin, with five colleagues, reports a 2026 study of cancer-related fatigue in people with advanced liver cancer around the time of a procedure. Fatigue is one of the most common and wearing effects of cancer, yet its drivers in this group were little studied. The team mapped how several factors link to fatigue and to each other.

The study enrolled 220 patients at a large cancer hospital who filled in surveys on their background, illness, mood, activity level, and fatigue. The mean fatigue score was 31.30 on the scale used, and 94.5 percent met the clinical bar for fatigue. Regression and path models then traced which factors tied to fatigue directly and which acted through others. The map aims to show care teams where support, such as activity or mood care, might ease the burden most.
pmc-13572874:
Jan Kollár argues that molecular methods have reached a stable equilibrium with traditional taxonomy rather than replacing it, publishing the essay in 2026. Since the 1990s, DNA tools moved from niche to mainstream, and some framed morphology as a legacy system headed for extinction, shifting funding toward molecular infrastructure. The author tests that story against bibliometric data covering over four million documents from 1988 to 2023.

Across animals, fungi, plants, protists, and cyanobacteria, the molecular share of taxonomic work rose steeply then levelled near one-third of output, typically between 25 and 45 percent. DNA excels at phylogeny and cryptic lineages but cannot capture form, function, or ecology alone, and sequences need voucher specimens for meaning. The essay defends sustained support for collections and organismal expertise as partners, not relics.
pmc-13573474:
Gaurav Patri and colleagues tested nanoparticle additives for improving mineral trioxide aggregate, a dental root cement, publishing the in vitro study in 2026. The cement seals and heals well in endodontics but sets slowly, handles awkwardly, and gains early strength slowly. The team blended 1 percent gallium oxide, cerium oxide, or graphene oxide into the powder and tested eighty specimens against unmodified cement.

All modified cements set significantly faster and held dimensions better, with strength rising over time and cerium and gallium variants strongest at thirty days. Solubility varied by particle: gallium gave the lowest long-term solubility while others ran slightly higher early. All stayed alkaline. The study shows targeted nanoparticles can sharpen a workhorse dental material's performance.
pmc-13575174:
Mouad Nechchad leads a 2026 study of a brain-computer interface that steers a robot using eye movements alone. Brain signals picked up by EEG, a scalp recording method, can stand in for hands for people who cannot move. The team decoded blinks and gaze direction into five control commands.

Data came from 15 participants, and eight learning methods were compared. A random forest model won, reaching 98.74 percent accuracy across the five classes. Commands were sent wirelessly to a small computer on a wheelchair-type robot, which turned them into safe movements. Indoor trials showed steady control and obstacle avoidance with no physical input. The authors note that response delay was not yet measured, and plan broader tests.
pmc-13579774:
Wanjun Chen and colleagues profile drug resistant staph bacteria that oddly fail to fully break down blood, in a 2026 study. The work comes from a teaching hospital in Inner Mongolia, China. Isolates gathered from patients between 2010 and 2024 numbered over eleven hundred. Close to three in ten showed the weak blood clearing trait, most of them from lower airway samples, with blood samples next.

Two clones ruled the weak group, one taking the vast bulk of cases. Toxin genes were common, and a third of isolates carried two of them at once. Biofilm output split across weak, middling, and strong bands, with the strong band the largest. Gene scans hunted a switch gene whose faults may explain the dim blood clearing and the tougher drug resistance this group is known for.
pmc-13579874:
Vicky Xu and Robert Brockman review the trial record for schema therapy as a treatment for depression, in a 2026 paper. The therapy targets deep life patterns laid down early, and a newer mode based version, which works with shifting emotional states, has spread in clinics faster than its proof. Five databases were searched through mid 2024 under standard review rules.

Seven studies with five hundred eighty patients qualified, all reporting clear symptom drops and large gains after treatment. The therapy matched cognitive behavioral therapy and supportive talk therapies in head to head tests. The mode model drew the stronger backing, and more sessions seemed to deepen the benefit, even in chronic and mixed cases. The authors stress the pool is small and call for direct model versus model trials.
pmc-13580674:
Huang and colleagues tested whether hydrogen sulfide can slow the formation of osteoclasts, the cells that break down bone. Hydrogen sulfide is a gas the body makes in small amounts, and it also calms cell damage. Excess osteoclast activity drives diseases where bone is eaten away. Their 2026 laboratory study used a mouse cell line pushed toward becoming osteoclasts by a signal protein called RANKL.

Huang added a hydrogen sulfide donor at several strengths and measured bone-eating cell formation, stress damage, and cell powerhouses. The treatment sharply reduced osteoclast formation and lowered marker proteins for bone breakdown, while easing oxidative stress, meaning damage from reactive oxygen, and restoring mitochondrial function. The effect ran through a defense switch called Nrf2 and a protective enzyme called GPX4. Blocking either one partly undid the benefit, marking this pathway as a candidate drug target.
pmc-13582774:
Andrew E Warfield and colleagues tested one-hour imaging review sessions led by second-year medical students for first-year anatomy students. Imaging is woven through seven anatomy blocks, yet time and instructor shortages limit teaching. Each optional session focused on high-yield exam concepts, with quizzes before and after and surveys afterward.

About fifty-one students attended each session on average, and post-session quiz scores improved in six of seven sessions. Students reported feeling more knowledgeable and better prepared for test questions, and end-of-course questions showed longer-term retention. Learners asked for more practice time and longer sessions, but rated the near-peer facilitators and content highly.
pmc-13582974:
Yingying Song and colleagues built BiSP-GP, a generative model that designs drug-like molecules and guesses their traits as one task. Drug design must satisfy both trait targets and shape limits, but most generative models flatten traits into numbers and miss the tangled links between shape and trait. Their 2026 model turns smooth traits into token strings, treating them jointly with drug shapes so making and trait-guessing run in both directions.

Scaffolds can be supplied as starting points to steer making. Tests showed strong results on guided making, trait guessing, and later tasks, and a case study on the target PAK1 gave molecules with better docking scores. The authors present two-way sequence work as a more controlled route to new drug candidates.
pmc-13584474:
Bin Tang and colleagues study what boarding does to rural schoolchildren in northwest China in this 2026 paper. Boarding has spread fast as small village schools closed and parents left for city jobs. Using records from 2019 and 2020, the team followed 10,923 pupils in 195 rural elementary schools and measured noncognitive skills, the habits and traits beyond test scores, such as grit and openness.

Boarding came out harmful on the whole, wearing down openness, grit, and liking for school. Yet the effect was not even: girls, younger pupils, richer pupils, and those with better-schooled mothers drew more benefit from boarding than others. The authors advise parents to guard boarders' emotional lives, schools to teach self-care and social skills, and officials to fund that work.
pmc-13585974:
Mariah Post and colleagues test mouth fluid as an easier way to watch for Salmonella in market-weight pigs. Checking droppings pen by pen is slow work on big farms, while pigs will chew ropes hung in the pen, leaving fluid that staff can collect fast. Their study paired mouth fluid and pooled dung from 51 pens at three Iowa finishing sites between February and May 2025.

Straight gene tests on raw samples found nothing in either type. After a growth step in the lab, both types turned positive, and culture of the mouth fluid gave living germs that could be typed. Salmonella showed up in most pens by at least one method, and mouth fluid matched dung testing closely. The team presents the rope method as a practical way to scale up herd watching.
pmc-13586474:
J Hearst and colleagues summarize an external evaluation of the Creative Health Associates program, which placed one associate in every NHS region in England from July 2023 to March 2025. The associates acted as bridges between public health and cultural sectors, embedding in integrated care systems to advance creative health. The evaluation used the Two Loops model of systems change to trace how new systems emerge.

Associates first made invisible creative-health activity visible to public health teams, then gave it a shared language that leaders could defend in strategy. They also convened cross-sector groups that uncovered duplication and redirected effort. Most impact sat in these early naming and connecting phases, laying groundwork for deeper transformation.
pmc-13591174:
Timothy R Dillingham and five colleagues test, in 2026, an adjustable prosthetic socket for children and teens who have lost a lower limb. Growing children outgrow fixed sockets fast, and each refit costs families time, travel, and school days. The tested socket fits at once and can be widened as the limb grows. Twenty eight young people took part; 15 finished follow up, comparing the new socket with their usual device.

Scores for ease of adjustment clearly favored the new socket, and users praised its cooler, less sweaty fit. Walking speed and pressure inside the socket matched the old devices, and no skin harm or breakage occurred. Dillingham and the team call the design a practical, lower cost option for growing users.
pmc-13591674:
Esmaeil Moshiri and three colleagues tally, in 2026, what a hospital stay for COVID-19 cost patients and families in Semnan, Iran. The study drew on 400 patients treated during the sixth wave of the illness, in summer and fall 2021. Costs came from medical records and patient interviews, and covered care bills, travel and lodging outlays, and lost income.

Each patient bore a monthly burden near 2,773 dollars in local terms. Direct medical costs made up about two thirds of that sum. Age, sex, place of residence, insurance type, other illness, and disease severity all shifted the total. Moshiri and the team stress the deep unfairness the sums reveal, with rural and poorer patients hit hardest.
pmc-13592474:
Gozde Erdemir leads a large team comparing, in 2026, world guidelines for infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, a severe baby epilepsy where fast care guards brain development. Their scoping review gathered 28 guidelines, half published and half shared by hospitals, spanning rich and poorer nations. Brain wave testing was advised nearly everywhere. Brain imaging and gene testing appeared far less often, they found.

Drug advice shifted over two decades: hormone treatment led early guidance, while steroid tablets and vigabatrin gained ground later. Combined therapy appeared after 2017 in a quarter of recent guidance. Poorer nations leaned uniformly on the cheap steroid, likely reflecting access and cost. Erdemir and the team call for shared global guidance to close the gap.
pmc-13592574:
İsmail Yaşartürk and four colleagues ask whether artificial intelligence can grade children's handwriting as fairly as a human expert. Their sample held 67 fourth grade pupils at a public school, each producing three kinds of writing: copied, dictated, and free. That gave 201 samples, scored on a multidimensional legibility scale by one researcher and by ChatGPT working from the same scale.

Across nearly every writing type and sub score, the two raters showed no meaningful gap. Their scores also correlated strongly and positively. The lone exception was slant in free writing. Yaşartürk and the team conclude that AI grading of legibility can match expert grading closely enough to serve as an objective aid, easing a heavy teacher workload.
pmc-13593674:
Katrin Kalies and co-authors report that briefly switching on the four Yamanaka reprogramming factors can make aged blood vessel lining cells act younger again. Their 2026 experiments used a drug cocktail, not gene therapy, on exhausted endothelial cells grown in the lab, then moved to old mice with blocked leg circulation.

Treated cells showed a short pulse of the reprogramming factors, lower levels of the aging markers p16 and p14, and steadier telomere length, the protective caps on chromosomes. The cells also grew, moved, and sprouted new vessel tubes better, and some gains lasted with continued culture. In 21-month-old mice, blood flow after the leg injury recovered clearly better at one and two weeks. The compounds are each approved for other uses, though the authors stress the combination itself is not yet ready for patients.
pmc-13593774:
Jakub Wójcik leads a ten-author team that modified fenoterol, a drug that activates beta-2 receptors, to see which versions best switch off a growth signal inside melanoma cells. Activating these receptors is known to quiet the ERK pathway that drives melanoma growth, and their 2026 study screened mirror-image variants of the drug in a human melanoma cell line.

One arrangement of the molecule, the R,R-prime form, consistently suppressed the ERK signal most strongly, and small changes to the molecule's side chain or ring shifted potency a great deal. The best ERK blocker barely slowed tumors in a zebrafish model, though. A close cousin with weaker ERK effects shrank tumors and killed cells far better. ERK suppression alone, the team concluded, does not predict anticancer power. Other mechanisms must be at work.
pmc-13594174:
Purba Mandal and colleagues compared the brains of people who died with Alzheimer's plaques and tangles yet stayed mentally sharp against those of people with full Alzheimer's disease. Drawing on protein and gene data from several cohorts, four brain regions, and many cell types, their 2026 study searched for what protects the resilient group.

The protected brains kept their mitochondria, the cells' energy plants, in far better shape, with stronger energy production, fat burning, and amino acid use, plus higher levels of several key mitochondrial proteins. Excitatory nerve cells showed the best-preserved energy function, while some inhibitory cell types were more numerous and more active. Support and immune cell shares ran lower than in Alzheimer's brains. The authors suggest that boosting NAD-related metabolism might help preserve thinking despite the disease's hallmark deposits.
pmc-13594874:
Jens Marquardt and co-authors reply to critics of their study of quality of life and healthcare use in patients with metabolic liver disease known as MASH. The letter from Zhuang and Shen had charged that the study's definition of additional heart, kidney, and metabolic conditions was circular, and this 2026 reply in JHEP Reports sets out the defense.

Every patient in the study already met at least one of the five cardiometabolic criteria needed for a MASH diagnosis. Additional comorbidity status was reserved for specific named diagnoses, from stroke and heart failure to kidney disease and type 2 diabetes, so the grouping did not simply restate the entry criteria. Patients were then compared across three groups defined by scarring stage and comorbidity presence. The authors welcome the scrutiny and use the reply to make their stratification logic explicit for readers judging the results.
pmc-13595474:
Luca Li and a team of co-authors measured ten DNA methylation markers of cell division and aging in nearly two thousand breast tumors and asked whether any forecast survival. Their 2026 study combined a Melbourne cohort with public datasets, computing four markers of how often cells have divided, two of calendar age, and four of biological age, then modeling five-year survival.

Tumors scoring high on the cell division markers came with worse survival, while high calendar-age marker scores pointed the other way, toward better outcomes. Biological age markers behaved inconsistently. Much of each link weakened once standard clinical features entered the model, and patterns differed across hormone receptor groups and subtypes. The authors judge the markers' added prognostic value limited, though the subtype differences may still reveal something real about tumor biology.
pmc-13612274:
Elisa Mansutti leads a seventeen-author team nudging lunch choices in three hospital canteens in northeastern Italy. Hospitals preach healthy eating, so the team tested posters, social-norm messages, and rearranged fruit and vegetable displays, photographing trays in one September week of 2022 and again in 2023. In total 2,851 trays were scored for nutrition and for carbon and water footprints.

Results split by canteen. Median meal energy rose slightly in two canteens, by 30 and 135 kilocalories, and fell by 118 in the third. Fat still supplied 30 to 39 percent of meal energy everywhere, above targets, while carbohydrates stayed low and fiber hit reference range in only two sites. Footprints barely budged: carbon between 966 and 1,227 grams of CO2 equivalent per meal, water above a thousand liters. The authors call the intervention a partial success at best. Their conclusion is blunt: educating diners is not enough, and the food on offer itself must change.
pmc-13614274:
Suzuki and colleagues published a 2026 study on making smooth films of lattice-like crystals. Covalent organic frameworks are crystals with neat pores and ordered layers. Growing them as even films on surfaces has proven stubbornly hard. The team found that room humidity during drying steers the whole process.

With humidity held steady, drop-cast films came out smooth and evenly faced. The method worked for several building-block pairs, not just one recipe. Orderly films let the team compare scent-sensing responses across film types fairly. Water in the air slows or speeds the linking steps, they propose. A simple humidity trick may thus unlock wider use of these films. Sensing and catalysis are named as early fields that could benefit.
pmc-13614974:
Matthew R. Boyce, Christine Crudo Blackburn, and Syeda Sharmin Duza report a 2026 survey study of how parents' social identities relate to skipping childhood vaccines through nonmedical exemptions in the United States. Such exemptions are rising and can erode the group immunity that protects children. The team surveyed parents and guardians of children aged five or younger online between August and September 2025.

Of 1,042 parents counted, 72 said a child of theirs had missed a vaccine through a nonmedical exemption. Rates differed clearly by race, political leaning, religious practice, and strength of vaccine-hesitant identity. The study treats exemption not as a lone medical choice but as part of who parents see themselves as. Health officials designing outreach may need to speak to identity and trust, not merely hand out facts.
pmc-13616274:
Xiu-wu Pan leads a large team tracing how kidney cancer cells learn to resist everolimus, a key drug for advanced clear cell kidney cancer, through a gene-cutting trick. The drug targets a growth pathway, yet tumours often escape. Single-cell gene readings linked a splicing controller, PTBP1, with both resistance and high pathway activity. Splicing is where a gene's message is edited before use, and PTBP1 steering it can favour a survival version of another gene.

Tests in patient tissue, animals, and dishes confirmed the chain: altered splicing of the DNAJB6 gene feeds a positive loop through partner proteins that switches the growth pathway back on. Cutting that loop could restore the drug's bite. For patients whose cancer has outgrown everolimus, the study names concrete points where a second drug might block the escape.
pmc-13616774:
Jiahua Hu, Lu Li, Xiaoli Yang, and Maohua Guo test whether a simple blood ratio predicts death within ninety days in liver failure. Most cases were the acute-on-chronic kind. In that form, a long-diseased liver suddenly worsens. The ratio divides the share of neutrophils, front-line infection fighters, by albumin, a protein marking nutrition and liver strength, so one number blends inflammation and nourishment. Charts covered 104 adults admitted between January 2022 and December 2024, of whom 89.4 percent had the acute-on-chronic form.

Models pairing the log-transformed ratio with the standard MELD severity score were checked by resampling a thousand times for stability. Short-term death in this condition is high, and a cheap flag drawn from routine blood work could help wards triage scarce intensive care. The study asks whether this two-part signal adds anything beyond the score doctors already use.
pmc-13618074:
Ahmed Mohammed Umar and four colleagues report a Nigerian case of Meleney's gangrene, a rapidly spreading flesh-destroying infection, triggered by a dislodged bladder catheter. The patient first arrived unable to pass urine, and after failed urethral attempts doctors placed an ultrasound-guided suprapubic tube through the abdominal wall into the bladder. Discharged home, he returned four days later with the tube dislodged and urine leaking through the opening, the surrounding skin already discolored and tender.

Despite a formal open procedure, the discoloration spread into full necrotizing infection. Surgeons cut away dead tissue, started broad-spectrum antibiotics, and later tried a skin graft, most of which failed before the wound healed by secondary intention. The authors argue the leaked urine, likely infected, chemically irritated tissue planes and fed bacterial spread along fascial layers. They urge teams to treat any suprapubic tube dislodgement as high risk.
pmc-13618274:
Rakesh Puttreddy, Sergi Burguera, Antonio Frontera, and Kari Rissanen report a chemistry study, published in 2026. It confirms a long-sought bonding set-up. One iodine atom with a positive charge sits midway between two oxygen atoms. Eight such complexes were built. They use pyridine N-oxide units. X-ray methods mapped their structure. Magnetic resonance methods studied them in solution.
