The iodine-oxygen bonds are the shortest of their kind. No halogen bond in N-oxide systems has been shorter. Maths compared oxygen, nitrogen, and sulphur versions. The oxygen complex behaves quite distinctly. It keeps a spare electron pair. This leaves it open to further interactions. That sets this bonding family apart.
pmc-13618774:
Young Rok Kim and two colleagues solve a light-trapping problem in top-emitting microcavity OLED displays. A Fabry-Perot cavity sharpens color and aims light forward but also confines much of it inside the device. Rough textures can free the trapped light yet disturb the cavity that gives the display its purity. Their answer is a gentle internal corrugation layer that reshapes the stack softly, paired with a narrowband emissive system tuned to the cavity's resonance.

Under identical conditions, the corrugation raised external quantum efficiency from about thirty-five percent to about sixty-nine percent, and roughly doubled power efficiency. It also cut the color shift seen at a sixty-degree viewing angle to less than half its former value. Current efficiency also climbed clearly. The authors argue the texture redistributes confined light into extractable channels while preserving the cavity's emission, a compatible route for high-resolution displays.
pmc-13619874:
Jia Guo, the sole author, proposes a new reconstruction method for arterial spin labeling MRI in a 2026 paper. That scan type tags blood water to measure flow without injected contrast, yet its signal is faint. Strong background suppression boosts the signal, but it can flip signal signs between the paired images, and ordinary subtraction then creates errors or wipes out real signal.

The method overlays a clean, high-quality reference scan onto the raw data before rebuilding the image, then subtracts the reference back out. Tests in four volunteers covered three labeling styles at several suppression levels on a three-tesla scanner. The approach removed sign-flip artifacts, recovered negative signals that other pipelines lost, and raised signal quality in both gray and white matter. It also tolerated small misalignments and worked with a common speed-up technique.
pmc-13619974:
Jaskaran Singh and five colleagues pooled evidence on whether image guidance during spine surgery keeps patients out of the operating room a second time. Surgeons place screws to stabilize the spine either freehand, by anatomy and feel, or with navigation and robotic help. The reviewers gathered twenty-one comparative studies covering more than ninety-one thousand patients, most of them freehand cases.

Guided placement came with lower odds of revision surgery for hardware problems and lower odds of any unexpected return to surgery. Returns for non-hardware reasons showed no difference. Navigation alone drove the clear gains, while robotic studies showed no firm advantage, though robotic cases were fewer and differed in mix. The authors warn that most source studies were backward-looking with high bias risk, so the pooled picture favors navigation without settling the robotics question.
pmc-13623374:
Mohamad Jamal Bark and co-authors grade the clear aligner information on Brazilian orthodontists' websites for quality, using the DISCERN tool, a standard checklist for judging consumer health information. Clear aligners are the near-invisible trays marketed heavily as an alternative to braces. Patients often meet the claims online first, so the accuracy of practice websites matters.

In July 2024 the team searched Google in Portuguese and kept 113 practice websites for scoring by two trained orthodontists, whose ratings agreed well. The average score reached barely a third of the maximum. Over half the sites rated very poor and none rated excellent. The weakest points were missing sources, missing dates, silence about uncertainty, and silence about treatment risks, with every site failing to say what happens without treatment. The authors urge orthodontists to publish balanced, referenced content that names risks and alternatives, so patients can decide with open eyes.
pmc-13623774:
Jefferson Rosi leads a five-year follow-up study of small, unruptured brain aneurysms left untreated. Aneurysms are balloon-like weak spots in brain arteries, and for those under five millimetres wide, doctors debate operating against watching. Reliable long-term data on what these small bulges do on their own have been thin.

The study followed 113 patients at one academic centre, most of them women near sixty years old, with repeat dye-based vessel imaging at five years. Across the whole follow-up nobody's aneurysm burst. More than three quarters of the bulges stayed exactly the same size. A tenth grew slightly but stayed under five millimetres, a few shrank, and a few vanished completely. Three patients grew brand-new aneurysms elsewhere. One odd result linked smoking to a higher chance of disappearance. The authors support watchful scanning for most such patients, with choices still tailored to each case.
pmc-13624374:
Muhammad Farhan leads a case report of a rare gallbladder tumour that mixes two cancer types in one mass, reported from a low-resource setting. The patient, a thirty-five-year-old woman, had a month of pain under the right ribs, nausea, and a palpable lump. Imaging showed a polyp-like growth in the gallbladder with enlarged nearby lymph nodes.

Surgeons removed the gallbladder and nodes in open surgery. Under the microscope, staining confirmed a mixed neuroendocrine and non-neuroendocrine neoplasm, a tumour defined by holding at least thirty percent of each component. Such mixed tumours make up a slice of digestive cancers, and no standard protocol exists for them. At twelve months the patient remained free of recurrence even though she received no chemotherapy after surgery. The authors stress careful tissue diagnosis and case-by-case planning for these rare tumours, particularly where resources limit options.
pmc-13626074:
Koichi Naito and colleagues check a wrist tracker against a research waist sensor in older heart patients. Fifty-one Japanese outpatients, most near eighty and split between heart failure and artery disease, wore a Fitbit Inspire 3 on the wrist and an Omron accelerometer at the waist for seven days. Sitting time was compared inside a fixed twelve-hour daytime window, minute by minute.

The two devices moved together closely across patients, yet the wrist tracker overcounted sitting by about an hour a day on average, with wide spread around that bias. A fixed correction steadied the readings in testing. For clinic use, the authors conclude, wrist trackers rank patients well but overstate total sitting time, which matters when doctors set activity goals for fragile hearts.
pmc-13627874:
Sarah Nafea and colleagues present a young woman whose stubborn pressure symptoms masked a dangerous clot in the brain's drainage veins. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis is a rare stroke that favors the young and often shows only a long headache. It is therefore commonly mistaken for idiopathic intracranial hypertension, a pressure disorder it resembles. In this case the thrombosis was extensive and blocked fluid flow, causing obstructive hydrocephalus, a swelling that can kill quickly.

The search for a cause found essential thrombocythemia, a bone marrow disorder that overproduces platelets and turns blood clot-prone, carrying the JAK2 mutation. The authors draw two lessons: pressure symptoms that defy standard treatment demand urgent brain imaging, and a venous clot with no obvious trigger demands a hunt for hidden marrow disease. Early anticoagulation, they note, is what saves function in most patients.
pmc-13627974:
José Alfredo Castillo-Guerrero and four colleagues report on the Laysan albatross colony on Clarion Island, off Mexico, where the birds have bred since the 1980s yet barely grown. Between 2016 and 2023 the team checked nests, watched for predators, tracked feeding trips with GPS devices, and tested blood samples.

Across those years the colony failed to raise young at all. The researchers point to two pressures: the island sits far from feeding grounds, so parents travel long distances for food, and predators killed hatchlings at very high rates. Their records give conservation planners a baseline for judging whether protection efforts can still save the colony.
pmc-13629274:
Selin Olenik and thirteen colleagues built a bioelectronic implant that folds down small for insertion under the skin, then unfolds itself into its full flat working shape. Published in 2026, the device tackles a core trade-off: implants must be tiny to limit surgical harm yet large enough to hold wireless power, communications, and sensing electronics.

Once in place, the implant measures acidity, temperature, heart and breathing activity, and lithium levels, a drug marker important in psychiatry. The team verified insertion, operation, and removal through bench, tissue, and live animal experiments. They pitch the suture-free, multiplexed monitoring as a step toward personalised care that gathers chemical information wearables on the skin cannot reach.
pmc-13629574:
Marco Juul Thomsen and five colleagues used Denmark's national health records to chart subacute thyroiditis. This painful thyroid condition often follows a viral infection. Their 2026 study found 1,763 cases diagnosed at Danish hospitals. The years ran from 1995 to 2016. That span covers the start of forced iodine fortification in 2000.

Recorded rates nearly doubled over the period. No gap appeared between eastern and western Denmark. The outcome data carry a warning. About a quarter of patients started thyroid hormone treatment afterwards. For nearly half of those, treatment ran beyond three years. That suggests lasting underactivity of the gland. The authors urge attention to long-term follow-up. This illness is often called temporary, but the record says otherwise.
pmc-13631274:
Ming Yan and six colleagues deliver the first complete genome of a freshwater bivalve, end to end. Their study appeared in 2026. They chose a vulnerable mussel found only in China. It is nicknamed the pig's ear mussel for its flattened shell. The species clings to Yangtze basin rivers and lakes. Kin mussels have vanished, and no quality genome existed to guide its protection.

Merging three sequencing methods, the team produced a genome of about three billion bases. It is over ninety-three percent complete. It is anchored to nineteen chromosomes. Comparing it with other freshwater mussel genomes named the European pearl mussel as its closest published kin. The authors present the assembly as a base for conservation genetics. The group it serves suffers steep declines.
pmc-13631374:
Garrett Ni and three colleagues pilot-tested a drug-free combined treatment for pattern hair loss. Eight patients took part: five men and three women. Their average age was in the mid-fifties. Each received 24 sessions of low-level laser therapy over three months. Three monthly infusions of a proprietary growth serum joined them. The infusions used a needle-free device.

Automated scalp imaging recorded clear gains over the three months. Hairs per square centimetre rose by about a quarter. Hairs per follicle rose by over two-fifths. The ratio of thick terminal hairs to fine vellus hairs rose by about a quarter too. Single hairs widened modestly. Patients' own impressions were more muted. All found the regimen tolerable and would recommend it. The authors call for larger controlled trials.
pmc-13633174:
Platon Braun and three colleagues published this 2026 review of hantavirus infection for emergency radiology teams. Hantaviruses usually pass from rodents to people through airborne particles from droppings. One type, Andes virus, can also pass between people, a fact underlined by severe cases aboard a cruise ship in April 2026. Infections can flood the lungs or damage the kidneys, and both forms can kill.

Imaging findings shift fast in these illnesses, so radiologists often spot the pattern early and shape triage. The review walks through how the virus injures the body, what scans typically show at each stage, and how the two syndromes differ. It also covers practical infection control for imaging departments, where close contact and shared equipment raise exposure risk. The authors stress exposure history as a key clue, since early illness can mimic common respiratory infections.
pmc-13635274:
Diele Carine Barreto Arantes and four colleagues published this 2026 review comparing artificial intelligence with human pathologists at predicting which mouth lesions turn cancerous. Oral epithelial dysplasia is a precancerous change in the mouth lining, graded under the microscope to guide care. The team gathered thirty-two studies published between 1998 and 2026. Nine tested AI risk models, while twenty-three relied on human grading, mostly in white or red patch mouth conditions.

Both approaches predicted later cancer, yet the AI models discriminated far more sharply in the pooled analysis. Their edge came mainly from precision: they ruled out low-risk cases more reliably, while their catch rate for true future cancers matched the humans'. Human results also swung widely between studies. The authors judge AI promising but not clinic-ready. Shared standards, outside validation, and larger multi-center datasets must come first, before these models steer real treatment choices.
pmc-13635674:
Shadi Moradi, Anupama Binoy, and Shouan Zhu built a workflow to prove that cartilage makes its own fat. Cartilage is usually cast as a quiet tissue that imports the lipids it needs. The team labeled living mice with heavy water, a harmless tracer whose atoms enter newly built fat molecules. They then measured tracer buildup in palmitate, a fatty acid, in blood and joint cartilage using chemical instruments.

The tracer appeared steadily in cartilage fat, direct proof of local production. Labeling ran slower in cartilage than in blood, matching the tissue's dense, slow-turnover structure. Mice engineered to lack a key fat-building enzyme in cartilage made fat with weaker early labeling and held less palmitate overall, though their new-synthesis share looked similar. The authors present heavy-water tracing as a solid measuring frame for joint fat metabolism, with the enzyme confirmed as a pool keeper.
pmc-13641874:
Nimrat Grewal and three colleagues published this 2026 analysis questioning whether Western guideline thresholds for aortic surgery fit the Indian population, whose aortas run smaller. Guidelines trigger surgery at set diameters drawn mainly from Western bodies. The authors set the size spread of 2,000 South Asian adults against the sizes of 71 patients with acute type A aortic dissection. They asked where dissections occur relative to the population's anatomy.

In the population the median ascending aorta measured 30.2 millimetres. Under one percent of people reached even the 45-millimetre guideline threshold. Dissection patients presented at a median of 52 millimetres. Their dissections clustered in the right tail of the population spread, a pattern that sharpened when sizes were indexed to body surface area. Many dissections occurred below guideline thresholds. The authors argue for reading aortic size against the local population rather than importing set cut-offs. They caution that anatomy alone does not prove thresholds wrong.
pmc-13643474:
Ayse Kubra Coskun and five colleagues present a 2026 national study of emergency department visits for suicidality among United States children and adolescents from 2016 to 2022. The data came from the Nationwide Emergency Department Sample for patients aged five to nineteen.

More than a million such visits were estimated in total, and girls accounted for about three quarters. Visits rose significantly among ten to fourteen year olds across all diagnoses, while suicide attempt visits also rose in older teens. Depression and anxiety were the commonest accompanying conditions. The authors press for earlier screening, quick follow-up after discharge, and stronger community mental health care.
pmc-13643774:
Dahlia M Nielsen presents a 2026 genetics study of how a plant-parasitic nematode rewires gene activity inside its hosts. The root-knot nematode Meloidogyne hapla feeds within plant tissue and bends host development to serve itself.

Tissue came from three host plant species infected by two genetically distinct worm strains. Which plant genes switched on or off depended on the worm's strain, and those strain-linked patterns stayed consistent across the distant host species. Public data confirmed shared infection responses, and the worms' own gene activity also varied by strain in every host. Parasite genetics, Nielsen concludes, steers a conserved host program.
pmc-13644474:
Yamei Li and colleagues compare amino acids in pristine samples from asteroids Bennu and Ryugu in a 2026 paper on the extraterrestrial roots of life's building blocks. Amino acids may have reached early Earth from space, and meteoritic amino acids famously show left-handed excess, matching biology's preference for left-handed forms. NASA's OSIRIS-REx returned Bennu material in 2023 and JAXA's Hayabusa2 returned Ryugu material three years earlier, letting researchers compare two water-rich asteroids without terrestrial contamination.

Bennu carried fourteen protein amino acid types, nearly twice Ryugu's eight, with glycine, alanine, beta-alanine, aspartic acid, and glutamic acid dominating. Ryugu instead favored non-protein amino acids, mainly beta-alanine and gamma-aminobutyric acid. Total amino acid abundance in Bennu, near 70 nanomoles per gram, ran about five times Ryugu's 15. Astrobiologists get a striking contrast: two similar asteroids preserved very different amino acid inventories, hinting at divergent chemical histories.
pmc-13645774:
Lok Lam Lorraine Cheng, Chun Chit Cheung, and Yiu Che Chan review human trials of 3D bioprinted scaffolds for hard-to-heal ulcers of the leg and foot. Bioprinting lays down living material in tissue-like patterns, aiming to speed skin closure. The team searched four databases for clinical studies from 2000 to June 2025, leaving out animal and lab work. Eight studies with 139 patients in total qualified.

Both randomized trials in the set showed faster full skin closure than standard dressings. In the single-arm studies, most ulcers closed fully within twelve weeks. No serious treatment-related side effects were reported. Study quality limits were plain, though: small groups, uneven blinding, and short follow-up. The authors call the approach promising and apparently safe, while saying larger, longer trials must confirm the benefit before wide clinical adoption.
pmc-13646274:
Abhishek Sengupta and six colleagues present the third version of a database for vitiligo, the skin disease that destroys pigment cells and leaves white patches, in a 2026 paper. The molecular basis of vitiligo is still poorly mapped. Their resource combines gene activity datasets, a network of interacting proteins with its hub proteins, and a library of natural compounds and approved drugs aimed at disease proteins. Fresh rebuilding of the platform's engine makes it faster and more scalable.

New tools let users normalize gene data, run multi-gene pathway queries, and compare gene networks between vitiligo and related autoimmune diseases. The database supports forming hypotheses, hunting biomarkers, and testing drug ideas in the computer before bench work. It is free to use online. The authors position the upgrade as shared infrastructure for a field that has lacked a dedicated systems biology home.
pmc-13646474:
Luca Ambrosio and ten colleagues report, in a 2026 study, how a cell-level skin imaging tool performs alongside the standard magnified skin exam at a large referral center. The tool, reflectance confocal microscopy, is used after dermoscopy when a spot's nature stays unclear. Records covered 886 patients and 1,057 lesions seen between October 2023 and September 2024. Agreement between the two methods, tissue-confirmed accuracy, and removal decisions were analyzed.

Where both readings existed, the two methods agreed in well under half of cases, though their patterns were clearly linked. Disagreement clustered in pigment-cell lesions, the category where cancers hide. Among removed pigment lesions, about one melanoma was found per four removals, a yield the authors treat as reasonable. Only a fifth of lesions had tissue confirmation, which limits certainty. The authors frame the imaging tool as a complement that refines which spots to remove, not a replacement for the first exam.
pmc-13649774:
Filippo Ruffini and colleagues built a survival forecast tool for lung cancer that works even when some patient data are missing, in a 2026 study. Full forecasts should join scans, tissue images, and clinic facts, yet real cohorts often lack one stream, and older tools dropped such patients or filled gaps with guesses.

Their system reads each stream with a pre-trained model, then fuses what exists through a code that flags what is absent. The fused form beat single-stream tools and both early and late fusion. Using all three streams gave the best score of all. Risk scores split patients into clear groups for spread and growth. The authors say the tool adapts its trust to whichever stream speaks loudest.
pmc-13649974:
Dandan Guo and two colleagues examine why students stay motivated to learn English in online settings where English is a foreign language. Their survey study connects four factors: emotional intelligence, meaning skill at reading and managing feelings, academic well-being, motivation to learn English, and how much digital support learners feel they receive.

Responses from 435 learners were modeled with a partial least squares method. Emotional intelligence was linked to both better well-being and stronger motivation, and well-being itself was linked to motivation. Digital support strengthened the tie between well-being and motivation. The authors stress that the design captures links at one point in time, not causes, and that some indirect results still need stronger testing.
pmc-13650774:
Yanli Zheng and six colleagues build a scan-based model to predict, before liver cancer surgery, whether tumor cells have invaded tiny blood vessels. That finding forecasts recurrence and shapes the treatment plan. The signal, they suspected, sits not inside the tumor but in the ring of liver tissue hugging it.

Magnetic resonance scans from 147 confirmed patients were mined for image texture features at three ring widths around each tumor. The narrowest ring, five millimeters, carried the most relevant information, clearly beating wider rings and the tumor interior. A combined model fusing those features with ordinary imaging and clinical findings discriminated invasion with excellent accuracy in both training and validation groups, and resampling checks confirmed its stability. The authors offer the model as a preoperative aid for surgical planning, noting the modest sample behind it.
pmc-13650974:
Luping Chen and twenty-four colleagues measure how well the influenza vaccine worked in China during the 2024–2025 season, and whether social contact patterns explain who caught the flu. Outpatients with flu-like illness at three sentinel hospitals in one autonomous prefecture were tested, forming a test-negative design where positive and negative patients are compared.

Of 907 patients in the vaccine analysis, 121 tested positive. The adjusted estimate put vaccine protection against medically attended influenza in the moderate range, a little above forty percent, with wide uncertainty. Among all participants, infected young children and infected older adults reported more frequent and longer social contacts than their test-negative peers. Sequencing of six positive samples found no major mismatch with vaccine strains, though the team stresses that six samples prove little. Observational design and self-reported contacts limit causal claims, and combined vaccine plus behavior strategies need further testing.
pmc-13651474:
Raju Vaishya and seven colleagues lay out a step-by-step technique for converting a failed partial knee replacement into a full one using an imageless robot system. The conversion is notoriously awkward: the old implant leaves uneven bone loss, the joint line sits wrong. Ligaments balance poorly, so surgeons often lean on stems and filler blocks that sacrifice bone.

Their workflow registers the knee twice. First the joint is mapped as if native, capturing overall alignment and soft-tissue behavior through movement. Once the old implant comes out, fresh reference points measure the true bone defect, and the plan for the new components is rebuilt around those measurements. Cuts and positioning can then be adjusted live, with gaps balanced across the whole bend. In the case shown, the conversion succeeded without stems or augments. The authors present the dual-stage mapping as the core innovation worth testing wider.
pmc-13651674:
Martin Kraepelien and seven colleagues test Lifefulness, a self-guided digital program meant to lift mental health in older Swedes. Adults past sixty-five already exceed a fifth of Sweden's population. Cheap, reachable behavioral tools are scarce relative to the need, so the team adapted cognitive behavioral therapy and healthy aging principles into a six-week online course.

Seventy-three recruits aged sixty-five to eighty-five took part, supported by three brief phone interviews averaging about half an hour of clinician time. Engagement ran high, with nearly three quarters using the program daily or several times weekly. Participants finished with better mental health symptom scores and higher quality-of-life ratings, and they rated the program satisfying. As a single-group feasibility study, the design cannot separate program effects from time or expectation. The authors recommend a randomized trial with long-term follow-up and healthcare-use tracking.
pmc-2375974:
Conesa and Gotz describe Blast2GO, a software suite for functional analysis in plant genomics. Giving new sequence data a functional label is a first need for using genomics in plant research. Sequences alone say little until each is tied to a known role.

Blast2GO matches new sequences against known ones, assigns function terms, and supports mining of the results in one package. It was aimed in particular at plant studies, where many species lack rich prior annotation. A single workflow from raw sequence to function helped smaller plant labs join genome-era research.
pmc-2872874:
Young, Wakefield, Smyth, and co-authors present GOseq, a method for Gene Ontology analysis of RNA sequencing data. Gene Ontology analysis asks which biological roles are over-represented among genes that change in an experiment. RNA-seq, though, carries a built-in length bias: long genes gather more reads.

GOseq takes that selection bias into account before testing for enriched roles. Without the correction, long-gene categories look important even when nothing biological changed. Their method gives cleaner answers about which processes an experiment truly affected, and it is widely used in transcript studies.  Pathway results after correction focus attention on fewer, more believable biological themes.
pmc-4328074:
Powell, Waltz, Chinman, and their team reported in 2015 a refined list of implementation strategies. Implementation science studies how to get proven care into routine practice. Work in the field was held back by inconsistent language and poor descriptions of the strategies used.

The ERIC project drew on expert recommendations to build a cleaner compilation. Each strategy got a clear name and definition that researchers and managers can share. A common vocabulary lets studies be compared and lets hospitals copy what worked elsewhere. The list has become a reference for teams planning how to change practice in clinics and health systems.
pmc-4383874:
Szklarczyk, Franceschini, Wyder, and their team updated the STRING database in 2014 with version ten. Proteins work through partnerships and interactions that sit at the core of cell life. Knowing that web of links gives context for systems biology, but records were scattered across many sources.

STRING gathers known and predicted protein interactions into one network resource. Version ten widened coverage across the whole tree of life. Users can enter a protein and see its partners, with evidence scores for each link. Such maps help researchers guess the role of a new protein and find pathways tied to disease.
pmc-6007674:
Marc Suchard, Philippe Lemey, Guy Baele, and coauthors described BEAST version 1.10 in 2018. BEAST is software for Bayesian analysis of evolutionary trees from DNA data. It combines tree building with models of traits and spread through space and time.

The update reports faster computation and better tools for joining sequence data with trait data. Users can estimate when ancestors lived and how lineages moved. Outbreak researchers use the same machinery to trace virus spread. The paper documents what changed so long-running projects can move to the new version with confidence.
pmc-6494974:
The GBD 2016 Stroke Collaborators published this global stroke analysis in 2019. Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. Treatment and long-term care after stroke carry heavy costs for families and systems.

The study gives comparable figures for stroke cases, deaths, and disability across most countries. It splits results by stroke type and by age and sex. Most of the burden falls on low and middle income countries, where risk control is weakest. The authors press for wider prevention, above all blood pressure treatment, as the cheapest way to cut the toll.
pmc-7062874:
Bruno Perillo, Marzia Di Donato, Antonio Pezone, and coauthors reviewed reactive oxygen in cancer therapy in 2020. Reactive oxygen species are reactive molecules that also run normal cell signaling. Moderate levels are required for healthy gene control and growth.

Cancer cells live with higher oxygen stress than normal cells, close to their limit. Pushing that stress higher can kill them while sparing healthy tissue. Many standard treatments already work partly through this route. The review gathers the mechanisms and the new drugs designed to exploit the bright side of this chemistry.
pmc-7611074:
Elizabeth Williamson and colleagues built a new kind of research platform in 2020 to learn who faces the greatest risk of dying from COVID-19. Working on behalf of the national health service in England, they created OpenSAFELY, a secure system for analyzing health records without moving private data around. It covered about seventeen million patients, a scale few studies had ever reached.

With that platform they examined which factors were tied to COVID-19 death, including age, other illnesses, and background. The size of the data let them separate real risks from apparent ones with unusual precision. Beyond its findings, the project showed how privacy protecting analysis of whole population records could be done quickly during a crisis.
pmc-7613574:
You Li and colleagues estimated in 2022 how much illness respiratory syncytial virus, known as RSV, causes in the youngest children worldwide. This virus is the most common cause of serious chest infections in children under five. The team's systematic analysis updates an earlier estimate for 2015 with newer data centered on the year 2019.

They gathered studies from around the world to count infections, hospital stays, and deaths linked to the virus in children from birth to five years. Their figures show a heavy toll concentrated in poorer countries, where care is hardest to reach. Such estimates guide decisions about vaccines and preventive antibodies, which were just arriving as this accounting was published.
priestley-experiments-observations-air-1:
Joseph Priestley, an English cleric and keen chemist, brought out this set of trials on air in three parts from 1774 to 1777. He worked with lenses, troughs of water, and mice in sealed jars. His lab was a plain room, yet the gains were huge.

Priestley made and named a string of new gases, one by one. The most famed was the pure air we now call oxygen, which he named dephlogisticated air. Odd as it sounds, he held to the phlogiston scheme all his life, while his finds broke it.
randolph-eulis-1874:
Paschal Beverly Randolph set out his most fought claim in Eulis!, his book of 1874. He held that the act of love, rightly used, is a rite of great force. Through it the soul can heal, see, and draw near to God. He taught this lore in hid groups for years ere he dared print it.

The print caused shock and rows at once. Yet his lore spread, by hid paths, to bands in the West for years. This book is the turn point of his life's work. It still sparks awe and doubt in kind. His heirs in hid bands kept the book in print by hand. That care shows how much weight his close fans gave these bold claims.
retz-memoirs-1774:
Jean François Paul de Gondi, Cardinal de Retz, wrote his Mémoires about the Fronde, the revolt that shook France in his youth. Retz was no bystander: he plotted, preached, and intrigued at the center of the rising against the young Louis XIV's court. The memoirs were first published in 1717, and the English translation of 1774 fills this text.

Retz tells his story with unmatched wit, candor about his own ambition, and a gambler's love of the game. He judges allies and enemies alike with a cool, amused eye. French readers rank the book among the most brilliant memoirs ever written. Its cynicism is matched only by its sparkle, page after page.
schweinfurth-heart-africa-vol1-1874:
Georg Schweinfurth, a German botanist, traveled the Bahr el Ghazal region of the Sudan from 1868 to 1871. Volume One of The Heart of Africa, from 1874, reports his route into lands then unknown to Europeans. He went for plants and stayed for the peoples.

Schweinfurth describes the river systems, the ivory trade, and the peoples of the region, including the Niam-niam, wrongly feared as cannibals. His plant collections were vast, and his maps fixed a blank space on the chart. He writes with a scientist's care and a traveler's relish. The volume opened the upper Nile country to European knowledge.
schweinfurth-heart-africa-vol2-1874:
Volume Two of Schweinfurth's Heart of Africa completes his three years in the unexplored Sudan. The botanist-explorer pushed south toward the Congo watershed. What he found there made the book famous across Europe.

He meets the Monbuttoo, with their fine crafts and great hall, and the Akka, a pygmy people of the forest. Schweinfurth gives the first reliable report of pygmies in the Congo basin. He also condemns the slave and ivory raids ruining the region. His return journey closes the work. Few African travel books of the age join science and story so well.
sea-monster-account-1674:
A True and Perfect Account of the Miraculous Sea-Monster is an English broadside of 1674. Broadsides were single printed sheets, cheap and loud, sold in streets and fairs. This one trumpets a marine marvel in bold black type for penny buyers passing by.

Such sheets promised a true report and delivered a woodcut wonder. Crowds who could barely read could still gape at the picture. The sheet belongs to a rich trade in popular marvels, whales, monsters, and strange fish. It tells us less about the sea than about its readers. Street print fished for wonder, and in 1674 a sea monster was fine bait.
smyth-our-inheritance-great-pyramid-1874:
Astronomer Charles Piazzi Smyth argued that the Great Pyramid hides divine measure and prophecy. His book Our Inheritance in the Great Pyramid first appeared in 1864. Smyth held Scotland's top post in astronomy.

He claims a sacred pyramid inch guides the building's design. Chambers and passages, he says, map sacred history in stone. His charts and numbers fill page after page. Fellow scientists mostly rejected the scheme. Yet the book launched pyramid prophecy as a lasting genre. It is a curious, earnest work from an age when faith and science still shared one desk.
stanley-coomassie-magdala-1874:
Henry Stanley reported two British campaigns in Africa for the New York Herald before he was famous as an explorer. Coomassie and Magdala, from 1874, gathers his dispatches from the Abyssinian campaign and the Ashanti expedition of 1873 and 1874. The reporting made his name.

Stanley marches with the troops to Magdala, where Emperor Theodore died, and into the Ashanti capital, Coomassie. He writes fast, vivid copy about heat, disease, and battle. The book shows a war correspondent inventing his own legend on the march. It is also a raw record of Britain's small, brutal African wars. His Herald editors printed the pieces first for American readers hungry for war news.
steller-kamchatka-1774:
Georg Wilhelm Steller sailed as naturalist on Vitus Bering's last voyage to the Pacific, and his account of Kamchatka came out in German in 1774. He died on the trip home, so the book came out years after his death. Kamchatka is the wild far east coast of Siberia.

Steller wrote of the land, its beasts and plants, and the Itelmen people who lived there. He gave the first account by a trained eye of Itelmen shamans and their rites. The book first opened that remote coast to European science. His notes on the great sea cow are still prized as well.
stubbs-constitutional-history-vol-1-1874:
William Stubbs published The Constitutional History of England, Volume 1, in 1874. Stubbs, a bishop and Oxford historian, founded English constitutional history as a discipline. This volume runs from the Anglo-Saxon settlements to the death of Richard I. He traces shires, courts, kingship, and the Norman settlement in fine detail.

Stubbs built his account from charters, chronicles, and law codes at first hand. His framework, often called Stubbsian, guided scholars for generations. Later research corrected his love of Teutonic origins and free assemblies. Even so, the mastery of sources still commands respect. The three volumes remain a monument of Victorian scholarship.
the-birth-of-chemistry-1874: Opening pages are a Google Books scanner wrapper, heavily garbled in its lettering, explaining that a public domain book was scanned from library shelves to make it discoverable online. It asks readers to make non-commercial use of the file, avoid automated queries, keep attribution, and check local copyright rules. No legible title page, author name, table of contents, or chapter text of a work on chemistry appears in these pages.
the-definite-object-a-romance-of-new-yor: Jeffery Farnol's The Definite Object, a romance of New York dated 1917, appears in this second record with a fuller chapter list of thirty entries. Beyond Mrs. Trapes and Spike, the headings add a night expedition, M'Ginnis threatening and going, the Old Un at tea. Hermione makes a fateful decision, and Geoffrey Ravenslee departs from Hell's Kitchen at the close. Only the title page and that full list are present here, so the novel itself does not appear.
the-memoirs-of-jacques-casanova-de-seing:
London to Berlin, part of In London and Moscow in Jacques Casanova's memoirs, follows the 1894 London edition in Arthur Machen's translation, with chapters discovered by Arthur Symons. Chapter Fourteen, titled Flight from London to Berlin, opens the morning after Casanova's arrest and release on bail. Pocchini, who robbed him at Stuttgart, tries to enter his house and is shouted away. Then Goudar brings a newspaper report of the arrest.

The report disguises Casanova's name but prints Bottarelli's plainly, praising his conduct. Casanova visits the man who bore false witness against him and finds misery: a wife and five children in rags, Bottarelli writing in an old dressing-gown. Bottarelli apologizes, pleading he had no bread for his children, and offers future service for nothing. Pity displaces revenge in the scene. Readers watch a legal enemy undone not by punishment but by poverty.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 269 of The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction, dated Saturday, August 18, 1827, leads with the Duke of Devonshire's villa at Chiswick. The death of George Canning has excited curiosity about the house where the statesman breathed his last. The magazine offers an original drawing made since that melancholy event. Chiswick House, readers learn, was built by the last Earl of Burlington, a recorded amateur of architecture.

A double flight of steps climbs to a portico of six fluted Corinthian columns, flanked by statues of Palladio and Inigo Jones. Quoting Horace Walpole, the article calls the house a model of taste borrowed from a villa of Palladio's, though not without faults. Too many corresponding doors and chimneys between windows earn criticism. Lord Hervey's wit is quoted too: the house was too small to inhabit, and too large to hang to one's watch.

Surrey Zoological Gardens return in No. 556 of The Mirror, dated July 7, 1832, with engravings of a circular building for lions and tigers, its interior, and rockwork for beavers. An editorial aside interrupts the visit. The magazine had widened its columns and cast entirely new type, gaining the space of two extra pages in every sheet at no cost to readers.

Six months had passed since the last visit, and Mr. Cross had worked without pause. Henry Phillips, author of Sylva Florifera, supervised the laying out of the grounds. Forest trees lined the avenues to each building, and every tree and new plant carried its name on a small tally, or label. A small botanical garden was also being talked of.
the-patrician-pg2774: Galsworthy’s 1911 novel of Lord Miltoun, torn between love and his order’s code. Restrained and noble, it is his kindest book. Duty and desire in high places, in high places, duty and desire contending in high places.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-complete-:
Motley's second complete portion, covering 1566 to 1574 and labeled volume two, book one, opens with a chapter summary on secret policy. Envoys Berghen and Montigny wait in Spain while debates at Segovia, letters between the Duchess and Philip, and secret instructions expose royal delay and dissimulation.

Egmont works in Flanders, Orange returns tolerant to Antwerp, and Horn holds Tournay amid excavations, packed preaching, and new temples, while Margaret praises the nobles publicly and defames them in secret letters. Court deceit and provincial pressure build together. The same chapter summary opens a later volume record in the set, and readers should expect overlapping text there.
the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volume-21:
Headed volume twenty-two in its own pages, though the record calls it volume twenty-one, this portion opens part four on the Grand Commander Requesens for 1573 and 1574. His earlier career, Philip's passion for detail, a bankrupt exchequer, and a costly war frame a universal desire for peace.

Middelburg is relieved after Mondragon capitulates, then Count Louis crosses the Rhine to face Avila at Mook, where battle on the heath ends with Louis overthrown and killed. A phantom battle follows in the summary. New command brings no relief to either side's exhaustion.
tob-0074:
Julian Morgenstern, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible, turned his tools on Babylon for a study of how its people understood sin. Mesopotamia's temples kept rites for guilt, stain, and cleansing long before Israel's psalms. Morgenstern reads those rites closely in an early work of comparative religion.

He describes confession, sorrowful hymns, and the fear that a hidden fault had angered a god. Priests acted as healers of both body and conscience, since sin and sickness blurred together. The study shows an old moral world in fine detail. Readers of the Bible will meet many echoes of its ideas next door in Babylon.
tob-10174:
Amos was a herdsman from Tekoa who spoke as a prophet to the kingdom of Israel in the eighth century before Christ. His short book stands as Book 30 in the King James Version of the Bible. Amos was no court prophet; he came from the fields to confront the rich.

He charges Israel's leaders with crushing the poor, cheating in trade, and mocking justice while keeping up fine worship. His best-known words demand that justice roll down like waters and righteousness like a strong stream. Of all the early prophets, Amos speaks most sharply about fairness for the poor.
tob-10274:
The Book of Jubilees retells Genesis and the start of Exodus as a secret account given to Moses by angels. It was written in Hebrew in the second century BC, most likely. R. H. Charles edited and translated the surviving text, which came down whole in Ethiopic.

The story is divided into blocks of forty-nine years, the jubilees that give the book its name. It adds detail on angels, the calendar, and laws it says the patriarchs already kept. The Ethiopian church counts it as scripture, while other churches treat it as apocrypha. It helps show how Jews of its age read the Bible.
tob-13329-15474:
Books one to three of the Mahabharata open Ganguli's translation in its Vyasa-titled copy. The Kuru kings rise, marry, and quarrel. A dice game in the royal hall, played with loaded stakes, costs the Pandava brothers their kingdom and sends them into the forest.

Thirteen years of exile follow, full of demons, pilgrimages, and stories nested inside stories. The brothers gather allies and grievances in equal measure. Ganguli, the first to render the whole epic into English prose, keeps the huge cast straight. Every feud that drives the later war is planted here, in the longest story ever told.
tob-4074:
L. W. de Laurence's 1916 Chicago edition presents the Goetia, the famous first book of the Lesser Key of Solomon, under the subtitle The Book of Evil Spirits. Seventy-two spirits are listed with their seals, ranks, and legions, alongside the ceremonies prescribed for calling and binding them. De Laurence's no-frills printing put ritual magic into mail-order reach.

His editions spread occult texts across America to readers far from metropolitan bookshops, a genuine landmark of occult publishing. The grimoire itself is medieval in origin, whatever its Solomonic branding claims. V1 evidence calls the volume a landmark whatever one makes of its contents; historians of American occultism would agree.
tob-4146-15474:
Kisari Mohan Ganguli spent years turning the Mahabharata, India's great Sanskrit epic, into English prose. Volume one covers the first three books. They tell of the Bharata clan's origins, the feud between the Pandava and Kaurava cousins, and the rigged dice game that ruins the Pandavas.

Losers in the game, the five Pandava brothers accept thirteen years of exile. Stories within stories fill the long forest years, since the epic pauses for tales of gods, kings, and lovers. Ganguli's Victorian prose moves steadily through it all. The longest poem in world literature opens here, with every thread of the coming war in place.
tob-4174:
The 1902 edition of Julian of Norwich's Revelations of Divine Love presents, in modernized spelling, the sixteen showings the anchoress received during a near-fatal illness. Julian, walled into a cell at Norwich, pondered the visions for twenty years. Their recurring promise, that all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well, anchors the whole work.

Julian's theology is tender and daring at once: God as mother, sin as somehow answered by love, and a hazelnut held in the palm standing for all creation loved by its maker. The first book in English known to be written by a woman, the Revelations reward the 1902 edition's easier spelling with immediate intimacy.
tob-9052-15474:
Ganguli's complete English Mahabharata begins, in this copy, with the epic's opening movement. Two branches of the Kuru house grow up rivals. A dice game, fixed against the honest Pandava brothers, strips them of kingdom, wealth, and freedom in one disastrous hall scene.

Sentenced to thirteen years of exile, the brothers withdraw to the forest. The long banishment fills with adventures, disguises, and tales told to pass the years. Every insult stays remembered; every debt will be called in. Readers meet the vast cast slowly, which suits a poem of this scale. The fuse for the great war is lit here, and it burns through the whole epic.
tob-9174:
Budge compiled his Egyptian Hieroglyphic Dictionary as the key to the carved and painted writings of ancient Egypt. Sign lists and vast word lists fill its volumes, the fruit of his decades at the British Museum. Generations of pupils learned to read the glyphs from Budge's pages.

The dictionary's learning is very much of the 1800s, and later Egyptology corrected it in many places. Its scale, though, commands respect: thousands of words gathered before modern corpora existed. Checked from the 1919 printing, the work stands as a high point of early Egypt lore and a tool that opened tombs and temples to readers.
un-ga-res-a-69-74: Africa's regional hub for peace and disarmament work is backed in Resolution A/69/74, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Africa gives staff support, on request, to the states of the region. The text recalls the chain of votes on the centre since 1985, and the Assembly's 2012 nod to the role of women in arms work. The centre's part in regional arms steps is restated with force.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl: Adopted at the sixty-ninth session in 2014, Resolution 69/74 of the General Assembly deals with the United Nations Regional Centre for Peace and Disarmament in Africa. It describes the Centre's cooperation with the African Union. That includes help in drafting the Union's small arms strategy and a common African position on the Arms Trade Treaty. It includes support for the Pelindaba Treaty through the African Commission on Nuclear Energy. It includes work behind the Kinshasa Convention. It urges African Union member states to fund its trust fund.
un-sc-res-1374:
Angola occupied the Council on 19 October 2001, when it unanimously adopted Resolution 1374 on Angola. Sanctions had targeted the UNITA rebel movement for years. A team of experts tracked how the rebels sold diamonds and got arms. The war's cost to civilians stayed severe.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council extends the expert monitoring team for six more months, to 19 April 2002. Four experts will serve on it. The team must file an action plan within sixty days. Its focus is rebel diamonds, arms-ban breaches, and rebel finances. The sanctions committee will review the team's past reports by year's end and guide its next steps.
un-sc-res-1474:
Somalia's arms embargo gained a new panel of experts under a Security Council decision of 8 April 2003. The embargo set in 1992 had been broken without pause, even after the Eldoret peace declaration of October 2002. Weapons and ammunition kept flowing in from abroad.

The Council stressed that every state had to obey resolution 733 (1992) in full, and that defiance breached the Charter. It welcomed the Panel of Experts' report of 25 March 2003 and re-established the panel for six months. Up to four experts, skilled in arms and related fields, would serve. Somali and regional parties had to cooperate with the panel fully. The panel owed a mid-term briefing and a final report. The Council also decided to send its sanctions committee on a mission to the region as soon as the panel was in place.
un-sc-res-1574:
A Council decision on Sudan took shape as Resolution 1574, adopted in Nairobi on 19 November 2004. The Council met away from New York to push the north-south peace talks to a close. The two sides signed a pledge that same day to finish their deal by 31 December. War in Darfur, though, kept spreading.

The text strongly backs a final Comprehensive Peace Agreement by that year-end date. Once signed, the Council stands ready to send a peace support operation. It extends the advance mission in Sudan by three months, until 10 March 2005. It also backs the African Union plan to grow its Darfur force to 3,320 staff.
un-sc-res-1674:
Protection of civilians in armed conflict was restated as doctrine on 28 April 2006. The Council built on resolutions 1265 (1999) and 1296 (2000) and its texts on children and on women, peace and security. It voiced deep regret that civilians form the vast majority of war's casualties. Illegal resource trading, small arms flows, and child recruitment drew its concern.

The Council stressed that preventing armed conflict comes first and that attacks aimed at civilians are grave breaches. It reaffirmed the 2005 World Summit's words on the responsibility to protect populations from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing, and crimes against humanity. All parties were told to obey the law of armed conflict strictly. Ending impunity was named essential, and states bore the duty to comply with their obligations and prosecute offenders. Regional bodies such as the African Union won praise for their protection work.
un-sc-res-1774:
The Rwanda war crimes tribunal needed its prosecutor renewed in 2007. On 14 September 2007 the Security Council reappointed Hassan Bubacar Jallow to the post. The Secretary-General had nominated him. His new term ran from 15 September 2007 for four years. The Council could end it early once the tribunal finished its work. The tribunal statute allows this way of filling the office.

The reappointment came as the tribunal raced a deadline. Resolution 1503 had told it to finish first-instance trials by the end of 2008. Jallow had led the prosecution since 2003. Keeping him in place avoided a change of leadership mid-stream. The court sat in Arusha, Tanzania.
un-sc-res-1874:
The matter of North Korea was settled for the Council in Resolution 1874, adopted on 12 June 2009. North Korea had set off a nuclear test on 25 May 2009. The test broke earlier Council orders and defied the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty. The country had also announced its exit from that treaty and kept firing missiles.

The Council condemns the test in the strongest terms and bans any further test or missile launch. The arms embargo widens to cover nearly all weapons, not just heavy arms. States must inspect suspect cargo at their ports and airports, and may seize banned goods. Banks must block funds tied to the nuclear and missile work. A panel of up to seven experts will watch for breaches for one year.
un-sc-res-274:
Improvements in Cyprus had held through the autumn of 1969, and the peacekeeping force was still required to protect them. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 3 December, said the force was still needed to maintain peace. It also noted that the situation on the island had kept improving. Cyprus's government agreed the force should stay beyond 15 December. Resolution 274 was adopted unanimously on 11 December 1969.

The Council reaffirmed its Cyprus resolutions, from Resolution 186 of 1964 onward. The parties were urged to act with the utmost restraint and to press on with their joint efforts. The force's stationing was extended for a further period, ending on 15 June 1970. The Council expected that progress toward a final settlement would be made by then. Renewals of this kind had become the rhythm of the Cyprus mission, term after term.
un-sc-res-2774: The Security Council's Resolution 2774 on the war between Russia and Ukraine was adopted on 24 February 2025. The short text mourns the tragic loss of life across the conflict. It recalls that the United Nations exists to keep peace and settle disputes without force. The Council implores a swift end to the fighting. It urges a lasting peace between Ukraine and the Russian Federation. The resolution came three years into the full-scale war, and its brevity itself marked a shift in the Council's stance.
un-sc-res-674:
Iraq's treatment of Kuwaitis and foreign nationals was condemned in October 1990. Baghdad's forces had taken third-state nationals hostage and seized diplomatic staff. Kuwaiti records were being destroyed, Kuwaitis forced out, and settlers moved in. Public and private property, hospital supplies among it, was looted or wrecked.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demanded that Iraq stop at once the taking of hostages and the abuse of Kuwaiti and foreign nationals. States were invited to gather solid evidence of Iraq's grave breaches for later use. Iraq had to let every foreign national who wished leave Kuwait and Iraq at once. Food, water, and basic services for Kuwaitis and foreigners had to be secured. Diplomatic staff and premises were to be protected. Iraq was reminded that it bears liability under the Convention for grave breaches, as do the persons who commit or order them.
un-sc-res-74: The Atomic Energy Commission sent the Council a letter in the summer of 1949. It carried two resolutions on atomic control, adopted that July. On 16 September 1949 the Security Council told the Secretary-General to pass the package on. The General Assembly and all member states would receive it. The record of the commission's debate went along with the papers. The one-sentence act kept atomic diplomacy in the open as the arms race began.
un-sc-res-874:
Nagorno-Karabakh received the Council's formal attention in Resolution 874, adopted on 14 October 1993. A cease-fire had been reached through direct talks backed by Russia. Leaders from the region had met in Moscow on 8 October. Still, the fighting had caused deep suffering and driven many civilians from their homes.

The Council calls on the parties to make the cease-fire firm and lasting. It commends the Minsk Group's adjusted timetable for carrying out its earlier resolutions. Forces must leave land taken in recent fighting, and blocks on transport and communications must go. The text backs a monitoring mission and asks for urgent aid so refugees can return home in safety and dignity.
un-sc-res-974: Readers meet Resolution 974 here as a Security Council record, catalogued with a date of 1995. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Ukraine fills the agenda of the Security Council's 8974th meeting, held on the night of February 23, 2022, and kept in this verbatim record. Russia's ambassador chaired the session while Russian forces massed on Ukraine's borders. The Secretary-General, António Guterres, opened with a direct plea to President Putin to stop his troops from attacking Ukraine and to give peace a chance.

As the meeting ran, word arrived that the attack was beginning. Delegates condemned the move in turn while the chair insisted Russia was acting in defense. The record captures, hour by hour, the moment diplomacy failed and a major war began.

Angola's civil war was still raging in the autumn of 2001. Resolution 1374, adopted unanimously on 19 October 2001, kept a team of outside investigators on the case. Their job was watching whether sanctions against the UNITA rebel movement were being obeyed or quietly broken.

The monitoring group's mandate grew by six months, ending on 19 April 2002. Four experts were to serve on it. Members demanded a detailed work plan within sixty days. The plan had to focus on UNITA's diamond trade, arms deals, and money. A review of earlier expert reports was also ordered by the end of 2001.

Resolution 1474, adopted unanimously on 8 April 2003, tries to give the Somalia arms embargo some teeth. The embargo, dating from 1992, had been violated continuously, even after Somali factions signed a ceasefire declaration at Eldoret the previous October. The Council worried about the money channels that paid for illegal weapons and military activity.

It backed the Somali reconciliation conference hosted in Kenya and insisted that states, especially in the region, stay out of Somalia's affairs. Its practical step was to set up a panel of experts to investigate embargo violations and report on how the ban could be enforced. The panel model, documenting routes, brokers, and financing, shaped UN monitoring of Somalia for years afterward.

Sudan's north-south peace deal nears completion in Resolution 1574, adopted on 19 November 2004 at a meeting in Nairobi. The six protocols between the government and the SPLM/A formed the core of a Comprehensive Peace Agreement. A memorandum signed that day set a deadline of 31 December 2004 for the final deal. In Darfur, insecurity and ceasefire breaches were growing.

The Council strongly backs the peace effort. It promises, once the agreement is signed, to help build a peaceful, united Sudan. It also promises to consider a UN peace support operation to back it. It extends the UN Advance Mission in Sudan, UNAMIS, by three months to 10 March 2005, with more staff. It urges fast preparation of a reconstruction package, including possible debt relief. It strongly supports expanding the African Union mission in Darfur to 3,320 personnel and demands an end to all violence.

Resolution 1674, adopted on 28 April 2006, renews and deepens the Council's doctrine on protecting civilians in armed conflict. It builds on the two earlier civilians resolutions of 1999 and 2000, and on its texts about children, women, and cooperation with regional bodies. The preamble regrets that civilians make up the vast majority of casualties in today's wars.

The resolution treats protection as a core Council task rather than a humanitarian afterthought. It condemns deliberate attacks on civilians, presses all parties to obey humanitarian law, and links civilian safety to the traffic in small arms and the looting of natural resources. Peacekeeping mandates written after 2006 routinely cite it when authorizing troops to shield civilians under threat.

Jamaica danced out of British rule on 6 August 1962. The isle was the first of Britain's Caribbean lands to go free. Its bid for a UN seat came on the heels of the fete. Resolution 174 passed with no dissent on 12 September 1962. The meet was the Council's 1018th.

The Council told the General Assembly to admit Jamaica. The Assembly did so in days. A twin text for Rwanda and Burundi had passed weeks past; now the Caribbean took its turn. Jamaica's voice at the UN grew fast past its size. Its chiefs spoke for small isles and poor lands in trade talks for years. The seat dates from this calm vote, a legal seal on a week of flags, song, and street dance in Kingston.

The Rwanda court's chief prosecutor kept his post by this vote of 2007. On 14 September, the Council adopted Resolution 1774. The prosecutor serves a four-year term under the court's statute. The Secretary-General had put the incumbent forward again. Hassan Bubacar Jallow had held the job since 2003. The court was then working to a tight finish plan.

The text reappoints Jallow from 15 September 2007 for four years. The term can end early once the court's work is done. The finish plan aimed to close trials by the end of 2008. All work was to wrap up in 2010. Those dates slipped in practice. Steady leadership at the top kept the genocide cases on track.

North Korea is sanctioned harder after a nuclear test in Resolution 1874, adopted unanimously on 12 June 2009. The DPRK had tested a nuclear device on 25 May 2009 in defiance of Resolution 1718 (2006) and announced withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty. The Council said Pyongyang could never have nuclear-weapon state status under the treaty.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council condemns the test in the strongest terms and demands no further tests or missile launches. It extends the 1718 arms embargo to all arms and related services, except small arms notified in advance. States are called on to inspect suspect cargo in their ports and, with flag-state consent, on the high seas, and to seize banned items; bunkering services to suspect DPRK vessels are prohibited. Financial services that could fund nuclear or missile programmes must be blocked. A Panel of Experts of seven is created for one year.

Resolution 274 is a UN Security Council renewal of the Cyprus peacekeeping force, adopted unanimously on 11 December 1969. The Secretary-General reported the force was still needed, noted that the island's situation had continued to improve, and recorded Cyprus's agreement to the force staying beyond mid-December.

The resolution reaffirms the full chain of earlier Cyprus texts, urges restraint and cooperative effort in the favorable climate, and extends the force to 15 June 1970. It voices the now-routine expectation that sufficient progress toward a final solution would then allow withdrawal or substantial reduction, closing out the mission's first six years of rolling renewals.

Resolution 2774, adopted by the Security Council on 24 February 2025, three years into the war, addresses the Russia-Ukraine conflict in a single operative paragraph. The Council mourns the tragic loss of life throughout the conflict and recalls that the United Nations' principal purpose is to maintain international peace and security and to settle disputes peacefully. It implores a swift end to the conflict and urges a lasting peace between Ukraine and the Russian Federation. The text names no aggressor, demands no withdrawal, and sets no conditions or deadlines.

Mozambique's admission is recommended in Resolution 374, adopted unanimously on 18 August 1975. Mozambique had applied under its formal state name. The country had won independence from Portugal in June of that year after a long liberation war. Several African states freed from Portuguese rule applied to the UN in the same season.

The resolution asks the General Assembly to admit Mozambique to membership, in the standard single-sentence form. Behind the formula sat a major change: another large African territory had left colonial rule, and the FRELIMO government now spoke for it in world forums. Mozambique's seat also strengthened the bloc pressing the Council on Rhodesia and apartheid South Africa.

Iraq's occupation of Kuwait in 1990 is the crisis behind Resolution 674. The Council condemned Iraqi forces for taking foreign nationals hostage, abusing Kuwaitis and foreigners, wrecking population records, forcing Kuwaitis out, and seizing public and private property, including hospital supplies. It said the Fourth Geneva Convention applied to Kuwait and that Iraq had to answer for grave breaches of it.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council demands that Iraq stop the hostage-taking and abuse at once. It demands that foreign nationals, including embassy staff, be free to leave and that food, water, and basic services reach people in Kuwait and Iraq. It reminds Iraq that it must pay for loss and harm caused by the invasion and asks states to gather records of claims. It warns that more steps will follow if Iraq does not comply.

Atomic energy talks hit the Council's desk in September 1949. The Atomic Energy Commission's chair had sent a letter on 29 July. Two of the body's own texts came with it. Resolution 74 passed on 16 September 1949. Nine members voted yes. The Ukrainian and Soviet teams held back.

The Secretary-General was told to pass the file along. The letter, the two texts, and the full debate record went to the General Assembly. Member states got copies too. The commission was the UN's first try at ruling the atom. By 1949 its work was stuck fast. The great powers could not agree on checks or bans. This text is a clerk's note on a dying effort, sent on for the record.

Nagorny Karabakh's war is addressed in Resolution 874, adopted on 14 October 1993. Fighting between Armenia and Azerbaijan had displaced large numbers of civilians and created a humanitarian emergency. Russian-assisted direct contacts had produced a ceasefire. The CSCE Minsk Group had drawn up an adjusted timetable of urgent steps. The steps were to carry out the Council's earlier resolutions 822 and 853.

The Council calls on the parties to make the ceasefire effective and permanent and to accept the Minsk Group's adjusted timetable. It demands the reciprocal steps at once: withdrawal of forces from recently occupied territories and removal of all obstacles to communications and transport. It backs an early Minsk Conference for a negotiated settlement. It supports the CSCE monitoring mission. It asks for urgent aid to the affected population. It also asks for help for refugees and displaced people to return home in safety and dignity.

Lebanon asked for more time for the United Nations force in its south in January 1995. Its request came in a letter dated 16 January. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 23 January, was also before the Council. The force, UNIFIL, had stood in southern Lebanon since 1978. Resolution 974 was adopted unanimously on 30 January 1995.

The Council extended UNIFIL's mandate for a further interim period of six months, until 31 July 1995. It restated its strong support for Lebanon's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence, within its recognized borders. The force was to carry out its original 1978 mandate in full. That mandate covered confirming Israel's withdrawal and helping Lebanon's government restore its authority in the south. The Council also backed the Secretary-General's plans to streamline the force's maintenance and supply work, in order to save money.
valera-pepita-jimenez-1874:
Juan Valera published Pepita Jimenez in 1874, a Spanish novel told mostly in letters. Luis de Vargas is a young man training for the priesthood. He returns to his village and meets Pepita, a young and charming widow. His letters to his uncle trace a growing love he feels he must resist.

The clash between duty and desire drives the whole story. Valera writes with warmth and gentle humor about faith, family, and small-town life. Pepita is no mere temptress but a strong and thoughtful woman. The English text here dates from 1886. The novel remains Valera's best-known work in any language.
verne-mysterious-island-1874:
Jules Verne published The Mysterious Island in 1874, a novel about five men cast away during the American Civil War. They escape by balloon and land on an unknown island in the Pacific. Led by the engineer Cyrus Smith, they build tools, a home, and even a telegraph. Almost nothing on the island is wasted.

Strange help arrives at key moments, and the men sense a hidden presence. Late in the book the source of that help is revealed, linking this story to Captain Nemo. The Kingston translation is the text given here. Readers value the novel as a hymn to skill, science, and teamwork.
wallace-defence-modern-spiritualism-1874:
Alfred Russel Wallace first spoke out for the faith in A Defence of Modern Spiritualism, a brief tract of 1874. Foes had mocked his faith in the dark room in the press. Wallace, a famed man of science, replies in calm print. He sums the proof as he sees it and asks for a fair test, not scorn.

The tract is short, clear, and brave for its day. It came ere his fat book of 1878 on the same theme. Here is the first time a top name in science stood up in print for the seance.
walras-elements-vol1-1874:
Léon Walras published the first part of his Elements of Pure Political Economy in French in 1874. Walras, teaching at Lausanne, aimed to do for economics what Newton had done for physics: state the whole system in exact, mathematical form. The first part lays the foundation with his theory of exchange.

He shows how prices form when many traders, each seeking the most satisfaction, meet in one market. From two traders and two goods he builds toward the general case, the whole economy balanced in a system of equations. Value, on his account, comes from scarcity joined to usefulness. The book founded general equilibrium theory, the idea that all markets clear together. Economics became a mathematical science in these pages, though the world took decades to notice.
walras-elements-vol2-1874:
The second part of Walras's Elements of Pure Political Economy followed the first in French in 1874. Part 1 had built the theory of exchange between traders. Part 2 works out the system in full, extending the equations to production, capital, and money.

Walras treats capital goods as sources of services that earn rent, and money as the good in which accounts are kept. His famous device of an auctioneer crying prices until supply meets demand shows how equilibrium could be found in practice. The mathematics scared off many early readers, and the book's fame grew slowly. By the mid-twentieth century it was honored as the most exact statement of the marginal revolution. The Lausanne master's complete theory stands in these two parts.
wundt-artzney-buchel-leonhart-bagasser-a: Wundt Artzney Büchel Leonhart Bagasser, 1570. The wound medicine book. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
zola-conquest-plassans-1874:
Chatto and Windus issued The Conquest of Plassans at London in 1917, in Vizetelly's English version. Twenty-two chapters carry the tale in the fourth Rougon-Macquart volume. The scene returns to Plassans, the small town where the family saga began.

A smiling young priest, Abbe Faujas, arrives and slowly takes hold of the town. His grip tightens on the sound Mouret household, which becomes his tool. Faith curdles into fanatic drive as ambition conquers from within. The tale ends in madness and fire, by the v1 account. Dark and tense, it ranks among the most gripping volumes of the whole cycle.
